Python Mastery

This course takes you from "I can write Python" to "people can rely on the Python I write." You will learn how Python works on the inside, so its surprises stop being surprises. You will learn to label your code with types, so a checking tool finds mistakes before anyone runs the program. You will learn the four ways Python can work on several jobs at once, and which job each one suits. You will learn to package your code so anyone can install it with one command. And you will meet the popular libraries that Python jobs expect you to know.

Start with four lines. Before you look at the output, guess what the last line prints:

a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a)

[1, 2, 3]

You changed b, and a changed too. If that surprised you, good: this course is about exactly that kind of moment.

Here is what happened. The line b = a did not copy the list. It stuck a second label, b, on the same list that a already labels. There is only one list, so a change through either name shows through both. §1.2 builds the whole picture from this one idea, and a surprising amount of Python follows from it.

Think of it like driving a car. You can already drive: you write loops, functions and classes, and your programs run. This course opens the bonnet. A driver hears a strange noise and hopes it goes away. A mechanic hears the same noise and knows which part is making it. By the end, when Python does something unexpected, you will know which part of the engine to look at.

The other half of the course is about trust. Programmers say code is in production when real people depend on it: a shop's checkout, a clinic's appointment list, a bank's monthly report. Code like that has to do more than run once on your laptop. Other people must be able to read it, install it and change it, and mistakes must be caught by tools before they reach a user. §6 and §11–§12 teach exactly those habits.

How to use this course

  • This course assumes you can already write Python. Loops, functions, classes, lists and dictionaries should be familiar. If they are not, work through the Foundations course first — this one starts where that one stops.
  • Everything here targets Python 3.14 (released October 2025, supported to October 2030). Where a feature is newer than 3.10, the section says which version introduced it, because for years to come you will be reading code written for older versions of Python.
  • Run every example. Python is an unusually honest language: almost every claim in this course can be confirmed in under ten seconds in the REPL, the interactive prompt you get by typing python3 on its own (the name stands for read, evaluate, print, loop: it reads a line, runs it, prints the result, and waits for the next one), and the ones that surprise you are the ones worth confirming. Every output block below was produced by actually running the code above it.
  • Every section follows the same shape. It opens with one small program you can run. It then adds one idea at a time, each with a short example and its real output, followed by a line-by-line reading of what happened. Each section has one everyday picture that it comes back to (a kitchen for concurrency, a nurse's ward round for the capstone), so a new idea always has something familiar to hang on. The section ends with exercises, and every exercise has a worked solution you can open.
  • Look underneath, not just at the surface. When Python surprises you, the explanation is usually one layer below the code you wrote. For example, when you write len(x), Python quietly calls a method named __len__ on x and hands back whatever that method returns (§1.1). A method whose name has two underscores on each side is a special method: you rarely call one yourself, but Python calls them for you all the time. The sections show you both layers, the line you wrote and what Python does with it.
  • Set yourself up before section 1:
python3 --version          # 3.14 or newer for the whole course
mkdir ~/python-mastery && cd ~/python-mastery
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate

The first line checks your Python version. The second makes a folder for your experiments and moves into it. The third creates a virtual environment (a private set of installed packages for this folder, explained properly in §11.8) and switches it on.

The versions behind the examples. The course was first written against Python 3.14.4 on Linux, and every example with printed output has since been re-run and checked under Python 3.14.8 on macOS. Where the two operating systems print different things (an error number, a default setting), the section says so and shows what holds on both. The test reports in §12 come from pytest 9.1.1 (the tool that runs your tests), and the type-checker reports in §6 from mypy 2.4 (the tool that checks your type labels). The third-party libraries in §13 were measured with pydantic 2.14, FastAPI 0.148, NumPy 2.5 and pandas 3.0.

What you are actually learning

Not a tour of features. The fourteen sections fall into five parts, and each part explains a whole family of behaviour that otherwise looks arbitrary. Every new word in the list below is explained from scratch in the section it points to; here it gets one sentence, so you know what you are heading towards.

Part 1: how Python works inside (§1–§5).

  1. The object model. This is Python's set of rules for how values are stored and found. Every value (a number, a list, even a function) is an object, and a variable name is only a label stuck on one. When you write obj.name, Python looks for name along a fixed route: the object itself, then its class, then the classes that class was built from. A handful of puzzles fall out of those few rules: why a list used as a default argument remembers values from earlier calls, the difference between "the very same object" (is) and "equal values" (==), and why += changes a list in place but builds a brand-new tuple (§1, with the += case in §2.6).
  2. The protocols the language calls for you. A protocol here is an agreement: give your class a method with a certain special name, and Python's built-in tools will use it. Write __len__ and len() works on your objects. Special methods like that make your own objects work with len, in, with, indexing (x[0]) and the operators such as + and == (§2). §3 then covers the tools for designing classes: dataclasses (classes that write their own routine setup code), __slots__ (a fixed list of attributes, which saves memory), descriptors (the machinery behind @property), abstract base classes (a class that says "every subclass must have these methods") and enums (a fixed set of named choices, like the four suits in a deck of cards).
  3. Functions and iteration. In Python a function is an object like any other, so you can store it in a variable or pass it to another function. That is what makes closures (functions that remember variables from the place they were created) and decorators (functions that wrap another function to add something, such as announcing each call or remembering answers it has already worked out) possible (§4). Iteration means going through items one at a time. Generators hand out items one at a time instead of building a whole list first, so a file larger than your computer's memory is no problem; and match picks apart structured data, checking its shape and pulling out the pieces in one step (§5).

Part 2: code that tells you when it is wrong (§6–§7).

  1. Types a checker enforces. A type is the kind of a value: text, a whole number, a list of names. Normally Python only discovers that a value is the wrong kind when that line runs, which may be months later, in front of a user. A type checker such as mypy reads your code without running it and points out those mistakes in advance. §6 teaches the type features real code needs (protocols, generics, variance, TypedDict, overloads and narrowing) and how teams run the checker in CI, short for continuous integration: a server that automatically checks every change before it is accepted. It also shows where type labels earn their keep and where they are just noise.
  2. Failure handled on purpose. Programs fail: files go missing and networks drop. §7 teaches you to fail clearly: your own family of exception (error) types, chaining, so a new error still records the original cause, exception groups for when several things fail at once, logging (a written record of what the program did) that you can search later, and the debugger, a tool that pauses a running program so you can look inside it.

Part 3: doing several things at once, and doing them fast (§8–§10).

  1. Concurrency matched to the workload. Concurrency means making progress on several jobs in the same stretch of time, like a cook with three pans on the stove. Python has four ways to do it (threads, processes, subinterpreters and asyncio), plus the free-threaded build, a version of Python that lets threads truly run side by side. Each one answers a different bottleneck, the slow part that everything else waits for: waiting on the network is a different problem from a long calculation, and the wrong choice can make a program slower than doing one thing at a time (§8–§9).
  2. Speed on evidence. Measure first, with a profiler (a tool that reports where the time and memory really go). Then fix the algorithm, the method the code uses to solve the problem, before shaving small costs off each step (§10).

Part 4: shipping (§11–§13). Shipping means handing your code to other people in a form they can install and run.

  1. An installable project. How import finds code; virtual environments; pyproject.toml, the one file that describes your project; a lockfile, which records the exact version of every library so everyone installs the same thing; and a package with an entry point, which turns your code into a command a user can type in the terminal (§11).
  2. Quality that runs by itself. Tests (small programs that check your program and fail when it is wrong), a linter (a tool that flags suspicious code) and a formatter (a tool that lays out code the same way every time), all run automatically, on every change, by CI (§12).
  3. The toolbox and the shop. The standard library is the toolbox that comes with Python (pathlib for files and folders, argparse for command-line options, json for reading and writing data, sqlite3 for a small database). The shop is the third-party libraries, code other people wrote that you install with pip from PyPI, the Python Package Index. You will meet the ones employers expect: pydantic (checks that incoming data has the right shape), FastAPI (builds web services that other programs talk to), NumPy (fast calculations on large lists of numbers) and pandas (tables of data, like a spreadsheet you control with code) (§13).

Part 5: putting it together (§14). The capstone builds Sentinel, a small program that watches a list of servers (computers that answer requests over a network) and reports which ones are down. It reads its settings from a config file, checks many servers at once with a time limit on each, tries again on the ones that fail, saves the results in SQLite, prints a report, and finishes with an exit code, a number that tells whatever started it whether everything was fine. It uses something from nearly every earlier section, and it ships as a real installable command with its own tests.

By the end you should be able to read an ordinary Python codebase without finding any part of it mysterious, and to make the choices (how to design classes, where to use types, which kind of concurrency, how to package) that decide whether people can rely on it in production.

SECTION 1

The Object Model

Python has a reputation for being simple. It is not simple. It is consistent.

Almost everything that surprises people about Python comes from one small set of rules:

  • what an object is,
  • how a name refers to an object,
  • how Python finds an attribute, a value or method attached to an object, such as the name in obj.name.

Learn those rules once and a very large amount of Python stops needing to be memorised. You will be able to predict what code does instead of remembering what it does.

This section is the foundation the rest of the course stands on. Every later section points back to it, so take it slowly. Each subsection starts with a small program; run it, look at the output, and only then read the explanation.

1.1 The Data Model Is the Language

Start with something you already know. len() works on a list and on a string:

print(len([10, 20, 30]))
print(len('hello'))

3
5

How does len know how to measure both? It does not. It asks the object. len(x) is defined as a call to a method named __len__ on x, and both list and str provide one.

That means your own class can join in. Here is a playlist that tells len how many songs it holds:

class Playlist:
    def __init__(self, songs):
        self.songs = songs

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.songs)

print(len(Playlist(['Intro', 'Verse', 'Outro'])))

3

Six lines, and len() treats a Playlist exactly like a list. Nothing about len changed. Playlist simply answered the question len asks.

The same is true of most of Python's syntax. Each piece is a call to a method with a fixed name:

  • len(x) calls x.__len__()
  • x + y calls x.__add__(y)
  • for i in x calls x.__iter__()
  • with x: calls x.__enter__() and later x.__exit__(...)

The data model is Python's specification of what an object is and how the interpreter interacts with it. In plainer words, it is the rulebook that says what an object is and how the interpreter (the program that reads and runs your Python: the python3 you type in the terminal) works with it. It is the reason len(x), x + y, for i in x and with x: work on your own classes exactly as they work on built-in ones: each of those syntaxes is defined as a call to a named method, and any object providing that method participates. Section 2 goes through those methods one by one.

This is the central design decision of the language. Many other languages treat their built-in types (the ones that come with the language, such as list and str) as special, with powers your own classes cannot have. Python does the opposite: it defines the built-ins in terms of the same rules it offers you. list gets no special treatment. It simply implements __len__, __getitem__, __iter__ and the rest, as Playlist implemented __len__.

Identity, type and value

Every object, built-in or yours, has three properties. Think of a library book:

  • its shelf location says which physical copy it is,
  • its kind (novel, atlas, dictionary) says what you can do with it,
  • its contents are what you read, and a notebook's contents can change while it stays the same notebook.

Python's names for these are identity, type and value. Only the third can ever change, and only for a mutable object: one that can be changed in place, such as a list. An immutable object, such as a number, a string or a tuple, can never change at all:

Property What it is Changes?
Identity Its address in memory, returned by id() Never
Type The class that defines its behaviour, returned by type() Effectively never
Value The data it holds Only if the type is mutable

Watch all three on one list:

x = [1, 2, 3]
print(id(x) == id(x))       # identity is stable
print(type(x).__name__)     # type is fixed
x.append(4)                 # value can change...
print(x, id(x) == id(x))    # ...without the identity changing

True
list
[1, 2, 3, 4] True

The list gained an element, so its value changed. Its id() did not, because it is still the same object.

An object's identity is fixed for its whole lifetime. Two things follow from that, and both come up in the next three subsections:

  • it is what makes is meaningful (§1.4 asks "is this the same object?"),
  • it is what makes a change visible through every name that refers to the object (§1.2).

1.2 Names Are Not Boxes

Many people first learn that a variable is a box: x = 10 puts 10 in the box called x. That picture works for a while, then it breaks. Here is a better one.

Think of a name as a sticky label. x = 10 sticks the label x on an object whose value is 10. Assignment moves a label; it never touches the object.

Start with numbers, where nothing surprising happens:

x = 10
y = x        # stick a second label, y, on the same object
x = 11       # move the label x to a different object
print(x, y)

11 10

y = x did not copy anything. It put a second label on the object x was attached to. Then x = 11 moved x to another object, and y stayed where it was.

Now do the same thing with a list. The only difference is that a list can be changed in place:

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a                # b is a second name for the SAME list
b.append(4)          # mutating through one name...
print(a)             # ...is visible through the other
b = [9, 9]           # rebinding b does NOT touch the list a refers to
print(a)

[1, 2, 3, 4]
[1, 2, 3, 4]

Read the output line by line:

  • The first [1, 2, 3, 4]: b.append(4) changed the one list that both labels are stuck on, so a sees the change.
  • The second [1, 2, 3, 4]: b = [9, 9] moved the label b to a brand-new list. The old list, and the label a on it, were not touched.
a
⟶
list object [1, 2, 3, 4]  id 0x7f…a10
b
⟶
↑ the same object, until b = [9, 9] rebinds it elsewhere

So the single most valuable correction to the picture most people start with is this: a Python variable is not a box that holds a value. It is a name bound to an object. In this course, "binding" a name means sticking the label on an object, and "rebinding" means moving it. Assignment never copies, and never mutates (changes) an object. It only rebinds.

The mutable-default surprise

This one rule explains the classic surprises. Before you look at the output, guess what the second call prints:

def add_item(items=[]):          # DANGER: evaluated ONCE, at def time
    items.append('x')
    return items

print(add_item())
print(add_item())                # the same list, still holding the first 'x'

['x']
['x', 'x']

Most people expect ['x'] twice. Here is what really happens:

  1. When Python runs the def statement, it creates one empty list and stores it inside the function object as the default. (In Python a function is itself an object, which §4.1 shows.)
  2. The first call uses that list and appends 'x'.
  3. The second call uses the same list, which still holds the first 'x', and appends another.

The default value is an object created when the def statement runs, bound into the function object, and reused on every call that does not supply an argument. It is not re-created per call. The fix is the standard sentinel idiom. An idiom is the usual way experienced programmers write something, and a sentinel is a stand-in value that means "nothing was passed". Use None as the default, and create a fresh list inside the function:

def add_item(items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append('x')
    return items

print(add_item(), add_item())

['x'] ['x']

Now the items = [] line runs on every call, so every call gets its own new list.

Passing an argument

Function arguments follow the same rule. When you call a function, Python sticks a new label (the parameter name) on the object you passed. Nothing is copied.

You may hear programmers who know other languages, such as C++, describe arguments as "pass by value" (the function gets a copy) or "pass by reference" (the function gets direct access to the caller's variable). Python is neither, in that sense. It passes the object, bound to a new local name: one that exists only inside the function. So:

  • mutating the object is visible to the caller, because the caller's label is on the same object;
  • rebinding the local name is not, because that only moves the function's own label.
def mutate(lst, num):
    lst.append(99)      # mutation — caller sees it
    num += 1            # rebinding a local name — caller does not
    return num

data, n = [1], 5
mutate(data, n)
print(data, n)

[1, 99] 5

data changed because lst.append changed the shared list. n is still 5 because num += 1 only moved the label num to a new integer, 6, inside the function.

1.3 The Standard Type Hierarchy

When you meet a value in Python, it helps to know which family it belongs to. The Language Reference (Python's official description of the language, on docs.python.org) sorts every built-in type into a hierarchy, a family tree of groups and subgroups. It is worth knowing, because a surprising number of "why does this work?" questions are answered by "because it is in that group."

Here are the families. You do not need to memorise them now; come back to this list when a later section mentions one.

  • None, NotImplemented, Ellipsis — singletons, meaning only one object of each exists. None is the sole instance of NoneType; that is why x is None is both correct and fast. NotImplemented is what a binary operator returns to say "I don't handle this type, try the other operand's method" (§2.4 uses it). A binary operator is one like + that works on two values, and each value is an operand. Ellipsis (...) is a real object, used heavily by NumPy (a library for large arrays of numbers, §13.10) to select parts of an array, and as a placeholder body for code you have not written yet.
  • Numbers — int (arbitrary precision: a whole number can grow as large as memory allows, so it never overflows, the wrap-around to a wrong value that fixed-size numbers suffer in some languages), float (a number with a fractional part, stored in 64 bits: what the C language calls a double), complex, and the separate Fraction/Decimal types. bool is a subclass of int (a class built on top of int that inherits everything it does; §3 covers subclasses), which is why True + True == 2 and why isinstance(True, int) is True.
  • Sequences — ordered collections you can index. Immutable ones (str, bytes, tuple, range) and mutable ones (list, bytearray).
  • Set types — set (mutable) and frozenset (hashable, so it can be a dict key; §1.5 explains "hashable").
  • Mappings — dict, plus types.MappingProxyType for a read-only view: a window onto a dictionary that lets you look but not change.
  • Callables — anything you can call with (): functions, methods, classes, and any instance with __call__.
  • Modules, classes, instances, exceptions — all ordinary objects with dictionaries you can inspect.

Two of those claims are easy to check:

print(isinstance(True, int), True + True)
print(type(...), type(NotImplemented))

True 2
<class 'ellipsis'> <class 'NotImplementedType'>

The first line shows that True really is an int whose value is 1. The second shows that ... and NotImplemented are real objects with real types, not special syntax.

1.4 Identity, Equality and Interning

Imagine two printed copies of the same newspaper. They are equal: every word matches. But they are not the same copy: if you write on one, the other stays clean.

Python has an operator for each of those questions:

  • == asks the objects whether they consider themselves equal (it calls __eq__). "Do these say the same thing?"
  • is asks whether they are literally the same object. "Is this the very same copy?"

They are different questions and they are not interchangeable.

a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
print(a == b, a is b)

True False

Two separate lists with the same contents: equal, but not the same object.

Interning: when Python reuses an object

Where this gets confusing is interning: CPython reuses certain immutable objects instead of creating new ones, as an optimisation. (CPython is the standard Python interpreter, the one you download from python.org.) Small integers from −5 to 256 are pre-created at startup, and many string literals (text written directly in the code, like 'hello') are cached: kept and reused.

Because of that, is sometimes says True for values you never expected to be the same object. Run this:

a, b = 256, 256
print(a is b)
c, d = 257, 257          # module-level constants folded by the compiler
print(c is d)
e = int('257'); f = int('257')   # built at runtime — genuinely distinct
print(e is f, e == f)

True
True
False True

Line by line:

  • 256 is 256 is True because 256 is one of the pre-created small integers.
  • 257 is 257 is also True, but not because 257 is interned. Before running your code, Python's compiler translates it into simpler instructions. Here it saw two identical literals in the same block of compiled code (a code object) and folded them into one constant.
  • int('257') builds each value while the program runs, so the two are genuinely distinct objects. is says False, and == still says True.

Build the values at runtime (while the program is running) and the illusion disappears. That is exactly why the rule is absolute:

Use is only for singletons — None, True, False, and sentinels you created yourself. Use == for values. Interning is a CPython implementation detail (a choice this one interpreter happens to make, not a promise of the language), it differs between versions and interpreters, and code that depends on it is broken code that happens to work.

Python 3.8 and later print a SyntaxWarning (a warning about code that is legal but almost certainly a mistake) when you compare a literal with is, precisely because it is so reliably a bug.

A sentinel of your own

Sometimes None is not enough. Suppose a function has an optional default argument, and None is a perfectly good value for a caller to pass. You then need a way to tell "the caller passed None" apart from "the caller passed nothing".

The idiomatic answer is a sentinel: a private object that nobody else can ever pass, compared with is:

_MISSING = object()          # unique, falsy-free, cheap

def get(cfg, key, default=_MISSING):
    if key in cfg:
        return cfg[key]
    if default is _MISSING:
        raise KeyError(key)
    return default

print(get({'a': 1}, 'a'), get({}, 'b', None))

1 None

The second call passed None on purpose, and got None back instead of a KeyError. Only a call with no default at all would raise.

1.5 Mutability, Hashing and the Contract Between Them

Think of a cloakroom. You hand over your coat and receive a ticket with a number. Later you show the number, and the attendant goes straight to the right hook. That only works if the number on your ticket never changes while the coat is hanging.

A dictionary works the same way. When you store a key, Python computes a number from it, called its hash, and uses that number to decide where the entry goes (its hash bucket). When you look the key up, Python computes the hash again and goes straight to that bucket.

An object is hashable if it has a __hash__ that stays constant for its lifetime and an __eq__ consistent with it. Dictionaries and sets require hashable keys, because they locate entries by hash bucket. A list can change, so its hash would change with it. That is why mutable built-ins deliberately set __hash__ = None, which makes them unhashable:

try:
    {[1, 2]: 'nope'}
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)
print(hash((1, 2)) == hash((1, 2)))

TypeError: cannot use 'list' as a dict key (unhashable type: 'list')
True

The list was refused as a key. The tuple, which cannot change, gives the same hash every time.

(That precise wording is a Python 3.14 improvement — earlier versions said only unhashable type: 'list', leaving you to work out where the unhashable value was being used. The bare form is still what hash() itself raises.)

The rule every hash must follow

The contract, the promise every hashable class must keep, is: equal objects must have equal hashes. If a == b, then hash(a) == hash(b).

The reverse is not required: different objects may share a hash (that is called a collision, and dictionaries handle it).

Break the forward direction and dictionaries silently misbehave. You insert a key and cannot find it again, because the lookup goes to the wrong bucket. This is why defining __eq__ on a class sets __hash__ to None automatically unless you define it too. Python would rather make your class unhashable than let it corrupt a dict. Section 2 covers how to do this correctly.

A tuple is only hashable if everything inside it is. A tuple holding a list could still change through that list, so it is refused:

print(hash(('a', 1)) is not None)
try:
    hash(('a', [1]))
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

True
TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'

1.6 How Attribute Lookup Actually Works

obj.attr looks like simply reading a field. It is really a search, and like any search it has an order.

Think of looking for your keys. You check your pockets first, then the hook by the door, and only if both fail do you ask someone to help. Python does the same thing for obj.attr, with a fixed order of places to look.

Technically, obj.attr is a method call — type(obj).__getattribute__(obj, 'attr') — and the default implementation follows a specific, learnable order. Two terms first:

  • The MRO (method resolution order) is the list of classes Python searches: the object's class, then its parents. §3.5 explains how it is built.
  • A descriptor is a class attribute with special methods that take over the access. Functions and property are descriptors. §3.4 explains them; for now, just note where they appear in the order.
1. Look in type(obj) and its MRO for a data descriptor (defines __set__ or __delete__) — if found, call its __get__ and stop.
2. Look in obj.__dict__ — if found, return it and stop.
3. Look in the type's MRO again for a non-data descriptor (only __get__, e.g. a plain function) or a plain class attribute.
4. Fall back to type(obj).__getattr__(obj, 'attr') if the class defines one; otherwise raise AttributeError.

For everyday classes, steps 2 and 3 are the ones that matter: first the instance's own dictionary (obj.__dict__), then the class. Two consequences follow immediately, and both come up constantly in real code.

Shared class attributes

Class attributes are shared until shadowed. To shadow something is to hide it behind something else with the same name. Assigning to self.x writes into the instance dictionary, hiding the class attribute rather than changing it. Watch a counter that is meant to be shared:

class Counter:
    total = 0                 # one object, shared by all instances

a, b = Counter(), Counter()
a.total += 1                  # reads class attr 0, writes INSTANCE attr 1
print(a.total, b.total, Counter.total)
print(a.__dict__, b.__dict__)

1 0 0
{'total': 1} {}

a.total += 1 is really a.total = a.total + 1. The right-hand side read total from the class (step 3) and got 0. The assignment then wrote 1 into a's own dictionary. The class still says 0, and so does b. The second line of output shows the new entry sitting in a.__dict__ only.

If the class attribute is mutable, there is no rebinding, so nothing gets shadowed and every instance shares one object. This is the class-level version of the mutable-default bug from §1.2:

class Basket:
    items = []                # shared by every Basket ever made

x, y = Basket(), Basket()
x.items.append('apple')
print(y.items)

['apple']

x.items.append found the class's list and changed it in place. y found the same list, so y has an apple it never asked for.

The fallback at the end

__getattr__ is a fallback, not a hook. A hook would run on every access; a fallback runs only when normal lookup has already failed (step 4). That makes it cheap, and safe for proxies (objects that stand in for another object and pass requests on to it) and for lazy loading (fetching data only when it is first asked for). Its cousin __getattribute__ runs on every access, and it is very easy to make it call itself forever (infinite recursion), because reading any attribute inside it triggers it again.

Here __getattr__ turns missing attributes into lookups in a dictionary:

class Config:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self._data = data
    def __getattr__(self, name):          # only called on failure
        try:
            return self._data[name]
        except KeyError:
            raise AttributeError(name) from None

c = Config({'host': 'localhost'})
print(c.host)
try:
    c.port
except AttributeError as exc:
    print('AttributeError:', exc)

localhost
AttributeError: port

c.host is not a real attribute, so normal lookup failed and __getattr__ found it in the dictionary. c.port is not in the dictionary either, so __getattr__ raised.

Raising AttributeError — not KeyError — is required, because hasattr(), getattr(obj, n, default) and copy/pickle (pickle turns objects into bytes for saving, §13.5) all probe with attribute access and expect that specific exception.

1.7 __slots__ and the Cost of a Dictionary

Every ordinary instance carries a __dict__: its own private dictionary of attributes. That is what makes Python objects so flexible: you can attach an attribute that the class never declared.

That flexibility has a memory price. One dictionary per object is fine for a hundred objects. For objects you create by the million, it is the dominant cost.

__slots__ is the trade. You tell the class, up front, the exact list of attributes it will ever have. The class then reserves a fixed set of places for exactly those attributes, instead of a dictionary (technically, one descriptor per name, §3.4). Think of a form with fixed boxes instead of a blank notebook: smaller, but you cannot add a box later.

import sys

class PointDict:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y

class PointSlots:
    __slots__ = ('x', 'y')
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y

d, s = PointDict(1, 2), PointSlots(1, 2)
print('dict version has __dict__:', hasattr(d, '__dict__'))
print('slots version has __dict__:', hasattr(s, '__dict__'))
d.z = 3                    # fine — arbitrary attributes allowed
try:
    s.z = 3
except AttributeError as exc:
    print('AttributeError:', exc)
print('slot descriptor:', type(PointSlots.x).__name__)

dict version has __dict__: True
slots version has __dict__: False
AttributeError: 'PointSlots' object has no attribute 'z' and no __dict__ for setting new attributes
slot descriptor: member_descriptor

The first two lines show the difference: the slots version has no __dict__ at all. The third line is the price: z was not in the list, so it cannot be added.

Note the last line: __slots__ is implemented with descriptors, the mechanism section 3 covers in full. The entries are not magic strings — they become class-level objects that know how to read and write a fixed position inside the object.

Practical rules:

  • The saving is real but not free: you lose dynamic attributes (adding new attributes on the fly), and you must repeat __slots__ in subclasses (a subclass without it regains a __dict__, undoing the benefit).
  • Multiple inheritance (a class built from two parent classes at once, §3.5) from two classes that both define non-empty __slots__ is an error.
  • Reach for it when profiling (measuring where a program really spends its time and memory, §10) says instance memory matters, not by default. dataclasses supports @dataclass(slots=True) since Python 3.10, which is the most convenient way to get it (§3.9 covers dataclasses).

1.8 Reference Counting

Go back to the labels from §1.2. An object can have several labels stuck on it. What happens when the last label is peeled off and nothing refers to the object any more? Nothing can ever reach it again, so its memory can be reused.

CPython reclaims memory primarily by reference counting: every object records how many references point at it, and when that count reaches zero the object is freed immediately and deterministically: at a predictable moment, the same on every run.

You can watch the moment it happens. __del__ is a method Python calls just before it frees an object, so this class announces its own end:

import sys

class Noisy:
    def __del__(self):
        print('freed')

n = Noisy()
m = n                        # count goes up
del n                        # ...down; still one reference left
print('still alive')
del m                        # count hits zero -> freed right here
print('after')

still alive
freed
after

del n removed one label, but m was still attached, so the object stayed alive. del m removed the last one, and freed printed right there, before after.

That determinism is a genuine feature. It is why open(...) without a with block usually still closes the file, and why you never free memory by hand, as C programmers must with free. Two cautions:

  • sys.getrefcount() always reports one extra, because passing the object to the function creates a temporary reference.
  • It is a CPython implementation detail. PyPy (another Python interpreter, built for speed) and the free-threaded build (a version of Python whose threads can truly run at the same time, section 8) do not promise prompt destruction. Never rely on __del__ running at a particular moment; use a context manager (an object used with with, which runs its cleanup code at a known moment; section 2 covers it) when cleanup timing matters.

1.9 Cycles and the Garbage Collector

Reference counting has one blind spot. Picture two people each holding the other's hand, standing in a room that everyone else has left. Nobody outside can reach them, but each is still "held" by the other, so neither count ever drops to zero.

That is a reference cycle. Reference counting alone cannot free a cycle: two objects that refer to each other never reach zero, even when nothing outside can reach them. CPython therefore also runs a second mechanism: generational garbage collection, a collector that periodically finds unreachable cycles and reclaims them.

import gc

class Node:
    def __init__(self):
        self.other = None

gc.collect()                      # start from a clean slate
a, b = Node(), Node()
a.other, b.other = b, a           # a cycle: each holds the other
del a, b                          # refcounts are 1, not 0 -> leaked so far
print('collected by cycle GC:', gc.collect() > 0)

collected by cycle GC: True

After del a, b, the two nodes are out of reach but still hold each other. Calling gc.collect() runs the collector by hand, and it reports that it found something to free.

"Generational" garbage collection means objects are tracked in three generations; survivors are promoted, and older generations are scanned less often, because experience shows that most objects are thrown away soon after they are made. gc.get_threshold() shows how many new objects (allocations) trigger a scan of each generation.

You rarely need to touch the collector, but three interventions are legitimate and appear in real systems:

  • gc.freeze() after startup, before forking worker processes (making copies of the running program, §8) — it moves existing objects to a permanent generation so the collector does not touch them, keeping copy-on-write memory shared instead of dirtied. Under the operating system's copy-on-write rule, the copies share the original's memory until one of them writes to it; a collector scan would write to every object and force each copy to make its own.
  • gc.disable() in a short-lived batch process (a program that runs one job and exits) with a known allocation pattern, where you would rather spend memory than collector time.
  • gc.set_debug(gc.DEBUG_LEAK) when hunting an actual memory leak: memory a program keeps holding but will never use again.

The collector only needs to watch objects that can hold other objects. Containers (objects that hold other objects, like lists and dictionaries) are tracked; simple immutable objects like a plain int are not, because they cannot participate in a cycle:

import gc
print(gc.is_tracked([]), gc.is_tracked(1), gc.is_tracked('abc'))

True False False

1.10 Weak References

Think of a balloon on a string. While someone holds the string, the balloon stays. Now imagine you only watch the balloon: you can see it and point at it, but you are not holding it. When the last person lets go, it floats away, and your watching does not stop it.

Sometimes you want that kind of reference: to refer to an object without keeping it alive. A cache (a store of results kept for reuse), an observer registry (a list of objects to notify when something happens), or a child's pointer back to its parent that must not create a cycle all need it. A weak reference does exactly that: it points at the object but does not raise its reference count.

import weakref

class Image:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

img = Image('cat.png')
ref = weakref.ref(img)
print(ref() is img)              # call it to dereference
del img
print(ref())                     # target is gone: the ref goes dead

True
None

You call the weak reference, ref(), to get the object back. While img held the object, that gave the image. After del img, nothing was holding it, so it was freed, and ref() returns None.

A cache that cleans itself

weakref.WeakValueDictionary is the practical form: a cache whose entries vanish as soon as the rest of the program stops using them, so the cache never keeps an object alive on its own.

import weakref

class Session:
    def __init__(self, sid):
        self.sid = sid

cache = weakref.WeakValueDictionary()
s = Session('abc')
cache['abc'] = s
print(len(cache))
del s                            # the last strong reference
print(len(cache))

1
0

Nobody removed the entry from the cache. It disappeared on its own when del s let go of the last strong reference (an ordinary one, the kind that keeps an object alive).

Limits

Two constraints worth knowing before you design around it:

  • not every object can be weakly referenced — int, str, tuple and plain list/dict instances cannot, and a class using __slots__ cannot unless '__weakref__' is included in the slots.
  • Use weakref.finalize() rather than __del__ when you need a cleanup callback (a function to run when the object goes away), because it runs reliably when Python shuts down and cannot accidentally resurrect the object, bringing it back to life, which __del__ can.

Here is a slotted class that opts back in:

import weakref

class Conn:
    __slots__ = ('name', '__weakref__')      # opt back in
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

c = Conn('db')
print(weakref.ref(c)() is c)

True

1.11 Looking at Objects From the Outside

Everything above can be inspected while the program runs: you can ask a live object what it holds and where it came from. That is one of Python's real advantages when debugging, because you can check a guess instead of reasoning about it. The tools worth having at your fingertips:

import sys

class Widget:
    kind = 'ui'
    def __init__(self):
        self.label = 'ok'

w = Widget()
print(w.__dict__)                       # instance state only
print(Widget.__mro__)                   # resolution order (section 3)
print([k for k in vars(Widget) if not k.startswith('_')])   # class namespace
print(type(w) is Widget, isinstance(w, object))
print(sys.getsizeof(1), sys.getsizeof(2**64))

{'label': 'ok'}
(<class '__main__.Widget'>, <class 'object'>)
['kind']
True True
28 36

Line by line:

  • w.__dict__ holds only label, set in __init__. kind lives on the class, as §1.6 described.
  • __mro__ is the search order from §1.6: Widget, then object.
  • vars(Widget) shows the class's own namespace (its table of names and values), where kind lives.
  • type(w) is Widget checks the exact class; isinstance also accepts parent classes, and every class descends from object.
  • sys.getsizeof reports an object's size in bytes.

That last line is a nice demonstration that int is arbitrary-precision: a value too large for a machine word (the 64-bit chunk the processor handles in one step) simply takes more bytes, with no overflow and no wraparound.

Exercises

Exercise 1.1 — Predict the output. Without running it, say what this prints and why.

def collect(value, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(value)
    return bucket

print(collect(1))
print(collect(2))
print(collect(3, []))
print(collect(4))
Solution 
[1]
[1, 2]
[3]
[1, 2, 4]

The default [] is created once, when the def statement executes, and stored on the function object. Calls 1, 2 and 4 all mutate that same list. Call 3 supplies its own list, so it is untouched by the others and does not affect the shared one. You can see the culprit directly:

def collect(value, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(value)
    return bucket

collect(1); collect(2)
print(collect.__defaults__)

([1, 2],)

Exercise 1.2 — Fix the shared-state bug. This class is supposed to give every robot its own log. Explain the bug and fix it.

class Robot:
    log = []
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def say(self, msg):
        self.log.append(f'{self.name}: {msg}')
Solution

log is a class attribute — one list shared by every instance. self.log.append(...) never rebinds self.log, so it never creates an instance attribute; it mutates the single shared list. Move the list into __init__ so each instance builds its own:

class Robot:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.log = []                # per instance
    def say(self, msg):
        self.log.append(f'{self.name}: {msg}')

a, b = Robot('R1'), Robot('R2')
a.say('hi')
print(a.log, b.log)

['R1: hi'] []

The general rule: a mutable class attribute is almost always a bug, because rebinding-shadows-but-mutation-shares. An immutable class attribute (kind = 'ui', MAX = 100) is fine and idiomatic.

Exercise 1.3 — Identity vs equality. Explain why the first comparison is True and the second is False, and say what you should have written instead.

a = 'hello'
b = 'hello'
print(a is b)

x = 'hello world!'
y = ''.join(['hello', ' ', 'world!'])
print(x is y)
Solution

Both print the same string value; only the object identity differs. 'hello' is a name-like literal, so CPython interns it at compile time and both names point at one cached object. The second string is built at runtime by join, producing a brand-new object that is never interned automatically.

The correct comparison in both cases is ==, which asks about value:

x = 'hello world!'
y = ''.join(['hello', ' ', 'world!'])
print(x == y, x is y)

True False

Interning is an optimisation, not a guarantee. It varies by CPython version, by whether the string looks like an identifier, and by whether the values sit in the same code object.

Exercise 1.4 — Attribute lookup order. Predict the output, then explain which step of the lookup algorithm produced each line.

class Base:
    greeting = 'class attribute'
    def __getattr__(self, name):
        return f'fallback for {name}'

b = Base()
print(b.greeting)
b.greeting = 'instance attribute'
print(b.greeting)
print(b.anything)
del b.greeting
print(b.greeting)
Solution 
class attribute
instance attribute
fallback for anything
class attribute

Line 1: nothing in the instance dict, so step 3 finds the plain class attribute. Line 2: the assignment put a key in b.__dict__, so step 2 wins and shadows the class. Line 3: neither the instance nor the class has anything, so normal lookup fails and step 4 calls __getattr__. Line 4: del removed the instance key, un-shadowing the class attribute — the class attribute was never modified, only hidden.

Note that __getattr__ was never consulted for greeting, on any line. It is a fallback that runs only after the normal search fails, which is exactly what makes it cheap.

Exercise 1.5 — Break a reference cycle with weakref. This parent/child pair leaks: the cycle keeps both objects alive until the cyclic collector happens to run. Rewrite the child's back-pointer so the pair is freed by reference counting alone.

class Parent:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = []
    def add(self, child):
        self.children.append(child)
        child.parent = self          # strong back-reference -> cycle

class Child:
    pass
Solution

Make the back-pointer weak. weakref.proxy is convenient here because it forwards attribute access, so calling code does not change:

import gc, weakref

class Parent:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.children = []
    def add(self, child):
        self.children.append(child)
        child.parent = weakref.proxy(self)

class Child:
    pass

gc.collect()
p = Parent('root')
p.add(Child())
print(p.children[0].parent.name)     # forwards like the real object
before = gc.collect()
del p
print('cycles collected on delete:', gc.collect())

root
cycles collected on delete: 0

The final 0 is the point: nothing was left for the cycle collector to do, because the only strong reference chain ran parent → children, and dropping p took the whole structure to zero immediately. With the original strong back-reference, that number is non-zero.

Use weakref.ref instead of proxy when you want explicit ref() calls and an obvious None when the target is gone; use proxy when you want transparent forwarding. Either way the parent must be kept alive by someone else — a weak reference is not ownership.

SECTION 2

Special Methods and Protocols

In §1.1 a six-line Playlist class defined __len__, and len() worked on it. That was one example of a much bigger idea. Section 1 said the data model is the language. This section is the proof: a tour of the special methods — the double-underscore, or dunder, methods — that every piece of Python syntax is defined in terms of.

Think of a wall socket. The socket does not care what you plug in: a lamp, a kettle, a phone charger. Anything with the right plug works. Python's syntax is a row of sockets, and each dunder method is the plug shape for one of them.

The mental shift to make here is that dunder methods are not "magic" and you do not call them. You implement them, and the interpreter calls them on your behalf when the corresponding syntax appears. len(x) is defined as "call type(x).__len__(x)". Nothing more mysterious than that is happening.

The section goes socket by socket: creating objects, printing them, comparing them, doing arithmetic with them, using them as containers, calling them, using them with with, testing them with if, and copying them. It ends with a map of every special method, for reference.

2.1 Syntax Is a Protocol

A protocol in Python is an informal interface: a set of dunder methods that, if you implement them, make your object work with a piece of syntax or a built-in function. An interface is a list of methods an object promises to have, and "informal" means you never declare that promise anywhere. Some languages make you write it down with an implements keyword; Python has no such keyword, and nothing to register. If your class has __len__, len() works on it. That is the whole contract.

Here is the same idea for the most common pieces of syntax. Read each row as "when you write the left side, Python runs the right side":

You write Python calls
len(x) type(x).__len__(x)
x[k] type(x).__getitem__(x, k)
x + y type(x).__add__(x, y), then type(y).__radd__(y, x)
for i in x type(x).__iter__(x), then __next__ repeatedly
with x: type(x).__enter__(x) … type(x).__exit__(x, …)
x(…) type(x).__call__(x, …)
if x: type(x).__bool__(x), else __len__, else True
repr(x) type(x).__repr__(x)

Now look at the right column again. Every row starts with type(x), not x. That is deliberate: lookup happens on the type, not the instance. This is the single most surprising rule about special methods, and it exists so the interpreter can remember where each method is and find it faster.

You can see it by trying to cheat. The first attempt puts __len__ on one object; the second puts it on the class:

class Sneaky:
    pass

s = Sneaky()
s.__len__ = lambda: 42          # attaches to the INSTANCE, not the type
try:
    print(len(s))
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

Sneaky.__len__ = lambda self: 42   # on the type — now it works
print(len(s))

TypeError: object of type 'Sneaky' has no len()
42

The first len(s) failed even though s.__len__ existed, because len never looked at the instance. Once the method was on the class, it worked. In practice this means: define special methods in the class body, as every example below does.

2.2 Construction: __new__ and __init__

Think of moving into a new house. First someone has to build the house. Then you furnish it. Two different jobs, done in order.

Creating an instance is two steps, not one, in the same way. __new__ allocates and returns the object (builds the house; to allocate is to reserve memory for it); __init__ initialises the object it is handed (furnishes it). type.__call__ runs both (it is the method that makes a class callable, §2.8), which is what happens when you write Traced(7). This class prints a line from each step so you can see the order:

class Traced:
    def __new__(cls, *args):
        print('  __new__ called, args =', args)
        return super().__new__(cls)      # actually allocate
    def __init__(self, value):
        print('  __init__ called, value =', value)
        self.value = value

print('constructing:')
t = Traced(7)
print(t.value)

constructing:
  __new__ called, args = (7,)
  __init__ called, value = 7
7

__new__ ran first and received the arguments. It returned a new, empty object. Python then passed that object to __init__ as self, along with the same arguments, and __init__ set self.value.

When you need __new__

You almost never need __new__; __init__ is where your setup code goes. The exceptions are genuine and worth recognising:

  • Subclassing an immutable type. By the time __init__ runs, a str or tuple already has its value; there is nothing left to initialise, so customisation has to happen in __new__. (The house is built with its walls painted, and they cannot be repainted.)
  • Caching or singletons — returning an existing instance instead of a fresh one.

Here is the first case: a string that is always upper case. The change has to happen before the string exists:

class Upper(str):
    def __new__(cls, value):
        return super().__new__(cls, value.upper())

u = Upper('hello')
print(u, type(u).__name__, u.startswith('HE'))

HELLO Upper True

The result is a real str (it has startswith), of type Upper, holding HELLO.

The rule that catches people: if __new__ returns an object that is not an instance of cls, __init__ is never called. Python only furnishes a house of the kind you asked for:

class Weird:
    def __new__(cls):
        return 'just a string'       # not a Weird
    def __init__(self):
        print('never runs')

print(repr(Weird()))

'just a string'

never runs did not print, and Weird() produced a plain string.

2.3 Representation: __repr__, __str__ and __format__

Python has two ways to turn an object into text. Two string conversions exist because they have two audiences: the developer debugging the program and the person using it.

  • __repr__ is for you — unambiguous, aimed at a developer reading a log or a REPL. The convention is that it should look like the expression that would rebuild the object.
  • __str__ is for the user — readable. It defaults to __repr__ if you do not define it, which is why __repr__ is the one to always write and __str__ is optional.

A third method, __format__, handles the part after the colon in an f-string, such as f'{m:short}'. Here is a money class with all three:

class Money:
    def __init__(self, amount, currency='GBP'):
        self.amount, self.currency = amount, currency
    def __repr__(self):
        return f'Money({self.amount!r}, {self.currency!r})'
    def __str__(self):
        return f'{self.amount:.2f} {self.currency}'
    def __format__(self, spec):
        if spec == 'short':
            return f'{self.currency}{self.amount:.0f}'
        return format(str(self), spec)

m = Money(12.5)
print(repr(m))
print(str(m))
print(f'{m}', f'{m:short}', f'{m:>12}')
print([m])                        # containers use repr of their elements

Money(12.5, 'GBP')
12.50 GBP
12.50 GBP GBP12    12.50 GBP
[Money(12.5, 'GBP')]

The first line is the developer's view: it looks like code you could paste. The second is the user's view. The third line shows three f-strings: plain, with the custom short spec, and right-aligned in 12 characters.

Three details in that example earn their keep:

  • Rounding. {m:short} prints GBP12, not GBP13, because format(12.5, '.0f') rounds half to even — the IEEE-754 default that Python uses everywhere, including the built-in round(). (IEEE-754 is the international standard for how computers store and round numbers with a fractional part; nearly every machine follows it.) It is not a bug, and it is the reason money should be stored as Decimal or as integer minor units (whole pence or cents) rather than as float.
  • !r. The !r conversion in the f-string calls repr() on the field, which is what makes the output round-trippable, meaning the text could be turned back into the same object: 'GBP' keeps its quotes.
  • Containers. Printing a list of objects shows their __repr__, never their __str__ — a container asks its elements for their unambiguous form. That is why a class with only __str__ produces the useless <__main__.Money object at 0x7f…> the moment you put it in a list.

2.4 Equality and Hashing, Done Correctly

Start with the problem. By default, two objects are equal only if they are the same object. That is rarely what you want for a value like a point:

class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y

print(Point(1, 2) == Point(1, 2))

False

Two points with the same coordinates, and Python says they differ, because without __eq__ the == operator falls back to is (§1.4).

Section 1 stated the contract: equal objects must hash equal (§1.5). So the fix needs two methods, __eq__ and __hash__. Here is how to satisfy it:

class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y
    def __repr__(self):
        return f'Point({self.x}, {self.y})'
    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Point):
            return NotImplemented          # let the other side try
        return (self.x, self.y) == (other.x, other.y)
    def __hash__(self):
        return hash((self.x, self.y))      # same fields as __eq__

a, b = Point(1, 2), Point(1, 2)
print(a == b, a is b)
print(len({a, b}))                          # equal + equal hash -> one entry
print({a: 'origin-ish'}[b])                 # b finds a's entry

True False
1
origin-ish

Now a == b is True, while a is b is still False: equal, but two objects. A set holding both keeps only one, and b can find the dict entry stored under a. Both of those depend on the hashes matching.

Three rules make this work every time:

  1. Hash the same fields you compare, as a tuple. If __eq__ looks at x and y, __hash__ must too.
  2. Return NotImplemented, not False, for unknown types. False asserts inequality; NotImplemented tells Python to try the reflected operation on the other operand (its mirror-image method, such as __radd__; §2.6 explains it), and only then fall back to identity comparison. Returning False breaks comparisons against types that would have known how to compare with yours.
  3. Only hash immutable state. If x can change after the object goes into a set, the object's hash bucket becomes wrong and it is effectively lost (the cloakroom ticket from §1.5 no longer matches the hook).

Forgetting __hash__

What if you write __eq__ and forget __hash__? Defining __eq__ sets __hash__ = None unless you also define __hash__, making the class unhashable:

class Mutable:
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.v = v
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return isinstance(other, Mutable) and self.v == other.v

print(Mutable.__hash__)
try:
    {Mutable(1)}
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

None
TypeError: cannot use 'Mutable' as a set element (unhashable type: 'Mutable')

That is Python protecting you, not obstructing you: a mutable object with value equality is genuinely unsafe as a dict key, so the default is to refuse.

2.5 Ordering

Version numbers are a good test of ordering. Sort them as plain strings and the answer is wrong:

print(sorted(['1.10.0', '1.2.0', '1.9.3']))

['1.10.0', '1.2.0', '1.9.3']

Strings compare character by character, and '1' comes before '2', so 1.10.0 lands first. A Version class can do better by teaching < what "earlier" means.

Six comparison dunders exist: __lt__, __le__, __gt__, __ge__, plus __eq__ and __ne__. Implementing all of them by hand is tedious and easy to get subtly wrong, so functools.total_ordering fills in the rest from __eq__ and one ordering method:

from functools import total_ordering

@total_ordering
class Version:
    def __init__(self, text):
        self.parts = tuple(int(p) for p in text.split('.'))
    def __repr__(self):
        return 'v' + '.'.join(map(str, self.parts))
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return isinstance(other, Version) and self.parts == other.parts
    def __lt__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Version):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.parts < other.parts

vs = [Version('1.10.0'), Version('1.2.0'), Version('1.9.3')]
print(sorted(vs))
print(Version('1.2.0') <= Version('1.9.3'))    # supplied by total_ordering
print(max(vs))

[v1.2.0, v1.9.3, v1.10.0]
True
v1.10.0

Note that this sorts 1.10.0 after 1.9.3, which string comparison would get backwards — the tuple of integers is doing the work: (1, 10, 0) is greater than (1, 9, 3). The class defined only __eq__ and __lt__, yet <= worked, because total_ordering wrote it.

Sorting, min, max, heapq and bisect all need only __lt__; that is the one to define if you define just one.

2.6 Operator Overloading

You can make +, * and the other operators work on your own classes. Giving an operator a meaning for your own class is called operator overloading. Arithmetic operators map to dunders in a symmetrical, three-stage system that is worth understanding in full because it explains how 2 * vector can work when int has never heard of your class.

Think of two people at a door, each politely offering the other the chance to go first. For x + y, Python asks x first, and if x declines, it asks y:

  1. type(x).__add__(x, y)
  2. If that returned NotImplemented, type(y).__radd__(y, x) — the reflected operation
  3. If that also declined, raise TypeError

Here is a small vector class that supports +, multiplying by a number on either side, and -v:

class Vec:
    def __init__(self, *xs):
        self.xs = tuple(xs)
    def __repr__(self):
        return f'Vec{self.xs}'
    def __add__(self, other):
        if isinstance(other, Vec):
            return Vec(*(a + b for a, b in zip(self.xs, other.xs)))
        return NotImplemented
    def __mul__(self, k):
        if isinstance(k, (int, float)):
            return Vec(*(a * k for a in self.xs))
        return NotImplemented
    __rmul__ = __mul__                      # scalar * vector == vector * scalar
    def __neg__(self):
        return self * -1

v, w = Vec(1, 2), Vec(10, 20)
print(v + w)
print(v * 3)
print(3 * v)          # int.__mul__(3, v) declines -> Vec.__rmul__ runs
print(-v)
try:
    v + 5
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

Vec(11, 22)
Vec(3, 6)
Vec(3, 6)
Vec(-1, -2)
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'Vec' and 'int'

Follow 3 * v, the interesting line. Python first asked int to multiply 3 by a Vec. int has never heard of Vec, so it returned NotImplemented. Python then asked the right-hand side, and Vec.__rmul__ did the work.

v + 5 failed in the same two steps, with nobody willing. That TypeError message is generated by the interpreter, not by you — it is what you get for free by returning NotImplemented instead of raising. Returning NotImplemented is how you say "not my job"; raising is how you say "nobody's job."

+=

In-place operators (+=) try __iadd__ first and fall back to __add__ followed by a rebind. This is the difference between list and tuple under +=:

a = [1, 2]
before = id(a)
a += [3]                 # list.__iadd__ mutates in place
print(a, id(a) == before)

t = (1, 2)
before = id(t)
t += (3,)                # no __iadd__ -> builds a new tuple, rebinds t
print(t, id(t) == before)

[1, 2, 3] True
(1, 2, 3) False

The list is still the same object (True): it was changed in place. The tuple cannot change, so += built a new tuple and moved the label t to it (False), as in §1.2.

The full operator set follows the same pattern throughout: __sub__/__rsub__/__isub__, __matmul__ for @ (matrix multiplication, used by NumPy), __truediv__ and __floordiv__, __mod__, __pow__, the bitwise family (operators such as & and | that work on the individual bits of a number), and the unary ones, which take a single value: __neg__, __pos__, __abs__, __invert__.

2.7 The Container Protocol

A container is anything that holds items: a list, a dict, a deck of cards. Four dunders make an object behave like a collection, and you can adopt as few as you need:

  • __len__ for len(d),
  • __getitem__ for d[0] and slices,
  • __setitem__ for d[0] = ...,
  • __contains__ for 'Q' in d.
class Deck:
    def __init__(self, cards):
        self._cards = list(cards)
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self._cards)
    def __getitem__(self, key):
        return self._cards[key]              # slices work for free
    def __setitem__(self, key, value):
        self._cards[key] = value
    def __contains__(self, card):
        return card in self._cards

d = Deck(['A', 'K', 'Q', 'J'])
print(len(d), d[0], d[-1], d[1:3])
print('Q' in d)
d[0] = '10'
print(list(d))                                # iterable via __getitem__ alone
print(list(reversed(d)))                      # reversed() too

4 A J ['K', 'Q']
True
['10', 'K', 'Q', 'J']
['J', 'Q', 'K', '10']

The first three lines are what you would expect. The last two are a bonus: Deck never defined __iter__, yet list(d) and reversed(d) both worked.

They are the payoff for a design decision made long before __iter__ existed: if a class has __getitem__ accepting integers from 0 upward, Python falls back to calling it with 0, 1, 2… until IndexError, giving you iteration, in, reversed() and unpacking (first, *rest = d) without writing another line. Section 5 covers __iter__, which is the modern and more efficient way to say the same thing.

One practical caveat, because it will bite you in a typed codebase: static type checkers do not model this fallback. A static type checker, such as mypy (§6), reads your code without running it. Fully annotate the class above and mypy still rejects list(d) with "No overload variant of list matches argument type Deck", because Iterable is defined structurally (by which methods an object has) as "has __iter__", and Deck does not. The code runs correctly; the checker is describing the modern protocol rather than the legacy one, the older way that Python still supports. If you want both the iteration and a clean type check, define __iter__ explicitly — which is the better habit anyway.

__contains__ is optional — without it, in falls back to a linear scan, checking the items one by one — but defining it lets you answer membership in better than O(n) when your data structure can. (O(n) means the time grows with the number of items; a set answers in roughly constant time.)

2.8 Callables

Any object with __call__ can be called with (), like a function. This gives you a function with state: something you call like a function that also remembers things between calls. That is often clearer than a closure (§4.3) and always easier to introspect (examine while the program runs, §1.11) and to pickle (save as bytes, §2.11).

Here is a rate limiter that allows a fixed number of requests, then refuses:

class RateLimiter:
    def __init__(self, limit):
        self.limit, self.count = limit, 0
    def __call__(self, request):
        self.count += 1
        if self.count > self.limit:
            return f'{request}: rejected'
        return f'{request}: allowed ({self.count}/{self.limit})'

allow = RateLimiter(2)
print(allow('GET /'), allow('GET /a'), allow('GET /b'), sep='\n')
print(callable(allow), callable(42))

GET /: allowed (1/2)
GET /a: allowed (2/2)
GET /b: rejected
True False

allow is an object, but it is used exactly like a function. Its counter lives in self.count, so the third call was rejected. callable() confirms that it can be called and a number cannot.

This is also why classes themselves are callable: type defines __call__, and calling a class is what triggers the __new__/__init__ pair from section 2.2.

2.9 The Context Manager Protocol

Think of borrowing a library book. You check it out, read it, and return it, and the return must happen even if you spill coffee on it halfway through. Lots of programming tasks have that shape: open a file and close it, take a lock (a token that lets only one part of a program use something at a time, §8) and release it, start a timer and stop it.

with is the syntax for that shape, and it is defined by exactly two methods. __enter__ runs on entry and its return value is bound by as; __exit__ runs on the way out — whether or not an exception occurred — which is what makes it the correct tool for any acquire/release pair: take something, then give it back.

This class prints a line on the way in and on the way out. The second with block raises an error halfway through:

class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        print('  acquiring')
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        print('  releasing; exception was', exc_type.__name__ if exc_type else None)
        return False                 # False/None -> propagate; True -> suppress

with Timer() as t:
    print('  body runs')

try:
    with Timer():
        raise ValueError('boom')
except ValueError as exc:
    print('caught outside:', exc)

  acquiring
  body runs
  releasing; exception was None
  acquiring
  releasing; exception was ValueError
caught outside: boom

In both blocks, releasing printed. In the second, __exit__ was told which exception happened (its three arguments describe it), and then the exception carried on to the except outside.

Swallowing an exception

The __exit__ return value is a genuine trap: returning a truthy value swallows the exception. A truthy value is one that counts as true in an if (§2.10), and swallowing an exception means stopping it so that it goes no further. Since a bare return gives None, the default is correct, and you should only return True deliberately — that is precisely how contextlib.suppress is implemented. Here is a small version of it:

class Suppress:
    def __init__(self, *types):
        self.types = types
    def __enter__(self):
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        return exc_type is not None and issubclass(exc_type, self.types)

with Suppress(ZeroDivisionError):
    1 / 0
print('still running')

still running

1 / 0 raised ZeroDivisionError, __exit__ returned True, and the program carried on as if nothing had happened.

Section 4 shows contextlib.contextmanager, which lets you write the same thing as a generator (a function that can pause at yield, §5.3) with one yield — usually the better choice for one-off cases. The class form is preferable when the manager holds real state, is reusable, or is also an async context manager (the async with version, §9).

2.10 Truthiness

if x: works on any object, not just on True and False. An empty list is false and a full one is true. How does Python decide for your own class?

Python calls a value truthy if if treats it as true, and falsy if if treats it as false. if x: consults, in order: __bool__, then __len__, then defaults to True. Only that last fallback surprises people — an object with neither method is always truthy, which is why a custom class that "looks empty" still enters the if.

class Bag:
    def __init__(self, items):
        self.items = list(items)
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.items)

class Plain:
    pass

print(bool(Bag([])), bool(Bag([1])))
print(bool(Plain()))

False True
True

Bag has __len__, so an empty bag is false and a full one is true. Plain has neither method, so it is always true.

Define __bool__ when emptiness and falsiness differ — a database row of all zeros exists and should be truthy even though it is "empty" in some other sense. Note also that __len__ returning 0 makes the object falsy for free, so containers rarely need __bool__ at all.

2.11 Copying and Serialisation Hooks

Copying is a protocol too, and knowing it prevents a very common class of bug: a "copy" that shares mutable internals (changeable parts inside it, such as a list) with the original.

Think of photocopying a page that lists the people on a team. The copy is a new sheet of paper, but the people on it are the same people. A shallow copy works like that. A deep copy is closer to cloning the team as well. Watch the difference:

import copy

class Team:
    def __init__(self, name, members):
        self.name, self.members = name, members

t = Team('red', ['ann', 'bo'])
shallow = copy.copy(t)
deep = copy.deepcopy(t)
shallow.members.append('cy')       # shared list!
print(t.members)
print(deep.members)

['ann', 'bo', 'cy']
['ann', 'bo']

Adding cy to the shallow copy also added them to the original, because both point at one list. The deep copy kept its own list and was not affected.

copy.copy creates a new object whose attributes point at the same sub-objects; copy.deepcopy recursively copies them, meaning it copies each sub-object, everything inside it, and so on all the way down, tracking already-seen objects so that cycles do not loop forever. Customise with __copy__ and __deepcopy__ when the default is wrong — an object holding an open socket (a network connection) or a thread lock cannot be meaningfully deep-copied and should say so.

Pickle

The same hooks drive pickle, Python's built-in object serialisation: turning an object into bytes you can save to a file or send elsewhere, and back again. __getstate__ returns what to save and __setstate__ restores it, which is how you exclude an unpicklable attribute:

import pickle

class Connection:
    def __init__(self, dsn):
        self.dsn = dsn
        self.socket = object()             # stands in for a real, unpicklable socket
    def __getstate__(self):
        state = self.__dict__.copy()
        del state['socket']                # never serialise the live handle
        return state
    def __setstate__(self, state):
        self.__dict__.update(state)
        self.socket = None                 # reconnect lazily

c = Connection('postgres://localhost/app')
restored = pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(c))
print(restored.dsn, restored.socket)

postgres://localhost/app None

The address survived the round trip. The socket was left out when saving and set to None when restoring, so the program knows it must reconnect.

A security warning that belongs next to every mention of pickle: unpickling executes arbitrary code by design, because the format includes instructions to call constructors, the calls that create objects. pickle.loads on untrusted bytes is remote code execution: whoever wrote the bytes can run any code on your machine. Use JSON for anything crossing a trust boundary: any data that comes from someone you do not control. Section 13 returns to this with the alternatives.

2.12 The Map

You have now met every socket that matters day to day. The table below lists all of them, grouped. Keep this as a reference; you will implement perhaps a dozen of these in a career, but recognising them all makes unfamiliar code readable. When you meet an unfamiliar dunder in someone else's code, find its group here, and you will know which piece of syntax it plugs into.

Group Methods
Construction & lifecycle __new__, __init__, __del__, __init_subclass__, __set_name__
Representation __repr__, __str__, __format__, __bytes__
Comparison & hashing __eq__, __ne__, __lt__, __le__, __gt__, __ge__, __hash__
Attributes __getattr__, __getattribute__, __setattr__, __delattr__, __dir__
Descriptors __get__, __set__, __delete__
Containers __len__, __length_hint__, __getitem__, __setitem__, __delitem__, __contains__, __missing__
Iteration __iter__, __next__, __reversed__, __aiter__, __anext__
Callables __call__
Numeric __add__, __sub__, __mul__, __matmul__, __truediv__, __floordiv__, __mod__, __divmod__, __pow__, __lshift__, __rshift__, __and__, __xor__, __or__ (+ r and i variants)
Unary & conversion __neg__, __pos__, __abs__, __invert__, __complex__, __int__, __float__, __index__, __round__, __trunc__
Context managers __enter__, __exit__, __aenter__, __aexit__
Truthiness __bool__
Copy & pickle __copy__, __deepcopy__, __getstate__, __setstate__, __reduce__
Classes & typing __class_getitem__, __instancecheck__, __subclasshook__

Exercises

Exercise 2.1 — A correct value object. Write a Temperature class storing degrees Celsius that: prints as 20.0°C for users and Temperature(20.0) for developers; compares and sorts by value; is usable as a dict key; and supports +/- with another Temperature and * with a number on either side.

Solution 
from functools import total_ordering

@total_ordering
class Temperature:
    __slots__ = ('celsius',)

    def __init__(self, celsius):
        self.celsius = float(celsius)

    def __repr__(self):
        return f'Temperature({self.celsius})'

    def __str__(self):
        return f'{self.celsius:.1f}\N{DEGREE SIGN}C'

    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Temperature):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.celsius == other.celsius

    def __lt__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Temperature):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.celsius < other.celsius

    def __hash__(self):
        return hash(self.celsius)

    def __add__(self, other):
        if isinstance(other, Temperature):
            return Temperature(self.celsius + other.celsius)
        return NotImplemented

    def __sub__(self, other):
        if isinstance(other, Temperature):
            return Temperature(self.celsius - other.celsius)
        return NotImplemented

    def __mul__(self, k):
        if isinstance(k, (int, float)):
            return Temperature(self.celsius * k)
        return NotImplemented

    __rmul__ = __mul__

a, b = Temperature(20), Temperature(20)
print(str(a), repr(a))
print(a == b, len({a, b}), sorted([Temperature(30), a, Temperature(-5)]))
print(a + Temperature(5), 2 * a, a * 2)
try:
    a + 5
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

20.0°C Temperature(20.0)
True 1 [Temperature(-5.0), Temperature(20.0), Temperature(30.0)]
25.0°C 40.0°C 40.0°C
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'Temperature' and 'int'

Note that the third line shows 25.0°C, not Temperature(25.0): print() calls str() on each argument, so __str__ wins there, while the sorted(...) list on the line above is a container and therefore shows __repr__.

The points that matter: __hash__ hashes exactly the field __eq__ compares; __slots__ plus float storage makes the object effectively immutable, which is what makes hashing it safe; NotImplemented produces the interpreter's own good error message; and __rmul__ = __mul__ is valid because multiplication by a scalar commutes.

Exercise 2.2 — Why is the copy shared? This cache is supposed to hand out independent snapshots. Explain the bug and give two different fixes.

import copy

class Snapshot:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data

original = Snapshot({'users': ['ann']})
clone = copy.copy(original)
clone.data['users'].append('bo')
print(original.data)
Solution
