copy.copy is a shallow copy: it makes a new Snapshot whose data attribute points at the very same dictionary — which in turn holds the very same list. Mutating anything nested is visible through both objects, so the original prints {'users': ['ann', 'bo']}.

Fix one — ask for a deep copy at the call site:

import copy

class Snapshot:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data

original = Snapshot({'users': ['ann']})
clone = copy.deepcopy(original)
clone.data['users'].append('bo')
print(original.data, clone.data)

{'users': ['ann']} {'users': ['ann', 'bo']}

Fix two — make the class copy correctly by default, so callers cannot get it wrong:

import copy

class Snapshot:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
    def __copy__(self):
        return Snapshot(copy.deepcopy(self.data))

original = Snapshot({'users': ['ann']})
clone = copy.copy(original)
clone.data['users'].append('bo')
print(original.data, clone.data)

{'users': ['ann']} {'users': ['ann', 'bo']}

The second is better when independence is part of the type's meaning: it puts the guarantee in one place instead of trusting every caller to remember. The general lesson is that "copy" is ambiguous in any language with references, and Python makes you choose which one you mean.

Exercise 2.3 — A context manager that suppresses selectively. Write ignore_missing, a context manager that swallows FileNotFoundError but lets every other exception through, and prove both behaviours.

Solution 
class ignore_missing:
    def __enter__(self):
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        return exc_type is not None and issubclass(exc_type, FileNotFoundError)

with ignore_missing():
    open('/no/such/file')
print('suppressed, still running')

try:
    with ignore_missing():
        raise PermissionError('denied')
except PermissionError as exc:
    print('propagated:', exc)

suppressed, still running
propagated: denied

The whole behaviour lives in __exit__'s return value: truthy suppresses, falsy propagates. The exc_type is not None guard matters because __exit__ also runs on the success path with all three arguments set to None, and issubclass(None, ...) would raise TypeError there — turning a clean exit into a crash.

The standard library already has this as contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError), which you should prefer in real code; writing it once is how you learn what it is doing.

Exercise 2.4 — Reflected operators. Predict what each line prints, and explain the third one in terms of the three-stage lookup.

class Metres:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
    def __repr__(self):
        return f'{self.n}m'
    def __add__(self, other):
        print('  __add__ tried')
        if isinstance(other, Metres):
            return Metres(self.n + other.n)
        return NotImplemented
    def __radd__(self, other):
        print('  __radd__ tried')
        if isinstance(other, (int, float)):
            return Metres(self.n + other)
        return NotImplemented

print(Metres(3) + Metres(4))
print(5 + Metres(3))
print(Metres(3) + 5)
Solution 
  __add__ tried
7m
  __radd__ tried
8m
  __add__ tried
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'Metres' and 'int'

Line 1: both operands are Metres, so __add__ handles it directly and __radd__ is never consulted.

Line 2: int.__add__(5, Metres(3)) returns NotImplemented because int has never heard of Metres, so Python tries the reflected method on the right operand — Metres.__radd__(Metres(3), 5) — which accepts.

Line 3 is the one worth getting right, because the natural guess is wrong. Metres.__add__(Metres(3), 5) runs and declines. Python then tries the reflected method on the right operand, which is int.__radd__ — and that declines too. It does not fall back to the left operand's own __radd__. Reflected methods belong to the other operand by definition, so Metres.__radd__ never gets a turn and the operation raises. Notice the trace: only one __add__ tried line appears and no second __radd__ tried line.

So 5 + Metres(3) works while Metres(3) + 5 does not — an asymmetry that looks like a bug to callers. The fix is to accept the type where it is actually reachable, in __add__:

class Metres:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
    def __repr__(self):
        return f'{self.n}m'
    def __add__(self, other):
        if isinstance(other, Metres):
            return Metres(self.n + other.n)
        if isinstance(other, (int, float)):
            return Metres(self.n + other)
        return NotImplemented
    __radd__ = __add__          # addition commutes, so one implementation serves both

print(Metres(3) + 5, 5 + Metres(3), Metres(3) + Metres(4))

8m 8m 7m

The design lesson has two halves. Decline by returning NotImplemented rather than raising, so the other operand still gets its turn — and remember that "the other operand" is the only one that gets a reflected call, so every type you intend to support must be handled in the forward method too.

SECTION 3

Classes in Depth

Section 1 explained how attributes are found. Section 2 explained the protocols objects implement, the methods that plug an object into Python's syntax. This section is about the machinery that sits between them: the tools Python gives you for controlling what a class is when it is created, and what its attributes do when they are touched.

Most of this material has a reputation for being advanced. Very little of it is difficult; it is just rarely explained in order. Here is the order this section uses, each step building on the one before:

  1. What a class body really is (§3.1).
  2. Methods and properties, the tools you use every day (§3.2–§3.3).
  3. Descriptors, the single idea underneath both (§3.4).
  4. Inheritance from several parents (§3.5).
  5. The heavier tools, from most to least often useful: abstract base classes, class-creation hooks (code that runs at the moment a class is created), metaclasses (the class of a class) (§3.6–§3.8).
  6. Dataclasses and enums, which you will use constantly and can now understand completely (§3.9–§3.10).

3.1 A Class Body Is Just Code

The most useful thing to know about classes is that class is a statement that executes, just like if or for. Python does not read a class like a form to fill in. It runs it.

The body runs top to bottom in a fresh namespace, and whatever names that namespace ends up holding become the class attributes. Watch when each line prints:

print('before')

class Demo:
    print('  class body running')
    x = 1
    y = x + 1                     # ordinary code: x is in scope here
    for i in range(2):
        pass

print('after')
print(Demo.x, Demo.y, Demo.i)

before
  class body running
after
1 2 1

Three things to notice:

  • class body running printed between before and after. The body ran the moment Python reached the class statement, before anyone created an instance.
  • y = x + 1 worked, because inside the body x is an ordinary variable.
  • Demo.i exists. The loop variable i leaked into the class namespace — because there is no magic, only a namespace being populated by ordinary execution. Every name left over when the body finishes becomes a class attribute.

That same rule explains two well-known oddities:

  • A class body cannot see names from an enclosing (surrounding) class.
  • Comprehensions (the one-line [x for x in ...] loops, §5.8) inside a class body famously cannot see the class's other attributes: the comprehension gets its own scope, its own region of the program where names live.

Once the body finishes, Python calls the metaclass — type by default — with the class name, its bases (the parent classes), and that namespace. That call is what turns the namespace into a class. §3.8 returns to this.

3.2 Methods Are Functions Until You Look Them Up

A def inside a class body creates a plain function, the same kind of object a def anywhere else creates. It becomes a method only when accessed through an instance, and that transformation is done by the descriptor protocol (§3.4).

Compare what you get when you reach the same function through the class and through an instance:

class Greeter:
    def hello(self):
        return f'hello from {self!r}'

    @classmethod
    def make(cls):
        return f'classmethod on {cls.__name__}'

    @staticmethod
    def util(x):
        return f'staticmethod got {x}'

g = Greeter()
print(type(Greeter.hello).__name__)      # a plain function
print(type(g.hello).__name__)            # bound to the instance
print(g.hello.__self__ is g)
print(Greeter.make(), Greeter.util(1))

function
method
True
classmethod on Greeter staticmethod got 1

Through the class, hello is still a plain function. Through the instance, it is a method: Python has attached g to it, and you can see g as __self__. That is how self gets filled in when you call g.hello() without passing anything. Think of a method as the function with the instance already clipped onto it.

The three kinds and when each is right:

  • Instance method — needs the instance. The default.
  • @classmethod — needs the class, not the instance. The canonical (standard, textbook) use is an alternative constructor: a second way to build an object, besides calling the class directly. It stays correct under subclassing because cls is whatever class it was called on.
  • @staticmethod — needs neither. A function that belongs in the class's namespace for organisation.

The alternative constructor

Suppose a Duration is stored in seconds, but people often have minutes. A class method gives them a second way to build one. Watch what happens when a subclass uses it:

class Duration:
    def __init__(self, seconds):
        self.seconds = seconds
    def __repr__(self):
        return f'{type(self).__name__}({self.seconds})'

    @classmethod
    def from_minutes(cls, minutes):
        return cls(minutes * 60)          # cls, not Duration

class PreciseDuration(Duration):
    pass

print(Duration.from_minutes(2))
print(PreciseDuration.from_minutes(2))    # returns the SUBCLASS

Duration(120)
PreciseDuration(120)

Called on the subclass, from_minutes received PreciseDuration as cls, so it built a PreciseDuration. Hard-coding Duration(...) there would return the wrong class for every subclass — a bug that only appears once someone subclasses you.

3.3 property: Attributes That Run Code

Start with the problem. A temperature class with a plain attribute accepts anything:

class Celsius:
    def __init__(self, degrees):
        self.degrees = degrees

c = Celsius(100)
c.degrees = -300          # colder than anything can be, and nobody objects
print(c.degrees)

-300

Nothing can be colder than −273.15 degrees, so you want to refuse that value. But other code already writes c.degrees = ... everywhere, and you do not want to change all of it to c.set_degrees(...).

A property turns attribute access into method calls without changing the interface, the way other code uses the class. Callers still write c.degrees; behind the scenes, your code runs. This is why Python has no culture of writing get_x()/set_x() up front (getter and setter methods, common in languages such as Java): you can start with a plain attribute and add validation later without breaking a single caller.

Here is the same class with the check added, plus a second property that is computed:

class Celsius:
    def __init__(self, degrees):
        self.degrees = degrees            # goes through the setter

    @property
    def degrees(self):
        return self._degrees

    @degrees.setter
    def degrees(self, value):
        if value < -273.15:
            raise ValueError('below absolute zero')
        self._degrees = float(value)

    @property
    def fahrenheit(self):                 # computed, read-only
        return self._degrees * 9 / 5 + 32

c = Celsius(100)
print(c.degrees, c.fahrenheit)
c.degrees = 0
print(c.degrees, c.fahrenheit)
try:
    c.degrees = -300
except ValueError as exc:
    print('ValueError:', exc)
try:
    c.fahrenheit = 100
except AttributeError as exc:
    print('AttributeError:', exc)

100.0 212.0
0.0 32.0
ValueError: below absolute zero
AttributeError: property 'fahrenheit' of 'Celsius' object has no setter

How it works:

  • The method under @property runs when you read c.degrees.
  • The method under @degrees.setter runs when you assign c.degrees = .... It checks the value and stores it in self._degrees, the real underlying attribute.
  • fahrenheit has no setter, so it can only be read.

Note that __init__ assigns to self.degrees, which runs the setter — so validation applies at construction too, with no duplicated code. A read-only property is simply one with no setter, and Python produces a clear error for you (the last line of output).

3.4 Descriptors

property is convenient for one attribute. Now imagine a Rectangle whose width and height must both be positive. With property you would write the same check twice, once per attribute. With ten such attributes, ten times.

What you want is to write the rule once, as an object, and attach it to any attribute. That object is a descriptor.

A descriptor is any object defining __get__, __set__ or __delete__, placed as a class attribute. Think of it as a guard posted at an attribute's door: instead of Python simply reading or writing the value, it asks the guard what to do. It is the mechanism underneath methods, property, classmethod, staticmethod and __slots__ — learning it once explains all of them at the same time.

Recall the lookup order from §1.6: data descriptors (defining __set__ or __delete__) beat the instance dictionary; non-data descriptors (only __get__) lose to it. That single asymmetry is why a method can be shadowed by an instance attribute but a property cannot. The end of this subsection proves it.

Here is the positive-number rule, written once and used for two attributes:

class Positive:
    """A data descriptor: validates on every assignment."""
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
        self.name = '_' + name            # told its own attribute name
    def __get__(self, obj, objtype=None):
        if obj is None:
            return self                   # accessed on the class
        return getattr(obj, self.name)
    def __set__(self, obj, value):
        if value <= 0:
            raise ValueError(f'{self.name[1:]} must be positive, got {value}')
        setattr(obj, self.name, value)

class Rectangle:
    width = Positive()
    height = Positive()
    def __init__(self, width, height):
        self.width, self.height = width, height
    def area(self):
        return self.width * self.height

r = Rectangle(3, 4)
print(r.area())
try:
    r.width = -1
except ValueError as exc:
    print('ValueError:', exc)
print(type(Rectangle.width).__name__)     # obj is None -> returns the descriptor

12
ValueError: width must be positive, got -1
Positive

Read the descriptor's methods as answers to three questions:

  • __set__ answers "someone is assigning r.width = value; what now?" It checks the value and stores it under _width on the instance.
  • __get__ answers "someone is reading r.width." It fetches _width back. When the read is on the class itself (Rectangle.width), obj is None and it returns the descriptor, which is the last line of output.
  • __set_name__ answers "what is my attribute called?" It is asked once, when the class is created.

Two validated attributes, one validator, written once. A property would need the logic duplicated per attribute; that is exactly when to reach for a descriptor instead.

__set_name__ (Python 3.6) is what makes this convenient: at class creation Python calls it on every descriptor in the body, telling it the attribute name it was assigned to. Without it you would have to write width = Positive('width') and keep the string in sync by hand.

The tools you already use are descriptors

Now the payoff — the standard tools are all descriptors:

class C:
    def method(self): ...
    @property
    def prop(self): return 1
    @staticmethod
    def stat(): ...
    __slots__ = ()

print('function is a non-data descriptor:',
      hasattr(C.method, '__get__'), hasattr(C.method, '__set__'))
print('property is a data descriptor:',
      hasattr(C.prop, '__get__'), hasattr(C.prop, '__set__'))

function is a non-data descriptor: True False
property is a data descriptor: True True

A plain function has __get__ (that is what turned hello into a bound method, the function with the instance clipped on, in §3.2) but no __set__. A property has both.

That is the whole explanation for a behaviour that otherwise looks arbitrary: obj.method = something works and shadows the method, because a function is a non-data descriptor and loses to the instance dict. obj.prop = something raises, because property is a data descriptor and wins.

3.5 Multiple Inheritance and the MRO

A class can inherit from more than one parent. When a class has several bases, Python needs a deterministic order in which to search them for a method. Think of a family asking for advice: the order in which you ask relatives has to be fixed, or the answer would change from day to day.

That order is the MRO (method resolution order), computed by an algorithm called C3 linearisation (a rule for merging the parents' search orders into one list), and it guarantees that a class always precedes its own bases and that the order of bases is preserved.

The classic test is a diamond: B and C both inherit from A, and D inherits from both. Each who method adds its own letter and then calls super():

class A:
    def who(self): return 'A'
class B(A):
    def who(self): return 'B -> ' + super().who()
class C(A):
    def who(self): return 'C -> ' + super().who()
class D(B, C):
    def who(self): return 'D -> ' + super().who()

print([c.__name__ for c in D.__mro__])
print(D().who())

['D', 'B', 'C', 'A', 'object']
D -> B -> C -> A

The first line is the MRO: the order Python searches. The second line follows it exactly.

Look carefully at that second line, because it is the point of the whole mechanism. B.who calls super().who() — and super() inside B resolved to C, not to A, even though B inherits from A and knows nothing about C.

super() does not mean "my parent". It means "the next class in the MRO of the actual instance". The instance is a D, so the list that matters is D's, and in that list the class after B is C. That is what makes cooperative multiple inheritance work, where every class passes the call along with super(): the diamond's shared base A runs exactly once, not twice.

Cooperating classes

The practical rules for cooperative classes:

  • Every class in the hierarchy must call super(), or the chain breaks at the first one that does not.
  • Signatures must be compatible along the chain (a signature is the list of parameters a method accepts, §4.2), which is why mixins conventionally accept and forward **kwargs, any extra keyword arguments, passed on unchanged. (A mixin is a small class meant to be combined with others to add one feature.)
  • If C3 cannot produce a consistent order, the class definition itself raises TypeError — the inconsistency is caught at definition time, not at call time.

Here is a service built from two mixins, each adding one entry to a log, and then a class whose bases cannot be ordered:

class Base:
    def __init__(self, **kw):
        self.log = ['Base']
class Loud(Base):
    def __init__(self, **kw):
        super().__init__(**kw)
        self.log.append('Loud')
class Timed(Base):
    def __init__(self, **kw):
        super().__init__(**kw)
        self.log.append('Timed')
class Service(Loud, Timed):
    def __init__(self, **kw):
        super().__init__(**kw)
        self.log.append('Service')

print(Service().log)

try:
    class Broken(Base, Loud): ...
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', str(exc)[:60])

['Base', 'Timed', 'Loud', 'Service']
TypeError: Cannot create a consistent method resolution order (MRO) for

The log reads bottom-up because each __init__ appends after delegating — every class runs, once, in reverse MRO order. Base appears once, even though both mixins inherit from it.

Broken(Base, Loud) asks for Base to come before Loud, but Loud is a child of Base and must come first. No order satisfies both, so Python refuses to create the class.

3.6 Abstract Base Classes

Think of a job description. It lists the duties every person in the role must perform, but it is not itself a person, and you cannot hire someone who skips a duty.

An abstract base class declares an interface that subclasses must implement, and refuses to instantiate (create an instance of) anything incomplete. Where a Protocol (§6.6) checks shape structurally at type-check time (a type checker compares which methods an object has, before the program runs), an ABC enforces inheritance at runtime.

Here is a storage interface with two required methods, one complete implementation, and one that forgot a method:

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Storage(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def save(self, key: str, value: bytes) -> None: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def load(self, key: str) -> bytes: ...

    def save_text(self, key: str, text: str) -> None:   # concrete: shared logic
        self.save(key, text.encode())

class MemoryStorage(Storage):
    def __init__(self):
        self._data = {}
    def save(self, key, value):
        self._data[key] = value
    def load(self, key):
        return self._data[key]

class Incomplete(Storage):
    def save(self, key, value): ...          # forgot load()

s = MemoryStorage()
s.save_text('greeting', 'hello')
print(s.load('greeting'))
try:
    Incomplete()
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

b'hello'
TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class Incomplete without an implementation for abstract method 'load'

MemoryStorage implemented both methods, so it works, and it also got save_text for free from the base class. Incomplete skipped load, and Python refused to create one, naming the missing method.

The failure happens at instantiation, not at definition — which is what allows an abstract subclass to add some methods and leave others for its own children.

The ABCs Python ships

collections.abc ships the interfaces the language itself uses — Iterable, Sequence, Mapping, Hashable — and inheriting from them gives you working mixin methods for free. Here is the deck of cards from §2.7 again, this time inheriting from Sequence:

from collections.abc import Sequence

class Deck(Sequence):
    def __init__(self, cards):
        self._cards = list(cards)
    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return self._cards[i]
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self._cards)

d = Deck(['A', 'K', 'Q'])
print('Q' in d, d.index('K'), list(reversed(d)), d.count('A'))

True 1 ['Q', 'K', 'A'] 1

Two methods written; __contains__, index, count, __iter__ and __reversed__ all supplied by the ABC.

ABC or Protocol? Use an ABC when you own the hierarchy and want shared implementation plus runtime enforcement; use a Protocol when you are typing objects you do not own, or want structural matching with no inheritance.

3.7 __init_subclass__: The Hook Before Metaclasses

Sometimes a parent class needs to know whenever someone creates a child class. A plugin system, a program that other people extend by writing small classes of their own, is the usual example: every plugin should be added to a list automatically, the moment its class is written, without anyone calling register().

Most reasons people reach for a metaclass are better served by __init_subclass__, which runs on the parent whenever a subclass is defined:

class Plugin:
    registry = {}

    def __init_subclass__(cls, /, name=None, **kwargs):
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)
        key = name or cls.__name__.lower()
        Plugin.registry[key] = cls

class JsonPlugin(Plugin): ...
class CsvPlugin(Plugin, name='csv-reader'): ...

print(sorted(Plugin.registry))
print(Plugin.registry['csv-reader'] is CsvPlugin)

['csv-reader', 'jsonplugin']
True

Nobody called any registration function. Writing class JsonPlugin(Plugin) was enough: Python called Plugin.__init_subclass__ with the new class, and it added itself to the registry.

Self-registering subclasses, validation of subclass definitions, and injected defaults (default values added to every subclass automatically) — all without a metaclass, and with none of a metaclass's inheritance conflicts. Note it can accept keyword arguments passed in the class header (the class ...: line), which is how CsvPlugin supplied its own name.

The companion hook is __set_name__ (§3.4), for the descriptor side. Between them they cover the large majority of class-creation customisation.

3.8 Metaclasses

Every object has a class: 5 is an instance of int. Classes are objects too (§1.3), so a class must also have a class. A metaclass is the class of a class. type is the default, and calling type(name, bases, namespace) is exactly what the class statement does after running the body (§3.1).

You can make the call yourself and build a class with no class statement at all:

def make_greet(self):
    return 'hi'

Dynamic = type('Dynamic', (), {'x': 1, 'greet': make_greet})
print(Dynamic.__name__, Dynamic().x, Dynamic().greet())
print(type(Dynamic), type(int), type(type))

Dynamic 1 hi
<class 'type'> <class 'type'> <class 'type'>

Dynamic is a real class, with an attribute and a method. The second line shows that its class is type, the same as int's, and that even type is an instance of itself.

Writing one

A custom metaclass subclasses type and overrides __new__ or __init__ (replaces them with its own versions) to intervene at class creation. This one refuses any subclass without a docstring (the string on the first line of a class or function that describes it), and adds an attribute to every class it creates:

class Validated(type):
    def __new__(mcls, name, bases, ns, **kw):
        if bases and not ns.get('__doc__'):
            raise TypeError(f'{name} must have a docstring')
        ns['created_by'] = 'Validated'
        return super().__new__(mcls, name, bases, ns, **kw)

class Model(metaclass=Validated):
    """Base."""

class Good(Model):
    """Documented."""

print(Good.created_by)
try:
    class Bad(Model): pass
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

Validated
TypeError: Bad must have a docstring

The error came from the class Bad line itself, before any instance existed: a metaclass runs when the class is created.

When to actually use one. Almost never. The honest list is:

  • when you must change the namespace before the class object exists,
  • when you need to control isinstance/issubclass via __instancecheck__,
  • when you are building a framework whose users write declarative class bodies (they list what they want as fields, and the framework works out the rest) — which is why ORMs (libraries that map classes onto database tables, such as Django's models) and abc itself use them.

The real cost is composability, how easily it combines with other code: a class can have only one metaclass, and combining two classes with different metaclasses is a TypeError your users cannot fix. __init_subclass__ has no such problem. The standard guidance stands:

If you are wondering whether you need a metaclass, you do not. People who genuinely need them know they do.

3.9 Dataclasses in Depth

Most classes you write are mostly data: a point, an order, a user record. For each one, you would normally write the same three methods by hand: an __init__ that stores every field, a __repr__ that prints them, and an __eq__ that compares them. That is a lot of typing, and easy to get out of step when a field is added.

@dataclass generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from annotated class attributes (attributes written with a type, such as x: int). You list the fields with their types; the decorator (the @ line above the class, §4.4) writes the methods. It is the right default for any class that is mostly data.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True, kw_only=True)
class Point:
    x: float
    y: float
    label: str = 'origin'
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)   # NOT tags: list = []

p = Point(x=1, y=2)
print(p)
print(p == Point(x=1, y=2))
try:
    p.x = 5
except AttributeError as exc:
    print('AttributeError:', exc)
try:
    hash(p)                                       # a mutable field is still in there
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

Point(x=1, y=2, label='origin', tags=[])
True
AttributeError: cannot assign to field 'x'
TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'

The first two lines are the generated __repr__ and __eq__. The third shows frozen=True refusing a change.

That last line is the trap worth learning. frozen=True generates a __hash__ over all the fields, which is precisely §2.4's contract — but it cannot make a list field hashable, and the failure appears when someone first calls hash(), not at class definition. A frozen dataclass is hashable only if every field is. Use a tuple instead of a list, or exclude the field:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Point:
    x: float
    y: float
    tags: tuple[str, ...] = ()                    # immutable -> hashable

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Other:
    x: float
    notes: list[str] = field(default_factory=list, compare=False, hash=False)

print(hash(Point(1, 2)) == hash(Point(1, 2)))
print(len({Point(1, 2), Point(1, 2)}))
print(hash(Other(1)) == hash(Other(1)))

True
1
True

Both fixes work: Point with a tuple hashes, and a set of two equal points holds one; Other keeps its list but leaves it out of comparison and hashing.

The options that matter

  • frozen=True makes instances immutable and hashable — provided every field is itself hashable, as above. This is the default you want for value objects.
  • slots=True (3.10) adds __slots__, giving §1.7's memory saving with none of the boilerplate, the repetitive code you would otherwise type by hand.
  • kw_only=True (3.10) forces keyword arguments, so adding a field later cannot silently reorder positional calls (calls that pass arguments by position rather than by name).
  • field(default_factory=...) is mandatory for mutable defaults — a bare tags: list = [] raises ValueError at class creation, because the dataclass machinery recognises §1.2's bug and refuses.
from dataclasses import dataclass

try:
    @dataclass
    class Bad:
        items: list = []
except ValueError as exc:
    print('ValueError:', exc)

ValueError: mutable default <class 'list'> for field items is not allowed: use default_factory

Other useful pieces:

  • field(compare=False) excludes a field from __eq__,
  • field(repr=False) hides a secret from logs,
  • __post_init__ runs after generated initialisation for derived values (values computed from other fields),
  • dataclasses.replace() produces a modified copy of a frozen instance.

For comparison: NamedTuple is immutable, indexable and tuple-compatible — good for lightweight records; TypedDict (§6.7) types a plain dict with no class at runtime; pydantic (§13.7) validates at runtime. Dataclasses sit in the middle and are the usual answer.

3.10 Enums

Start with the problem. Statuses stored as plain strings let typos through silently:

from enum import Enum

status = 'active'
print(status == 'actve')          # a typo, and Python cannot tell

class Status(Enum):
    PENDING = 'pending'
    ACTIVE = 'active'

try:
    Status.ACTVE                  # the same typo, caught at once
except AttributeError as exc:
    print('AttributeError:', exc)

False
AttributeError: type object 'Status' has no attribute 'ACTVE'

The string comparison simply came out False, and a bug like that can hide for months. The enum has a fixed list of members, so a misspelled one is an error the first time the line runs.

An Enum gives a fixed set of named constants that are singletons, comparable by identity, and self-documenting in tracebacks (the error reports Python prints when something fails, §7.7) and logs. Python ships several kinds; here are the three you will use most:

  • Enum, the plain kind,
  • StrEnum, whose members are also real strings,
  • IntFlag, whose members are bits you can combine with |.
from enum import Enum, StrEnum, IntFlag, auto

class Status(Enum):
    PENDING = 'pending'
    ACTIVE = 'active'

class Colour(StrEnum):                 # 3.11: is a real str
    RED = 'red'
    GREEN = 'green'

class Perm(IntFlag):
    READ = auto()
    WRITE = auto()
    EXEC = auto()

print(Status.ACTIVE, Status.ACTIVE.value, Status('active') is Status.ACTIVE)
print(Colour.RED == 'red', f'{Colour.RED} works in strings')
rw = Perm.READ | Perm.WRITE
print(repr(rw), Perm.WRITE in rw, Perm.EXEC in rw)
print(rw, int(rw))                     # str() is int's, since 3.11
print([s.name for s in Status])

Status.ACTIVE active True
True red works in strings
<Perm.READ|WRITE: 3> True False
3 3
['PENDING', 'ACTIVE']

Line by line:

  • Status('active') looks a member up by its value, and gives back the very same object (is is True).
  • A StrEnum member equals its string and drops straight into an f-string.
  • READ | WRITE combines two flags; in tests whether a flag is set.
  • Iterating over an enum gives its members in order.

Note the difference between the two flag lines. repr() shows the readable <Perm.READ|WRITE: 3>, but str() gives 3 — since Python 3.11 IntEnum, IntFlag and StrEnum inherit their __str__ from int/str rather than from Enum, specifically so they interpolate into strings and format as the underlying value. It is what you want for serialisation and a surprise in log messages, so reach for repr() or .name when you are logging a flag.

StrEnum and IntEnum are the interoperability escape hatches, a way out of the enum's strictness when working with code that expects plain strings or numbers — members really are str/int, so they serialise to JSON and compare with raw values, at the cost of being implicitly usable where a plain string was expected. IntFlag gives you combinable bit flags with readable repr() output. Use @enum.unique to forbid aliases (two names for the same value), and auto() when the values themselves carry no meaning.

Exercises

Exercise 3.1 — Why does this validation not run? The author expected assigning to temp to be validated. Explain why it is not, and fix it.

class Reading:
    def __init__(self, temp):
        self.temp = temp

    def temp(self):
        if self.temp < -273.15:
            raise ValueError('too cold')
        return self.temp
Solution

Two separate problems, and the first hides the second.

temp is defined as a plain method, which is a non-data descriptor. Per §1.6 and §3.4, non-data descriptors lose to the instance dictionary — so self.temp = temp in __init__ writes straight into self.__dict__, shadowing the method entirely. Nothing is ever validated, and Reading(5).temp returns 5 rather than a bound method.

Even if it were reached, the method is infinitely recursive: self.temp inside temp would call itself.

A property is a data descriptor, so it wins over the instance dict and cannot be shadowed. The stored value needs a different name to avoid the recursion:

class Reading:
    def __init__(self, temp):
        self.temp = temp                  # goes through the setter

    @property
    def temp(self):
        return self._temp

    @temp.setter
    def temp(self, value):
        if value < -273.15:
            raise ValueError('too cold')
        self._temp = value

r = Reading(20)
print(r.temp)
try:
    r.temp = -300
except ValueError as exc:
    print('ValueError:', exc)
try:
    Reading(-300)
except ValueError as exc:
    print('rejected at construction too:', exc)

20
ValueError: too cold
rejected at construction too: too cold

The general lesson is the data/non-data asymmetry: if you want an attribute that cannot be bypassed by assignment, it must define __set__. That is exactly the difference between a method and a property.

Exercise 3.2 — Predict the MRO. Give D.__mro__ and the output of D().go(), then explain why B's super() reaches what it does.

class A:
    def go(self): return ['A']
class B(A):
    def go(self): return ['B'] + super().go()
class C(A):
    def go(self): return ['C'] + super().go()
class D(C, B):
    def go(self): return ['D'] + super().go()
Solution 
class A:
    def go(self): return ['A']
class B(A):
    def go(self): return ['B'] + super().go()
class C(A):
    def go(self): return ['C'] + super().go()
class D(C, B):
    def go(self): return ['D'] + super().go()

print([c.__name__ for c in D.__mro__])
print(D().go())

['D', 'C', 'B', 'A', 'object']
['D', 'C', 'B', 'A']

Note the bases are (C, B) here, the reverse of §3.5's example, and the MRO reverses with them: C3 preserves the order in which bases are declared.

The instructive part is C.go calling super().go() and reaching B — a class C does not inherit from and has no knowledge of. super() is not "my parent"; it is "the next class after me in type(self).__mro__". Since self is a D, that MRO is D → C → B → A, so C's super() is B.

This is the entire reason A.go runs once rather than twice. If each class had hard-coded A.go(self) instead of super(), the diamond would call A twice — the classic multiple-inheritance bug that C3 and cooperative super() exist to prevent.

Because behaviour depends on the MRO of the runtime instance, a mixin cannot know statically who follows it. That is why cooperative classes forward **kwargs and always call super().

Exercise 3.3 — Replace repetition with a descriptor. This class validates three fields with near-identical code. Rewrite it so the validation is written once, and the error message still names the right field.

class Product:
    def __init__(self, price, weight, quantity):
        if price <= 0: raise ValueError('price must be positive')
        self._price = price
        if weight <= 0: raise ValueError('weight must be positive')
        self._weight = weight
        if quantity <= 0: raise ValueError('quantity must be positive')
        self._quantity = quantity
Solution

A data descriptor holds the rule once; __set_name__ supplies the field name so the message stays specific.

class Positive:
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
        self._name = name
        self._store = '_' + name

    def __get__(self, obj, objtype=None):
        if obj is None:
            return self
        return getattr(obj, self._store)

    def __set__(self, obj, value):
        if value <= 0:
            raise ValueError(f'{self._name} must be positive')
        setattr(obj, self._store, value)

class Product:
    price = Positive()
    weight = Positive()
    quantity = Positive()

    def __init__(self, price, weight, quantity):
        self.price, self.weight, self.quantity = price, weight, quantity

p = Product(10, 2, 5)
print(p.price, p.weight, p.quantity)
for field, args in [('price', (0, 1, 1)), ('weight', (1, -1, 1)), ('quantity', (1, 1, 0))]:
    try:
        Product(*args)
    except ValueError as exc:
        print('ValueError:', exc)

10 2 5
ValueError: price must be positive
ValueError: weight must be positive
ValueError: quantity must be positive

Three fields, one validator, and validation still applies on later assignment (p.price = -1 raises) because __set__ runs on every write — something the original __init__-only checks did not do.

Two details that matter. __get__ must handle obj is None and return the descriptor itself, or Product.price raises instead of being introspectable. And the value is stored under a different name (_price) than the descriptor occupies (price); storing it under the same name would make __set__ call itself forever.

When to prefer what: one validated attribute is a property; three or more sharing a rule is a descriptor; a whole class of validated fields declared from types is pydantic (§13), which is descriptors all the way down.

Exercise 3.4 — Registry without a metaclass. A plugin system uses a metaclass to auto-register subclasses. Rewrite it without one, and explain what problem that removes.

class PluginMeta(type):
    registry = {}
    def __new__(mcls, name, bases, ns):
        cls = super().__new__(mcls, name, bases, ns)
        if bases:
            PluginMeta.registry[name.lower()] = cls
        return cls

class Plugin(metaclass=PluginMeta):
    pass
Solution

__init_subclass__ does the same job as a plain classmethod on the base:

class Plugin:
    registry = {}

    def __init_subclass__(cls, /, name=None, **kwargs):
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)
        Plugin.registry[name or cls.__name__.lower()] = cls

class JsonPlugin(Plugin): ...
class XmlPlugin(Plugin, name='xml'): ...

print(sorted(Plugin.registry))
print(Plugin.registry['xml'] is XmlPlugin)

['jsonplugin', 'xml']
True

The problem it removes is metaclass conflict. A class has exactly one metaclass, and that metaclass must be a subclass of the metaclasses of all its bases. So with the original design, a user who wants a plugin that is also an abc.ABC gets:

TypeError: metaclass conflict: the metaclass of a derived class must be a (non-strict) subclass of the metaclasses of all its bases

— because ABCMeta and PluginMeta are unrelated. The user cannot fix this without editing your library. With __init_subclass__ there is no metaclass at all, so class Thing(Plugin, ABC) simply works.

The rewrite also gains keyword arguments in the class header (name='xml') essentially for free, and is materially easier to read for anyone who has not memorised the type.__new__ signature. This is why §3.8's guidance is that the genuine remaining uses for metaclasses are narrow: controlling isinstance, or needing to alter the namespace before the class object exists.

SECTION 4

Functions, Closures and Decorators

In Python a function is a value, like a number or a string. You can store it in a variable, put it in a list, pass it to another function, and get one back. Functions in Python are ordinary objects that happen to be callable.

Once that clicks, decorators stop being syntax to memorise and become an obvious consequence: if a function is a value, you can write a function that takes one and returns another.

The section climbs to decorators one step at a time:

  1. Functions as values (§4.1) and their parameters (§4.2).
  2. Closures: functions that remember (§4.3).
  3. Decorators, built from those two ideas (§4.4–§4.7).
  4. The standard-library tools built on decorators: functools and contextlib (§4.8–§4.10).

4.1 Functions Are Objects

A def statement creates an object and binds it to a name, just as x = 5 binds a name to a number (§1.2). That object carries attributes you can read, modify and use. Ask a function about itself:

def greet(name: str, greeting: str = 'Hello') -> str:
    """Return a greeting."""
    return f'{greeting}, {name}!'

print(greet.__name__, '|', greet.__doc__)
print(greet.__defaults__, greet.__annotations__['return'])

alias = greet                       # just another name for the same object
greet.calls = 0                     # functions accept arbitrary attributes
print(alias('world'), alias.calls)

greet | Return a greeting.
('Hello',) <class 'str'>
Hello, world! 0

Line by line:

  • The function knows its own name and docstring.
  • It stores its default values ('Hello') and its type annotations.
  • alias = greet stuck a second label on the same function (§1.2), so calling alias calls greet, and alias.calls reads the attribute set through greet.

Functions in a dictionary

Because functions are values, they can be stored in dicts, passed to other functions, and returned from them. Here is a tiny calculator. Instead of if op == '+': ... elif op == '-': ..., a dict maps each symbol to the function that does the work. A dispatch table, a lookup table from a key to the function that handles it, is often clearer than a chain of ifs:

def add(a, b): return a + b
def sub(a, b): return a - b

OPS = {'+': add, '-': sub, '*': lambda a, b: a * b}
print([OPS[op](6, 3) for op in ('+', '-', '*')])

[9, 3, 18]

OPS['+'] is the function add itself, and OPS['+'](6, 3) calls it. Adding an operator means adding one line to the dict, not another branch.

lambda

The * entry used lambda. lambda is the same thing without a name, limited to a single expression. When to use which:

  • Use lambda for throwaway callables (anything that can be called with (), §1.3) passed to sorted, map or a dict like the one above.
  • Use def the moment the function needs a name in a traceback, a docstring, or more than one line.

4.2 The Signature

A function's signature is its list of parameters: what you may pass, in what order, and by what name. Python's parameter syntax is richer than most people use, and the markers are worth knowing because they appear throughout the standard library and its documentation.

Here is one function with all three kinds of parameter. The / and * in the list are not parameters; they are markers that divide it:

def f(pos_only, /, standard, *, kw_only):
    return pos_only, standard, kw_only

print(f(1, 2, kw_only=3))
print(f(1, standard=2, kw_only=3))
try:
    f(pos_only=1, standard=2, kw_only=3)
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

(1, 2, 3)
(1, 2, 3)
TypeError: f() got some positional-only arguments passed as keyword arguments: 'pos_only'

The first two calls work: standard can be passed either way. The third fails, because pos_only sits before the / and can only be passed by position. What the two markers mean:

  • / marks everything before it positional-only (3.8). Use it to keep parameter names out of your public API (the part of your code other people are meant to call), so you can rename them later without breaking callers. This is why len(obj) refuses len(obj=x).
  • * marks everything after it keyword-only. Use it for options and flags, where a bare True at a call site (the place in the code where the function is called) would be unreadable: connect(host, retry=True) says what it means; connect(host, True) does not.

Collecting and unpacking

*args and **kwargs collect the rest: extra positional arguments go into a tuple, extra keyword arguments into a dict. The same symbols unpack at a call site, spreading a list or dict back out into separate arguments:

def report(*args, **kwargs):
    return f'args={args} kwargs={kwargs}'

print(report(1, 2, mode='fast'))
values = [1, 2]
options = {'mode': 'fast'}
print(report(*values, **options))         # unpacking, the mirror image

args=(1, 2) kwargs={'mode': 'fast'}
args=(1, 2) kwargs={'mode': 'fast'}

The two lines are identical. The second call unpacked values and options into exactly the arguments the first call wrote out by hand.

Reading a signature at runtime

inspect.signature reads all of this back at runtime, which is how frameworks like pytest and FastAPI decide what to pass your function. pytest, for example, looks at your test's parameter names to decide which fixtures to give it (prepared inputs, such as a temporary folder; §12.4):

import inspect

def handler(request, /, timeout=30, *, retries=3):
    ...

sig = inspect.signature(handler)
for name, param in sig.parameters.items():
    print(f'{name:8} {str(param.kind):24} default={param.default!r}')

request  POSITIONAL_ONLY          default=<class 'inspect._empty'>
timeout  POSITIONAL_OR_KEYWORD    default=30
retries  KEYWORD_ONLY             default=3

Each parameter reports its kind and its default. request has no default, which inspect shows with the special marker inspect._empty.

4.3 Closures

Imagine a function that carries a small private notebook. Each time you call it, it reads and writes the notebook. Nobody else can open it. Two copies of the function each get their own notebook.

A closure is that: a function that remembers names from the scope where it was defined, even after that scope has returned (that is, even after the function that created it has finished). The remembered variables live in cells attached to the function object (the cells are the notebook).

Here a function builds and returns a counter. Each counter remembers its own count:

def make_counter(start=0):
    count = start
    def increment(by=1):
        nonlocal count            # rebind the enclosing variable
        count += by
        return count
    return increment

c1, c2 = make_counter(), make_counter(100)
print(c1(), c1(), c2(), c1())
print(c1.__closure__[0].cell_contents)
print([v for v in c1.__code__.co_freevars])

1 2 101 3
3
['count']

Read the first line as four calls: c1 gives 1 and 2, c2 starts from 100 and gives 101, then c1 carries on with 3. make_counter had already returned, yet each counter still had its count.

Two independent counters, each with private state that no outside code can reach except through the function. __closure__ exposes the cells and co_freevars names them — proof the state is real and attached to the function object.

nonlocal

nonlocal is required to rebind. Without it, count += by would treat count as local to increment and raise UnboundLocalError, because assignment anywhere in a function makes the name local throughout it. Here is the same counter with the nonlocal line left out:

def broken():
    count = 0
    def inc():
        count += 1               # no nonlocal -> count is local here
        return count
    try:
        inc()
    except UnboundLocalError as exc:
        print('UnboundLocalError:', exc)

broken()

UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'count' where it is not associated with a value

Python saw the assignment count += 1 and decided count belongs to inc. Then it tried to read that local count before anything had been assigned to it. Reading an outer variable needs no keyword; only assigning to one does.

The loop-variable trap

The classic closure trap is a loop variable, which is captured by reference, not by value. A closure remembers the variable, not the value it held at the time. Before you read the output, predict the first line:

funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in funcs])                     # all see the final i

fixed = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]       # bind now, via a default
print([f() for f in fixed])

[2, 2, 2]
[0, 1, 2]

Most people expect [0, 1, 2] both times. All three lambdas share one cell holding i, and by the time they are called the loop has finished, so i is 2.

The default-argument fix works because defaults are evaluated at definition time (§1.2 — the same rule that causes the mutable-default bug, here doing something useful). Each lambda stores the current i as its own default. functools.partial (§4.8) is the other standard fix.

4.4 Decorators From First Principles

Suppose you want several functions to announce each call: print a line before, run, print the result after. Copying those prints into every function is tedious, and you would have to remove them all again later.

Instead, write the announcing once, as a function that wraps any other function. A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a replacement. @ is only shorthand.

def announce(fn):
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        print(f'  calling {fn.__name__}')
        result = fn(*args, **kwargs)
        print(f'  {fn.__name__} returned {result}')
        return result
    return wrapper

@announce
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

# exactly equivalent to:
def sub(a, b):
    return a - b
sub = announce(sub)

add(2, 3)
sub(5, 2)

  calling add
  add returned 5
  calling sub
  sub returned 3

add used the @ form and sub used the long form, and both behave the same way. Follow the long form to see what happens:

  1. announce(sub) builds a new function, wrapper, that remembers sub as fn. wrapper is a closure (§4.3).
  2. sub = announce(sub) moves the label sub onto wrapper.
  3. Calling sub(5, 2) now calls wrapper, which prints, calls the original, prints again, and returns the result.

@announce above def add means precisely add = announce(add). Everything else follows:

  • the wrapper must accept whatever arguments the original takes (hence *args, **kwargs),
  • and must return the original's result, or callers silently get None.

4.5 functools.wraps

There is a catch in §4.4. After sub = announce(sub), the label sub is on wrapper, so anything that asks "what is this function called?" gets the wrong answer.

A naive (simple, first-attempt) decorator replaces the function object, so the name, docstring and signature of the original are lost. That breaks documentation tools, debuggers and any framework that introspects (that is, inspects your functions at runtime, as §4.2's pytest does). Compare a decorator without the fix and one with it:

import functools

def bare(fn):
    def wrapper(*a, **k):
        return fn(*a, **k)
    return wrapper

def kept(fn):
    @functools.wraps(fn)                 # copies __name__, __doc__, __wrapped__, ...
    def wrapper(*a, **k):
        return fn(*a, **k)
    return wrapper

@bare
def alpha(x):
    """Alpha docs."""

@kept
def beta(x):
    """Beta docs."""

print(alpha.__name__, alpha.__doc__)
print(beta.__name__, beta.__doc__)

import inspect
print('signature recovered:', str(inspect.signature(beta)))

wrapper None
beta Beta docs.
signature recovered: (x)

alpha now calls itself wrapper and has lost its docstring. beta kept both, because functools.wraps copied them from the original onto the wrapper.

Without wraps, every decorated function in your codebase is called wrapper in tracebacks. It also sets __wrapped__, which is how inspect.signature sees through the decorator to the real signature — the line above proves it: (x) is beta's signature, not the wrapper's (*a, **k).

Always use functools.wraps. There is no case where omitting it is correct.

4.6 Decorators That Take Arguments

Some decorators need a setting: @repeat(times=3) should run a function three times. Notice the parentheses. @decorator(arg) calls decorator(arg) first and applies the result. So repeat(times=3) must return a decorator. That means one more layer of nesting: a function returning a decorator.

Read the three layers from the outside in. Each one takes one thing:

import functools

def repeat(times):                       # takes the argument
    def decorator(fn):                   # takes the function
        @functools.wraps(fn)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):    # takes the call
            return [fn(*args, **kwargs) for _ in range(times)]
        return wrapper
    return decorator

@repeat(times=3)
def roll():
    return 4

print(roll())

[4, 4, 4]

In order: repeat(times=3) returned decorator; decorator(roll) returned wrapper; and calling roll() ran wrapper, which called the original three times and collected the results.

With or without parentheses

Some decorators work both ways, as @trace and as @trace(prefix='DEBUG'). In the first form Python passes the function straight in; in the second it calls trace with only options. To support both @decorator and @decorator(...), check whether the first argument is callable — here, whether a function was passed at all:

import functools

def trace(fn=None, *, prefix='TRACE'):
    def decorator(inner):
        @functools.wraps(inner)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            print(f'{prefix}: {inner.__name__}')
            return inner(*args, **kwargs)
        return wrapper
    return decorator(fn) if fn is not None else decorator

@trace
def one(): return 1

@trace(prefix='DEBUG')
def two(): return 2

one(); two()

TRACE: one
DEBUG: two

@trace passed one as fn, so trace decorated it immediately. @trace(prefix='DEBUG') passed no function, so trace returned the decorator for Python to apply to two.

The * in trace's signature is what makes this unambiguous: options must be keyword arguments (§4.2), so a positional first argument can only ever be the decorated function.

4.7 Decorating Classes, and Class-Based Decorators

Decorators apply to classes too — @dataclass (§3.9) and @functools.total_ordering (§2.5) are exactly this. A class decorator receives the class and returns a replacement, usually the same class with additions. This one gives any class a readable repr:

def add_repr(cls):
    def __repr__(self):
        fields = ', '.join(f'{k}={v!r}' for k, v in vars(self).items())
        return f'{cls.__name__}({fields})'
    cls.__repr__ = __repr__
    return cls

@add_repr
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y

print(Point(1, 2))

Point(x=1, y=2)

Point never defined __repr__. The decorator added one to the class and handed the class back.

A decorator that is a class

A decorator can also be a class, using __call__ from §2.8. Applying it creates an instance, and calling the decorated name calls that instance. This is the readable choice when the decorator holds real state, such as a counter:

import functools

class CountCalls:
    def __init__(self, fn):
        functools.update_wrapper(self, fn)     # the wraps equivalent for instances
        self.fn = fn
        self.count = 0
    def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        self.count += 1
        return self.fn(*args, **kwargs)

@CountCalls
def ping():
    return 'pong'

ping(); ping(); ping()
print(ping.count, ping.__name__)

3 ping

After @CountCalls, the name ping is a CountCalls instance. Each call went through __call__, which counted it, and update_wrapper kept the name ping.

One caveat: a class-based decorator applied to a method does not become a bound method automatically, because the instance is a class instance rather than a function. Making it work requires implementing __get__ — descriptors again (§3.4). For methods, a closure-based decorator is simpler.

4.8 functools

functools is the standard library's toolbox for working with functions. It is the module worth reading end to end. The pieces you will use constantly start with caching.

Caching

First, the problem. The textbook Fibonacci function (each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two before it: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8…) calls itself twice for every number, and does the same work over and over. Count the calls:

calls = 0

def fib(n):
    global calls
    calls += 1
    return n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

print(fib(20), calls)

6765 21891

Almost 22,000 calls to compute the 20th number, because fib(18) is computed again inside fib(19), and so on down. Each step up roughly multiplies the work by 1.6.

A cache is a memo pad: the first time the function sees an argument, it writes down the answer; the next time, it reads the answer off the pad instead of recomputing. functools.cache adds one with a single line:

import functools

@functools.cache                       # 3.9: unbounded memoisation
def fib(n):
    return n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

print(fib(60))
print(fib.cache_info())

@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=128)      # bounded: evicts least-recently-used
def slow_lookup(key):
    return key.upper()

slow_lookup('a'); slow_lookup('a'); slow_lookup('b')
print(slow_lookup.cache_info())

1548008755920
CacheInfo(hits=58, misses=61, maxsize=None, currsize=61)
CacheInfo(hits=1, misses=2, maxsize=128, currsize=2)

fib(60) returns instantly instead of taking longer than the age of the universe, because each subproblem, each smaller question like fib(18), is computed once. Note the counts: 61 misses for 61 distinct inputs, and 58 hits. A miss is a first-time computation; a hit is an answer read from the pad.

lru_cache is the bounded version: it keeps at most maxsize answers and throws away the least recently used one when full. In the last line, the second 'a' was a hit and 'b' was a new miss.

Three rules for caching:

  • Arguments must be hashable — the cache is a dict, so a list argument raises TypeError (§1.5).
  • Use cache only for pure functions. A pure function's result depends only on its arguments. Caching something that reads a database or the clock returns stale (out-of-date) data forever.
  • cache is unbounded. On a method, or with many distinct arguments, it is a memory leak; lru_cache(maxsize=...) bounds it. functools.cached_property is the right tool for a per-instance computed value.

The rest of the toolbox

The rest:

  • partial freezes some of a function's arguments, giving a new function that needs fewer.
  • reduce folds a list into a single value by applying a two-argument function repeatedly.
  • total_ordering fills in comparison methods (§2.5).
  • cached_property computes an attribute once per instance and then remembers it.
import functools, operator

double = functools.partial(operator.mul, 2)      # freeze an argument
print(double(21))

print(functools.reduce(operator.add, [1, 2, 3, 4]))

@functools.total_ordering                        # §2.5
class T:
    def __init__(self, n): self.n = n
    def __eq__(self, o): return isinstance(o, T) and self.n == o.n
    def __lt__(self, o): return self.n < o.n

print(T(1) < T(2), T(2) >= T(1))

class Circle:
    def __init__(self, r): self.r = r
    @functools.cached_property                   # computed once per instance
    def area(self):
        print('  computing')
        return 3.14159 * self.r ** 2

c = Circle(2)
print(c.area, c.area)

42
10
True True
  computing
12.56636 12.56636

Line by line: double(21) is operator.mul(2, 21); reduce computed ((1 + 2) + 3) + 4; T defined only __lt__, yet >= worked.

cached_property printed computing once for two accesses — it replaces itself in the instance dictionary after the first call, which works precisely because it is a non-data descriptor and therefore loses to __dict__ on every subsequent lookup (§3.4).

4.9 singledispatch

Imagine a function that must describe any value: an int one way, a string another, a list a third. The obvious version is a chain of if isinstance(value, int): ... elif isinstance(value, str): ..., and every new type means editing that chain.

functools.singledispatch gives you function overloading (several versions of one function, with Python choosing between them) on the type of the first argument — a clean alternative to a chain of isinstance checks, and open for extension without editing the original. You write one general version, then register a specialised version for each type:

import functools
from decimal import Decimal

@functools.singledispatch
def describe(value):
    return f'some object: {value!r}'

@describe.register
def _(value: int) -> str:
    return f'int with {value.bit_length()} bits'

@describe.register
def _(value: str) -> str:
    return f'string of length {len(value)}'

@describe.register(list)
def _(value) -> str:
    return f'list of {len(value)} items'

print(describe(255))
print(describe('hello'))
print(describe([1, 2, 3]))
print(describe(Decimal('1.5')))          # falls back to the base implementation
print(describe(True))                    # bool is a subclass of int

int with 8 bits
string of length 5
list of 3 items
some object: Decimal('1.5')
int with 1 bits

The first three calls each reached the version registered for their type. Nobody registered Decimal, so it fell back to the general version.

Look at the last line: describe(True) printed int with 1 bits, reaching the int implementation.

Registration reads the type annotation of the first parameter, or takes the type as an argument. Dispatch, choosing which version to run, follows the MRO, which is why True reached the int implementation — bool is a subclass of int (§1.3), and there is no more specific registration.

singledispatchmethod does the same for methods. The genuine advantage over if isinstance(...) chains is extensibility: a different module can register a handler for its own type without touching yours, which is how you write a library that others can teach about their data.

4.10 contextlib.contextmanager

Section 2.9 built context managers from __enter__/__exit__, which takes a whole class. For one-off cases, writing a generator is far less code: everything before yield is the setup, everything after is the teardown, the cleanup.

(A generator is a function containing yield; it pauses at the yield and resumes later. Section 5 covers them fully. Here you only need the pause: the body of the with block runs while the function is paused.)

This one prints an opening tag, pauses while the body runs, then prints the closing tag:

import contextlib

@contextlib.contextmanager
def tag(name):
    print(f'<{name}>')
    try:
        yield name                        # the value bound by `as`
    finally:
        print(f'</{name}>')               # runs even on exception

with tag('div') as t:
    print(f'  inside {t}')

try:
    with tag('p'):
        raise ValueError('boom')
except ValueError:
    print('handled outside')

<div>
  inside div
</div>
<p>
</p>
handled outside

In the second block the body raised ValueError, yet </p> still printed before handled outside.

The try/finally is not optional. Without it, an exception in the body propagates (travels outward) out of the yield and the teardown never runs — which is the entire point of a context manager. To suppress an exception, catch it around the yield and simply do not re-raise it (raise it again).

The rest of contextlib

The rest of contextlib earns its place:

  • suppress ignores the exceptions you name (§2.9 built one by hand).
  • redirect_stdout sends everything print writes somewhere else for the length of the block.
  • ExitStack manages any number of context managers at once.
import contextlib, io

with contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError):      # §2.9, written for you
    open('/no/such/file')
print('suppressed')

buffer = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buffer):
    print('captured')
print('buffer holds:', buffer.getvalue().strip())

with contextlib.ExitStack() as stack:             # a dynamic number of managers
    files = [stack.enter_context(io.StringIO(f'file{i}')) for i in range(3)]
    print('open:', len(files))
print('all closed:', all(f.closed for f in files))

suppressed
buffer holds: captured
open: 3
all closed: True

ExitStack is the answer whenever the number of resources is not known until runtime — it guarantees everything entered is exited, in reverse order, even if one of them raises. Here it opened three in-memory files (file-like objects that live in memory rather than on disk) and closed all three when the block ended. contextlib.asynccontextmanager (§9.8) is the async twin.

Exercises

Exercise 4.1 — Explain the output. Predict what this prints, then fix it so each function returns its own multiplier.

multipliers = []
for n in range(1, 4):
    multipliers.append(lambda x: x * n)

print([m(10) for m in multipliers])
Solution

It prints [30, 30, 30]. All three lambdas close over the same variable n, not over its value at the time each was created. By the time any of them runs, the loop has finished and n is 3.

This is the §4.3 trap, and it is the single most common closure bug. Two correct fixes:

# Fix 1: bind the value now, via a default argument
multipliers = [lambda x, n=n: x * n for n in range(1, 4)]
print([m(10) for m in multipliers])

# Fix 2: a factory, so each call gets its own scope
def make_multiplier(n):
    def multiply(x):
        return x * n
    return multiply

multipliers = [make_multiplier(n) for n in range(1, 4)]
print([m(10) for m in multipliers])

# Fix 3: functools.partial
import functools, operator
multipliers = [functools.partial(operator.mul, n) for n in range(1, 4)]
print([m(10) for m in multipliers])

[10, 20, 30]
[10, 20, 30]
[10, 20, 30]

Fix 1 is shortest but leaks a parameter into the public signature — a caller could pass m(10, 99). Fix 2 is the clearest and the one to reach for when the closure is non-trivial: each make_multiplier call creates a fresh scope, so each multiply gets its own cell. Fix 3 is idiomatic when you are merely freezing an argument.

Note this is not a quirk of lambdas — def inside the loop behaves identically. The rule is that closures capture variables, not values.

Exercise 4.2 — Write a @retry decorator. It should take attempts and retry the function that many times, re-raising the last exception if all attempts fail, and preserve the wrapped function's name and docstring.

Solution 
import functools

def retry(attempts=3, exceptions=(Exception,)):
    def decorator(fn):
        @functools.wraps(fn)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            last = None
            for attempt in range(1, attempts + 1):
                try:
                    return fn(*args, **kwargs)
                except exceptions as exc:
                    last = exc
                    print(f'  attempt {attempt} failed: {exc}')
            raise last
        return wrapper
    return decorator

calls = []

@retry(attempts=3)
def flaky():
    """Fails twice, then succeeds."""
    calls.append(1)
    if len(calls) < 3:
        raise ConnectionError(f'call {len(calls)}')
    return 'ok'

print(flaky())
print(flaky.__name__, '|', flaky.__doc__)

@retry(attempts=2, exceptions=(ValueError,))
def always_bad():
    raise ValueError('nope')

try:
    always_bad()
except ValueError as exc:
    print('gave up:', exc)

  attempt 1 failed: call 1
  attempt 2 failed: call 2
ok
flaky | Fails twice, then succeeds.
  attempt 1 failed: nope
  attempt 2 failed: nope
gave up: nope

The points that matter:

  • Three layers, because the decorator takes arguments: retry(attempts) → decorator(fn) → wrapper(*args).
  • functools.wraps keeps __name__ and __doc__, as the output confirms.
  • raise last re-raises the real exception rather than a generic one, so the caller keeps the original type and traceback.
  • Catch a specific tuple, defaulting narrowly. A retry that catches bare Exception will happily retry a TypeError caused by a bug, turning a fast failure into a slow one.

A production version would add exponential backoff with jitter (time.sleep(base * 2 ** attempt + random.uniform(0, 1))) and would not retry non-idempotent operations at all.

Exercise 4.3 — Why is this cache a memory leak? Explain the problem and give the correct alternative.

import functools

class UserService:
    @functools.cache
    def get_profile(self, user_id):
        return {'id': user_id}
Solution

The cache is stored on the function, which lives on the class — so it is shared by every instance and every call, for the lifetime of the process. Its keys are (self, user_id) tuples, which means the cache holds a strong reference to every UserService instance it has ever seen. Those instances can never be garbage collected (§1.8), no matter how short-lived they were meant to be.

It is also unbounded: one entry per distinct user_id, forever, with no eviction.

Which fix is right depends on what you meant:

import functools

# 1. Per-instance cached value, computed once, freed with the instance
class UserService:
    def __init__(self, user_id):
        self.user_id = user_id
    @functools.cached_property
    def profile(self):
        print('  fetching')
        return {'id': self.user_id}

s = UserService(1)
print(s.profile, s.profile)

# 2. A bounded cache on a plain function -- no self in the key
@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=1024)
def fetch_profile(user_id):
    return {'id': user_id}

class UserService2:
    def get_profile(self, user_id):
        return fetch_profile(user_id)

print(UserService2().get_profile(7))
print(fetch_profile.cache_info().currsize)

  fetching
{'id': 1} {'id': 1}
{'id': 7}
1

Option 1 when the value depends on the instance: cached_property stores the result in self.__dict__, so it dies with the instance and there is no shared state at all.

Option 2 when the value depends only on the arguments: move the cache to a module-level function so self never enters the key, and bound it with maxsize.

The general rule: functools.cache on a method is almost always wrong. If you genuinely need a bounded per-method cache keyed on the instance, use a weakref.WeakKeyDictionary (§1.10) so instances can still be collected.

Exercise 4.4 — Replace the isinstance chain. Rewrite this so a new type can be supported from another module without editing this function.

def to_json(value):
    if isinstance(value, str):
        return f'"{value}"'
    elif isinstance(value, bool):
        return 'true' if value else 'false'
    elif isinstance(value, int):
        return str(value)
    elif isinstance(value, list):
        return '[' + ','.join(to_json(v) for v in value) + ']'
    raise TypeError(f'cannot serialise {type(value).__name__}')
Solution

functools.singledispatch moves each branch into its own registered implementation, and registration is open — any module can add a type.

import functools
from decimal import Decimal

@functools.singledispatch
def to_json(value):
    raise TypeError(f'cannot serialise {type(value).__name__}')

@to_json.register
def _(value: str) -> str:
    return f'"{value}"'

@to_json.register
def _(value: bool) -> str:              # MUST be registered before/apart from int
    return 'true' if value else 'false'

@to_json.register
def _(value: int) -> str:
    return str(value)

@to_json.register
def _(value: list) -> str:
    return '[' + ','.join(to_json(v) for v in value) + ']'

# a "different module" extending it without touching the code above
@to_json.register
def _(value: Decimal) -> str:
    return str(value)

print(to_json(['a', 1, True, [2]]))
print(to_json(Decimal('1.5')))
try:
    to_json({1, 2})
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

["a",1,true,[2]]
1.5
TypeError: cannot serialise set

The subtle part is bool. In the original chain the bool check had to come before int or True would serialise as 1 — an ordering dependency that is easy to break. singledispatch removes it: dispatch walks the MRO and bool is more specific than int, so the right implementation wins regardless of registration order. Verify it, though — this exact case is why §4.9 shows describe(True) reaching the int handler when no bool handler exists.

The real payoff is the Decimal registration: it demonstrates a type being added from outside, which the isinstance chain structurally cannot allow without editing the function. That is the difference between a closed and an open dispatch mechanism.

SECTION 5

Iteration, Generators and Pattern Matching

You have written for x in something hundreds of times. It works on a list, a string, a dict, a file, a range. This section opens up that loop and shows what it actually asks of an object. Then it builds on the answer:

  1. How a for loop really works: the iterator protocol (§5.1) and making your own objects loopable (§5.2).
  2. Generators, which make that protocol cheap to write and cheap in memory (§5.3), chained into pipelines (§5.4), delegating (handing over to another generator) with yield from (§5.5), and receiving values (§5.6).
  3. The standard toolkit built on top: itertools (§5.7) and comprehensions (§5.8).
  4. match, the other way Python takes data apart (§5.9).

Iteration is the most-used protocol in Python, and generators are the feature that makes it cheap. Together they let you process data larger than memory, build pipelines out of small pieces, and write loops that read like a description of what you want.

5.1 The Iterator Protocol

Start with something you already know works. The same for loop runs over very different objects:

for letter in 'abc':
    print(letter, end=' ')
print()
for key in {'x': 1, 'y': 2}:
    print(key, end=' ')
print()

a b c 
x y

A string gives you its characters. A dict gives you its keys. The loop does not know what a string or a dict is. It only knows how to ask an object for its items, one at a time. That way of asking is the iterator protocol, and it has two parts.

Think of a book and a bookmark:

  • The book holds the pages. Many people can read the same book.
  • A bookmark remembers where one reader is. It only moves forward, and once it reaches the last page it is done.

In Python the book is an iterable and the bookmark is an iterator:

  • An iterable has a method __iter__ that hands out a new iterator.
  • An iterator has a method __next__ that returns the next item, and raises StopIteration when there is nothing left.

You can drive the protocol by hand. iter() calls __iter__, and next() calls __next__:

nums = [1, 2, 3]
it = iter(nums)                  # calls nums.__iter__()
print(type(it).__name__)
print(next(it), next(it), next(it))
try:
    next(it)
except StopIteration:
    print('exhausted')
print(iter(it) is it)            # an iterator is its own iterable

list_iterator
1 2 3
exhausted
True

Line by line:

  • iter(nums) gave back a list_iterator: the bookmark for this list.
  • Three next() calls moved it across the three items.
  • The fourth call raised StopIteration. That is not an error in the usual sense. It is the signal "no more items".
  • Asking an iterator for an iterator gives back the same object. That way you can pass an iterator straight to a for loop.

What for does

A for loop is exactly that sequence, written for you. Here it is spelled out as a while loop:

nums = [1, 2, 3]
it = iter(nums)
while True:
    try:
        x = next(it)
    except StopIteration:
        break
    print(x, end=' ')
print()

1 2 3

Get a bookmark, read pages until StopIteration, stop. Every for loop in Python, and every function that loops for you (sum, list, max, sorted, zip), does this.

Once, or many times

Here is the difference that causes real bugs: an iterable can be looped over repeatedly; an iterator is consumed once. A list is a book. Each loop gets a fresh bookmark. A generator (§5.3) is a bookmark, so a second pass starts at the end and sees nothing. Predict the second line before you read it:

nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(sum(nums), sum(nums))              # iterable: fine twice

gen = (n for n in [1, 2, 3])
print(sum(gen), sum(gen))                # iterator: second pass is empty

6 6
6 0

No error, no warning: just a silent 0. That is a genuine production bug. Picture a function that takes "anything iterable" and loops over it twice: once to count, once to total. Tested with a list, it is correct. Called with a generator, it quietly returns the wrong answer.

Two ways out:

  • If you must loop twice, turn the input into a list first: items = list(items).
  • Or ask for a Sequence in the type hints (§6.3), which a generator is not.

5.2 Making Your Own Iterable

Now make one of your own. The goal: a Countdown(3) object that a for loop turns into 3, 2, 1.

You need the two roles from §5.1:

  • Countdown is the book. Its __iter__ hands out a new bookmark.
  • CountdownIterator is the bookmark. It remembers where it is, and its __next__ gives the next number.

Keeping the two roles in separate classes means each loop gets its own fresh cursor, the bookmark's record of where it is:

class Countdown:
    def __init__(self, start):
        self.start = start
    def __iter__(self):
        return CountdownIterator(self.start)

class CountdownIterator:
    def __init__(self, current):
        self.current = current
    def __iter__(self):
        return self
    def __next__(self):
        if self.current <= 0:
            raise StopIteration
        self.current -= 1
        return self.current + 1

c = Countdown(3)
print(list(c), list(c))          # reusable, because __iter__ makes a new cursor

[3, 2, 1] [3, 2, 1]

Both calls to list(c) gave the full countdown, because each one asked c for a new CountdownIterator.

What would go wrong with one class? Suppose Countdown.__iter__ returned self, and Countdown kept the cursor itself. Then the object would be its own bookmark, and the second list(c) would be empty: the §5.1 bug, self-inflicted.
