mypy annotated_reveal.py

annotated_reveal.py:8: note: Revealed type is "str"
Success: no issues found in 1 source file

Plain str. Every string method is allowed, and the note costs the checker nothing.

This is the mechanism behind FastAPI's Annotated[str, Query(max_length=50)] and pydantic's constrained fields (fields with limits, such as a maximum length). It is the sanctioned (officially supported) way to carry runtime validation rules in an annotation without inventing a parallel system, and include_extras=True is how you retrieve them. Section 13 shows both libraries reading these notes for real.

6.12 The Escape Hatches

The type system will sometimes be wrong, or unable to express what you know. Five tools exist for that, in rough order of preference. Here they are together, then one at a time:

from typing import Self, Never, cast, NoReturn

class Builder:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.parts: list[str] = []
    def add(self, part: str) -> Self:        # Self: correct under subclassing
        self.parts.append(part)
        return self
    def build(self) -> str:
        return ' '.join(self.parts)

def fail(msg: str) -> NoReturn:              # never returns normally
    raise RuntimeError(msg)

raw: object = ['a', 'b']
items = cast(list[str], raw)                 # asserts; checks nothing at runtime
print(Builder().add('hello').add('world').build(), len(items))

hello world 2
  • Self (3.11) is the right return type for fluent methods (methods that return the object itself, so calls can be chained: b.add(x).add(y)) and __enter__. A subclass of Builder gets SubBuilder back, not Builder, which hard-coding the class name would get wrong.
  • NoReturn marks a function that always raises or exits. The checker then knows code after fail(...) is unreachable, which improves narrowing elsewhere.
  • Never is the empty type — the type of a value that cannot exist. It is what assert_never expects.
  • cast(T, x) is a pure assertion to the checker. It performs no runtime check whatsoever and compiles to returning x unchanged. Being wrong produces a crash later, far from the cast.
  • # type: ignore[code] silences one error on one line. Always include the bracketed error code, so it does not accidentally hide a different error that appears later.

Self: why not just write the class name?

A fluent method returns self so calls can be chained. The obvious annotation is the class's own name. Watch what it does to a subclass. Save this as builder_named.py:

class Builder:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.parts: list[str] = []
    def add(self, part: str) -> 'Builder':
        self.parts.append(part)
        return self

class HtmlBuilder(Builder):
    def bold(self, part: str) -> 'HtmlBuilder':
        return self.add(f'<b>{part}</b>')

print(HtmlBuilder().add('hi').bold('there').parts)

['hi', '<b>there</b>']

It runs fine: add really does return the HtmlBuilder it was called on. But the annotation says it returns a plain Builder, and the checker believes the annotation:

mypy builder_named.py

builder_named.py:10: error: Incompatible return value type (got "Builder", expected "HtmlBuilder")  [return-value]
builder_named.py:12: error: "Builder" has no attribute "bold"  [attr-defined]
Found 2 errors in 1 file (checked 1 source file)

Two false alarms, both caused by one wrong annotation. Self means "the type of whatever object this was called on". Replace both annotations with it and save the result as builder_self.py:

from typing import Self

class Builder:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.parts: list[str] = []
    def add(self, part: str) -> Self:
        self.parts.append(part)
        return self

class HtmlBuilder(Builder):
    def bold(self, part: str) -> Self:
        return self.add(f'<b>{part}</b>')

print(HtmlBuilder().add('hi').bold('there').parts)

['hi', '<b>there</b>']

mypy builder_self.py

Success: no issues found in 1 source file

Same runtime, no errors. When the checker is wrong because the annotation is wrong, fix the annotation; no escape hatch is needed at all.

NoReturn: a function that never comes back

A helper that always raises is common: fail('no port configured'). Without NoReturn, the checker assumes it might return, and so assumes the code after it can still see the value it was guarding against. Save this as noreturn.py:

from typing import NoReturn, reveal_type

def fail(msg: str) -> NoReturn:
    raise RuntimeError(msg)

def parse_port(text: str | None) -> int:
    if text is None:
        fail('no port configured')
    reveal_type(text)
    return int(text)

mypy noreturn.py

noreturn.py:9: note: Revealed type is "str"
Success: no issues found in 1 source file

The None case went into fail, and NoReturn told the checker it never comes back out. So after the if, text can only be a str, and int(text) is accepted. NoReturn and Never are the same empty type: NoReturn is the older name, kept for return annotations.

cast: a promise nobody checks

cast tells the checker "trust me, this is a list[str]". The danger is that nothing else checks it either:

from typing import cast

raw: object = [1, 2]
items = cast(list[str], raw)      # a lie: these are ints
print(type(items).__name__, items)
try:
    print(items[0].upper())
except AttributeError as e:
    print(f'AttributeError: {e}')

list [1, 2]
AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'upper'

mypy reports no issues for this file, because the cast told it the items are strings. The crash happens on a different line from the lie. In a real program it may be in a different file, days later. Use cast only when you know something the checker cannot, and keep it right next to the check that justifies it.

# type: ignore: always name the error

The bracketed code limits the ignore to one kind of error, so a new and different mistake on the same line still shows up. Save this as ignores.py:

def double(x: int) -> int:
    return x * 2

double('ha')            # type: ignore[arg-type]
double('ha').upper()    # type: ignore[arg-type]

mypy ignores.py

ignores.py:5: error: "int" has no attribute "upper"  [attr-defined]
ignores.py:5: note: Error code "attr-defined" not covered by "type: ignore[arg-type]" comment
Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)

Line 4 is silenced, as intended. Line 5 has a second problem, .upper() on an int, and the checker still reports it, because the ignore only covered arg-type. A bare # type: ignore would have hidden both. This is why every error message ends with its code in brackets.

In order of preference

Prefer narrowing over cast, and cast over type: ignore, and type: ignore over Any. Each step gives up more checking than the last.

Think of fire exits. You use the nearest safe one, not the first door you see:

  1. Narrowing (§6.9) checks at runtime and informs the checker. Nothing is given up.
  2. cast gives up checking for one value, at one point.
  3. # type: ignore[code] gives up one kind of error, on one line.
  4. Any gives up checking for everything that value touches, wherever it flows (§6.1).

6.13 Running a Checker for Real

Annotations are worthless unless a checker runs them in CI. Like a smoke alarm, a type checker that is not switched on protects nobody. The two mainstream options are mypy (the reference implementation, the original checker the others are measured against) and pyright (faster, used by Pylance, the Python extension for the VS Code editor). They agree on the standard and differ at the edges; pick one for CI and stay with it.

Configuration lives in pyproject.toml:

[tool.mypy]
python_version = "3.14"
strict = true
warn_unreachable = true
warn_return_any = true

# Third-party packages without type information: silence them narrowly,
# never by weakening the settings above for your own code.
[[tool.mypy.overrides]]
module = ["legacy_vendor.*"]
ignore_missing_imports = true

strict = true is a bundle of about a dozen flags. The two that catch the most real bugs are disallow_untyped_defs (an unannotated function is a hole in your coverage) and warn_return_any (an Any escaping into a typed return is exactly the leak §6.1 warned about).

Here are both, on two files from earlier in this section. In §6.1, the default settings let gradual.py's unannotated function through, and said nothing about ports.py's Any. Strict mode:

mypy --strict gradual.py ports.py

gradual.py:1: error: Function is missing a type annotation  [no-untyped-def]
gradual.py:5: error: Returning Any from function declared to return "int"  [no-any-return]
gradual.py:5: error: "int" has no attribute "anything"  [attr-defined]
ports.py:6: note: Revealed type is "Any"
ports.py:7: error: Returning Any from function declared to return "int"  [no-any-return]
Found 4 errors in 2 files (checked 2 source files)

Line by line:

  • gradual.py:1: the unannotated function is now an error in itself, no-untyped-def. That is disallow_untyped_defs at work.
  • ports.py:7: the function promised an int and returned the Any from json.loads. That is warn_return_any. It does not find the 'prot' typo by itself, but it points at the exact line where checking stopped, and the fix — validating the parsed JSON before returning it — fixes the typo too.
  • gradual.py:5 gets a no-any-return as well: once x.anything was an error, mypy treats its result as Any.

Adopting types on an existing codebase works, but only in this order:

  1. Turn the checker on with everything permissive and get to zero errors. This is the baseline that lets CI fail meaningfully.
  2. Enable disallow_untyped_defs for one module at a time, using per-module overrides (settings that apply to one module only). Annotate that module, merge (add the change to the shared code), repeat.
  3. Type the leaf modules with no internal dependencies first: modules that import none of your other modules. Types flow upward from the bottom of the import graph (the map of which module imports which); typing a caller before its callees (the functions it calls) means annotating against Any and learning nothing.
  4. Install stub packages (types-requests, pandas-stubs) rather than adding ignore_missing_imports globally. A blanket ignore turns every symbol (every name: function, class, constant) from that package into Any.

A stub package holds only type information for a library that ships none: the signatures, with ... for every body, like the overload stubs in §6.8.

Run it exactly as CI does, so results are reproducible, the same on every machine:

mypy --python-version 3.14 src/
mypy --strict src/mypackage/core.py      # tighten one module at a time

One habit is worth more than any flag: when the checker rejects something, assume it is right first. Most of the time the annotation is a bad description of what the code does, and fixing the code is the correct response. The Builder in §6.12 is the pattern: the checker's complaint pointed at a wrong annotation, and fixing it removed both errors. Reaching immediately for cast or type: ignore turns a working type system into decoration.

Exercises

Exercise 6.1 — Why is this rejected? A checker rejects the call on the last line. Explain precisely why, then give two different fixes and say when you would choose each.

def total(values: list[float]) -> float:
    return sum(values)

counts: list[int] = [1, 2, 3]
total(counts)
Solution

list is invariant, so list[int] is not a list[float] even though int is compatible with float. The reason is mutability: total is free to do values.append(1.5), which would put a float into a list the caller still believes is list[int]. The checker cannot know that this particular function does not mutate, so it refuses the whole class of call.

Fix one — widen the parameter to a covariant read-only type. This is right when the function only reads, which is the overwhelmingly common case:

from collections.abc import Sequence

def total(values: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return sum(values)

counts: list[int] = [1, 2, 3]
print(total(counts))

6

Fix two — change the variable's declared type, right when the list really is meant to hold floats:

def total(values: list[float]) -> float:
    return sum(values)

counts: list[float] = [1, 2, 3]
print(total(counts))

6

Choose the first by default: Sequence documents that the function does not mutate its argument, and it accepts tuples and other sequences for free. Choose the second only when the caller's list genuinely is a float list that was annotated too narrowly.

(Iterable[float] would also work here since sum only iterates, and is even more permissive — the general rule from §6.3 is to accept the weakest abstraction that does the job.)

Exercise 6.2 — Type a duck-typed function. This function works on anything with a read() returning str. Type it so that both classes below are accepted without either inheriting from anything, and so a class with a wrong-shaped read is rejected.

def load_config(source):
    return source.read().strip()

class FileSource:
    def read(self) -> str:
        return '  host=localhost  '

class HttpSource:
    def read(self) -> str:
        return '  host=example.com  '
Solution

This is exactly what Protocol is for — the two classes share a shape, not an ancestor.

from typing import Protocol

class Readable(Protocol):
    def read(self) -> str: ...

def load_config(source: Readable) -> str:
    return source.read().strip()

class FileSource:
    def read(self) -> str:
        return '  host=localhost  '

class HttpSource:
    def read(self) -> str:
        return '  host=example.com  '

print(load_config(FileSource()))
print(load_config(HttpSource()))

host=localhost
host=example.com

A class whose read returns bytes is rejected, because the protocol's method signature must match — structural typing checks the shape properly, not merely that a read attribute exists.

Why not an abstract base class? An ABC would require both classes to inherit from it. That is impossible for classes you do not own, which is the usual reason for reaching here: Readable also accepts a real file object and an io.StringIO without either of them knowing your protocol exists.

Note the protocol is defined in terms of what the function needs, not what the classes are. Naming it Readable rather than FileLike is deliberate — a protocol describing one capability stays small and gets reused.

Exercise 6.3 — Fix the decorator. This decorator works at runtime but destroys type information: after decoration the checker accepts charge('not a number'). Fix it so the wrapped function keeps its exact signature.

import functools
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Any

def retry(fn: Callable[..., Any]) -> Callable[..., Any]:
    @functools.wraps(fn)
    def wrapper(*args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
        try:
            return fn(*args, **kwargs)
        except ValueError:
            return fn(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper

@retry
def charge(amount: float) -> str:
    return f'charged {amount}'
Solution

Callable[..., Any] says "some callable taking anything, returning anything" — so the decorated charge is typed as accepting literally any arguments. ParamSpec captures the parameter list and a type variable captures the return type, so both survive:

import functools
from collections.abc import Callable

def retry[**P, R](fn: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R]:
    @functools.wraps(fn)
    def wrapper(*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R:
        try:
            return fn(*args, **kwargs)
        except ValueError:
            return fn(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper

@retry
def charge(amount: float) -> str:
    return f'charged {amount}'

print(charge(9.99))

charged 9.99

Now charge('nope') is an error again and charge(1).upper() is known to be valid. The three pieces that must line up: **P declares the ParamSpec, the wrapper's parameters must be exactly *args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs (the checker recognises that specific pattern and nothing else), and the return annotation Callable[P, R] reuses both variables.

functools.wraps is separate and still needed — it copies __name__, __doc__ and __wrapped__ at runtime, which the type system knows nothing about. §4 covers why omitting it breaks introspection and debugging.

Exercise 6.4 — Exhaustiveness. Rewrite this so that adding a new Shape variant becomes a type error at every place that switches on it, rather than a runtime surprise.

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Circle:
    radius: float

@dataclass
class Square:
    side: float

type Shape = Circle | Square

def area(s: Shape) -> float:
    if isinstance(s, Circle):
        return 3.14159 * s.radius ** 2
    return s.side ** 2
Solution

The return s.side ** 2 line is the problem: it is a catch-all that happens to be correct today. Add a Triangle variant and it silently computes a square's area from an attribute that does not exist, failing at runtime. assert_never makes the checker prove the switch is exhaustive:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import assert_never

@dataclass
class Circle:
    radius: float

@dataclass
class Square:
    side: float

type Shape = Circle | Square

def area(s: Shape) -> float:
    match s:
        case Circle():
            return 3.14159 * s.radius ** 2
        case Square():
            return s.side ** 2
        case _:
            assert_never(s)

print(area(Circle(1)), area(Square(2)))

3.14159 4

Note the 4 rather than 4.0, which is §6.2 demonstrating itself: Square(2) was annotated side: float but was given an int, and nothing at runtime converted or complained. 2 ** 2 is an int. The annotation described an intention the interpreter never enforced — a checker would flag the call, but the running program simply does integer arithmetic.

In the final case the checker has eliminated both variants, so s narrows to Never and assert_never(s) type-checks. Introduce Triangle into the union and that narrowing fails: the checker reports Argument 1 to "assert_never" has incompatible type "Triangle"; expected "Never", pointing directly at every switch that needs a new branch.

At runtime assert_never raises AssertionError if it is ever somehow reached, so the guarantee degrades safely rather than falling through and returning None.

This pattern is the main practical reason to model closed sets of variants as a union of dataclasses rather than as a class hierarchy with an overridden method — you get compiler-enforced exhaustiveness at every call site, not just in the one place the base class defined.

SECTION 7

Errors, Exceptions and Logging

Start with a line of code that cannot work:

try:
    int('abc')
except ValueError as exc:
    print('caught:', exc)
print('the program carries on')

caught: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
the program carries on

int('abc') has no sensible answer. So instead of returning a wrong number, Python raises an exception: an object that says "something I assumed was not true". The except clause caught it, and the program carried on.

That is the whole mechanism. Using it well is a matter of judgement, and this section is about that judgement:

  1. Which exceptions exist, and which ones you must never catch (§7.1).
  2. What to catch, and where (§7.2), and the two clauses people forget, else and finally (§7.3).
  3. How to turn a low-level failure into a meaningful one without losing the original (§7.4), and how to define your own exceptions (§7.5).
  4. Reporting several failures at once (§7.6).
  5. Reading and capturing tracebacks (§7.7).
  6. Recording what happened, with logging (§7.8), and stopping inside a running program, with pdb (§7.9).

The goal behind all of it: when something fails at three in the morning, the person on call (the engineer whose turn it is to respond when something breaks) can find out what happened without a debugger.

7.1 The Hierarchy

Exceptions come in families. Try opening a file that does not exist, but catch a broader type than the one raised:

try:
    open('/no/such/file.txt')
except OSError as exc:
    print(type(exc).__name__, 'caught by except OSError')

FileNotFoundError caught by except OSError

Python raised FileNotFoundError, yet except OSError caught it. That works because FileNotFoundError is a subclass of OSError.

Think of a supermarket's signs. "Dairy" covers milk, cheese and yoghurt. If someone asks you to fetch "anything from dairy", milk counts. An except clause works the same way: it catches the class it names and every class below it.

So the family tree matters. Every exception inherits from BaseException. The split just below it is the one that matters.

BaseException
SystemExit, KeyboardInterrupt, GeneratorExit — do not catch these
Exception — everything you might reasonably handle
ValueError · TypeError · KeyError · OSError · RuntimeError · …

Two branches:

  • Exception holds the failures a program might reasonably handle: a bad value, a missing key, a file that is not there.
  • The three classes beside it are not really failures. They are instructions:
  • KeyboardInterrupt means the user pressed Ctrl-C.
  • SystemExit means the code called sys.exit().
  • GeneratorExit is how Python tells a generator (§5.3) to shut down.

Picture the big red emergency-stop button on a factory machine. A worker who catches every problem on the line should still never catch the emergency stop. KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit sit outside Exception deliberately, so that except Exception: does not swallow Ctrl-C or a deliberate sys.exit().

You can check the family tree yourself:

print(issubclass(KeyboardInterrupt, Exception))
print(issubclass(KeyboardInterrupt, BaseException))
print(issubclass(FileNotFoundError, OSError), issubclass(OSError, Exception))
print([c.__name__ for c in FileNotFoundError.__mro__[:4]])

False
True
True True
['FileNotFoundError', 'OSError', 'Exception', 'BaseException']

Line by line:

  • KeyboardInterrupt is not an Exception. That is the emergency stop staying out of reach.
  • It is a BaseException. Everything is.
  • FileNotFoundError is an OSError, and OSError is an Exception. That chain is why the first example worked.
  • The __mro__ (method resolution order, §3.5) lists the whole line of ancestors, from the specific class up to the root.

The bare except:

This is where the hierarchy turns into a rule. Never write a bare except:. It catches BaseException, which means Ctrl-C stops working and your program becomes unkillable in a loop. If you truly need a catch-all, write except Exception: and re-raise.

7.2 Catching Well

You know how to catch. The harder question is what to catch. A receptionist is a good model. They handle appointment requests themselves. A complaint they cannot resolve goes to the manager, unchanged. A good receptionist never answers every question with "the doctor is busy", because then nobody learns what was actually wrong.

The guiding principle is: catch the narrowest exception you can actually handle, at the level where you can do something about it.

Here is that principle in a small function that reads a network port number from text:

def parse_port(raw):
    try:
        port = int(raw)
    except ValueError:
        return None                    # a specific, expected failure
    return port if 0 < port < 65536 else None

print(parse_port('8080'), parse_port('nope'), parse_port('99999'))

8080 None None

What makes it good:

  • It catches ValueError only. That is the one failure int() produces for bad text, and the function knows what to do about it: return None.
  • Only the line that can fail is inside try.
  • The range check is ordinary code. A number out of range is not an exception, so it does not need one.

Several types at once

Sometimes two different exceptions mean the same thing to you. A timeout and a refused connection are both "the network let us down". Put them in one clause as a tuple:

def fetch(source):
    try:
        return source()
    except (TimeoutError, ConnectionRefusedError) as exc:
        return f'network problem: {type(exc).__name__}'

def boom():
    raise ConnectionRefusedError('refused')

print(fetch(boom))

network problem: ConnectionRefusedError

as exc gives you the exception object, so the message can still say which of the two happened.

Python 3.14 (PEP 758) allows omitting the brackets when there is no as clause — except TimeoutError, ConnectionRefusedError:. Keep the brackets when you bind with as, and prefer them generally: the parenthesised form works on every version you are likely to support.

Two anti-patterns

Now the receptionist who gets it wrong. Here are two handlers you should learn to recognise on sight. Read the last line of the code and predict the output before you look:

def bad_silent(fn):
    try:
        return fn()
    except Exception:
        pass                  # the bug is now invisible; debugging starts from zero

def bad_broad(fn):
    try:
        return fn()
    except Exception:
        return 'network error'    # was it? or a typo in your own code?

def typo():
    return {}['missing']          # a KeyError, nothing to do with the network

print(bad_silent(typo), '|', bad_broad(typo))

None | network error

What went wrong in each:

  • bad_silent swallowed the error and returned None. Removing the battery from a smoke alarm stops the noise. It does not put out the fire.
  • bad_broad is worse. A KeyError caused by a bug in your own code was reported as a network error. That is worse than crashing, because it sends whoever is debugging in the wrong direction.

The fix for both is the principle above: name the exceptions you expect, and let everything else crash loudly.

7.3 else and finally

The full try statement has four clauses, and the two people forget are the useful ones. In order:

  • try — the code that might fail.
  • except — what to do if it did.
  • else — what to do if it did not.
  • finally — what to do no matter what.

Start with else, in the smallest useful form:

def double(raw):
    try:
        n = int(raw)
    except ValueError:
        return 'not a number'
    else:
        return n * 2

print(double('21'), double('x'))

42 not a number

n * 2 could have gone inside the try. Putting it in else says: "only int() is allowed to fail here". You will see why that matters in a moment.

Now watch all four clauses at once. This function records which clauses ran, for three different inputs:

def read(source, fail=False, boom=False):
    log = []
    try:
        log.append('try')
        if fail:
            raise ValueError('bad')
        if boom:
            raise KeyError('unhandled')
    except ValueError as exc:
        log.append(f'except {exc}')
    else:
        log.append('else — only when no exception')
    finally:
        log.append('finally — always')
    return log

print(read(None))
print(read(None, fail=True))
try:
    read(None, boom=True)
except KeyError:
    print('finally ran, then KeyError propagated')

['try', 'else — only when no exception', 'finally — always']
['try', 'except bad', 'finally — always']
finally ran, then KeyError propagated

Line by line:

  • No failure: try, then else, then finally.
  • A handled failure (ValueError): try, then except, then finally. The else was skipped.
  • An unhandled failure (KeyError, which no clause names): finally still ran, and then the exception carried on up to the caller.

The third call never returns its list — the KeyError escaped before the return — but the finally clause still ran on the way out. That is the guarantee.

Why else exists

Use else to keep the try block minimal. Only the line that can raise belongs inside try; everything that should run on success goes in else. Otherwise you risk catching an exception from code you never meant to guard.

Picture double with the multiplication moved inside the try. It works today. Then someone changes n * 2 into a call to a helper with a bug that raises ValueError. The except clause now reports that bug as "not a number", which is the §7.2 anti-pattern arriving by accident.

Why finally exists

finally is for clean-up: closing a file, releasing a lock, turning off the oven before you leave the kitchen. It happens whether dinner went well or burned.

finally runs on every path — success, handled exception, unhandled exception, even return. That last one is a trap: a return inside finally discards the exception entirely, and Python 3.14 (PEP 765) now emits a SyntaxWarning for exactly this. See it for yourself:

def swallow():
    try:
        raise ValueError('lost')
    finally:
        return 'finally won'

print(swallow())

finally won

The ValueError vanished. No traceback, no trace at all. Under Python 3.14 the run also prints this warning (on stderr, the error stream from §6.1, so it is not part of the output above):

SyntaxWarning: 'return' in a 'finally' block

The rule: clean up in finally, but never return, break or continue out of it.

In everyday code you often do not write finally at all. A with block (§2.9) runs its clean-up the same way, and it reads better.

7.4 Exception Chaining: raise ... from ...

Here is a common situation. Your configuration loader calls int() on a setting. int() raises ValueError. But the person calling your loader does not care about int(). They care that the configuration is wrong. So you catch the ValueError and raise your own, more meaningful error.

Doing that throws away the original, unless you keep it. Think of a doctor's referral letter. The specialist needs the letter ("suspected fracture"), and they also need the original X-ray stapled to it.

When you catch a low-level exception and raise a domain-level one (one that speaks the language of your program's own subject, such as "bad configuration"), keep the original. Python does this automatically — the mechanism is called exception chaining — and from lets you say what you mean by it.

class ConfigError(Exception):
    pass

def load(raw):
    try:
        return int(raw)
    except ValueError as exc:
        raise ConfigError(f'invalid port {raw!r}') from exc

try:
    load('abc')
except ConfigError as exc:
    print(type(exc).__name__, '|', exc)
    print('__cause__:  ', repr(exc.__cause__))
    print('__context__:', type(exc.__context__).__name__)

ConfigError | invalid port 'abc'
__cause__:   ValueError("invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'")
__context__: ValueError

Line by line:

  • The caller sees a ConfigError with a clear message. That is the referral letter.
  • __cause__ holds the original ValueError. That is the X-ray, stapled on by from exc.
  • __context__ also points at the ValueError. Python sets it on its own, whenever an exception is raised while another one is being handled.

Three ways to raise inside except

Three forms, three meanings:

  • raise New() from exc — sets __cause__. "This failure was caused by that one." The traceback says The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception.
  • raise New() inside an except — sets __context__ automatically. The traceback says During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred, which reads as incidental.
  • raise New() from None — suppresses the chain. Use it when the internal cause is noise that would leak implementation detail, as §1.6's Config.__getattr__ did.

Here are all three side by side. For each form, the loop prints __cause__, __context__, and a flag called __suppress_context__, which tells the traceback printer whether to hide the context:

def convert(raw, mode):
    try:
        return int(raw)
    except ValueError as exc:
        if mode == 'from':
            raise RuntimeError('bad setting') from exc
        if mode == 'plain':
            raise RuntimeError('bad setting')
        raise RuntimeError('bad setting') from None

for mode in ['from', 'plain', 'none']:
    try:
        convert('x', mode)
    except RuntimeError as exc:
        print(f'{mode:5}', type(exc.__cause__).__name__,
              type(exc.__context__).__name__, exc.__suppress_context__)

from  ValueError ValueError True
plain NoneType ValueError False
none  NoneType ValueError True

Reading the rows:

  • from exc: the cause is the ValueError. The traceback shows it as the direct cause.
  • plain raise: no cause (NoneType means None), but the context is still the ValueError. The traceback shows it as something that happened during handling.
  • from None: still no cause, and the flag is now True. The context is kept on the object, but the traceback hides it.

Always prefer from exc. Losing the original exception is the most common way a stack trace (another name for a traceback, §7.7) stops being useful.

7.5 Custom Exceptions

Python's built-in exceptions describe programming problems: a bad value, a missing key. Your program has its own problems: a card was declined, an item is out of stock. Give them their own names. Defining one takes two lines:

class OutOfStock(Exception):
    pass

try:
    raise OutOfStock('only 2 left')
except OutOfStock as exc:
    print('sorry,', exc)

sorry, only 2 left

That is all a custom exception needs: a class that inherits from Exception. The message passed in becomes its text.

A family of your own

As soon as there are several, organise them like a shop's departments. A customer can ask the whole "payments" desk for help, or go straight to the one person who handles declined cards.

Define a base class per library or subsystem (one large part of a program, such as payments), so callers can catch everything from you with one clause, and specific problems with a narrower one.

class PaymentError(Exception):
    """Base for everything this module raises."""

class CardDeclined(PaymentError):
    def __init__(self, code, message='card declined'):
        super().__init__(f'{message} ({code})')
        self.code = code                     # structured data for the handler

class InsufficientFunds(CardDeclined):
    def __init__(self, shortfall):
        super().__init__('51', 'insufficient funds')
        self.shortfall = shortfall

try:
    raise InsufficientFunds(shortfall=250)
except PaymentError as exc:                  # broad: anything from this module
    print(type(exc).__name__, '|', exc)
    print('code:', exc.code, '| shortfall:', exc.shortfall)

InsufficientFunds | insufficient funds (51)
code: 51 | shortfall: 250

Line by line:

  • The code raised the most specific class, InsufficientFunds.
  • except PaymentError caught it anyway, because of the family tree from §7.1.
  • The message came from CardDeclined.__init__, which InsufficientFunds called through super().
  • The handler read code and shortfall straight off the object.

Attach structured attributes, not just a formatted string. A handler that needs the shortfall should not have to parse it out of a message. Text is for people. Attributes are for code.

7.6 Exception Groups and except*

Everything so far handles one failure at a time. But think about a teacher marking an exam. If they stopped at the first mistake and handed the paper back, the student would fix one answer, resubmit, find the next mistake, and so on. A good teacher marks every mistake in one pass.

Some operations fail in several ways at once — a TaskGroup (§9.5) where three tasks raised, a validator collecting every problem rather than stopping at the first. ExceptionGroup (Python 3.11, PEP 654) represents that, and except* handles it.

Here is a validator that marks the whole paper:

def validate(record):
    problems = []
    if not record.get('name'):
        problems.append(ValueError('name is required'))
    if record.get('age', 0) < 0:
        problems.append(ValueError('age must be non-negative'))
    if not isinstance(record.get('email', ''), str):
        problems.append(TypeError('email must be a string'))
    if problems:
        raise ExceptionGroup('validation failed', problems)
    return record

try:
    validate({'age': -1, 'email': 42})
except* ValueError as eg:
    print('ValueErrors:', [str(e) for e in eg.exceptions])
except* TypeError as eg:
    print('TypeErrors: ', [str(e) for e in eg.exceptions])

ValueErrors: ['name is required', 'age must be non-negative']
TypeErrors:  ['email must be a string']

What happened:

  • The record had three problems, so validate raised one ExceptionGroup holding three exceptions.
  • except* ValueError received a smaller group with just the two ValueErrors.
  • except* TypeError received the one TypeError.

Both handlers ran. That is the whole difference: a normal except chain picks one clause, whereas except* clauses each take the part of the group that matches them and let the rest continue to the next clause.

Think of sorting a pile of post. Each except* clause takes the letters addressed to it from the pile. Whatever nobody takes stays in the pile.

What nobody handles

So what happens to letters nobody takes? Here a group holds three exceptions, but only two kinds are handled:

try:
    try:
        raise ExceptionGroup('mixed', [ValueError('v'), TypeError('t'), KeyError('k')])
    except* ValueError:
        print('handled the ValueError')
    except* TypeError:
        print('handled the TypeError')
except ExceptionGroup as remaining:
    print('still propagating:', remaining.message,
          [type(e).__name__ for e in remaining.exceptions])

handled the ValueError
handled the TypeError
still propagating: mixed ['KeyError']

The unhandled KeyError propagates on, still wrapped in a group — nothing is silently dropped, and the group keeps its original message. Left uncaught it prints with the tree-shaped traceback that exception groups use:

  + Exception Group Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  | ExceptionGroup: mixed (1 sub-exception)
  +-+---------------- 1 ----------------
    | KeyError: 'k'
    +------------------------------------

Choosing between them

A plain except ExceptionGroup: still works and catches the whole thing at once. Use except* when different failure types need different handling; use except Exception: when you just want to know it failed.

7.7 Tracebacks

When an exception is not caught, Python prints a traceback and stops. Many beginners read it from the top, get lost in the first few lines, and give up. The trick is the opposite direction.

Save this as app.py:

def price_with_tax(item):
    return item['price'] * 1.2

def basket_total(items):
    total = 0
    for item in items:
        total += price_with_tax(item)
    return total

print(basket_total([{'price': 10}, {'cost': 5}]))
# the second item has no 'price' key: this crashes with a KeyError

Run it:

python app.py

Python 3.14 prints this (the full path to the file is shortened to app.py):

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "app.py", line 10, in <module>
    print(basket_total([{'price': 10}, {'cost': 5}]))
          ~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "app.py", line 7, in basket_total
    total += price_with_tax(item)
             ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^
  File "app.py", line 2, in price_with_tax
    return item['price'] * 1.2
           ~~~~^^^^^^^^^
KeyError: 'price'

Each File ... entry, with the source line under it, is a frame: one function call that was still in progress when the error happened. Read it bottom up:

  1. The last line says what went wrong: a KeyError, for the key 'price'.
  2. The frame just above says where: line 2, inside price_with_tax, on item['price'].
  3. The frames above that say how you got there: the top level called basket_total on line 10, which called price_with_tax on line 7.

"Most recent call last" means exactly that. The list runs from the oldest call at the top to the newest at the bottom. Here the second item has a 'cost' key instead of 'price', so the fix is in the data, not in price_with_tax.

Fine-grained locations

Notice the ~~~~^^^^ marks under each line. Since Python 3.11 tracebacks include fine-grained error locations, underlining the exact sub-expression that failed rather than just naming the line:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "app.py", line 3, in <module>
    print(config['db']['host']['port'])
          ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^
TypeError: string indices must be integers, not 'str'

That ^^^^ marks which subscript (which [...] lookup) raised, which on a line with four of them saves real time. Here, config['db']['host'] turned out to be a string, so the last ['port'] failed.

A traceback is an object

So far the traceback was printed and the program died. But inside an except block, the traceback is data you can keep. A traceback is an object, and you can capture, format and store it rather than printing it.

import traceback

def inner():
    raise ValueError('the original problem')

def outer():
    inner()

try:
    outer()
except ValueError as exc:
    lines = traceback.format_exception(exc)
    print('frames captured:', sum(1 for l in lines if l.strip().startswith('File')))
    print('last line:', lines[-1].strip())
    print('functions:', [f.name for f in traceback.extract_tb(exc.__traceback__)])

frames captured: 3
last line: ValueError: the original problem
functions: ['<module>', 'outer', 'inner']

Line by line:

  • format_exception returns the traceback as a list of strings, exactly the text Python would have printed. It had three File lines: the top level, outer and inner.
  • Its last line is the familiar one, the type and the message.
  • extract_tb returns the same frames as objects, so you can read .name, .lineno and .filename instead of parsing text.

traceback.extract_tb gives structured frames — file, line, function, source text — which is what you want for sending errors to a monitoring system (a service that collects errors from running programs and alerts people) rather than a log file.

7.8 Logging

You have probably debugged with print. It works on your laptop. Then the program runs on a server for a month. Now you need answers to questions print cannot give: when did this happen? How serious was it? Which part of the program said it? Can I hide the chatty messages without deleting them?

print is not logging. The logging module gives you levels, per-module control, structured output and destinations you can change without touching the code that logs.

Start with the smallest working setup:

import logging, sys

logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, level=logging.INFO,
                    format='%(levelname)s %(message)s')
logging.debug('loop variable is 3')
logging.info('server started on port 8080')
logging.warning('disk 91% full')

INFO server started on port 8080
WARNING disk 91% full

Three messages went in and two came out. The debug message was filtered out, because basicConfig set the level to INFO.

Levels

Every message has a level, and every level is just a number:

import logging

for name in ['DEBUG', 'INFO', 'WARNING', 'ERROR', 'CRITICAL']:
    print(f'{name:8}', getattr(logging, name))

DEBUG    10
INFO     20
WARNING  30
ERROR    40
CRITICAL 50

A level setting is a volume knob. Set it to INFO (20), and everything at 20 or above gets through, while DEBUG (10) is muted. You turn the knob up in production and down when you are investigating, and the code that logs does not change.

What each level is for:

  • DEBUG — detail you only want while investigating.
  • INFO — normal events worth recording: started, finished, connected.
  • WARNING — something unexpected that the program survived.
  • ERROR — an operation failed.
  • CRITICAL — the program itself may not be able to continue.

With no configuration at all, the knob sits at WARNING. logging.info('hidden') prints nothing, and logging.warning('disk 91% full') prints WARNING:root:disk 91% full on stderr. That surprise is the most common "my logging does nothing" question.

Loggers have names

A bigger program needs more than one voice. Loggers are named with dots, and the dots make a hierarchy, like an organisation chart:

import logging

pay = logging.getLogger('shop.payments')
shop = logging.getLogger('shop')
print(pay.parent is shop, shop.parent.name)

True root

shop.payments reports to shop, and shop reports to the root logger at the top. A message logged on shop.payments travels up that chain to the handlers above it. That is why you can turn up the detail for shop.payments alone, or for all of shop, without touching anything else.

A complete example

Now the pieces together. A logger decides whether a message counts. A handler decides where it goes (here, standard output). A formatter decides what the line looks like:

import logging, sys

logger = logging.getLogger('shop.payments')     # module-scoped, dotted
handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter('%(levelname)-8s %(name)s: %(message)s'))
logger.addHandler(handler)
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

logger.debug('not shown — below the level')
logger.info('charging %s for %.2f', 'user-1', 9.99)   # %s, NOT an f-string
logger.warning('retrying')
try:
    1 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    logger.exception('charge failed')            # ERROR + full traceback

INFO     shop.payments: charging user-1 for 9.99
WARNING  shop.payments: retrying
ERROR    shop.payments: charge failed
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 13, in <module>
    1 / 0
    ~~^~~
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

Line by line:

  • The debug call is missing from the output: below the level.
  • The info line was built from 'charging %s for %.2f' and its two arguments.
  • logger.exception printed an ERROR line and the traceback of the exception being handled.

Pass arguments, not finished strings

Why does the info call pass %s placeholders instead of an f-string? Watch what each version costs when the message is filtered out:

import logging

class Report:
    def __str__(self):
        print('  (building the report text)')
        return 'big report'

logger = logging.getLogger('demo')
logger.setLevel(logging.WARNING)

logger.debug('value: %s', Report())
print('after the %s version')
logger.debug(f'value: {Report()}')
print('after the f-string version')

after the %s version
  (building the report text)
after the f-string version

Both debug calls were filtered out, and neither printed a log line. But the f-string version still built the text, because Python evaluates an f-string before calling the function. The %s version handed over the pieces, and logging never needed to assemble them. For a cheap message the difference is small. For a big object, or a message inside a hot loop (one that runs a very large number of times), it is not.

The rules that matter

The details that separate working logging from cargo-culted logging, copied from somewhere without understanding why it works:

  • logging.getLogger(__name__) in every module. The dotted hierarchy means you can raise the level for shop.payments alone without touching anything else.
  • Pass arguments, do not format. logger.info('charging %s', user) defers formatting until the record (Python's object for one log message) is actually emitted, that is, written out; an f-string pays the cost even when the message is filtered out, and loses the structured arguments.
  • logger.exception(...) inside an except block logs at ERROR with the traceback. It is the single most useful call in the module.
  • Libraries add a NullHandler and configure nothing. Configuration is the application's decision; a library that calls basicConfig hijacks its user's logging.

__name__ is the module's own dotted name (shop.payments for shop/payments.py), so the hierarchy follows your package layout without any extra typing.

Configure once, at startup

The example above wired a handler by hand, which is fine for learning. A real application sets everything in one place, when it starts. Configure once, at startup, with dictConfig:

import logging.config

logging.config.dictConfig({
    'version': 1,
    'disable_existing_loggers': False,
    'formatters': {'plain': {'format': '%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s'}},
    'handlers': {'console': {'class': 'logging.StreamHandler', 'formatter': 'plain'}},
    'root': {'level': 'INFO', 'handlers': ['console']},
    'loggers': {'shop.payments': {'level': 'DEBUG'}},   # noisier, just this one
})
print('configured')

configured

Reading the dictionary:

  • formatters names a line layout, plain, with the time, level, logger name and message.
  • handlers sends records to the console using that layout.
  • root sets the default: INFO and above, to the console.
  • loggers turns the knob down to DEBUG for shop.payments only. Its records still travel up to the root's console handler.
  • 'disable_existing_loggers': False keeps loggers that modules created before this call working. The default, True, silences them, which is a classic surprise.

For services, log JSON rather than prose so the lines are queryable (a log search tool can filter them by field), and attach request context (details such as which web request a line belongs to) automatically with contextvars (§9.12) rather than passing an ID through every signature.

7.9 pdb

Logging tells you what happened after the fact. Sometimes you want to stop the program at the moment it goes wrong, and look around. A debugger is a pause button for a running program. While it is paused, you can look at every variable, then step forward one line at a time.

The debugger is in the standard library and is usually faster than adding print statements.

def buggy(items):
    total = 0
    for item in items:
        # breakpoint()          # <- uncomment to stop here
        total += item
    return total

print(buggy([1, 2, 3]))

6

Uncomment the breakpoint() line and run the file again. The program stops at that line, and you get a (Pdb) prompt. Type p total to print total, n to run the next line, c to carry on to the next stop.

breakpoint() (3.7) is the entry point — it honours the PYTHONBREAKPOINT environment variable (a named setting the shell passes to every program it starts), so PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 disables every breakpoint in the codebase without editing files, and PYTHONBREAKPOINT=ipdb.set_trace swaps in a different debugger.

The commands worth memorising:

Command Does
n / s next line / step into a call
c continue to the next breakpoint
r run until the current function returns
l / ll list source around here / the whole function
p expr / pp expr print / pretty-print an expression
w where — the stack (the chain of calls in progress)
u / d move up / down a stack frame
b file:line set a breakpoint
interact drop into a full REPL in this frame

You do not need all of them on day one. p, n, c and q (quit) are enough to start.

Two workflows

Two workflows that are worth more than the command list:

python -m pdb -c continue script.py    # run until it crashes, then inspect
python -m pdb -p 12345                 # 3.14: attach to a RUNNING process

The first is post-mortem debugging: the program runs normally and you land in the debugger at the point of the unhandled exception, with the whole stack live. import pdb; pdb.post_mortem() does the same inside an except block.

Here it is on a real crash. Save this as buggy.py:

def average(nums):
    total = 0
    for n in nums:
        total += n
    return total / len(nums)

print(average([4, 8]))
print(average([]))
# an empty list: this crashes with a ZeroDivisionError

Run it under the debugger, then type p total and p nums at the prompt:

python -m pdb -c continue buggy.py

Python 3.14 prints this (the traceback is cut to its last lines, and the paths to buggy.py are shortened):

6.0
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File "buggy.py", line 5, in average
    return total / len(nums)
           ~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
Uncaught exception. Entering post mortem debugging
Running 'cont' or 'step' will restart the program
> buggy.py(5)average()
-> return total / len(nums)
(Pdb) p total
0
(Pdb) p nums
[]

Line by line:

  • The first call worked and printed 6.0.
  • The second call crashed, and instead of exiting, Python stopped inside average, on the failing line.
  • p nums shows the cause at once: the list was empty, so len(nums) was 0.

No print statements were added and nothing was re-run. You looked at the scene of the crash while it was still there.

Attaching to a running program

The second is new in Python 3.14 (PEP 768): a safe, zero-overhead interface (it costs nothing while unused) for attaching to a process that is already running, without restarting it or having prepared it in advance. For a wedged production service (stuck, but still running) this is a substantial improvement over guessing from logs. The related python -m asyncio ps <PID> (§9.11) does the equivalent for asyncio tasks.

12345 stands for the process ID, which tools such as ps or top show you.

Exercises

Exercise 7.1 — Diagnose the handler. This code hides bugs. Identify every problem and rewrite it.

def load_user(user_id):
    try:
        data = fetch_from_db(user_id)
        profile = data['profile']
        return parse_profile(profile)
    except:
        return None
Solution

Four distinct problems.

  1. Bare except: catches BaseException — including KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit. Ctrl-C during this function does nothing, and in a retry loop the process becomes unkillable.
  2. It returns None on failure, so the caller cannot distinguish "no such user" from "the database is down" from "there is a typo in parse_profile".
  3. The try block is too wide. Three operations are guarded, so a KeyError from a bug inside parse_profile is indistinguishable from the missing 'profile' key.
  4. Nothing is logged, so the failure leaves no trace at all.
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

class UserNotFound(Exception):
    pass

def fetch_from_db(user_id):
    return {'profile': {'name': 'ada'}} if user_id == 1 else {}

def parse_profile(profile):
    return profile['name'].upper()

def load_user(user_id):
    try:
        data = fetch_from_db(user_id)
    except (TimeoutError, ConnectionError) as exc:
        logger.exception('database unreachable for user %s', user_id)
        raise                                    # infrastructure: caller decides
    try:
        profile = data['profile']
    except KeyError as exc:
        raise UserNotFound(f'no profile for user {user_id}') from exc
    return parse_profile(profile)                # bugs here propagate, as they should

print(load_user(1))
try:
    load_user(2)
except UserNotFound as exc:
    print(type(exc).__name__, '|', exc, '| caused by', type(exc.__cause__).__name__)

ADA
UserNotFound | no profile for user 2 | caused by KeyError

The principles applied: each try guards exactly one thing that can fail; the expected failure becomes a domain exception with from exc preserving the cause; infrastructure failures are logged and re-raised rather than converted; and parse_profile is left outside any handler so its bugs crash loudly instead of masquerading as a missing user.

Exercise 7.2 — Collect every error, not the first. Rewrite this so a caller learns about all the invalid rows in one pass, with the row number attached.

def import_rows(rows):
    out = []
    for row in rows:
        out.append(int(row['qty']))
    return out
Solution

An ExceptionGroup reports every failure at once, which is what a bulk import needs — telling a user about one bad row at a time turns a ten-second fix into ten round trips.

class RowError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, index, message):
        super().__init__(f'row {index}: {message}')
        self.index = index

def import_rows(rows):
    out, problems = [], []
    for i, row in enumerate(rows):
        try:
            out.append(int(row['qty']))
        except (KeyError, ValueError, TypeError) as exc:
            problems.append(RowError(i, str(exc)))
    if problems:
        raise ExceptionGroup(f'{len(problems)} of {len(rows)} rows failed', problems)
    return out

rows = [{'qty': '3'}, {'qty': 'abc'}, {}, {'qty': '7'}, {'qty': None}]
try:
    import_rows(rows)
except* RowError as eg:
    for exc in eg.exceptions:
        print(exc)

print(import_rows([{'qty': '3'}, {'qty': '7'}]))

row 1: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
row 2: 'qty'
row 4: int() argument must be a string, a bytes-like object or a real number, not 'NoneType'
[3, 7]

Three failures reported together, each carrying its row index as a structured attribute rather than only inside the message.

Two design notes. The group is raised only if there were problems, so the success path is unchanged and still returns a plain list. And catching (KeyError, ValueError, TypeError) is deliberately specific — a bare except Exception here would also swallow a bug in your own code and report it as a bad row, which is exactly the §7.2 anti-pattern.

If you want to keep the good rows and report the bad ones, return both rather than raising — an exception is for when the caller cannot proceed.

Exercise 7.3 — Fix the logging. Three things here are wrong or wasteful. Find them.

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)

def charge(user, amount):
    logging.info(f'charging {user} {amount}')
    try:
        result = 1 / 0
    except Exception as e:
        logging.error('failed: ' + str(e))
        raise
Solution

1. The root logger is used directly. logging.info(...) logs to the root logger, so every message from every module lands in one undifferentiated stream with no way to change the level for this module alone. Use logging.getLogger(__name__).

2. An f-string builds the message unconditionally. f'charging {user} {amount}' is formatted even when the level filters it out. Passing %s arguments defers that work and keeps the arguments available as structured fields.

3. logging.error('failed: ' + str(e)) throws away the traceback. Inside an except block, logger.exception(...) logs at ERROR and attaches the full traceback — without it you get a one-line message and no idea where it came from.

A fourth, more subtle: calling basicConfig at import time is fine in a script but wrong in a library, where it hijacks the application's logging configuration.

import logging, sys

logger = logging.getLogger('shop.payments')
handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter('%(levelname)-8s %(name)s: %(message)s'))
logger.addHandler(handler)
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

def charge(user, amount):
    logger.info('charging %s %.2f', user, amount)     # deferred formatting
    try:
        return 1 / 0
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        logger.exception('charge failed for %s', user)  # ERROR + traceback
        raise

try:
    charge('user-1', 9.99)
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print('propagated to caller')

INFO     shop.payments: charging user-1 9.99
ERROR    shop.payments: charge failed for user-1
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 12, in charge
    return 1 / 0
           ~~^~~
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
propagated to caller

Note that charge both logs and re-raises. That is correct here because the function cannot handle the failure — but be careful not to make it a habit: logging the same exception at every level of the stack produces the same traceback five times. Log where you handle, or log once at the boundary.

SECTION 8

Concurrency: Threads, Processes and the GIL

Start with a program that spends its time waiting. Each call to wait() stands in for something slow that is not your code: a web request, a database query, a file on a network drive.

import threading, time

def wait():
    time.sleep(0.1)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(3):
    wait()
print('one after another:', round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 1), 'seconds')

t0 = time.perf_counter()
threads = [threading.Thread(target=wait) for _ in range(3)]
for t in threads: t.start()
for t in threads: t.join()
print('three threads:', round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 1), 'seconds')

one after another: 0.3 seconds
three threads: 0.1 seconds

Line by line:

  • The loop runs the three waits one after another, so they add up: 0.3 seconds.
  • The second half starts three threads, one per wait. Each thread waits on its own, at the same time as the others, so the whole thing takes as long as one wait.

That is concurrency: making progress on several things in the same stretch of time. Here it made the program three times faster without changing wait() at all.

Now the catch. Python offers four different ways to do more than one thing at a time, and they are good at different jobs. Choosing the wrong one is the most expensive mistake in this area, because it produces code that is more complicated and no faster. This section explains what each mechanism actually does, so the choice stops being a guess:

  1. The four mechanisms and the one question that picks between them (§8.1).
  2. The GIL, the lock that decides what threads can and cannot speed up (§8.2).
  3. Threads (§8.3), and the bugs that come with sharing data between them (§8.4).
  4. concurrent.futures, the one API you will use most (§8.5).
  5. Processes, for real parallel computing, where work truly happens at the same moment on several processor cores (§8.6), and how processes share data (§8.7).
  6. The two newest options in Python 3.14: free-threaded Python (§8.8) and subinterpreters (§8.9).
  7. Running other programs from Python (§8.10), and how to choose in practice (§8.11).

8.1 Four Mechanisms, One Decision

Think of a restaurant kitchen. There are two very different reasons a meal can be slow:

  • The cook is waiting: the oven is on, the water has not boiled yet, the delivery has not arrived. One cook could look after many of these at once, because waiting takes no effort.
  • The cook is working: chopping, stirring, plating. One cook can only chop one onion at a time. To chop faster, you need more cooks.

Programs have the same two kinds of slowness:

  • I/O-bound work spends its time waiting for something outside the program: the network, the disk, a database. "I/O" means input and output.
  • CPU-bound work spends its time computing: arithmetic, parsing, compressing, resizing an image. The processor (the CPU) is the limit.

Python's four mechanisms are four ways of organising the kitchen:

Threads — one process, shared memory, preemptive. Overlap waiting. Limited for CPU work while the GIL exists.
Processes — separate memory, true parallelism. Real multi-core CPU work. Expensive to start, data must be pickled.
Asyncio — one thread, cooperative switching at await. Thousands of concurrent I/O waits, cheaply. Section 9.
Subinterpreters — isolated interpreters in one process, own GIL each. New in 3.14. Between threads and processes.

Three words in those boxes need a sentence each:

  • A process is a running program, with its own memory. Two processes cannot see each other's variables.
  • A thread is a line of execution inside a process. All the threads of one process share the same memory, so they see the same variables.
  • Preemptive means the system decides when to pause one thread and run another, at any moment, without asking the thread. Asyncio is the opposite, cooperative: a task runs until it says "I am waiting now" with await.

In kitchen terms: threads are several cooks in one kitchen, sharing the same counter. Processes are separate kitchens. Asyncio is one very organised cook who starts the oven, then the kettle, then the rice, and goes back to whichever one is ready. Subinterpreters are separate kitchens inside one building.

You do not need to memorise the table below yet. Every row gets its own subsection. The point is that the decision comes down to one question — is the work waiting, or computing?

Your work is Use Because
Waiting on network/disk, thousands of them asyncio cheapest possible concurrency for I/O
Waiting, but the library is blocking threads a blocking call in a thread does not block the loop (asyncio's scheduler, §9)
Computing, multi-core processes sidesteps the GIL entirely
Computing, and you control the build free-threaded Python real threads, no GIL (§8.8)
Mixed, with isolation wanted subinterpreters cheaper than processes, isolated unlike threads

Read it as two halves:

  • The first two rows are waiting work. Asyncio and threads both let one program wait on many things at once. Which one depends on the library you call: a blocking library (one whose functions do not return until the work is done, like requests or most database drivers) needs threads.
  • The last three rows are computing work. Here you need more than one CPU core actually running Python at the same moment (a core is one independent processor inside the CPU; most machines have several), and §8.2 explains why threads normally cannot do that.

8.2 The GIL

Try to speed up computing work with threads, the same way the opener sped up waiting work:

import sys, time, threading

def spin(n):
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        total += i * i
    return total

N = 2_000_000
t0 = time.perf_counter()
spin(N); spin(N)
sequential = time.perf_counter() - t0

t0 = time.perf_counter()
threads = [threading.Thread(target=spin, args=(N,)) for _ in range(2)]
for t in threads: t.start()
for t in threads: t.join()
threaded = time.perf_counter() - t0

print('GIL enabled:', sys._is_gil_enabled())
print('threads gave a real speedup:', threaded < sequential * 0.7)

GIL enabled: True
threads gave a real speedup: False

Line by line:

  • spin is pure computing: a loop doing multiplication and addition, no waiting at all.
  • The first timing runs spin twice, one call after the other.
  • The second timing runs the same two calls in two threads.
  • The last line asks whether the threads finished in less than 70% of the sequential time. They did not.

Two threads, more than one core on the machine, and no speedup whatsoever. It is often slightly worse than sequential. The opener's threads were three times faster. What is different?

One knife in the kitchen

Imagine a kitchen with a rule: there is only one knife, and only the cook holding it may chop. You can hire four cooks, but at any moment only one of them is chopping. The other three stand there waiting for the knife.

Waiting for the oven does not need the knife, though. A cook can put a tray in, hand the knife over, and let the next cook chop while the tray bakes.

That knife is the GIL. The Global Interpreter Lock is a mutex inside CPython that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. (A mutex is a lock that only one holder can have at a time. Bytecode is the list of small instructions Python compiles your code into; §8.4 shows some.)

Why would anyone design it that way? It exists because CPython's memory management — the reference counting from §1.8 — is not thread-safe (correct even when several threads use it at once), and a single coarse lock, one lock covering everything, was dramatically simpler and faster for single-threaded code than locking every object individually. Every object carries a count of how many names point at it. If two threads changed one count at the same moment, the count could end up wrong, and Python would free an object that is still in use. One big lock prevents that cheaply.

Note the name: the Global Interpreter Lock is global to an interpreter, not to a process — which is exactly the door subinterpreters (§8.9) walk through.

What the GIL means for your code

The consequences are precise, and both halves matter:

  • Two Python threads never run bytecode simultaneously. CPU-bound multithreading gives no speedup on a GIL-enabled build.
  • The GIL is released during I/O, and by C extensions (Python modules written in the C language, for speed) that opt in (NumPy, compression, hashing, most database drivers). Threads waiting on a socket, sleeping, or crunching inside NumPy do overlap.

That explains both experiments:

  • In the opener, time.sleep releases the GIL, so three threads wait at the same time. Waiting is the oven.
  • In spin, every instruction is Python bytecode, so each thread needs the GIL for its whole run. Chopping is the knife.

Why is it sometimes slower than sequential? Because the threads pay to hand the lock back and forth. A thread holding the GIL is asked to give it up at regular intervals, so the others get a turn. sys.getswitchinterval() reports how often that happens:

import sys
print(sys.getswitchinterval())

0.005

That is 0.005 seconds: 5 ms by default. Every handover costs a little, and those costs are pure overhead when only one thread can make progress anyway.

The GIL is not part of the Python language

The GIL is a CPython implementation detail, not a language rule. CPython is the standard Python, the one you download from python.org. Jython and IronPython (Python interpreters that run on the Java platform and on .NET) never had one, and as of Python 3.13 CPython itself can be built without it (§8.8).

So for the rest of this section, keep the two cases apart:

  • Waiting work: threads help, GIL or not.
  • Computing work: threads do not help while the GIL exists. You need processes (§8.6), a free-threaded build (§8.8) or subinterpreters (§8.9).

8.3 Threads

The previous subsection could make threads sound useless. They are not. Threads are still the correct tool whenever the work is waiting and the library is blocking.

Starting and joining a thread

First the mechanics, on the smallest possible example:

import threading

def greet(name):
    print('hello,', name, 'from', threading.current_thread().name)

t = threading.Thread(target=greet, args=('Ada',))
t.start()
t.join()
print('back in', threading.current_thread().name)

hello, Ada from Thread-1 (greet)
back in MainThread

Line by line:

  • threading.Thread(target=greet, args=('Ada',)) describes a thread: which function to run, and with which arguments. Nothing runs yet. Note the comma in ('Ada',): args must be a tuple, and ('Ada') is just a string in brackets.
  • t.start() starts it. From this point greet runs on its own, alongside the main program.
  • t.join() means "wait here until that thread has finished". Without it, the main program would carry straight on.
  • Every program starts with one thread, called MainThread. The new one is named Thread-1 (greet): a number, plus the function it runs.

Think of starting the washing machine, the dishwasher and the oven before you leave the kitchen. start() presses each button. join() is waiting by the door until all three have beeped.

Threads for waiting work

Now a realistic shape: five downloads, each one a blocking call.

import threading, time

def download(name, delay, out):
    time.sleep(delay)                  # stands in for a blocking network call
    out.append(name)

results = []
t0 = time.perf_counter()
threads = [threading.Thread(target=download, args=(f'file{i}', 0.1, results))
           for i in range(5)]
for t in threads: t.start()
for t in threads: t.join()
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0

print(sorted(results))
print('five 0.1s waits overlapped:', elapsed < 0.3)

['file0', 'file1', 'file2', 'file3', 'file4']
five 0.1s waits overlapped: True

Line by line:

  • Each thread sleeps for 0.1 seconds, then appends its file name to the shared results list.
  • The first loop starts all five. The second loop waits for all five.
  • sorted(results) is printed, not results, because the threads can finish in any order. Sorting makes the output the same on every run.
  • The timing check passes: five 0.1-second waits finish in about 0.1 seconds, because time.sleep releases the GIL.

This is exactly the case where threads earn their keep — and exactly what asyncio.to_thread does under the hood in §9.10. Start and join every thread like this, two loops, and do not start a thread inside the loop that joins them: that would wait for each one before starting the next, which is the sequential version again.

Daemon threads

Sometimes you want a background thread that should not keep the program alive, such as one that refreshes a cache every minute. Python has a flag for that.

Daemon threads die when the main thread exits, without running finally blocks. You create one with threading.Thread(target=f, daemon=True). The word comes from old Unix vocabulary for a background helper.

Picture the cleaner who leaves the building the moment the last manager locks up, mid-mop, bucket still on the floor. That is fine for mopping. It is not fine for someone halfway through writing the accounts.

Use them only for work that is safe to abandon; anything holding a resource should be a normal thread you join(). "Holding a resource" means an open file, a database transaction, a half-written message: anything that a finally block (§7.3) would have tidied up.

8.4 Race Conditions

Threads share memory. That is what makes them convenient: the five downloads above all appended to one list. It is also what makes them dangerous.

Picture two booking clerks at a theatre, each on the phone with a customer. Both look at the seating chart, both see that seat 14 is free, and both say "it is yours". Two people now hold a ticket for one seat. Neither clerk did anything wrong on their own. The problem is when they looked.

That is a race condition: a bug whose result depends on the timing of two threads, as if they were racing each other. Shared mutable state plus preemptive scheduling (the system deciding which thread runs when) equals a race.

Why counter += 1 is not one step

The textbook demonstration is counter += 1, which is not one operation. It looks like one line, but Python compiles it into several bytecode instructions. The dis module ("disassemble") shows them:

import dis

def increment():
    global counter
    counter += 1

print([i.opname for i in dis.get_instructions(increment)])

['RESUME', 'LOAD_GLOBAL', 'LOAD_SMALL_INT', 'BINARY_OP', 'STORE_GLOBAL', 'LOAD_CONST', 'RETURN_VALUE']

(Run dis.dis(increment) instead for the full human-readable listing with line numbers and arguments; the list of opcode names (each one the name of a single bytecode instruction) is used here because it is what the statement compiles to, without the formatting noise.)

Four bytecodes do the work:

  1. LOAD_GLOBAL reads the current value of counter.
  2. LOAD_SMALL_INT loads the number 1.
  3. BINARY_OP adds them.
  4. STORE_GLOBAL writes the result back into counter.

The other three (RESUME, LOAD_CONST, RETURN_VALUE) are the function starting and returning None.

Load, load, add, store. If a thread is suspended between the BINARY_OP and the STORE_GLOBAL, another thread's update is overwritten and silently lost. Step by step, starting from counter = 5:

  • Thread A reads 5 and computes 6. Then it is paused.
  • Thread B reads 5 (A has not stored yet), computes 6, stores 6.
  • Thread A wakes up and stores its 6.

Two increments ran, and the counter went up by one.

Why you might never see it

Now for the part most tutorials get wrong. Run four threads incrementing that counter a million times each on CPython 3.14 and you will very likely get the right answer, even with sys.setswitchinterval(1e-6).

The reason is that CPython does not check whether to switch threads between every pair of bytecodes — it checks at specific points, chiefly backward jumps and calls. A backward jump is the end of a loop iteration, going back to the top. There is no such point inside that four-instruction sequence, so in practice it usually completes without interruption.

This makes the bug more dangerous, not less. The race is real, it is not guaranteed to be prevented, and it depends on details that change between releases — a free-threaded build (§8.8) has no GIL to serialise anything (here the word means forcing things to happen one at a time, not §2.11's turning objects into bytes), and other implementations differ. Code that is correct only because of an interpreter's instruction scheduling is not correct.

It is like crossing a road without looking because there has never been a car at that hour. The habit works every day, right up to the day it does not.

Making the race happen on purpose

To see a race reliably you need a real switch point between the check and the act, which is what any function call, any I/O, or any await gives you. A Barrier makes it deterministic. A barrier is a meeting point: each thread that calls barrier.wait() stops there until all four have arrived, and then all four continue together.

Here are four clerks, each trying to sell the last 100 tickets:

import threading

stock = 100
barrier = threading.Barrier(4)

def sell(n):
    global stock
    can_sell = stock >= n          # CHECK
    barrier.wait()                 # every thread checks before any of them acts
    if can_sell:
        stock -= n                 # ACT

threads = [threading.Thread(target=sell, args=(100,)) for _ in range(4)]
for t in threads: t.start()
for t in threads: t.join()

print('stock:', stock)
print('all four sold the same 100 units:', stock == -300)

stock: -300
all four sold the same 100 units: True

Line by line:

  • Each thread first checks: is there enough stock? All four read 100, so all four get can_sell = True.
  • The barrier holds every thread until all four have checked.
  • Then each one acts on its old answer and subtracts 100. The stock ends at 100 - 400 = -300.

Four threads each sold the last 100 units, because each one checked before any of them acted. The barrier only makes the interleaving reproducible; the bug is present without it and will surface under production load.

This check-then-act shape — read a value, decide, then write based on the stale reading — is the pattern to recognise, and it is far more common in real code than a bare +=. "Stale" means out of date: by the time the thread acts, the value it read is no longer true. It is the two theatre clerks exactly.

The GIL does not protect you from any of this. It guarantees only that one thread runs bytecode at a time, never that a statement completes atomically. Atomic means "all or nothing, with nobody able to see or change it halfway".

Locks

The fix for the clerks is a rule: only the clerk holding the seating chart may check a seat and write a name on it. Everyone else waits for the chart.

Think of the key to a café toilet, chained to a big wooden spoon. Whoever has the key is inside. Everyone else waits until it is handed back. That is a lock.

import threading
lock = threading.Lock()
print(lock.locked())
with lock:
    print(lock.locked())
print(lock.locked())

False
True
False

with lock: takes the key at the start of the block and hands it back at the end, even if the block raises an exception. Inside, locked() is True; after the block it is False again. A second thread reaching with lock: while it is held simply waits.

A Lock makes the sequence atomic:

import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def increment(n):
    global counter
    for _ in range(n):
        with lock:              # always use `with`, never manual acquire/release
            counter += 1

threads = [threading.Thread(target=increment, args=(50_000,)) for _ in range(4)]
for t in threads: t.start()
for t in threads: t.join()

print(counter, counter == 200_000)

200000 True

Four threads add 50,000 each, and the total is exactly 200,000. With the lock held around counter += 1, no thread can be paused halfway through somebody else's load-add-store.

Why with and never lock.acquire() followed by lock.release()? Because if the code between them raises, release() never runs, and every other thread waits for that key forever. That is a deadlock: threads waiting for each other, none able to move.

The rest of the toolkit

The rest of the toolkit: RLock (re-entrant, for recursive acquisition by one thread), Semaphore (cap concurrency), Event (signal), Condition (wait for a predicate), and Barrier (rendezvous).
