A boundary is the one place where ordinary code hands over to async code: usually the last line of a script, or the web framework that calls your async def handlers for you. Above it, everything is sync. Below it, everything that waits is async.

9.11 The Five Classic Mistakes

Almost every asyncio bug in production is on this list. Each one has a symptom you will recognise, so learn them as a checklist to run through when something is wrong.

1. Blocking the loop. time.sleep, requests.get, a big json.loads, or any CPU-heavy loop stops every task. Symptom: latency (the time a request takes to be answered) that spikes for unrelated requests. Fix: asyncio.to_thread, or an async-native library (httpx instead of requests).

This is §9.1's time.sleep demo, in production. The tell-tale sign is that the slowness spreads: one slow page makes every page slow, because they all share one thread. An async-native library is one written with async def all the way down, so its waits are awaits rather than blocking calls.

2. Fire-and-forget tasks that vanish. The loop keeps only a weak reference to a task, so a task nobody holds can be garbage-collected mid-flight:

import asyncio

async def background():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return 'finished'

async def main():
    tasks = set()
    t = asyncio.create_task(background())
    tasks.add(t)                          # keep a strong reference
    t.add_done_callback(tasks.discard)    # release it when done
    await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
    print(t.result(), 'tracked:', len(tasks))

asyncio.run(main())

finished tracked: 0

§1 explained weak references with a balloon: holding a string keeps it from floating away, and the loop only watches the balloon, it does not hold it. If you write asyncio.create_task(background()) and throw the returned task away, nothing holds it. Line by line, the fix:

  • tasks.add(t) keeps a normal, strong reference in a set, so the task cannot be collected while it runs.
  • t.add_done_callback(tasks.discard) asks the task to call tasks.discard(t) when it finishes, so the set does not grow forever.
  • The output shows the task finished, and the set is empty again: tracked: 0.

Better still, use a TaskGroup and let it own the lifetime.

3. Swallowing CancelledError. Covered in §9.6 — catch it, clean up, re-raise.

4. Unawaited coroutines. A forgotten await is a silent no-op, an operation that does nothing. Run with PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 (or asyncio.run(main(), debug=True)) and the loop reports them, along with any callback that blocks for more than 100 ms.

Debug mode is a smoke alarm for mistakes 1 and 4. It slows the loop a little, so use it in development and tests, not in production. PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 is an environment variable: set it in the shell before running the program, and debug mode is on without changing any code.

5. Unbounded concurrency. gather over ten thousand URLs opens ten thousand sockets and gets you rate-limited or out of file descriptors. Cap it with a Semaphore, as in §9.9.

A file descriptor is the number the operating system gives a program for each open file or connection, and every process has a limit on how many it may hold at once. Being rate-limited means the server you are calling refuses requests because you sent too many too fast. Both are the car park in §9.9 without the barrier.

You can confirm that debug mode is on from inside the program:

import asyncio

async def main():
    print('debug mode:', asyncio.get_running_loop().get_debug())

asyncio.run(main(), debug=True)

debug mode: True

Python 3.14 adds genuinely useful introspection for a running process: python -m asyncio ps <PID> lists its tasks and python -m asyncio pstree <PID> shows the await tree — the fastest way to find which task is stuck without attaching a debugger.

A PID is a process ID, the number the operating system gives each running program; ps in a terminal shows it. The await tree shows which task is awaiting which: "main is waiting on handler, which is waiting on fetch". When a program hangs, the deepest entry in the tree is usually the culprit.

9.12 contextvars: State That Follows a Task

A web server handles many requests at the same time. When it writes a log line, you want to know which request the line belongs to. Passing a request_id argument through every function just for logging is tedious and easy to forget.

Thread-local storage does not work in asyncio, because thousands of tasks share one thread. contextvars is the correct mechanism: each task gets its own copy of the variable, inherited at creation.

(Thread-local storage is a variable that has a separate value in each thread. It solved this problem for threaded servers, where each request had its own thread. In asyncio, all requests share one thread, so they would all share one value.)

Think of the name badges at a conference. Everybody walks around the same building, but each person carries their own badge, and anyone they talk to can read it. A context variable is a badge each task carries:

import asyncio, contextvars

request_id = contextvars.ContextVar('request_id', default='-')

async def handler(rid):
    request_id.set(rid)                 # local to THIS task
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return log('handled')

def log(msg):                           # ordinary sync function, no plumbing
    return f'[{request_id.get()}] {msg}'

async def main():
    print(await asyncio.gather(handler('req-1'), handler('req-2')))
    print(log('outside'))               # unchanged in the parent context

asyncio.run(main())

['[req-1] handled', '[req-2] handled']
[-] outside

Line by line:

  • ContextVar('request_id', default='-') creates the variable once, at module level. The name is used in error messages; the default is what get() returns when nothing was set.
  • Each handler runs as its own task, and sets the variable to its own request ID.
  • Both then pause at the await, so the two tasks are interleaved — and yet each one's log call read its own value.
  • Back in main, log('outside') sees the default -, untouched by either task.

Two tasks set the same variable to different values and neither saw the other's, while log — a plain synchronous function that takes no arguments about requests — read the right one in each. This is how structured logging attaches a request ID to every line without threading it through every signature (passing it along as an argument to every function), and it is what logging, OpenTelemetry and most tracing libraries use internally. (Tracing records the path one request takes through a system; OpenTelemetry is the most widely used tool for it.)

The parent's value was never touched, which is the key rule: a task copies the context at creation, so writes do not propagate back up.

In badge terms: each task is handed a photocopy of its parent's badges when it is created. Writing on your photocopy does not change the original. That is exactly the behaviour you want for a request: whatever a handler sets is visible to everything it calls, and disappears when it is done.

Exercises

Exercise 9.1 — Why is this not concurrent? This is supposed to fetch three URLs at once and takes three times as long as expected. Explain precisely why, and fix it two different ways.

import asyncio

async def fetch(url):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    return f'{url}: ok'

async def main():
    results = []
    for url in ['a', 'b', 'c']:
        results.append(await fetch(url))
    return results
Solution

await means "run this and wait for it", not "start this". The loop awaits fetch('a') to completion before it even creates the coroutine for 'b'. Nothing overlaps, so the total is 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1.

Awaiting is not what makes things concurrent — scheduling them as tasks is. Fix one, gather:

import asyncio, time

async def fetch(url):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    return f'{url}: ok'

async def main():
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(u) for u in ['a', 'b', 'c']))
    print(results, f'{time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f}s')

asyncio.run(main())

['a: ok', 'b: ok', 'c: ok'] 0.1s

Fix two, a TaskGroup — preferable in new code because a failure cancels the siblings instead of leaving them running:

import asyncio, time

async def fetch(url):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    return f'{url}: ok'

async def main():
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tasks = [tg.create_task(fetch(u)) for u in ['a', 'b', 'c']]
    print([t.result() for t in tasks], f'{time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f}s')

asyncio.run(main())

['a: ok', 'b: ok', 'c: ok'] 0.1s

Both take 0.1s instead of 0.3s. The general diagnostic: an await inside a for loop is sequential by definition. If you meant concurrency, the loop should build tasks and the await should happen once, afterwards.

Exercise 9.2 — Find the blocking call. This handler makes the whole server unresponsive under load even though it is written with async def. Identify every problem and rewrite it.

import asyncio, time

async def handle(request_id):
    time.sleep(0.05)                      # simulate a slow library call
    total = sum(i * i for i in range(200_000))
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return f'{request_id}: {total}'
Solution

There are two blocking operations, and async def protects against neither.

time.sleep(0.05) is synchronous: it blocks the entire thread, so every other task in the process is frozen for 50 ms. The sum(...) is CPU-bound, which is worse in a sense — there is no await point anywhere inside it, so the loop cannot switch away even in principle.

Push both off the loop with asyncio.to_thread:

import asyncio, time

def slow_library_call():
    time.sleep(0.05)                       # I/O-ish: releases the GIL
    return sum(i * i for i in range(200_000))   # CPU: holds the GIL

async def handle(request_id):
    total = await asyncio.to_thread(slow_library_call)
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return f'{request_id}: {total}'

async def main():
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(handle(i) for i in range(4)))
    threaded = time.perf_counter() - t0

    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(4):
        slow_library_call()
    sequential = time.perf_counter() - t0

    print(results[0])
    print('handled:', len(results), '| threaded beat sequential:', threaded < sequential)

asyncio.run(main())

0: 2666646666700000
handled: 4 | threaded beat sequential: True

The loop is now free while the threads wait, and the four handlers overlap instead of queueing.

But measure the size of the win, because it is not 4×. On the machine this was written on the threaded version takes about 0.19s against 0.29s sequential — better, and nowhere near the ~0.06s you would get from perfect overlap. The reason is visible in the two comments: time.sleep releases the GIL, so those waits genuinely overlap, while the sum holds it, so that ~0.10s of CPU work is serialised no matter how many threads you use. Section 8 covers this properly; the short version is that threads overlap waiting, not computing.

That gives the decision rule. If the blocking call is mostly I/O, to_thread is the right fix. If the CPU portion dominates, use loop.run_in_executor with a ProcessPoolExecutor instead, or run on a free-threaded build. And the best fix for a "slow library call" is usually to stop needing the thread at all — httpx rather than requests.

Exercise 9.3 — Bound the concurrency. Rewrite this so at most 5 requests are ever in flight, while still processing all 50 and returning results in the original order.

import asyncio

async def fetch(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return n * 2

async def main():
    return await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(i) for i in range(50)))
Solution

gather starts all 50 immediately. A Semaphore caps how many get past the gate at once, and because gather still preserves argument order, the results stay ordered:

import asyncio

async def fetch(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return n * 2

async def bounded(sem, n, active, peak):
    async with sem:
        active[0] += 1
        peak[0] = max(peak[0], active[0])
        try:
            return await fetch(n)
        finally:
            active[0] -= 1

async def main():
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(5)
    active, peak = [0], [0]
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(bounded(sem, i, active, peak) for i in range(50)))
    print(results[:5], '...', results[-1])
    print('count:', len(results), 'peak in flight:', peak[0])

asyncio.run(main())

[0, 2, 4, 6, 8] ... 98
count: 50 peak in flight: 5

The try/finally matters: without it, a failing fetch would leave the counter wrong. The semaphore itself is released correctly regardless, because async with guarantees it.

Note the semaphore wraps the await, not the task creation — all 50 coroutines are still scheduled, they simply queue at the gate. That is fine for 50. For 50,000 you would want a worker-pool shape instead: a fixed number of tasks pulling from an asyncio.Queue, so you never materialise 50,000 coroutine objects at once.

Exercise 9.4 — Cancellation done right. This worker holds a resource and is cancelled during shutdown, but the resource is never released and shutdown hangs. Find both bugs.

import asyncio

async def worker(resource):
    try:
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
            resource['ticks'] += 1
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print('cancelled, cleaning up')
        await asyncio.sleep(5)          # "flush buffers"
        resource['open'] = False
Solution

Two bugs, and the second is the one that hangs shutdown.

Bug 1: CancelledError is never re-raised. Swallowing it makes the task complete normally, so the canceller sees a task that ignored its cancellation. In a TaskGroup this can block the group from ever exiting.

Bug 2: slow cleanup inside the cancellation handler. The task is being torn down; awaiting 5 seconds there delays the whole shutdown, and the cleanup will itself be cancelled if the canceller has a deadline — leaving resource['open'] set to True after all.

import asyncio

async def worker(resource):
    try:
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
            resource['ticks'] += 1
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print('cancelled, cleaning up')
        raise                             # bug 1: propagate
    finally:
        resource['open'] = False          # bug 2: fast, and always runs

async def main():
    resource = {'ticks': 0, 'open': True}
    task = asyncio.create_task(worker(resource))
    await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
    task.cancel()
    try:
        await task
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        pass
    print('open:', resource['open'], 'cancelled:', task.cancelled(),
          'ticked:', resource['ticks'] > 0)

asyncio.run(main())

cancelled, cleaning up
open: False cancelled: True ticked: True

Putting the release in finally is the real fix: it runs on cancellation, on error, and on normal exit, and it does not depend on catching anything. The except clause now does nothing but log and re-raise, which is exactly what a cancellation handler should do.

If cleanup genuinely must perform I/O — closing a network connection politely — wrap only that part in asyncio.shield() and give it a short asyncio.timeout(), so a slow peer cannot hold your shutdown open forever.

SECTION 10

Performance and Profiling

Start with a small program that does two jobs. One job looks expensive: square roots and sines. The other looks harmless: it removes repeated numbers from a list. Before you read the output, guess which one is slow.

import cProfile, pstats, math

def fancy_maths(numbers):          # looks expensive
    return [math.sqrt(x) * math.sin(x) for x in numbers]

def remove_repeats(numbers):       # looks harmless
    seen = []
    for x in numbers:
        if x not in seen:
            seen.append(x)
    return seen

def report(numbers):
    fancy_maths(numbers)
    remove_repeats(numbers)

numbers = [i % 2000 for i in range(10_000)]
profiler = cProfile.Profile()
profiler.runcall(report, numbers)

stats = pstats.Stats(profiler).stats
mine = {name: total for (_, _, name), (_, _, total, _, _) in stats.items()
        if name in ('fancy_maths', 'remove_repeats')}
print('slowest:', max(mine, key=mine.get))

slowest: remove_repeats

Line by line:

  • cProfile.Profile() is a profiler: a tool that watches a program run and writes down how long every function took. §10.3 explains it properly.
  • profiler.runcall(report, numbers) runs report(numbers) with the profiler watching.
  • The last three lines dig the two functions out of the profiler's notes and print the one that took longer.

The harmless-looking function lost. fancy_maths does 10,000 calculations, and each one is a single fast call into C. remove_repeats does x not in seen 10,000 times, and every one of those checks walks along the seen list from the start, which grows to 2,000 numbers. That is millions of comparisons hiding inside one innocent not in.

That is the whole section in miniature. Python is slower than C and that is usually irrelevant. What matters is whether your program is fast enough, and when it is not, which specific part is responsible. This section is about answering that question with measurements rather than intuition, and about the small number of changes that reliably pay off:

  1. Why you measure before you change anything, and how much any one fix can give back (§10.1).
  2. Timing a small piece of code properly with timeit (§10.2).
  3. Finding the slow function in a whole program with cProfile (§10.3).
  4. Finding where the memory goes with tracemalloc (§10.4).
  5. Why the right data structure beats every clever trick (§10.5).
  6. The short list of changes that reliably pay (§10.6).
  7. What to do when Python itself is the limit (§10.7).

10.1 Measure First, and Measure the Right Thing

Think of a car that has started making a strange noise. A good mechanic does not replace the engine, the brakes and the exhaust one after another to see which fixes it. They listen, test, find the one broken part, and replace that.

Slow code is the same. The rule that saves the most wasted effort: you cannot guess where the time goes. The opening example showed it in twenty lines. Experienced developers are wrong about this routinely, because the bottleneck is usually somewhere boring:

  • a database query inside a loop,
  • a file opened again for every row,
  • a regular expression (a pattern for searching text, such as "three digits, then a dash") compiled again a million times.

A bottleneck is the one part of the program that the rest is waiting on, like the narrow neck of a bottle that decides how fast everything pours. Speeding up anything else changes nothing you can feel.

So the work always goes in the same four steps:

1. Establish it is too slow against a real requirement, not a feeling.
2. Profile to find where the time goes — cProfile for CPU, tracemalloc for memory.
3. Fix the biggest item, usually by changing an algorithm or a data structure.
4. Measure again. If it did not move the number, revert it — you have added complexity for nothing.

Read the four steps as questions:

  • Step 1: is there a problem at all? "The page must load in under 200 ms" is a requirement. "It feels a bit sluggish" is not, because you cannot tell when you are done.
  • Step 2: where is it? Profiling means measuring a running program to see where its time or memory goes. You do it before you touch the code, because otherwise you are guessing.
  • Step 3: fix the biggest thing first. The biggest wins come from doing less work, not from doing the same work slightly faster. §10.5 shows why.
  • Step 4: did it help? A change that did not move the measurement is not an improvement. It is only extra code to maintain.

How much can one fix give back? Picture a one-hour journey to work: five minutes walking to the station, then a 55-minute train. Even if you could walk to the station instantly, you would still arrive after 55 minutes. You saved five minutes at most, because walking was only five minutes of the trip.

That idea has a name. Amdahl's law sets the ceiling: optimising code that accounts for 5% of runtime can never give you more than 5% back, even if you make it infinitely fast. Here is the formula as a function you can play with:

def overall_speedup(fraction, factor):
    """fraction: share of the runtime you speed up; factor: how much faster it gets."""
    return 1 / ((1 - fraction) + fraction / factor)

print(round(overall_speedup(0.05, 1_000_000), 3))   # 5% of the time, made a million times faster
print(round(overall_speedup(0.80, 2), 2))           # 80% of the time, made twice as fast

1.053
1.67

Line by line:

  • fraction is how much of the total runtime the part you are fixing takes. factor is how many times faster you make that part.
  • The first line makes 5% of the program a million times faster. The whole program becomes only 1.053 times faster: about 5% quicker, exactly the ceiling.
  • The second line makes 80% of the program merely twice as fast, and the whole program becomes 1.67 times faster. A modest fix to a big part beats a heroic fix to a small part.

This is why step 2 comes before step 3. Profiling tells you the fraction, and without it you do not know whether a fix is worth anything.

10.2 timeit: Micro-benchmarks

Sometimes the question is small and exact: "Which of these two lines is faster?" Answering it with a stopwatch is harder than it looks. A single run of a short line takes a few millionths of a second, which is shorter than the noise around it: other programs, the operating system, the CPU changing speed.

A benchmark is a measurement of how long some code takes. A micro-benchmark measures something tiny, one line or one small function. timeit is the standard library's tool for them.

timeit runs a snippet many times and reports the best result, handling the traps that make hand-rolled timing wrong:

  • it disables the cyclic garbage collector, so a collection (§1.9) that happens to start mid-measurement does not land in your number,
  • it uses the highest-resolution clock (the most precise one available), time.perf_counter,
  • and it repeats to reduce noise.

Two arguments control the repetition:

import timeit

times = timeit.repeat('sorted(data)', setup='data = list(range(1000, 0, -1))',
                      number=1000, repeat=5)
print('runs:', len(times))
print('fastest is never above the average:', min(times) <= sum(times) / len(times))

runs: 5
fastest is never above the average: True

Line by line:

  • setup runs once before timing starts. It builds the data, so building it is not counted.
  • number=1000 runs sorted(data) a thousand times in a row and times the whole batch. A batch is long enough for the clock to measure accurately.
  • repeat=5 does that whole batch five times, and returns a list of five totals. That is the runs: 5.
  • The last line is true by arithmetic: the smallest of five numbers can never be bigger than their average. Keep it in mind for the next example.

Now a real comparison: three ways to double every number in a list.

import timeit

setup = 'items = list(range(1000))'

def best(stmt):
    # repeat() then min(): the fastest run is the one with least interference
    # from the OS scheduler. Averaging would fold that noise into the answer.
    return min(timeit.repeat(stmt, setup=setup, number=2000, repeat=5))

loop = best('out = []\nfor i in items: out.append(i * 2)')
comp = best('[i * 2 for i in items]')
mapl = best('list(map(lambda i: i * 2, items))')

print('all three produce the same thing:',
      [i * 2 for i in range(4)] == list(map(lambda i: i * 2, range(4))))
print('measured three variants:', all(t > 0 for t in (loop, comp, mapl)))

all three produce the same thing: True
measured three variants: True

The two printed lines only prove that the code ran and the three versions agree. The interesting numbers are loop, comp and mapl, and they are different on every machine, so the example does not print them. Run it and print them yourself.

On the machine this was written on the list comprehension is consistently the fastest and the explicit append loop the slowest, by somewhere between 5% and 35% depending on system load — a comprehension uses a specialised bytecode instead of looking up and calling the append method on every iteration.

Note the methodology in best(): repeat() and then min(), never a mean. Think of driving the same road to work every day. A red light or a traffic jam can make you late. Nothing can make you arrive faster than the empty road allows. So your fastest trip is the best estimate of the road itself, and your average trip mixes in the traffic.

Timing noise works the same way. Timing noise is one-sided — an interrupted run can only be slower, never faster — so the minimum is the closest estimate of the code's real cost, while averaging deliberately mixes in the scheduler's behaviour. The scheduler is the part of the operating system that decides which program runs on the CPU next; when it pauses yours to run something else, your timing gets longer.

The gap here is also a good lesson in not trusting a single measurement. It is small enough that a single timeit.timeit() call on a loaded machine will report the orderings in either direction. If a difference is not large enough to survive repetition, it is not large enough to justify changing your code.

From the command line, which is how you will usually reach for it:

python -m timeit -s "items = list(range(1000))" "[i * 2 for i in items]"
python -m timeit -s "d = {i: i for i in range(1000)}" "500 in d"
python -m timeit -s "l = list(range(1000))" "500 in l"
  • -s is the setup, run once.
  • The last string is the statement being timed.
  • python -m timeit chooses number for you (it keeps increasing it until one batch takes at least 0.2 seconds) and repeats 5 times.

Each command prints one line. Measured on this Mac under Python 3.14.8, the three printed 20000 loops, best of 5: 12.5 usec per loop, 20000000 loops, best of 5: 12.1 nsec per loop and 100000 loops, best of 5: 2.61 usec per loop. (usec is microseconds, millionths of a second; nsec is nanoseconds, billionths of a second.) Your numbers will differ; the shape will not. Read the last two together: finding 500 in a dictionary took about 12 nanoseconds, and in a list about 2,600. The dictionary jumps straight to the answer, while the list checks 500 items first. §10.5 is about exactly that difference.

Two rules for micro-benchmarks. Benchmark something representative — timing an empty loop teaches nothing about your program. And never optimise on a micro-benchmark alone: a 30% gain in a function that runs 0.1% of the time is not a gain. That second rule is §10.1's journey to work again: a faster walk to the station does not change the train.

10.3 cProfile: Where the Time Actually Goes

timeit answers "how fast is this one line?". Most of the time you do not know which line to ask about. You need the opposite question: "here is my whole program; where does its time go?"

cProfile is the deterministic profiler in the standard library. "Deterministic" here means it records every call. Picture an office where every employee fills in a timesheet for every task, all day. You get a complete record, but filling in timesheets takes time too, so the office runs a little slower while it is being watched.

That is the trade-off it makes: complete data, at the cost of adding overhead to every call — which is why the ratios it reports are trustworthy and the absolute timings are not. If one function took 60% of the time while being watched, it takes roughly 60% without being watched as well. The exact seconds are inflated.

Sampling profilers (py-spy, scalene, austin) make the opposite trade and are what you use for profiling a live production process. Instead of timesheets, picture a manager who walks past every desk once a minute and writes down what each person is doing at that moment. Nobody is slowed down, and after a day the notes show where the time went just as well.

Here is cProfile comparing a slow and a fast way of doing the same lookup:

import cProfile, pstats, io

def slow_lookup(items, targets):
    return [t for t in targets if t in items]      # O(n) scan per target

def fast_lookup(items, targets):
    seen = set(items)
    return [t for t in targets if t in seen]       # O(1) per target

def main():
    items = list(range(20_000))
    targets = list(range(0, 20_000, 100))
    slow_lookup(items, targets)
    fast_lookup(items, targets)

buf = io.StringIO()
profiler = cProfile.Profile()
profiler.enable()
main()
profiler.disable()

stats = pstats.Stats(profiler, stream=buf).sort_stats('cumulative')
stats.print_stats(10)
report = buf.getvalue()
print('slow_lookup appears:', 'slow_lookup' in report)
print('fast_lookup appears:', 'fast_lookup' in report)
print('report has the standard columns:',
      all(c in report for c in ('ncalls', 'tottime', 'cumtime')))

slow_lookup appears: True
fast_lookup appears: True
report has the standard columns: True

Line by line:

  • profiler.enable() and profiler.disable() switch the watching on and off around main(). Everything called in between is recorded.
  • pstats.Stats turns the raw notes into a report. sort_stats('cumulative') puts the most expensive call paths first, and print_stats(10) keeps the top ten rows.
  • The report is written into buf, a string in memory, so the example can check it. The real numbers change on every run, so the example prints only facts that do not: both functions were recorded, and the report has its usual columns.

In practice you run it from the command line and read the table:

python -m cProfile -s cumulative script.py | head -20
python -m cProfile -o profile.out script.py     # save for later analysis
  • The first line profiles the whole of script.py, sorts by cumulative time and shows the top of the table.
  • The second saves the raw data to profile.out instead, so you can load it later with pstats.Stats('profile.out') and sort it different ways without running the program again.

The columns and what they mean:

Column Meaning
ncalls number of calls (12/4 means 12 calls, 4 of them non-recursive)
tottime time in this function excluding sub-calls
cumtime time in this function including sub-calls
percall the above divided by ncalls

The difference between tottime and cumtime is the most important idea in this table. Back to the office: a manager spends the morning handing out three big tasks and then waits while the team does them.

  • The manager's own time, handing the tasks out, is small. That is tottime.
  • The manager's time including everything the team did for them is the whole morning. That is cumtime.

Here is that office in code, along with a recursive function to explain the odd 12/4 in ncalls:

import cProfile, pstats

def worker():
    return sum(i * i for i in range(300_000))

def manager():
    return [worker() for _ in range(3)]

def countdown(n):
    if n:
        countdown(n - 1)

def main():
    manager()
    countdown(3)
    countdown(3)

profiler = cProfile.Profile()
profiler.runcall(main)
stats = {name: row for (_, _, name), row in pstats.Stats(profiler).stats.items()}

primitive, total, tottime, cumtime, _ = stats['manager']
print('manager tottime is tiny:', tottime < cumtime / 10)
primitive, total, tottime, cumtime, _ = stats['countdown']
print('countdown ncalls:', f'{total}/{primitive}')

manager tottime is tiny: True
countdown ncalls: 8/2

Line by line:

  • pstats.Stats(profiler).stats is the raw data behind the report: one row per function, holding the primitive call count, the total call count, tottime, cumtime and who called it.
  • manager spent less than a tenth of its cumtime in its own code. All the real work happened inside worker.
  • countdown(3) calls itself for 2, 1 and 0, so one outside call is four calls in total. main makes two outside calls, which gives 8 calls in all, 2 of them from outside. The report prints that as 8/2. A primitive call is one that did not come from the function itself, which is what the table means by non-recursive.

Sort by tottime to find the function doing the work; sort by cumtime to find the call path responsible. A function with high cumtime and low tottime is not slow itself — it is calling something that is. The usual way to read a report is to start at the top of the cumtime order and follow the path down until you reach a function whose tottime is big. That one is your bottleneck.

Two limitations to know.

  • cProfile adds per-call overhead, so it distorts programs dominated by many tiny calls. If a program makes ten million calls to a one-line function, the timesheets become a large part of the work, and the report overstates how much those calls cost.
  • Threads: before Python 3.12 it profiled only the calling thread. Since 3.12 it is built on sys.monitoring, which watches the whole interpreter, and measured on 3.14 a function running in a second thread started after enable() appears in the report too. If your program uses threads, check which version you are on before trusting what is missing from the report.

For production, a sampling profiler (py-spy, austin) interrupts periodically instead, with near-zero overhead and no code changes — py-spy top --pid 1234 attaches to a running process. Here 1234 is the process ID, the number the operating system gives every running program; ps or top will show it. Since Python 3.12 CPython also supports the Linux perf profiler directly (python -X perf), so Python frames appear in native (machine-level) flame graphs: pictures where each function is a bar as wide as the time spent in it.

To find which line is to blame inside one hot function (per-line attribution), line_profiler and its @profile decorator are the standard tool. A hot function is one where a program spends a large share of its time. Once cProfile has named the hot function, line_profiler tells you which of its lines is the expensive one.

10.4 tracemalloc: Where the Memory Goes

Some programs are not slow but greedy: they use more and more memory until the machine runs out. Memory problems need a different instrument. tracemalloc records the allocation site of every object, so you can compare two points in time and see what grew.

An allocation is Python asking for a piece of memory to hold a new object. The allocation site is the line of code that asked. Think of a stock-take in a warehouse: count everything on the shelves on Monday, count again on Friday, and compare. The items that grew are the ones to ask about, and each box is labelled with the supplier that sent it.

import tracemalloc

tracemalloc.start()
snapshot_before = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()

leaky = [str(i) * 50 for i in range(20_000)]       # the allocation we want to find

snapshot_after = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
top = snapshot_after.compare_to(snapshot_before, 'lineno')[0]
print('biggest growth is in this file:', top.traceback[0].filename.endswith('.py'))
print('grew by more than 1 MB:', top.size_diff > 1_000_000)
current, peak = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
print('peak exceeded current:', peak >= current)
tracemalloc.stop()
print('kept alive:', len(leaky))

biggest growth is in this file: True
grew by more than 1 MB: True
peak exceeded current: True
kept alive: 20000

Line by line:

  • tracemalloc.start() begins recording. Memory allocated before this line is invisible to it.
  • take_snapshot() is the Monday stock-take. The second one, after building leaky, is Friday's.
  • compare_to(snapshot_before, 'lineno') lists the differences grouped by line, biggest first. [0] is the line that grew the most, and its traceback[0].filename says which file it is in.
  • That line grew by more than a megabyte: 20,000 strings of 50 to 250 characters each.
  • get_traced_memory() returns two numbers: the memory traced right now, and the highest it has been since start(). The peak can never be lower than the current value.

The workflow that finds real leaks: take a snapshot after warm-up, run the suspect workload, take another, and compare_to them. The top entries name the exact line that allocated the memory still held. A leak here means memory that the program keeps holding after it no longer needs it, usually because something still refers to the objects (§1.8 showed how references keep objects alive). "After warm-up" matters because a program fills its caches and imports its modules in the first few minutes, and that growth is normal.

The peak number answers a different question: not "what is still held?" but "what was the most I ever needed?". A program that needs 2 GB for one second will be killed on a machine with 1 GB, even if it gives everything back a moment later:

import tracemalloc

def build_report():
    rows = [str(i) * 50 for i in range(20_000)]    # big, but only for a moment
    return len(rows)

tracemalloc.start()
count = build_report()
current, peak = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
tracemalloc.stop()

print('rows built:', count)
print('peak above 1 MB:', peak > 1_000_000)
print('now under 100 KB:', current < 100_000)

rows built: 20000
peak above 1 MB: True
now under 100 KB: True

Line by line:

  • rows is a local variable, so when build_report returns, nothing refers to the list any more and Python frees it straight away.
  • So current is small again, under 100 KB, but peak remembers the moment when all 20,000 strings existed at once.

When memory is the problem, look at both numbers: a high current that keeps growing is a leak, while a high peak with a low current is a program that needs too much memory at one moment. The usual fix for the second is to process the data in pieces, for example with a generator (§5.3), instead of building the whole list first.

sys.getsizeof measures one object shallowly — it does not follow references — which is a common source of confusion:

import sys

inner = [0] * 1000
outer = [inner, inner, inner]
print('outer looks tiny:', sys.getsizeof(outer))
print('inner is the real cost:', sys.getsizeof(inner) > 8000)

outer looks tiny: 80
inner is the real cost: True

Line by line:

  • outer is a list of three references. sys.getsizeof(outer) counts only the list itself: its header plus three slots, 80 bytes on a 64-bit build.
  • The thousand-element list those slots point to is not counted, because a list holds references to its items, not the items themselves (§1.2's sticky labels).
  • inner on its own is more than 8,000 bytes: a thousand 8-byte slots.

An address book is the right picture. The address book is small, even if the houses it lists are enormous. sys.getsizeof weighs the address book. tracemalloc is the right tool when you want to know about the houses.

10.5 Complexity Beats Micro-optimisation

Imagine looking for a word in a dictionary by reading every page from the start. Now imagine opening it at the right letter. No amount of reading faster makes the first method competitive, because the second one skips almost all the work.

Code is the same. The largest wins are almost always algorithmic. To see why, count work instead of timing it. The class below counts how many times Python compares two objects with ==:

class Spy:
    comparisons = 0
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
    def __eq__(self, other):
        Spy.comparisons += 1
        return self.value == other.value
    def __hash__(self):
        return hash(self.value)

for n in (10, 100, 1000, 10_000):
    as_list = [Spy(i) for i in range(n)]
    as_set = set(as_list)
    Spy.comparisons = 0
    Spy(n - 1) in as_list
    in_list = Spy.comparisons
    Spy.comparisons = 0
    Spy(n - 1) in as_set
    print(f'{n:>6} items: list {in_list:>6} comparisons, set {Spy.comparisons}')

    10 items: list     10 comparisons, set 1
   100 items: list    100 comparisons, set 1
  1000 items: list   1000 comparisons, set 1
 10000 items: list  10000 comparisons, set 1

Line by line:

  • Each Spy wraps a number, and its __eq__ adds one to a counter every time Python compares two of them (§2.4 covered __eq__ and __hash__).
  • Spy(n - 1) in as_list looks for the last item. A list has no way to know where it is, so it compares from the front, one item at a time, until it finds it: n comparisons.
  • Spy(n - 1) in as_set uses the hash to jump straight to the right place (§1.5's cloakroom ticket), then compares once to make sure: 1 comparison, whatever the size.

That growth pattern is what complexity, or "Big-O", describes. The list search is O(n): the work grows in step with the number of items n. Ten times the data, ten times the work. The set search is O(1), "constant time": the work stays the same however big the set gets. Big-O ignores the exact numbers and keeps only the shape of the growth, because the shape is what decides whether a program survives ten times more data.

This is the single most valuable table in the section:

Operation list set / dict deque
x in c O(n) O(1) O(n)
append / add O(1)* O(1) O(1)
pop from end O(1) — O(1)
pop from front O(n) — O(1)
index access O(1) — O(n)

*amortised

Two terms in it need a word:

  • Amortised O(1) means "O(1) on average over many calls". A list keeps spare room at its end, so most appends just use it. Now and then the room runs out and the list moves everything into a bigger block, which is slow, but this happens rarely enough that the average cost per append stays constant.
  • A deque (from collections, pronounced "deck") is a double-ended queue: a sequence built to add and remove at both ends quickly. It gives up fast index access to get that.

Now the timing that follows from the first row:

import time

n = 30_000
haystack_list = list(range(n))
haystack_set = set(haystack_list)
needles = range(0, n, 3)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
found_list = sum(1 for x in needles if x in haystack_list)
list_time = time.perf_counter() - t0

t0 = time.perf_counter()
found_set = sum(1 for x in needles if x in haystack_set)
set_time = time.perf_counter() - t0

print('same answer:', found_list == found_set)
print('set was at least 10x faster:', list_time > set_time * 10)

same answer: True
set was at least 10x faster: True

Line by line:

  • needles is 10,000 numbers to look for, and both versions look for all of them in the same 30,000 numbers.
  • time.perf_counter() reads the high-resolution clock; the difference between two readings is the time taken.
  • Both versions find the same numbers. The set does it more than ten times faster, and on most machines the real ratio is in the hundreds.

That is not a 30% tuning gain; it is the difference between O(n·m) and O(m), and it grows with the data. Here m is the number of needles: each of them costs O(n) in a list and O(1) in a set. Double the haystack and the list version takes twice as long, while the set version does not change. No amount of micro-optimising the in operator on a list would ever close it.

The same reasoning applies to the front of a list. Picture a queue of people standing on numbered squares. When the person on square 1 leaves, everyone else has to step forward one square, so the cost of one person leaving grows with the length of the queue. That is list.pop(0): a list keeps its items packed from position 0, so removing the first one moves all the others.

A deque is a queue where the front simply moves: the person leaves, and the square behind them becomes the new front. Nobody steps anywhere.

import collections, time

def with_list(n):
    q = list(range(n))
    while q:
        q.pop(0)                 # O(n) each time -> O(n^2) total

def with_deque(n):
    q = collections.deque(range(n))
    while q:
        q.popleft()              # O(1) each time -> O(n) total

n = 20_000
t0 = time.perf_counter(); with_list(n); list_time = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter(); with_deque(n); deque_time = time.perf_counter() - t0
print('deque was faster:', deque_time < list_time)
print('by more than 5x:', list_time > deque_time * 5)

deque was faster: True
by more than 5x: True

Line by line:

  • with_list empties a list from the front. Each pop(0) moves every remaining item, so emptying n items costs about n×n/2 moves in total: O(n²), "quadratic". Double the data and it takes four times as long.
  • with_deque empties a deque from the front. Each popleft() is O(1), so the whole job is O(n).

If your code uses a list as a queue, taking work from the front, it is a deque waiting to happen. It is a one-line change.

10.6 Optimisations That Reliably Pay

Once the profiler has named the hot spot, here is what to try. In rough order of value per unit of effort:

1. Do less work. Cache with functools.cache (§4.8), batch database calls, avoid recomputation. The fastest code is code that does not run. Batching means asking for many things in one trip instead of one thing per trip: one query that fetches 100 rows instead of 100 queries that fetch one each, like buying all the week's groceries in one visit to the shop.

2. Use the right data structure. As above — usually a one-line change.

3. Hoist invariants out of loops. An invariant is a value that is the same on every pass of the loop. To hoist it is to compute it once, before the loop starts. It is the difference between looking a word up in the dictionary every time you meet it in a book, and writing its meaning on a sticky note the first time.

import re, time

text = 'the year 2026 and the year 1999'
pattern = r'\d{4}'

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(20_000):
    re.findall(pattern, text)                # re-looks-up the compiled cache
uncompiled = time.perf_counter() - t0

compiled = re.compile(pattern)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(20_000):
    compiled.findall(text)                   # no lookup at all
precompiled = time.perf_counter() - t0

print('precompiling helped:', precompiled < uncompiled)

precompiling helped: True

Line by line:

  • A regular expression has to be compiled into an internal matching program before it can be used.
  • re.findall(pattern, text) compiles pattern the first time, and then keeps the result in a cache inside the re module. Every later call still has to look the pattern up in that cache, on all 20,000 passes.
  • re.compile(pattern) does that work once, before the loop. Inside the loop compiled.findall(text) goes straight to matching.

The gain here is modest, because re's cache already saves the expensive part. The habit matters more in your own code, where nothing caches for you: a value computed from the same inputs on every pass is computed once, before the loop.

4. Build strings with join, not += in a loop. Strings cannot be changed in place (they are immutable, §1.5), so s += 'x' normally builds a brand-new string and copies everything so far into it. It is like rewriting a whole letter by hand every time you want to add one word. Repeated concatenation is O(n²) because each + copies everything so far.

import time

n = 40_000
t0 = time.perf_counter()
s = ''
for i in range(n):
    s += 'x'
concat = time.perf_counter() - t0

t0 = time.perf_counter()
s2 = ''.join('x' for _ in range(n))
joined = time.perf_counter() - t0

print('same result:', s == s2)
print('join was faster:', joined < concat)

same result: True
join was faster: True

Line by line:

  • The first loop grows s one character at a time, 40,000 times.
  • ''.join(...) collects all the pieces first, works out the total length, and builds the final string once.
  • Both produce the same 40,000-character string, and join is faster.

Going deeper: the trick that sometimes hides this. CPython has an optimisation for one special case. When s += 'x' runs inside a function, and s is the only reference to the string, nobody else can see the old string, so CPython may extend it in place instead of copying. The example above runs at the top level of a module, where the trick does not apply. Inside a function it often does, and then a single extra name pointing at the old string is enough to switch it off again:

import time

def grow(n):
    s = ''
    for _ in range(n):
        s += 'x'
    return s

def grow_with_backup(n):
    s = ''
    for _ in range(n):
        backup = s          # a second name for the same string
        s += 'x'
    return s

def seconds(fn, n):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    fn(n)
    return time.perf_counter() - t0

print('same text:', grow(10) == grow_with_backup(10))
print('the backup made it 10x slower:',
      seconds(grow_with_backup, 200_000) > seconds(grow, 200_000) * 10)

same text: True
the backup made it 10x slower: True

Line by line:

  • grow is the loop from before, moved into a function. Here CPython's trick works, and the loop is fast.
  • grow_with_backup is identical except for backup = s. Now the old string has two names, so it must not change, and every += has to copy it. On the machine this was written on the difference was about 60 times.

That is why the rule stays the same: use join. The trick belongs to CPython only, it depends on details you cannot see in the code, and one harmless-looking extra line removes it. PEP 8, Python's style guide, says the same: do not rely on it in code that needs to perform, and use ''.join() instead.

5. Prefer built-ins and comprehensions. sum, min, sorted, any and list comprehensions run their loops in C rather than in the interpreter. The interpreter has to read and dispatch each Python instruction one at a time; a C loop is compiled machine code with none of that overhead. Calling sum(numbers) hands the whole loop to a machine instead of doing it by hand.

6. Use __slots__ or dataclass(slots=True) when instance count is in the millions (§1.7). Each instance then stores its attributes in fixed slots instead of carrying its own dictionary, which saves memory per object and makes attribute access slightly faster.

7. Use local variables in hot loops. Local lookups are an array index; global and attribute lookups are dictionary lookups. Think of a carpenter who keeps the hammer in hand instead of walking to the shed for it before every nail. append = out.append before a tight loop is a real, if small, win — and a readability cost, so only where profiling justifies it.

Notice the order. The first two items can turn hours into seconds. The last two shave off a few percent. Work down the list, and measure after each step (§10.1, step 4).

10.7 When Python Itself Is the Limit

If the algorithm is right and it is still too slow, the remaining options leave pure Python behind. The idea behind almost all of them is the same: keep Python for the parts that organise the work, and move the inner loop, the code that runs millions of times, into compiled machine code.

It is the difference between carrying boxes up the stairs one at a time and using a lift. You still decide which boxes go where; the lift does the carrying.

  • NumPy — vectorised array operations in C, with the GIL released. For numerical work this is usually a 10–100× improvement and should be the first thing tried, not the last. "Vectorised" means one operation applies to a whole array at once: prices * 1.2 multiplies a million numbers in a single call, and the loop runs in C. The GIL (§8.2) is released during that work, so other threads can run.
  • A C extension — the traditional route. A C extension is a module written in C and compiled, which Python then imports like any other module; much of the standard library, including math, is built this way. You write C against the CPython API, or use ctypes/cffi to call an existing shared library without compiling anything yourself.
  • Cython — annotate Python with static types and compile it to a C extension. The gentlest path from working Python to fast native code. You start from the Python you already have and add types to the hot function until it is fast enough.
  • PyO3 / Rust — Rust is a newer language for fast, low-level code, and PyO3 connects it to Python. Increasingly the modern choice for new extensions; memory-safe, and what pydantic-core, ruff and uv are built with. "Memory-safe" means the Rust compiler rejects the kinds of bugs, such as reading memory that has already been freed, that make C extensions crash.
  • The JIT. CPython 3.13 added an experimental copy-and-patch JIT (named after its technique: stitching together pieces of machine code prepared in advance), and 3.14 ships it in the official Windows and macOS binaries, the ready-to-run downloads from python.org. It is off by default and its gains are modest so far; it is a direction of travel rather than a lever to pull today. A JIT ("just-in-time" compiler) turns frequently run Python code into machine code while the program is running.
  • PyPy — an alternative interpreter with a mature tracing JIT (one that watches which paths the code actually takes and compiles those), often several times faster on long-running pure-Python workloads. The constraint is C extension compatibility: a package built for CPython's C API may not work on PyPy, or may run slower there.

ctypes, from the standard library, is the quickest way to see the idea at work. A shared library is a file of compiled functions that many programs can use: libm is the C maths library that comes with the operating system. ctypes loads it and calls a function in it directly:

import ctypes, ctypes.util

libm = ctypes.CDLL(ctypes.util.find_library('m'))
libm.sqrt.restype = ctypes.c_double            # you MUST declare the types
libm.sqrt.argtypes = [ctypes.c_double]
print(libm.sqrt(144.0))

12.0

Line by line:

  • ctypes.util.find_library('m') finds the maths library's file on this system (its name differs between Linux and macOS, which is why you ask rather than hard-coding it).
  • ctypes.CDLL(...) loads it, and libm.sqrt is the C function sqrt.
  • argtypes and restype tell ctypes what C types go in and come out. A C library file stores only machine code, not the types of its functions, so Python cannot find them out for itself.

That is C called from Python with no compiler involved. Note the explicit restype/argtypes: ctypes assumes int returns otherwise, and omitting them produces silently wrong numbers rather than an error.

It is like phoning a specialist who speaks only in numbers: you must say whether you are giving them metres or centimetres, because they will never ask. Leaving out argtypes gives you one of the lucky failures, an error, because ctypes refuses to guess how to pass a Python float:

import ctypes, ctypes.util

libm = ctypes.CDLL(ctypes.util.find_library('m'))
try:
    libm.sqrt(144.0)                           # no argtypes declared
except ctypes.ArgumentError as error:
    print(error)

argument 1: TypeError: Don't know how to convert parameter 1

Leaving out only restype is the unlucky failure: the call runs, and ctypes reads the answer as an int from the wrong place, so you get a number that has nothing to do with the square root and no error at all. Declare both, every time.

Before reaching for any of this, confirm the problem is CPU-bound Python. If it is I/O, sections 8 and 9 are the answer; if it is a database, an index (a lookup structure that lets the database find rows without reading them all) or one fewer query will beat any of this by an order of magnitude, roughly ten times. A program that spends 90% of its time waiting for a database will be at most 10% faster even if a C extension made its Python part infinitely fast: §10.1's journey to work, one last time.

Exercises

Exercise 10.1 — Find and fix the bottleneck. This takes far longer than it should. Profile it mentally, name the complexity, and fix it.

def find_duplicates(records):
    duplicates = []
    for i, record in enumerate(records):
        if record in records[i + 1:]:
            if record not in duplicates:
                duplicates.append(record)
    return duplicates
Solution

Three separate O(n) operations nested inside an O(n) loop:

  1. records[i + 1:] builds a new list on every iteration — O(n) copying, n times, so O(n²) just in allocation.
  2. record in records[i + 1:] is an O(n) scan.
  3. record not in duplicates is another O(n) scan.

Overall O(n²) with a large constant. A Counter does it in one pass:

import collections, time

def find_duplicates_slow(records):
    duplicates = []
    for i, record in enumerate(records):
        if record in records[i + 1:]:
            if record not in duplicates:
                duplicates.append(record)
    return duplicates

def find_duplicates(records):
    counts = collections.Counter(records)
    return [item for item, n in counts.items() if n > 1]

data = [i % 800 for i in range(4000)]
t0 = time.perf_counter(); slow = find_duplicates_slow(data); slow_t = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter(); fast = find_duplicates(data); fast_t = time.perf_counter() - t0

print('same answer:', sorted(slow) == sorted(fast))
print('items found:', len(fast))
print('at least 10x faster:', slow_t > fast_t * 10)

same answer: True
items found: 800
at least 10x faster: True

Counter is O(n) and hashes each record once. Note the requirement it introduces: records must be hashable (§1.5). If they are dicts, key on a tuple of the fields that define identity, or use frozenset(d.items()).

The general pattern to recognise: a membership test inside a loop over the same data is nearly always O(n²) and nearly always fixable with a set or a Counter. Slicing inside a loop is the other tell — it is easy to miss because it looks like indexing.

Exercise 10.2 — Which measurement tool? For each symptom, say which tool you would reach for and what you would look at.

  1. A web request takes 3 seconds and you do not know why.
  2. A worker process grows from 200 MB to 4 GB over a day.
  3. You want to know whether dict.get(k, d) is faster than try/except KeyError.
  4. A production service is wedged right now and you cannot restart it.
Solution

1. Three-second request — cProfile, sorted by cumtime. Sort by cumulative time first to find the call path responsible, then by tottime to find the function actually burning CPU. If neither shows much CPU, the time is I/O — a database query or an HTTP call — and the profiler will show it as time inside a read/recv. In that case the answer is in section 9, not here. For a real service, prefer a sampling profiler or distributed tracing so you are measuring production rather than a synthetic run.

2. Growth to 4 GB — tracemalloc. Snapshot after warm-up, snapshot again later, compare_to(..., 'lineno') and read the top entries: they name the exact allocation site of memory still held. Common causes are an unbounded cache (§4.8 — functools.cache on a method), a module-level list that only ever grows, and reference cycles holding large objects (§1.9). gc.set_debug(gc.DEBUG_LEAK) helps with the last of these. objgraph is worth knowing for visualising what refers to what.

3. dict.get vs try/except — timeit. This is exactly what micro-benchmarks are for. Benchmark both branches, though: try/except is very cheap when the key is usually present and relatively expensive when it usually is not, so the answer depends on your hit rate. Then remember §10.2's second rule and check the function is hot enough for the difference to matter at all.

4. Wedged service — attach to it. py-spy dump --pid <PID> shows the current stack of every thread with no restart and near-zero overhead; py-spy top gives a live view. On Python 3.14, python -m pdb -p <PID> (PEP 768) attaches the standard debugger to a running process, and python -m asyncio ps <PID> shows the asyncio task tree (§9.11). Look for a thread blocked on a lock, a socket read with no timeout, or a deadlock between two locks acquired in different orders.

The pattern: CPU → cProfile or a sampler; memory → tracemalloc; micro-comparison → timeit; live process → attach, never restart. Restarting destroys the evidence.

SECTION 11

Imports, Environments and Packaging

Start with a tiny experiment. The program below writes a one-line module called greet.py into a temporary folder, tells Python to look in that folder, and then imports the module twice. Before you read the output, guess how many times greet.py is running appears.

import sys, tempfile, pathlib

folder = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(folder / "greet.py").write_text('print("greet.py is running")\nWORD = "hello"\n')
sys.path.insert(0, str(folder))

import greet
import greet                       # the second import prints nothing
print(greet.WORD)
print("same object both times:", greet is sys.modules["greet"])

greet.py is running
hello
same object both times: True

Line by line:

  • tempfile.mkdtemp() makes an empty folder, and write_text puts a two-line Python file in it. The file prints a message and defines one name, WORD.
  • sys.path.insert(0, ...) adds the folder to the list of places Python searches for modules. §11.2 is about that list.
  • The first import greet finds the file and runs it, so the message appears.
  • The second import greet runs nothing. Python remembers modules it has already loaded and hands back the same one.
  • sys.modules is where Python keeps that memory. The last line proves the name greet and the remembered entry are one and the same object.

So an import is not a copy-and-paste of a file. It is a small, predictable procedure: find the file, run it once, remember the result. Everything in this section is a procedure like that.

Everything so far has been about code that runs. This section is about code that ships: how Python finds the modules you import, how environments keep one project's dependencies from breaking another's, and how a directory of .py files becomes something a colleague can pip install. These are the parts of Python most often learned by superstition:

  • a sys.path.append that fixes an import for reasons nobody can explain,
  • a requirements.txt that produces a different set of packages every time it is installed,
  • a "just delete the virtual environment and try again" that works without anyone knowing why.

All of it is mechanical, and once you have seen the mechanism the superstitions go away. The section runs in three parts:

  1. How importing works (§11.1-§11.7): the four steps of import, where Python looks, packages, relative imports, circular imports and lazy imports.
  2. Keeping projects apart (§11.8): virtual environments.
  3. Turning a project into something installable (§11.9-§11.14): pyproject.toml, building, dependencies and lockfiles, uv, entry points and publishing to PyPI.

11.1 What import Actually Does

Think of borrowing a book from a library. You ask at the desk. The librarian first checks whether you already have that book out; if you do, there is nothing to fetch. If not, they search the catalogues, fetch the book from the right shelf, record the loan, and hand it to you with a label on it.

import json works the same way. It looks like a keyword doing something magical. It is not. Python's import system is four steps, all of them written in Python and all of them inspectable — importlib in the standard library is the import system, and the import statement is a call into it.

1. Check sys.modules — a plain dict of every module already imported. A hit ends the process immediately; this is why importing something twice is free.
2. Ask each finder in sys.meta_path for a spec. The last one, PathFinder, is the one that walks sys.path.
3. The spec's loader creates a module object, inserts it into sys.modules before executing it, then runs the file's code in that module's namespace.
4. Bind a name in the importing namespace. import json binds json; from json import loads binds loads.

Three new words appear in those steps. Here they are in plain terms:

  • A finder is an object whose only job is to answer "do you know where module X lives?". Python keeps a short list of finders in sys.meta_path and asks them in order, like a librarian checking one catalogue after another.
  • A spec (short for "module specification") is the finder's answer: the module's name, where it was found, and which loader can load it. It is a description, not the module itself.
  • A loader is the object that turns the spec into a real module: it reads the file and runs its code.

The library analogy maps onto the four steps one to one: the "already on loan" check is sys.modules, the catalogues are the finders, fetching the book is the loader, and the label on the book is the name bound in your code.

The next program watches each step happen, using json as the guinea pig.

import sys
import importlib.util

print('json loaded already?', 'json' in sys.modules)
import json
print('json loaded now?    ', 'json' in sys.modules)
print('the name and the cache entry are one object:', json is sys.modules['json'])

spec = importlib.util.find_spec('json')          # step 2, without doing step 3
print('name:  ', spec.name)
print('loader:', type(spec.loader).__name__)
print('origin:', '/'.join(spec.origin.split('/')[-2:]))
print('is a package (has search locations):', spec.submodule_search_locations is not None)

print('sys origin:', importlib.util.find_spec('sys').origin)
print('sys is compiled into the interpreter:', 'sys' in sys.builtin_module_names)
# meta_path holds classes as often as instances, so ask for the right name:
names = [f.__name__ if isinstance(f, type) else type(f).__name__ for f in sys.meta_path]
print('the last three finders:', names[-3:])

json loaded already? False
json loaded now?     True
the name and the cache entry are one object: True
name:   json
loader: SourceFileLoader
origin: json/__init__.py
is a package (has search locations): True
sys origin: built-in
sys is compiled into the interpreter: True
the last three finders: ['BuiltinImporter', 'FrozenImporter', 'PathFinder']

Line by line:

  • The first three lines show step 1. Before the import, json is not in sys.modules; after it, it is, and the name json in your code is that exact cache entry.
  • find_spec('json') runs step 2 on its own and returns the spec without loading anything. The spec says the module is called json, that a SourceFileLoader (a loader for ordinary .py files) will load it, and that it lives in json/__init__.py.
  • "is a package" is True because json is a folder of modules rather than one file. §11.3 explains packages.
  • sys has the origin built-in. It is not a file at all; it was compiled into the Python program itself.
  • The last line prints the end of the finder list. BuiltinImporter handles modules compiled into the interpreter, FrozenImporter handles a few modules stored inside the interpreter as ready-made bytecode, and PathFinder searches the disk.

Three consequences worth holding on to.

Module-level code runs exactly once per process. A module body is not a definition, it is a script that happens to define things. If it opens a database connection or reads an environment variable, that happens at import time, in whatever order the imports resolve — which is why import-time side effects (actions beyond defining names, such as opening a connection) are a recurring source of bugs that only appear in one deployment: one installed, running copy of the program, such as the live website.

The opening greet example showed this: the print happened on the first import only. A process here means one run of the Python program, from start to exit. Start the program again and every module runs again, once.

sys.modules is writable. Deleting an entry forces a re-import; assigning a fake module is how unittest.mock.patch replaces a dependency (§12.6). importlib.reload(mod) re-executes the file in the existing module object, so old references survive — which is why reload is useful in a REPL and dangerous anywhere else.

To see why "old references survive" is dangerous, imagine a module defines a class Order and you have created ten Order objects. After a reload, the module holds a brand-new Order class, but your ten objects still point at the old one. isinstance(order, mod.Order) is now False for all of them, and nothing warns you.

Builtins have no file. sys reports origin: built-in: it was compiled into the interpreter, and BuiltinImporter claims it before PathFinder ever looks at the disk. That ordering is why you cannot shadow sys with a local sys.py, but can shadow json.

Which modules are compiled in is a property of the build, not of the language. On the Linux build this course was written on, math was built in too. In the macOS Homebrew build of 3.14 it is a separate extension module under lib-dynload, found by PathFinder like any other file — so there, a local math.py in the script's directory does shadow it. sys.builtin_module_names lists what is compiled into the interpreter in front of you, and it is the only reliable answer.

A build here means one particular compiled copy of Python: the one Homebrew installs, the one in a Docker image, the one your Linux distribution ships. They all run the same language, but each was compiled with slightly different choices. An extension module is a module written in C and compiled into a separate file (.so on Linux and macOS, .pyd on Windows) that Python loads from disk.

11.2 sys.path: Where Python Looks

Imagine a postman with a letter addressed only to "Sam". The postman walks down the street in house order and delivers it to the first house where someone called Sam lives. If your neighbour at number 2 is also called Sam, the letter meant for you at number 40 never reaches you.

sys.path is that street. It is a plain list of folders. PathFinder walks sys.path in order and takes the first match. The list is assembled at startup from four sources, and knowing which entry comes first explains most "why is it importing the wrong thing" incidents.

Position Entry Comes from
First the script's directory python app.py → the directory containing app.py
First the current directory ('') python -c ..., python -m mod, and the REPL
Then $PYTHONPATH entries the environment variable, split on :
Then the standard library the interpreter's own installation
Last site-packages added by the site module at startup

Reading the table:

  • The two "First" rows are alternatives: which one you get depends on how you started Python. Running a file puts that file's folder first. Running -c, -m or the interactive prompt (the REPL) puts the current folder first.
  • PYTHONPATH is an environment variable you can set to add folders. Most projects should not need it.
  • The standard library is everything that ships with Python: json, random, pathlib and the rest.
  • site-packages is the folder where pip installs third-party packages. It comes last.

The first row is the trap. Name a file random.py, email.py, types.py or token.py and every import of that name in your project — including imports made by libraries you did not write — resolves to your file instead. The failure is rarely a clean ImportError; it is usually an AttributeError from deep inside a dependency.

Here is the trap in action. The program writes its own calendar.py into a folder, puts that folder first (which is exactly what running a script from that folder does), and imports calendar.

import sys, tempfile, pathlib

folder = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(folder / "calendar.py").write_text('print("you got MY calendar.py")\n')
sys.path.insert(0, str(folder))     # what running a script from that folder does

import calendar
print("has month_name?", hasattr(calendar, "month_name"))

you got MY calendar.py
has month_name? False

Line by line:

  • The standard library has a real calendar module with names like month_name.
  • Our folder is first on sys.path, so PathFinder finds our calendar.py there and stops looking. The real one is never reached.
  • hasattr(calendar, "month_name") is False: the code that wanted the real calendar gets a stranger instead. In a real project that would be an AttributeError somewhere far from the cause.

Nothing in that program is wrong, and Python did exactly what the list told it to. The fix is never "be careful with imports"; it is to know what is on the list. These three commands help:

python -c "import random; print(random.__file__)"   # confirm what you actually got
python -P app.py             # 3.11+: do NOT put the script's directory first
PYTHONSAFEPATH=1 python app.py                      # same thing, as an env var
  • random.__file__ is the path of the file that was actually loaded. When an import behaves strangely, print it first.
  • -P (Python 3.11 and later) tells Python not to put the script's folder at the front of sys.path, so a stray file there cannot shadow anything.
  • PYTHONSAFEPATH=1 does the same through an environment variable, which is handy when you cannot change the command line.

Python 3.13 added a related diagnostic. When an import fails and the failing module lives in the directory you launched Python from, the error gains a hint: consider renaming /path/to/random.py if it has the same name as a library you intended to import. It is a genuinely useful nudge — but note the cost, because it costs a different message: that hint replaces the circular-import hint, so a circular import between two top-level modules in your working directory reports a filename clash instead of the cycle. Move the same two modules into a package and the message becomes "partially initialized module … most likely due to a circular import". Same bug, two different explanations.

Measured on 3.14 with two modules, a.py and b.py, that import each other (§11.6 explains why that fails). Run from their own folder, the last line of the error is:

ImportError: cannot import name 'f' from 'a' (consider renaming '/…/a.py' if it has the same name as a library you intended to import)

Moved into a package called pkg, with nothing else changed:

ImportError: cannot import name 'f' from partially initialized module 'pkg.a' (most likely due to a circular import) (/…/pkg/a.py)

(The /…/ stands for the folder on the machine that ran it.) So when the renaming hint makes no sense, because there is no library called a, suspect a circular import.

Appending to sys.path at runtime works and is almost always the wrong fix. It hides the real problem — a project that is not installed — and it only works for code launched from one specific directory. The right fix is §11.9: an installable project, installed in editable mode.

The examples in this section do insert into sys.path, but only to point Python at a temporary folder they just created. That is a demonstration technique, not a pattern for real projects.

11.3 Packages and __init__.py

A single .py file is fine for a small program. A bigger program needs folders, just as a filing cabinet has drawers. In Python a folder of modules is called a package, and a special file inside it marks the drawer and decides what is shown on its front.

A package is a directory Python imports as a module. shop/__init__.py makes shop a package; importing shop.models.order executes shop/__init__.py, then shop/models/__init__.py, then shop/models/order.py, in that order — importing a submodule always imports its ancestors first.

A submodule is a module inside a package: order is a submodule of shop.models, which is itself a subpackage of shop. The dots in shop.models.order follow the folders on disk.

The next program builds exactly that tree in a temporary folder. Each file prints a line when it runs, so you can watch the order.

import sys, tempfile, pathlib, textwrap

root = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(root / "shop" / "models").mkdir(parents=True)

(root / "shop" / "__init__.py").write_text(textwrap.dedent("""
    print("shop/__init__.py runs")
    from .models.order import Order          # re-export, so callers say shop.Order
    __all__ = ["Order"]
"""))
(root / "shop" / "models" / "__init__.py").write_text('print("shop/models/__init__.py runs")\n')
(root / "shop" / "models" / "order.py").write_text(textwrap.dedent("""
    print("shop/models/order.py runs")
    class Order:
        def __init__(self, total): self.total = total
"""))

sys.path.insert(0, str(root))
import shop

print("---")
print("public name:", shop.Order(19.99).total)
print("everything imported:", sorted(n for n in sys.modules if n.startswith("shop")))
print("shop.__path__ has one directory:", len(shop.__path__) == 1)

shop/__init__.py runs
shop/models/__init__.py runs
shop/models/order.py runs
---
public name: 19.99
everything imported: ['shop', 'shop.models', 'shop.models.order']
shop.__path__ has one directory: True

Line by line:

  • import shop runs shop/__init__.py first. Its second line imports .models.order, which makes Python run shop/models/__init__.py and then order.py. Parents always run before children.
  • The from .models.order import Order line is a re-export: it pulls Order up to the top of the package, so callers can write shop.Order instead of shop.models.order.Order. It is like putting the most popular item in the shop window.
  • sys.modules now holds three entries, one per module that ran.
  • shop.__path__ is the list of folders Python searches for shop's submodules. An ordinary package has exactly one: its own folder. §11.4 shows a package with more than one.

What belongs in __init__.py. Re-exports that define the package's public surface (the names it offers its users), __all__, and nothing expensive. What does not belong: database connections, config loading, logging configuration (§7.8), and long import chains. Every one of those runs before the caller has done anything, and a package whose __init__.py imports its entire subtree makes import shop cost as much as importing all of shop. §11.7 shows how to defer that.

The test for anything you want to put there is one question: should this happen for every program that touches any part of the package, even one that only wants a small helper? A re-export passes. Opening a database connection fails, because a test that imports one helper should not need a database.

__all__ does two things and neither is access control. It sets what from shop import * binds, and it tells type checkers and linters which names are deliberate re-exports rather than accidental leakage. Nothing stops anyone importing a name you left out.

Python has no truly private names. __all__ is a list of names you recommend, like the "staff only" sign from §6: it guides polite readers and tools, and stops nobody. If a name should not be used from outside, the convention is to start it with an underscore, _helper, and to leave it out of __all__.

11.4 Namespace Packages

Picture a library where the "Travel" shelf is split across two bookcases at opposite ends of the room. Readers still think of it as one Travel section, and the catalogue knows to look in both places. Python can do the same with a package, and that is what a namespace package is.

A directory with no __init__.py can still be imported — as a namespace package (PEP 420, Python 3.3+). Its distinguishing property is that it can be assembled from several directories on sys.path at once.

A PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) is the document in which a change to Python is proposed, discussed and recorded. When this section cites "PEP 420" it means the document that defined namespace packages. You never need to read a PEP to use the feature, but the number is how you find the authoritative rules.

The program below creates two separate folders, dist-a and dist-b, each holding one part of a package called acme, and neither with an acme/__init__.py:

import sys, tempfile, pathlib

root = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
for portion, sub in (("dist-a", "alpha"), ("dist-b", "beta")):
    d = root / portion / "acme" / sub          # note: no acme/__init__.py anywhere
    d.mkdir(parents=True)
