    (d / "__init__.py").write_text(f'NAME = "{sub}"\n')
    sys.path.insert(0, str(root / portion))

import acme.alpha, acme.beta
print("both halves import:", acme.alpha.NAME, acme.beta.NAME)
print("acme.__file__:", acme.__file__)
print("__path__ type:", type(acme.__path__).__name__)
print("portions found:", len(list(acme.__path__)))

both halves import: alpha beta
acme.__file__: None
__path__ type: _NamespacePath
portions found: 2

Line by line:

  • acme.alpha lives under dist-a, acme.beta under dist-b, and both import as if they shared one folder.
  • acme.__file__ is None: there is no acme/__init__.py, so the package itself has no file.
  • acme.__path__ holds two folders, one from each place. Each piece is called a portion.

acme has no file of its own, and its __path__ is a live _NamespacePath that re-scans sys.path when it changes. That is the whole feature: two separately distributed packages, acme-alpha and acme-beta, can both install into acme/ and coexist. Large organisations use this for a shared top-level namespace across many repositories (separate code projects, each under version control).

"Separately distributed" means two projects, built and released on their own schedules, perhaps by different teams. Without namespace packages, whichever of them provided acme/__init__.py would own the name, and installing the other one would overwrite or conflict with it.

Use it deliberately, or not at all. The common encounter with namespace packages is accidental: you forget an __init__.py, the directory becomes a namespace package, and imports mostly work — until the day a test runner collects two directories with the same name and silently merges them, or a build backend excludes your code from the wheel because it was not recognised as a package (§11.9 and §11.10 explain build backends and wheels). If a directory is one package, give it an __init__.py. Empty is fine.

That is the practical rule for almost everyone: every folder of your own code gets an __init__.py, even an empty one. Namespace packages are a tool for people splitting one name across several releases, and you will know if you are one of them.

11.5 Relative Imports and python -m

"The room next door" is a perfectly clear direction if you know which building you are standing in, and meaningless if you do not. Relative imports are directions of that kind, and the whole difficulty with them is that Python sometimes does not know which building it is in.

Inside a package, from .models import Order is a relative import: one dot means "this package", two means "the parent". Relative imports are resolved from __package__, not from the filesystem, which is why they behave differently depending on how you started Python.

from . import config              # sibling module in the same package
from .models.order import Order   # deeper in the same package
from ..shared import retry        # up one level, then down

__package__ is a variable every module gets automatically: the name of the package the module belongs to. It is the "which building am I in" answer. The dots are counted from there.

Run python shop/cli.py and __package__ is empty, __name__ is "__main__", and every relative import fails with ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package. Run python -m shop.cli and Python imports the shop package first, sets __package__ = "shop", and the same imports resolve.

You can watch both happen. The program builds a shop package whose cli.py uses a relative import, then runs it both ways as a separate Python process and prints the last line of what each one said:

import subprocess, sys, tempfile, pathlib

root = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(root / "shop").mkdir()
(root / "shop" / "__init__.py").write_text("")
(root / "shop" / "config.py").write_text("CURRENCY = 'EUR'\n")
(root / "shop" / "cli.py").write_text(
    "from .config import CURRENCY\n"
    "print('__name__ =', __name__, '| __package__ =', __package__, '|', CURRENCY)\n")

for command in (["shop/cli.py"], ["-m", "shop.cli"]):
    done = subprocess.run([sys.executable, *command], cwd=root,
                          capture_output=True, text=True)
    last_line = (done.stdout or done.stderr).strip().splitlines()[-1]
    print("python", *command, "->", last_line)

python shop/cli.py -> ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package
python -m shop.cli -> __name__ = __main__ | __package__ = shop | EUR

Line by line:

  • subprocess.run([sys.executable, ...], cwd=root) starts a fresh Python (the same one running this program) inside the project folder, exactly as if you had typed the command there. §8.10 covers subprocess.
  • Run as a file path, cli.py is just a script. Python has no idea it belongs to shop, so the dot in .config has nothing to be relative to.
  • Run with -m shop.cli, Python imports shop first and records __package__ = "shop", so .config means shop.config.
  • Notice that __name__ is __main__ in both cases. Whichever module you start is the main program, however you start it.

The rule: run modules inside packages with -m. It also fixes sys.path[0] — -m puts the current directory there rather than the script's directory, so the package is importable at all. -m is why python -m pytest, python -m venv and python -m http.server are written that way.

The if __name__ == "__main__": guard is the same mechanism seen from the other side. A module's __name__ is its import name normally, and "__main__" when it is the program's entry point. The guard means "only when run directly", and it is not optional decoration: multiprocessing with the spawn start method (§8.6) re-imports your __main__ module in the child, and without the guard the child re-runs your program.

In practice the guard looks like this, at the bottom of a module that is both importable and runnable:

def main():
    print("running the report")

if __name__ == "__main__":       # true only when this file is the program being run
    main()

running the report

Imported by another module, the file defines main and does nothing else. Run directly, it calls main(). One file, two roles, and the guard decides which.

A package can also be executed: python -m shop runs shop/__main__.py. That file, plus a console script (§11.13), is how a package gets a command-line interface.

11.6 Circular Imports

Two colleagues each refuse to sign a form until the other has signed first. Nobody is being unreasonable on their own, and yet the form never gets signed. Modules can get stuck the same way.

Two modules that import each other are a cycle. Whether it fails depends on precisely when each name is needed.

import sys, tempfile, pathlib, textwrap

root = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(root / "app").mkdir()
(root / "app" / "__init__.py").write_text("")
(root / "app" / "orders.py").write_text(textwrap.dedent("""
    from app.invoices import make_invoice
    class Order:
        def bill(self): return make_invoice(self)
"""))
(root / "app" / "invoices.py").write_text(textwrap.dedent("""
    from app.orders import Order
    def make_invoice(order): return f"invoice for {type(order).__name__}"
"""))
sys.path.insert(0, str(root))

try:
    import app.orders
except ImportError as exc:
    print(type(exc).__name__ + ":", str(exc).split(" (/")[0])   # trim the file path
    print("failing module:", exc.name)

ImportError: cannot import name 'Order' from partially initialized module 'app.orders' (most likely due to a circular import)
failing module: app.orders

Read the sequence and the message stops being mysterious. app.orders starts executing and is placed in sys.modules immediately — as an empty module. Its first line imports app.invoices, which imports app.orders, gets the cache hit, and asks for Order, which the class statement has not reached yet. "Partially initialized" is literal.

The same story as numbered steps:

  1. import app.orders starts. Python creates an empty app.orders module, puts it in sys.modules (step 3 of §11.1), and starts running orders.py from the top.
  2. The first line of orders.py needs app.invoices, so Python pauses orders.py and starts running invoices.py.
  3. The first line of invoices.py asks for Order from app.orders. The module is already in sys.modules, so Python does not run it again. It looks inside for Order.
  4. Order is not there yet. orders.py is still paused on its first line, and the class Order statement is further down. Python raises ImportError.

The key fact is in step 1: a module goes into sys.modules before its code runs. That is what stops a cycle from looping forever, and it is also why the second module sees a half-built first one.

Three fixes, in order of preference.

  1. Break the cycle. A cycle is usually a design signal: the two modules share a concept that belongs in a third. Move Order to app/models.py and have both import from there.
  2. Import the module, not the name. import app.orders inside invoices.py, then use app.orders.Order at call time. Module objects exist from the first line; the attribute is only looked up when the function runs, by which point both modules are complete. Note this only works if the use is inside a function — at module level it fails identically.
  3. Import inside the function. A deferred import is a legitimate tool, not a hack. It costs one sys.modules dict lookup per call.

Fix 2 is the least obvious, so here it is working. The modules are the same pair, renamed billing so the example stands alone, and both now import the module:

import sys, tempfile, pathlib, textwrap

root = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(root / "billing").mkdir()
(root / "billing" / "__init__.py").write_text("")
(root / "billing" / "orders.py").write_text(textwrap.dedent("""
    import billing.invoices                  # the module, not a name from it
    class Order:
        def bill(self): return billing.invoices.make_invoice(self)
"""))
(root / "billing" / "invoices.py").write_text(textwrap.dedent("""
    import billing.orders                    # the module, not a name from it
    def make_invoice(order):
        assert isinstance(order, billing.orders.Order)   # looked up at call time
        return f"invoice for {type(order).__name__}"
"""))
sys.path.insert(0, str(root))

import billing.orders
print(billing.orders.Order().bill())

invoice for Order

Line by line:

  • invoices.py still runs while orders.py is paused, exactly as before. But import billing.orders only asks for the module object, and that object already exists in sys.modules, half-built. Nothing inside it is needed yet, so nothing fails.
  • billing.orders.Order is written inside make_invoice, so Python looks it up when the function is called. By then both files have finished running and Order exists.
  • Move that isinstance check to the top level of invoices.py and it would fail just like the first example, because it would run while orders.py is still paused.

For imports needed only by annotations, there is a fourth answer that costs nothing at runtime. typing.TYPE_CHECKING is a constant that is False at runtime and True to every type checker, so an import inside if TYPE_CHECKING: is read by mypy and never executed:

from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

if TYPE_CHECKING:                       # never runs; mypy reads it anyway
    from app.invoices import Invoice

def latest(order: "Order") -> "Invoice | None":
    ...

On Python 3.14 the annotations themselves are already lazy (§6.2), so the names need no quotes there; the quotes above are what you write for 3.13 and earlier, where from __future__ import annotations gives the same behaviour. Either way, a cycle that exists purely because two modules annotate each other's types is not a real cycle.

Why does this work? A type checker such as mypy (§6) reads your code without running it, so it sees the import inside the if block and learns what Invoice is. Python itself runs the code, sees if False:, and skips the import entirely. The cycle only ever existed for the type checker, and the type checker does not mind cycles.

11.7 Lazy Imports and Import Hooks

A restaurant does not cook every dish on the menu when it opens in the morning. It cooks each dish when someone orders it. A lazy import is the same idea: a module promises a name but only loads the code behind it when someone first asks for it.

A library with a large surface (many public names) faces a conflict: from toolkit import Frame should work, but importing toolkit should not drag in NumPy for someone who only wanted the CSV parser. PEP 562 (3.7+) resolves it with a module-level __getattr__, called only when normal attribute lookup on the module fails.

You met __getattr__ on classes in §1.6, as the fallback that runs only when normal attribute lookup has failed. Defined at the top level of a module, it plays the same role for the module: Python calls it only when someone asks for a name the module does not have.

import sys, tempfile, pathlib, textwrap

root = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(root / "toolkit").mkdir()
(root / "toolkit" / "__init__.py").write_text(textwrap.dedent('''
    __all__ = ["parse_csv", "Frame"]

    def __getattr__(name):                     # PEP 562: module-level __getattr__
        if name == "Frame":
            from .heavy import Frame
            return Frame
        raise AttributeError(f"module {__name__!r} has no attribute {name!r}")

    def __dir__():                             # keep tab-completion honest
        return sorted(__all__)

    def parse_csv(text):
        return [line.split(",") for line in text.splitlines()]
'''))
(root / "toolkit" / "heavy.py").write_text(
    'print("   heavy.py is executing")\nclass Frame:\n    pass\n')
sys.path.insert(0, str(root))

import toolkit
print("after import, heavy loaded?", "toolkit.heavy" in sys.modules)
print("cheap call:", toolkit.parse_csv("a,b\nc,d"))
print("now touching toolkit.Frame:")
Frame = toolkit.Frame
print("heavy loaded now?", "toolkit.heavy" in sys.modules)
print("dir(toolkit):", dir(toolkit))
try:
    toolkit.nope
except AttributeError as exc:
    print("AttributeError:", exc)

after import, heavy loaded? False
cheap call: [['a', 'b'], ['c', 'd']]
now touching toolkit.Frame:
   heavy.py is executing
heavy loaded now? True
dir(toolkit): ['Frame', 'parse_csv']
AttributeError: module 'toolkit' has no attribute 'nope'

Line by line:

  • After import toolkit, the heavy module has not been loaded. The package is cheap to import.
  • parse_csv is an ordinary function defined in __init__.py, so calling it costs nothing extra.
  • toolkit.Frame is not a name the module has, so Python calls the module's __getattr__("Frame"). That function imports heavy.py (you see its message) and returns the class.
  • dir(toolkit) lists Frame even though it was never a real attribute, because __dir__ says so.
  • toolkit.nope reaches __getattr__ too, finds no match, and gets a proper AttributeError.

Two details make this production-grade rather than a trick. The fallback raise AttributeError is required — without it, every failed lookup returns None and hasattr lies. And __dir__ (also PEP 562) is what keeps dir() and REPL completion (the suggestions you get by pressing Tab) showing the lazy names, which __getattr__ alone cannot do because there is nothing to enumerate.

Here is why the missing raise makes hasattr lie. A function that ends without a return returns None. So without the last line, toolkit.nope would quietly give None, and hasattr(toolkit, "nope") would say True for a name that does not exist.

Below that sits the import system's extension point for the truly unusual case: sys.meta_path. Inserting a finder there lets you import from a database, a zip file, an encrypted archive, or nothing at all. This is how zipimport works, how import-time instrumentation (code that measures or records every import) works, and how tools that need to see every import — coverage measurement, lazy-loading frameworks — hook in. You will read code that does this more often than you will write it, but knowing the list is ordered and writable is the difference between "magic" and "a list of objects with a find_spec method".

Such a finder is called an import hook. In the library picture from §11.1 it is an extra catalogue added to the front of the librarian's list: every request now passes through it first, and it can answer, or say "not mine" and let the request carry on.

python -X importtime app.py prints the cumulative and self time of every import, which is the correct way to find out whether any of this is worth doing. Startup time is nearly always import time.

-X importtime writes one line per imported module to the error output. "Self" is the time spent running that module's own code. "Cumulative" adds the time of everything it imported in turn. It is the same split as tottime and cumtime in §10.3, and you read it the same way: look for the biggest numbers, then decide whether a lazy import would help.

11.8 Virtual Environments

Imagine two carpenters sharing one toolbox. One needs a 10 mm drill bit for every job; the other swaps it for a 12 mm bit and puts the 10 mm one away. Each carpenter's work is fine on its own, and every morning one of them finds the wrong bit in the box. The fix is not more care. It is a toolbox each.

Two projects need different versions of the same library. Without isolation, one of them is broken. A virtual environment is the isolation, and it is far simpler than its reputation: a directory with its own site-packages, a pyvenv.cfg file, and symlinks to an existing interpreter.

Two terms from that sentence:

  • site-packages is the folder that holds installed third-party packages (§11.2). A venv has its own, so packages installed into it do not touch anyone else's.
  • A symlink (symbolic link) is a file that points at another file, like a shortcut on a desktop. The venv's python is a shortcut to the real interpreter, not a copy of it.

The everyday commands:

python3 -m venv .venv          # create
source .venv/bin/activate      # Linux/macOS
.venv\Scripts\activate         # Windows
deactivate                     # leave

The interesting part is what the first command made. Open the configuration file it wrote:

$ cat .venv/pyvenv.cfg
home = /usr/bin
include-system-site-packages = false
version = 3.14.4
executable = /usr/bin/python3.14
command = /usr/bin/python3 -m venv /home/ada/project/.venv

That file is the virtual environment. When the interpreter at .venv/bin/python starts, it finds pyvenv.cfg next to itself, sets sys.prefix to the venv and sys.base_prefix to home, and builds sys.path with the venv's site-packages instead of the system one. The standard library still comes from the base installation — a venv copies almost nothing.

Reading the file line by line:

  • home is the folder of the real Python this venv borrows.
  • include-system-site-packages = false means packages installed globally are invisible inside the venv. That is what makes it isolated.
  • version, executable and command record which Python made it and how. Python ignores them at startup; they are notes for people and tools.
$ .venv/bin/python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix); print(sys.base_prefix)"
/home/ada/project/.venv
/usr

sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix is the reliable test for "am I in a virtual environment", and it works without activation.

The paths in those two transcripts come from the Linux machine this course was first written on. Yours will differ, so here is the same experiment as a program that works anywhere. It creates a venv with the standard library's venv module and asks the venv's own Python the question:

import subprocess, tempfile, pathlib, venv

folder = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / ".venv"
builder = venv.EnvBuilder(with_pip=False)     # skip pip: faster, same structure
builder.create(folder)
python = builder.ensure_directories(folder).env_exec_cmd

cfg = (folder / "pyvenv.cfg").read_text().splitlines()
print("pyvenv.cfg keys:", [line.split(" = ")[0] for line in cfg])

check = "import sys; print('in a venv:', sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix)"
print(subprocess.run([python, "-c", check], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip())

pyvenv.cfg keys: ['home', 'include-system-site-packages', 'version', 'executable', 'command']
in a venv: True

Line by line:

  • venv.EnvBuilder(...).create(folder) does what python -m venv does. with_pip=False skips installing pip into it, which saves a few seconds and changes nothing else about the structure.
  • env_exec_cmd is the path of the venv's own Python: .venv/bin/python on Linux and macOS, .venv\Scripts\python.exe on Windows. Asking the builder avoids guessing.
  • The keys of pyvenv.cfg are the five you just read.
  • Run through that Python, sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix is True, and nothing was activated.

Activation is only convenience. All activate does is prepend .venv/bin to $PATH (and set VIRTUAL_ENV), so that python and pip resolve to the venv's copies. .venv/bin/python -m pip install requests does exactly the same thing with no activation at all — which is what you want in a Dockerfile (the recipe for a Docker container, §8.6), a systemd unit (a Linux service definition) or a cron job (a scheduled task), where there is no shell to activate anything in.

$PATH is the list of folders your shell searches when you type a command name, much as sys.path is the list Python searches for a module. Putting .venv/bin at the front means that typing python finds the venv's Python first. That is all "activated" means, and deactivate simply puts $PATH back.

Four rules that prevent the usual mess:

  • One venv per project, in the project, named .venv, and git-ignored. Every tool looks for that name.
  • Never sudo pip install. It writes into the interpreter your operating system depends on. Modern Python refuses anyway: the externally-managed-environment error (PEP 668) exists precisely to stop this, and --break-system-packages is named as a warning, not a suggestion.
  • Do not commit the venv. It contains absolute paths and platform-specific binaries (compiled files that only work on one kind of machine). Commit the lockfile (§11.11) instead.
  • python -m pip, not pip. It guarantees the pip you run belongs to the interpreter you mean. A bare pip on $PATH may belong to something else entirely.

The reasons behind each rule, in plain words:

  • "Git-ignored" means listed in .gitignore, so version control never stores it. (Git is the version-control tool most projects use: it records the history of your files, and each saved snapshot of changes is a commit.) The .venv name is a convention that editors and tools look for automatically.
  • On Linux and macOS, the operating system's own tools are often written in Python. Replacing a library they rely on can break the system itself, which is why it refuses.
  • A venv is cheap to rebuild and specific to one machine. What you share is the description of what goes in it, and §11.9-§11.12 are about that description.
  • python -m pip runs pip as a module of that exact Python, so packages land where that Python will find them. A bare pip is whichever pip comes first on $PATH.

For throwaway command-line tools, pipx (or uv tool install) installs each into its own private venv and puts only the entry point on $PATH — the right way to install ruff, httpie or black globally without them sharing dependencies.

11.9 pyproject.toml

A packet of food carries a label: what it is, what is in it, how to cook it, who made it. A shop does not need to open the packet to know all that. pyproject.toml is that label for a Python project.

pyproject.toml (PEP 518/621) is the single declarative description of a Python project: what it is, what it needs, how to build it, and how its tools are configured. It replaced setup.py, setup.cfg, requirements.txt and a scattering of tool-specific dotfiles.

"Declarative" means it describes the project instead of running code to set it up. The older setup.py was a Python program, so installing a package meant running a stranger's code just to learn its name. A TOML file can be read without running anything. TOML is a simple configuration format: key = value lines grouped under [section] headings.

[build-system]                       # who builds this, and what they need
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]                            # PEP 621 metadata — backend-independent
name = "textwrangler"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Tidy up messy text files."
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
license = "MIT"
authors = [{ name = "Ada Lovelace", email = "ada@example.com" }]
dependencies = ["click>=8.1"]

[project.optional-dependencies]      # extras: pip install textwrangler[fast]
fast = ["orjson>=3.9"]

[dependency-groups]                  # PEP 735: for developers, never installed by users
dev = ["pytest>=8", "mypy>=1.11", "ruff>=0.6"]

[project.scripts]                    # becomes a `wrangle` command on PATH
wrangle = "textwrangler.cli:main"

[project.urls]
Homepage = "https://github.com/ada/textwrangler"

[tool.ruff]                          # tool config lives here too
line-length = 100

Three tables, three jobs. [build-system] is read first, by the frontend (pip, uv, build), which installs those requirements into an isolated environment and hands control to the named backend — hatchling, setuptools, flit_core, pdm-backend, uv_build, or maturin for Rust extensions. [project] is standardised metadata that every backend understands identically. [tool.*] is a namespace each tool owns; ruff, mypy, pytest and coverage all read their configuration from here.

A "table" is TOML's name for a [section]. Two roles in that paragraph are worth separating, because they are easy to blur:

  • A frontend is the tool you type: pip install ., python -m build, uv build. It reads [build-system] and sets things up.
  • A backend is the library that actually turns your source folder into an installable package. The frontend calls it. You choose one by name in build-backend and rarely think about it again.

Think of the frontend as the shop counter where you place an order, and the backend as the workshop behind it that makes the thing. Any counter can send work to any workshop, because the order form between them is standardised.

The other tables, read top to bottom:

  • requires-python = ">=3.11" tells installers which Python versions the project supports. pip refuses to install it on an older one.
  • dependencies are what the project needs to run. Every install gets them. §11.11 explains the >=8.1 part.
  • [project.optional-dependencies] declares extras: groups of additional dependencies a user can opt into with square brackets, as in pip install textwrangler[fast].
  • [dependency-groups] lists tools for people working on the project: test runners, linters, type checkers. They are never part of the published package.
  • [project.scripts] turns a function into a terminal command. §11.13 shows what that creates.

Use the src layout.

textwrangler/
├── pyproject.toml
├── README.md
├── src/
│   └── textwrangler/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       └── cli.py
└── tests/
    └── test_cli.py

Putting the package under src/ means the project directory is not on sys.path, so your tests cannot accidentally import the source tree instead of the installed package. That sounds pedantic until a package ships with a missing module that every local test passed against, because the tests were importing the working copy rather than the wheel. The src layout makes that failure impossible.

A car maker does not test the prototype on the designer's desk and then ship whatever came off the production line. It tests a car that came off the line. The src layout makes your tests do the same: they import the installed package, which is built the same way your users' copy will be. The alternative, with the package folder right next to pyproject.toml, is called the flat layout, and it lets tests quietly use the desk prototype.

Install it into the active venv in editable mode, which is how you work on it:

python -m pip install -e .              # editable: code changes take effect immediately
python -m pip install -e ".[fast]"      # with an extra
python -m pip install --group dev       # PEP 735 group (pip 25.1+)

Editable installs work by putting a pointer in site-packages that leads back to src/. Nothing is copied, so there is no stale-copy problem — but note that newly added entry points and metadata changes still need a re-install, because those are recorded in the .dist-info directory at install time.

Measured with hatchling and pip 26.2 on Python 3.14, an editable install of the project above leaves exactly two entries in the venv's site-packages:

  • textwrangler-0.1.0.dist-info, a folder of metadata: the name, version, dependencies and entry points, recorded at install time.
  • _editable_impl_textwrangler.pth, a one-line text file whose only content is the path of the project's src/ folder.

A .pth file is a small text file in site-packages. At startup, Python's site module reads every one and adds each path it finds to sys.path. So the editable install is a bookmark rather than a photocopy: Python follows it to your working folder, and edits to the code there show up on the next run. Other backends do the same job with a small import hook (§11.7) instead of a .pth file; the effect for you is the same.

11.10 Building: sdist and Wheel

Furniture can reach your home in two ways. A flat-pack box holds the parts and the instructions, and you need tools and time to assemble it. Or it arrives already assembled, and you just put it in place. Python packages travel in both forms.

Two distribution formats, and the difference matters.

An sdist (textwrangler-0.1.0.tar.gz) is the source: your package, pyproject.toml, README, and a PKG-INFO. Installing one requires running the build backend on the target machine.

A wheel (textwrangler-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl) is the built artefact, the finished file a build produces: a zip file whose contents are laid straight into site-packages. No build step, no arbitrary code executed at install time. Wheels are why installing is fast.

"sdist" is short for source distribution. The flat-pack box is the sdist: everything needed to build the package, plus a PKG-INFO file with the same metadata as pyproject.toml in a standard format. The assembled piece is the wheel. For a pure-Python project "assembling" is quick, but for a package with C or Rust code it means compiling, which needs a compiler on the machine doing it.

The standard tool that makes both is called build:

python -m pip install build
python -m build              # writes both into dist/

$ python -m build
* Creating isolated environment: venv+pip...
* Installing packages in isolated environment:
  - hatchling
* Getting build dependencies for sdist...
* Building sdist...
* Building wheel from sdist
Successfully built textwrangler-0.1.0.tar.gz and textwrangler-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl

That transcript is shortened. Recent versions of build print a few more lines after "Building wheel from sdist", because they set up a second isolated environment for the wheel step, but the order is the same.

Note the third line: build makes the wheel from the sdist, not from your working directory. That catches the most common packaging bug — a file that works locally because it is on disk and is missing from the distribution.

Put in furniture terms: build packs the flat-pack box first, then assembles the wheel using only what is in the box. If a part never made it into the box, the assembly fails now, on your machine, rather than later on a user's.

A wheel is a zip; open it.

$ unzip -l dist/textwrangler-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
textwrangler/__init__.py
textwrangler/cli.py
textwrangler/filters.py
textwrangler-0.1.0.dist-info/METADATA
textwrangler-0.1.0.dist-info/WHEEL
textwrangler-0.1.0.dist-info/entry_points.txt
textwrangler-0.1.0.dist-info/RECORD

Note what is not there: no src/ (the backend strips it), no tests/, no pyproject.toml. METADATA holds the [project] table rendered into the standard format, RECORD lists every file with a SHA-256 hash (a fingerprint of the file's bytes, §11.11) and a size, and WHEEL describes the format itself.

Installing a wheel is therefore mostly unzipping. The package folder goes into site-packages, the .dist-info folder goes next to it so tools can later ask "what is installed, and which version?", and RECORD tells pip exactly which files to delete when you uninstall.

The filename is structured — {name}-{version}-{python tag}-{abi tag}-{platform tag}.whl:

Filename Means
textwrangler-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl pure Python, any Python 3, any platform — one wheel serves everyone
numpy-2.3.5-cp314-cp314-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl compiled for CPython 3.14 on 64-bit Linux
numpy-2.3.5-cp314-cp314t-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl the t suffix is the free-threaded build (§8.8)

Because the parts are separated by hyphens, the name splits apart with one line of code:

filename = "numpy-2.3.5-cp314-cp314-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl"
name, version, python_tag, abi_tag, platform_tag = filename.removesuffix(".whl").split("-")
print("project: ", name, version)
print("python:  ", python_tag)
print("abi:     ", abi_tag)
print("platform:", platform_tag)

project:  numpy 2.3.5
python:   cp314
abi:      cp314
platform: manylinux_2_28_x86_64

What each tag means:

  • The python tag says which Python can run it. py3 is any Python 3; cp314 is CPython 3.14 specifically, because compiled code is built against one version.
  • The ABI tag names the binary interface the compiled code expects. ABI (application binary interface) is the low-level agreement between compiled code and the interpreter about how data is laid out in memory. none means there is no compiled code, so no agreement is needed.
  • The platform tag names the operating system and processor. manylinux_2_28_x86_64 means any Linux whose C library (glibc) is version 2.28 or newer, which covers most Linux distributions (Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora and the rest) released since about 2019, on 64-bit Intel or AMD chips. any means anywhere.

(The split works because a project name inside a wheel filename never contains a hyphen: hyphens in the name are written as underscores there.)

pip picks the most specific wheel matching your interpreter and platform, and falls back to the sdist only if there is none — which is when you discover you need a C compiler. When a compiled dependency has no wheel for your platform, that is the reason, and the fix is a different platform, an older version, or a manylinux wheel from the maintainers.

So the error you meet in practice is usually a long compiler failure while installing something like a database driver on a brand-new Python version. It does not mean the package is broken. It means nobody has published an assembled wheel for your exact combination yet, and pip fell back to the flat-pack box.

11.11 Dependencies, Constraints and Lockfiles

A shopping list says "milk". The receipt says "Brand X semi-skimmed, 2 litres, barcode 5012345678900, £1.45". Both are about milk, and they answer different questions: the list says what you want, the receipt says exactly what you got. Python projects need both.

A dependency specifier is a name plus an optional constraint (PEP 508).

Specifier Means
click any version — almost never what you want
click>=8.1 8.1 or newer, no upper bound
click>=8.1,<9 the usual shape: allow fixes, exclude the next major
click~=8.1.2 compatible release: >=8.1.2,<8.2.0
click==8.1.7 exactly this — correct for an application's lockfile, wrong in a library
orjson; python_version < "3.13" an environment marker: only install where the condition holds

Two words in the table need defining:

  • A constraint is the part after the name that limits which versions are acceptable. A comma means "and": >=8.1,<9 is "at least 8.1 and below 9".
  • A major version is the first number in 8.1.7. By convention (§11.14) it only goes up when something breaks for existing users, so <9 means "nothing that might break us".

Libraries and applications need opposite policies. A library should declare the widest range it actually supports, because a hard pin in a library becomes an unresolvable conflict for anyone who depends on two libraries with different pins. An application should pin everything, transitively, so that today's deploy and next month's deploy install the same bytes.

Some definitions, because the rest of this section leans on them:

  • A library is code other people's code imports: click, httpx, requests. You never control the other packages installed beside it.
  • An application is the thing that finally runs: your website, your command-line tool, your data pipeline. You control everything installed with it.
  • To pin is to name one exact version with ==.
  • Transitively means "including the dependencies of your dependencies, all the way down". httpx needs anyio, which needs idna, and so on.

Why the library rule? Suppose library A says click==8.1.7 and library B says click==8.1.8. An application that wants both A and B now needs two versions of click at once, and Python can only load one. The installer gives up. If A and B had said click>=8.1,<9, one version would satisfy both.

That second requirement is what a lockfile is for. pyproject.toml states intent (click>=8.1); the lockfile records the resolution (click==8.1.7, plus every transitive dependency, plus a hash of each artefact). You commit both, and the difference between them is exactly the difference between "what we need" and "what we tested".

Resolution is the installer's job of picking one exact version of every package that satisfies all the constraints at once. The lockfile is the receipt of that job. Here is one entry from uv.lock, the lockfile uv writes (§11.12):

[[package]]
name = "httpx"
version = "0.28.1"
source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" }
dependencies = [
    { name = "anyio" },
    { name = "certifi" },
    { name = "httpcore" },
    { name = "idna" },
]
sdist = { url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/.../httpx-0.28.1.tar.gz", hash = "sha256:6..." }
wheels = [
    { url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/.../httpx-0.28.1-py3-none-any.whl", hash = "sha256:d..." },
]

Reading the entry:

  • version = "0.28.1" is the pin, and source says which package index it came from.
  • dependencies lists what httpx itself needs. Each of those has its own [[package]] entry further down the file, which is what makes the lock transitive.
  • sdist and wheels give the download address and the hash of each file. (The hashes are cut short here for space; real ones are 64 characters.)

Those hashes are the security property, not a detail. An install from a lockfile verifies each downloaded file against a hash you committed, so a compromised (hacked) index or a re-uploaded artefact fails the install rather than shipping.

A hash is a short fingerprint computed from every byte of a file. Change a single byte and the fingerprint changes completely. It works like a tamper-evident seal on a jar: you cannot see inside, but you can tell at once whether anyone opened it. This program shows the check an installer does:

import hashlib

wheel = b"PK... the bytes of httpx-0.28.1-py3-none-any.whl ..."
locked = hashlib.sha256(wheel).hexdigest()          # what the lockfile records

download = wheel                                    # an honest download
tampered = wheel.replace(b"httpx", b"httpz")        # one letter changed
print("honest download matches:  ", hashlib.sha256(download).hexdigest() == locked)
print("tampered download matches:", hashlib.sha256(tampered).hexdigest() == locked)
print("hash length in hex digits:", len(locked))

honest download matches:   True
tampered download matches: False
hash length in hex digits: 64

Line by line:

  • hashlib.sha256(...).hexdigest() computes the SHA-256 fingerprint as 64 hexadecimal digits. That is what the lockfile stores.
  • An honest download has the same bytes, so the same fingerprint.
  • Changing one letter produces a completely different fingerprint, and the installer refuses the file. Nobody can change a file and keep its hash.

A hand-written requirements.txt is not a lockfile. It usually lists direct dependencies only, with loose constraints and no hashes, so two installs a month apart can differ in dozens of transitive packages. The tools that do produce real lockfiles are uv (uv.lock), pip-tools (pip-compile → a fully pinned, hashed requirements.txt), poetry (poetry.lock) and pdm (pdm.lock). Pick one; the failure mode is not choosing.

In shopping terms, a hand-written requirements.txt is a second shopping list, not a receipt. "Direct dependencies" are only the ones you named yourself; the packages they need are left for the installer to choose afresh each time, which is exactly how two installs drift apart.

One more rule decides whether two spellings name the same project. Installers compare names after normalising them (PEP 503): lower case, and any run of -, _ or . becomes a single -.

import re

def normalise(name):
    """How installers compare project names (PEP 503)."""
    return re.sub(r"[-_.]+", "-", name).lower()

for name in ("csvkit-lite", "csvkit_lite", "CSVKit.Lite", "csvkit--lite"):
    print(f"{name:14} -> {normalise(name)}")

csvkit-lite    -> csvkit-lite
csvkit_lite    -> csvkit-lite
CSVKit.Lite    -> csvkit-lite
csvkit--lite   -> csvkit-lite

All four spellings are the same project to pip. So pip install CSVKit.Lite and csvkit_lite>=1.0 in a constraint both find it, and nobody can upload a separate project called csvkit_lite to pretend to be yours.

11.12 uv

Think of a coffee table covered in remote controls: one for the television, one for the sound bar, one for the streaming box. A universal remote does all their jobs with one set of buttons. uv is the universal remote of Python packaging.

uv is a package and project manager written in Rust that replaces pip, venv, pip-tools, pipx and pyenv behind one command, and is fast enough to change how you work — resolution and installation that took a minute take under a second, so uv sync in a hook (a command run automatically, for example before every commit, §12.12) stops being an annoyance.

The tools it replaces, each in a few words:

  • pip installs packages; venv creates virtual environments (§11.8).
  • pip-tools produces a lockfile from loose constraints (§11.11).
  • pipx installs command-line tools each in their own venv (§11.8).
  • pyenv installs several versions of Python itself side by side.

The commands you will actually type:

uv init --lib reportgen        # create a project: pyproject.toml, src/, .python-version
uv add "httpx>=0.27"           # resolve, install, update pyproject.toml AND uv.lock
uv add --dev pytest ruff mypy  # into the dev dependency group
uv remove httpx
uv sync                        # make .venv match uv.lock exactly
uv sync --frozen               # ...and fail if the lock is out of date (use this in CI)
uv lock --upgrade-package httpx
uv run pytest                  # run a command in the project env, syncing first
uv python install 3.14         # it manages interpreters too
uv tool install ruff           # pipx equivalent: isolated env, entry point on PATH
uvx ruff check .               # run a tool without installing it at all

What a few of those do behind the scenes, checked with uv 0.13:

  • uv init --lib writes pyproject.toml, a README.md, a .python-version file naming the Python to use, and a src layout (§11.9) with an empty __init__.py. The [build-system] it writes names uv's own backend, uv_build.
  • uv add --dev pytest adds pytest under a dev list in [dependency-groups], the same PEP 735 table you saw in §11.9, and installs it.
  • uv sync --frozen installs exactly what uv.lock says and refuses to update the lock, which is what a build server should do: test the receipt you committed, not a fresh shopping trip.

One warning from that check: uv init fills the authors field from your git configuration, so look at it before you publish anything.

Here is what adding one dependency looks like:

$ uv add "httpx>=0.27"
Resolved 9 packages in 412ms
Installed 8 packages in 96ms
 + anyio==4.14.2
 + certifi==2026.7.22
 + h11==0.16.0
 + httpcore==1.0.9
 + httpx==0.28.1
 + idna==3.19
 + typing-extensions==4.16.0

Reading the transcript:

  • You asked for one package and uv resolved nine: httpx plus everything it needs, all the way down. That is the transitive tree from §11.11.
  • Each + line is a package installed into .venv, with the exact version uv chose. The same versions went into uv.lock.
  • The times are in milliseconds. That speed is the reason uv spread so quickly.

The mental model differs from pip's in one important way: you do not activate a venv and install into it. You describe the project, and uv makes .venv match the lockfile whenever you run something. uv run syncs first, so the environment cannot silently drift from the file you committed. uv pip install exists as a compatibility layer for the old workflow, and it is a transition aid rather than the intended path.

Compare the two habits:

  • The pip habit: activate the venv, pip install things into it, and hope requirements.txt still matches what is installed.
  • The uv habit: edit the description (uv add, uv remove), and let uv run rebuild the environment from it every time. The environment is never the source of truth; the files are.

None of this is required knowledge for reading Python, and all of it is required for working in a team that has adopted it — which, since 2024, is a rapidly growing share of them. The concepts are the same ones in §11.11; only the speed and the convenience changed.

11.13 Entry Points

A large office building has a board in the lobby: "Accounts, 3rd floor. Legal, 5th floor." You can find any department by reading the board, without walking into every office. Entry points are that board for installed Python packages.

An entry point is a name in your package's metadata that other code can look up without importing your package first. Two kinds matter.

Console scripts turn a function into a command. wrangle = "textwrangler.cli:main" under [project.scripts] makes the installer generate an executable named wrangle in the environment's bin/ that imports textwrangler.cli and calls main(). The function takes no arguments and its return value becomes the exit code — return 1 or call sys.exit(1) to signal failure (§13.3).

The value textwrangler.cli:main reads as "the module textwrangler.cli, then the name main inside it". The colon separates the module from the object.

Nothing magic is generated. With pip 26.2 on macOS, installing the §11.9 project created this file as .venv/bin/wrangle (the first line is shortened):

#!/…/.venv/bin/python
import sys
from textwrangler.cli import main
if __name__ == '__main__':
    sys.argv[0] = sys.argv[0].removesuffix('.exe')
    sys.exit(main())

Line by line:

  • The first line, the shebang, tells the operating system which program runs this file: the venv's own Python. That is why the command works without activating anything.
  • The middle lines import your function and call it.
  • sys.exit(main()) is where "the return value becomes the exit code" comes from: whatever main() returns is handed to sys.exit. None means success, 1 means failure.
  • On Windows the installer makes a small wrangle.exe instead, which does the same job.

Plugin groups are the general form, and they are how a library lets strangers extend it. pytest finds its plugins this way, as do flake8 (a linter), sphinx (a documentation builder) and pygments (a code highlighter). Declare a group in pyproject.toml; anyone who installs a package that advertises that group is discovered automatically.

A plugin is a separate package that adds a feature to another program without that program's authors changing anything. A group is the name of the slot the plugin fits into, like the department name on the lobby board. In a plugin's pyproject.toml it looks like this:

[project.entry-points."textwrangler.filters"]
upper = "textwrangler.filters:upper"

The program below plays the installer's part by hand, then plays the host application looking for plugins:

import sys, tempfile, pathlib
from importlib.metadata import entry_points, version, distribution

# What an installer writes into site-packages. Building it by hand shows there
# is no magic here: entry points are a text file inside a .dist-info directory.
tmp = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
dist = tmp / "textwrangler-0.1.0.dist-info"
dist.mkdir()
(dist / "METADATA").write_text(
    "Metadata-Version: 2.5\nName: textwrangler\nVersion: 0.1.0\n"
    "Requires-Dist: click>=8.1\n")
(dist / "entry_points.txt").write_text(
    "[console_scripts]\nwrangle = textwrangler.cli:main\n\n"
    "[textwrangler.filters]\nupper = textwrangler.filters:upper\n")
sys.path.insert(0, str(tmp))

print("version: ", version("textwrangler"))
print("requires:", distribution("textwrangler").requires)

for ep in entry_points(group="textwrangler.filters"):
    print(f"  plugin {ep.name!r} -> module={ep.module} attr={ep.attr}")
    # ep.load() would import the module and return the object.

print("console script:", [e.value for e in entry_points(group="console_scripts", name="wrangle")])

version:  0.1.0
requires: ['click>=8.1']
  plugin 'upper' -> module=textwrangler.filters attr=upper
console script: ['textwrangler.cli:main']

Line by line:

  • The first half writes a .dist-info folder like the one a real install leaves in site-packages (§11.9): a METADATA file and an entry_points.txt file. Both are plain text.
  • version("textwrangler") and distribution(...).requires read METADATA. Notice that the textwrangler package itself does not even exist here; only its metadata does.
  • entry_points(group="textwrangler.filters") reads every installed package's entry_points.txt and returns the entries in that group. Each one knows its module and attribute but has loaded nothing.
  • The console script is just another group, called console_scripts.

The host application's side is a loop over entry_points(group=...) calling ep.load(). Note the property that makes this worth the ceremony: discovery costs no imports. Reading metadata is a file read, so an application can list twenty available plugins and import only the one that is used. importlib.metadata is also where version() comes from, which is the correct way for a package to report its own version — read it from the installed metadata rather than duplicating a string in __init__.py that will drift from pyproject.toml.

"Drift" is what happens to any fact written in two places: someone updates one and forgets the other. With version() the version lives only in pyproject.toml, and the installed package reports whatever was actually installed.

11.14 Publishing

PyPI, the Python Package Index at pypi.org, is the public library that pip install downloads from by default. Publishing means uploading your sdist and wheel there so that anyone can install them by name. A published version is like a printed book: once copies are in readers' hands, you cannot change the text; you can only print a new edition.

The tools for the upload:

python -m build                                   # dist/*.whl and dist/*.tar.gz
python -m pip install twine
twine check dist/*                                # does the README render on PyPI?
twine upload --repository testpypi dist/*         # rehearse on TestPyPI first
twine upload dist/*                               # the real thing
  • twine is the standard upload tool. twine check reads the metadata and README before anything leaves your machine.
  • TestPyPI (test.pypi.org) is a separate practice copy of PyPI. Uploads there do not affect the real index, so it is the place to rehearse your first release.

Four things to get right before the first upload.

Claim the name early; PyPI names are first-come and cannot be transferred casually. Check availability before you settle on one.

Remember the name normalisation from §11.11: my_tool, my-tool and My.Tool are one name to PyPI, so if any spelling is taken, all of them are.

Use Trusted Publishing rather than an API token. Configure your PyPI project to trust a specific GitHub Actions workflow (GitHub Actions is GitHub's built-in CI service; a workflow is one script of steps it runs) in a specific repository, and the workflow exchanges an OIDC identity for a short-lived token at publish time. There is no long-lived secret to leak, rotate (replace on a schedule), or accidentally commit. If you must use a token, scope it to the single project, never to the whole account.

In plain terms:

  • An API token is a long password-like string that lets a program upload in your name. Anyone who copies it can publish to your project until you revoke it.
  • OIDC (OpenID Connect) is a standard way for one service to vouch for another. Here, GitHub tells PyPI "this upload really comes from workflow X in repository Y", and PyPI hands out a token that works for a few minutes only.
  • So Trusted Publishing is like a guest list at a door instead of a key under the mat: there is no key to lose.

A version can never be replaced. PyPI refuses a re-upload of an existing version, deliberately, so that a hash pinned in someone's lockfile always means the same bytes. A bad release is fixed by publishing the next version. yank (PEP 592) is the intermediate tool: a yanked version stays installable for anyone who pinned it exactly, and is ignored by resolvers choosing a new version — the right response to a release with a serious bug.

Back to the printed book. You cannot recall a printed edition, but a bookshop can take it off the shelf of new copies. Yanking is exactly that: readers who already asked for that specific edition (an == pin) still get it, and anyone simply asking for "the latest" never sees it.

Version deliberately. Semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) is the default expectation: patch for fixes, minor for backwards-compatible additions, major for anything that breaks callers. Calendar versioning (2026.8.1) suits applications and things that track the outside world. Either is fine; picking neither is not, because your version number is a promise other people's constraint specifiers rely on. Use 0.x while you are still willing to break things, and deprecate with a DeprecationWarning for at least one minor release before removing anything.

"Backwards-compatible" means code that worked with the old version still works with the new one. The <9 constraints in §11.11 only make sense because maintainers keep this promise: a user who wrote click>=8.1,<9 is trusting that no 8.x release breaks them.

One practical trap: a version number is a sequence of numbers, not a string. Compared as text, 0.10.0 sorts before 0.9.0, because the character 1 comes before 9:

old, new = "0.9.0", "0.10.0"
print("as strings: ", new > old)

def as_numbers(v):
    return tuple(int(part) for part in v.split("."))

print("as numbers: ", as_numbers(new) > as_numbers(old), as_numbers(new))

as strings:  False
as numbers:  True (0, 10, 0)

Installers compare the numbers, so 0.10.0 is correctly newer than 0.9.0. Your own scripts must do the same, or use a library built for it (packaging.version is the one pip uses). Real version strings can also carry suffixes such as 1.0rc1, which is one more reason not to write that comparison by hand.

Finally, the release checklist that catches nearly everything: build, twine check, install the built wheel into a fresh venv, import it, run its console script, and only then upload. Testing the wheel rather than the working tree is the whole point — it is the only way to find out what you forgot to include.

That checklist pulls the whole section together: build makes the wheel from the sdist (§11.10), a fresh venv (§11.8) guarantees nothing from your machine leaks in, importing it proves the package is complete (§11.3, §11.9), and running the console script proves the entry point (§11.13). Each step is a small, mechanical check, and together they replace "it works on my machine" with "it works when installed".

Exercises

Exercise 11.1 — Diagnose four import failures. For each, name the mechanism and give the fix.

  1. A script that works from the project root fails with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'shop' when run from anywhere else.
  2. from .models import Order raises ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package.
  3. A colleague's machine imports a json module that is missing loads.
  4. Tests pass locally, and the published wheel is missing shop/utils.py entirely.
Solution

1. sys.path[0] is the script's directory, not the project root. It works from the root because the current directory happened to contain shop/. The fix is not sys.path.append — it is to make the project installable (pyproject.toml with the src layout) and pip install -e . into the venv. Then shop is importable from any directory, in tests, and in production, for the same reason.

2. Run it with -m. A file executed as a script has __name__ == "__main__" and no __package__, so there is no "current package" for the dot to be relative to. python -m shop.cli imports shop first and sets __package__, and the relative import resolves. The other half of the fix, if this is a CLI, is to declare a console script (§11.13) so users never type either form.

3. A json.py in the current directory shadows the standard library. PathFinder walks sys.path in order, and the script's directory is first. Confirm with python -c "import json; print(json.__file__)", then rename the file — and delete the __pycache__/json.*.pyc next to it, which will otherwise still be found. On 3.14 the error message may say so itself: consider renaming …. Note that the same trick does not work for sys, which is always compiled into the interpreter and is claimed by BuiltinImporter before sys.path is consulted at all. (math is compiled in on some builds and a separate file on others, so whether it can be shadowed depends on the build: §11.1.)

4. The tests were importing the source tree, not the package. A flat layout puts the project root on sys.path, so import shop finds the working copy and never touches what the backend actually packaged. Move to src/, and make the release check "install the wheel into a fresh venv and import it" rather than "run the tests".

The unifying idea: three of the four are the same bug. sys.path contains a directory you did not intend, and something was found there instead of where you meant.

Exercise 11.2 — Write the pyproject.toml. A library called csvkit-lite exposing a csvlite command, requiring Python 3.11+, depending on click 8.1 or newer but not 9, with an optional excel extra pulling in openpyxl, and dev tooling of pytest, ruff and mypy. Use hatchling and the src layout.

Solution 
[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
name = "csvkit-lite"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A small CSV toolkit."
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
license = "MIT"
authors = [{ name = "Your Name", email = "you@example.com" }]
dependencies = ["click>=8.1,<9"]

[project.optional-dependencies]
excel = ["openpyxl>=3.1"]

[dependency-groups]
dev = ["pytest>=8", "ruff>=0.6", "mypy>=1.11"]

[project.scripts]
csvlite = "csvkit_lite.cli:main"

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]
packages = ["src/csvkit_lite"]

Four points that are easy to get wrong.

The distribution name and the import name differ. csvkit-lite on PyPI, csvkit_lite in import. That is normal (pillow/PIL, beautifulsoup4/bs4), and the hyphen is not legal in an import name. Names are normalised for comparison — csvkit-lite, csvkit_lite and CSVKit.Lite are the same project to a resolver.

<9 belongs in a library; ==8.1.7 does not. Two libraries that both pin exactly and disagree cannot be installed together at all.

The dev tools are in [dependency-groups], not [project.optional-dependencies]. An extra is part of your published metadata — anyone can pip install csvkit-lite[dev] and it is downloaded from PyPI. A PEP 735 group is local to the source checkout and is never published, which is where test and lint tooling belongs.

The [tool.hatch...] table is needed because the distribution name does not match the directory. Hatchling infers src/csvkit_lite/ from a name of csvkit-lite in the simple cases; state it explicitly and the build cannot guess wrong.

Exercise 11.3 — Make this package cheap to import. analytics/__init__.py takes 1.4 seconds to import because of the first three lines. Rewrite it so that importing the package is fast, from analytics import load_frame still works, and analytics.CONFIG is still available.

# analytics/__init__.py
import pandas as pd
from .frames import load_frame
from .plotting import plot_series

CONFIG = _read_config_file()          # reads ~/.analytics.toml at import time
Solution 
# analytics/__init__.py
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

__all__ = ["load_frame", "plot_series", "CONFIG"]

if TYPE_CHECKING:                     # type checkers see the real names...
    from .frames import load_frame
    from .plotting import plot_series

_config = None

def __getattr__(name):                # ...and at runtime nothing is imported until used
    global _config
    if name == "load_frame":
        from .frames import load_frame
        return load_frame
    if name == "plot_series":
        from .plotting import plot_series
        return plot_series
    if name == "CONFIG":
        if _config is None:
            _config = _read_config_file()
        return _config
    raise AttributeError(f"module {__name__!r} has no attribute {name!r}")

def __dir__():
    return sorted(__all__)

import pandas disappears entirely — it was never used in __init__.py, only in frames.py, and it will be imported when frames is. That one line is usually most of the 1.4 seconds.

CONFIG becomes lazy and cached. Reading a file at import time is the more serious defect of the two: it makes import analytics fail on a machine with no config file, it makes the value impossible to override in a test, and it happens even for callers that never look at it. Deferring it to first access fixes all three.

TYPE_CHECKING keeps the tooling working. A module-level __getattr__ is invisible to a type checker, so without that block from analytics import load_frame becomes an error in mypy and loses autocompletion. The block costs nothing at runtime (§11.6).

Measure before and after with python -X importtime -c "import analytics". And note the trade-off honestly: import errors in frames.py now surface at first use rather than at import, which is worse for a small package. Lazy imports are for packages with heavy or optional dependencies, not for every __init__.py.

Exercise 11.4 — Application or library? For each decision, say which policy applies and why.

  1. Pin requests==2.32.3 in pyproject.toml.
  2. Commit uv.lock.
  3. Publish a 0.x version for a year.
  4. Add numpy to dependencies because one optional feature uses it.
Solution

1. Application: correct — but in the lockfile, not pyproject.toml. Even for an application the two files have different jobs: pyproject.toml says what you support, the lock says what you tested. Pinning in both means every upgrade is two edits. Library: wrong, and actively harmful — a hard pin propagates to every consumer and conflicts with any other library that pinned differently. Declare requests>=2.32,<3.

2. Application: yes, always. It is the artefact that makes deploys reproducible and the hashes that make them verifiable. Library: no — nothing installs your lockfile, since a consumer resolves your constraints against everything else in their tree. Committing it for local development is fine, but treat it as a dev convenience and test against the oldest versions you claim to support as well as the newest, or your lower bounds are fiction.

3. Both: fine, and honest. 0.x communicates "the interface may change". The failure is staying there indefinitely while thousands depend on you — at that point the version number is lying, and a 1.0 costs nothing.

4. Wrong for both. A dependency needed by one optional feature belongs in [project.optional-dependencies] as an extra, imported lazily (§11.7) and guarded with a clear error if missing. Putting it in dependencies forces a ~60 MB download on everyone who installs your package for the other features.

The one-line version: a library states the widest range it truly supports and pins nothing; an application pins everything and commits the lock. A project that is both — a library with a CLI — follows the library rule for its metadata and keeps a lockfile for its own CI.

SECTION 12

Testing and Code Quality

Start with the smallest test there is. The program below has a function that prices one line of a shopping cart, and a second function that checks it. Then someone "tidies up" the pricing function and accidentally drops the discount. Watch what the check does.

def line_total(price, quantity, discount=0.0):
    return round(price * quantity * (1 - discount), 2)

def test_line_total_applies_discount():
    assert line_total(10.0, 3, discount=0.1) == 27.0

test_line_total_applies_discount()
print("first version: test passed")

def line_total(price, quantity, discount=0.0):     # the "tidied" version
    return round(price * quantity, 2)              # the discount is gone

try:
    test_line_total_applies_discount()
    print("second version: test passed")
except AssertionError:
    print("second version: test FAILED, the discount is missing")

first version: test passed
second version: test FAILED, the discount is missing

Line by line:

  • line_total multiplies price by quantity and takes the discount off. Three items at 10.0 with 10% off is 27.0.
  • test_line_total_applies_discount is an ordinary function. Its one line says "this must be true". If it is, nothing happens. If it is not, assert raises AssertionError.
  • The first call passes silently, so the program prints first version: test passed.
  • Then line_total is redefined without the discount. Nobody touched the test. Calling it again now computes 30.0, the assert fails, and the except branch reports it.

That is the whole idea of a test: a small program that checks another program, and complains loudly when the answer changes. The person who "tidied" line_total did not need to remember that discounts existed. The test remembered for them.

Think of a tightrope walker's safety net. The net does not make anyone walk better. It makes it safe to try something bold, because a fall is caught. A test suite is the same thing for code: it lets you change code you no longer remember writing, and it is the difference between a codebase that gets better over time and one that nobody dares touch.

A test suite is not a box to tick. This section covers the tools professional Python projects actually run — pytest, coverage, Hypothesis, ruff, mypy, pre-commit — and, more importantly, how to use them so that a green suite means something. It runs in three parts:

  1. Writing tests (§12.1-§12.8): what makes a good test, pytest, fixtures, parametrisation, fakes and mocks, and the built-in helpers.
  2. Judging tests (§12.9-§12.10): what coverage measures, and how Hypothesis finds the inputs you never thought of.
  3. Making quality automatic (§12.11-§12.13): the linter and formatter, the git hook that runs them, and the CI pipeline that runs everything.

The pytest transcripts in this section were measured with pytest 9.1.1. A few are from a Linux machine (you can tell by platform linux and a /home/... path); the timings in them will differ on yours, and nothing else should.

12.1 What a Test Is For

A test answers one question: if I change this, will I find out that I broke it? Everything else — coverage percentages, test counts, framework choice — is only a means to that end.

The opening example is the whole cycle in miniature: the code changed, the test noticed. A test that would not have noticed is not a weak test. It is no test at all, however green it looks.

Three properties separate a suite people trust from one they learn to ignore.

Deterministic. The same code gives the same result every run. A test that fails one run in twenty trains everyone to re-run it, and then to ignore it.
Independent. Any test can run alone, and in any order. Shared mutable state between tests is the most common cause of "it passes locally".
About behaviour, not implementation. A test that asserts how a function works breaks every time you refactor, which is exactly when you needed it to hold still.

Each of those has an everyday version:

  • Deterministic. Picture a warning light on a car dashboard that flickers on at random. The first few times you pull over. After that you ignore it — including the day the engine really is overheating. A flaky test is that light.
  • Independent. Picture an exam where question 3 says "use your answer to question 2". Get question 2 wrong and question 3 fails too, for a reason that has nothing to do with question 3. Tests that rely on what an earlier test left behind fail the same way: in the wrong place, for the wrong reason.
  • About behaviour. When you check a cake, you taste it. You do not check which spoon the baker used. A test that checks which internal helper a function called is checking the spoon: change the recipe's method without changing the cake, and the test fails anyway.

Arrange, Act, Assert

The structure of a good test is Arrange, Act, Assert, in that order and visibly separated: set up the world, do the one thing under test, check one outcome. If a test has three "Act" steps it is really three tests, and when it fails you will not know which one broke.

It is the shape of a school science experiment:

  1. Arrange — set up the equipment: the inputs, the objects, any fake services.
  2. Act — do the one thing you are investigating: call the function.
  3. Assert — write down what you observed and compare it with what you expected.

Here is the opening test written out that way, with the three parts labelled:

def line_total(price, quantity, discount=0.0):
    return round(price * quantity * (1 - discount), 2)

def test_line_total_applies_discount():
    # Arrange
    price, quantity, discount = 10.0, 3, 0.1
    # Act
    total = line_total(price, quantity, discount=discount)
    # Assert
    assert total == 27.0

test_line_total_applies_discount()
print("passed")

passed

Most real tests do not need the comments; a blank line between the three parts says the same thing. What matters is that a reader can point at the one line that is "the thing being tested".

Names that explain the failure

Name tests for the behaviour they pin down. test_line_total_applies_discount tells you what broke from the failure line alone; test_1 sends you reading code.

Think of the labels on the switches in a fuse box. "Kitchen sockets" tells you what lost power the moment it trips. "Switch 7" sends you round the house trying lights. When a test fails at 2 a.m. in a CI log, its name is the only thing you read first, so make the name do the explaining.

12.2 pytest and Assertion Rewriting

The opening example ran its test by calling it by hand. Real projects have hundreds of tests, so they need a test runner: a program that finds every test, runs each one, catches the failures, and prints a report.

Python has two in common use.

  • unittest ships with Python and follows the JUnit tradition (JUnit is Java's classic test framework) — a TestCase subclass, self.assertEqual, setUp and tearDown. It works, and you will read it in older codebases.
  • pytest is a third-party package (pip install pytest). Everything new uses pytest, because a test is a plain function and an assertion is a plain assert.

Here is a small test file. It assumes a cart package with a pricing module that holds the line_total from the opening example, plus a check that rejects negative quantities.

# tests/test_pricing.py
import pytest
from cart.pricing import line_total

def test_line_total_applies_discount():
    assert line_total(10.0, 3, discount=0.1) == 27.0

def test_rejects_negative_quantity():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="negative"):
        line_total(10.0, -1)

def test_broken_on_purpose():
    order = {"id": 7, "items": ["apple", "pear"], "total": 27.0}
    assert order == {"id": 7, "items": ["apple", "plum"], "total": 27.5}

Three tests:

  • the first is the opening test again;
  • the second says "calling line_total with a negative quantity must raise ValueError, and its message must mention negative" (§12.7 explains pytest.raises);
  • the third is broken on purpose, so you can see what a failure looks like.

What a plain assert throws away

Before running it, look at the problem pytest has to solve. A bare assert in plain Python only tells you that it failed:

order = {"id": 7, "items": ["apple", "pear"], "total": 27.0}
try:
    assert order == {"id": 7, "items": ["apple", "plum"], "total": 27.5}
except AssertionError as exc:
    print("type:   ", type(exc).__name__)
    print("message:", repr(str(exc)))

type:    AssertionError
message: ''

The message is empty. Python evaluated order == {...}, got False, and raised. It did not keep the two dictionaries, so it cannot tell you which key differed. With three keys you could spot it by eye; with a 40-field API response you could not.

A bare assert normally throws away everything about why it failed. pytest gets that back by rewriting the bytecode of your test modules at import time, so a failing comparison can report both sides:

$ pytest
============================= test session starts ==============================
platform linux -- Python 3.14.4, pytest-9.1.1, pluggy-1.6.0
rootdir: /home/ada/cart
configfile: pyproject.toml
testpaths: tests
collected 3 items

tests/test_pricing.py ..F                                                [100%]

=================================== FAILURES ===================================
____________________________ test_broken_on_purpose ____________________________

    def test_broken_on_purpose():
        order = {"id": 7, "items": ["apple", "pear"], "total": 27.0}
>       assert order == {"id": 7, "items": ["apple", "plum"], "total": 27.5}
E       AssertionError: assert {'id': 7, 'it...'total': 27.0} == {'id': 7, 'it...'total': 27.5}
E
E         Omitting 1 identical items, use -vv to show
E         Differing items:
E         {'items': ['apple', 'pear']} != {'items': ['apple', 'plum']}
E         {'total': 27.0} != {'total': 27.5}
E         Use -v to get more diff

tests/test_pricing.py:13: AssertionError
=========================== short test summary info ============================
FAILED tests/test_pricing.py::test_broken_on_purpose - AssertionError: assert...
========================= 1 failed, 2 passed in 0.11s ==========================

"Rewriting the bytecode" sounds alarming, so here is what it means. When pytest imports a test file, it does not hand it to Python unchanged. It first edits each assert so that, before comparing, it saves both sides in variables. If the comparison fails, it still has them, and it can print them. Your source file is never modified; only the in-memory copy is. (It does this only for test files and conftest.py, not for your application code.)

A football referee who only blows the whistle is the bare assert. One who blows the whistle and says "offside, number 9, by half a metre" is pytest.

Reading the report from the top:

  • The header names the Python and pytest versions, the project folder, and the config file it found.
  • collected 3 items — it found three tests.
  • ..F — one character per test, in order: a dot is a pass, F is a failure. [100%] is progress through the run.
  • The FAILURES block shows the failing test's source, with > on the line that failed and E on the lines that explain it.
  • The last line is the summary you check first: 1 failed, 2 passed.

Read what it did: it identified the two differing keys out of three and hid the identical one. That diffing (working out exactly what differs) is per-type — sets report missing and extra members, strings report the first differing position, and long sequences report the index. This is why assert a == b in pytest is more informative than self.assertEqual(a, b), not less.

The flags you use every day

The flags that carry the day-to-day work:

pytest                       # everything
pytest tests/test_pricing.py::test_rejects_negative_quantity   # one test
pytest -x                    # stop at the first failure
pytest --lf                  # re-run only last-failed
pytest --ff                  # failures first, then the rest
pytest -k "discount and not slow"     # select by name substring expression
pytest -m integration        # select by marker
pytest -q                    # quiet;  -v verbose;  -vv full diffs
pytest -s                    # do not capture stdout (print() becomes visible)
pytest --pdb                 # drop into the debugger at the failure (§7.9)
pytest -p no:randomly -n auto         # disable a plugin / run on all cores (pytest-xdist)

A few of those deserve a sentence each:

  • tests/test_pricing.py::test_rejects_negative_quantity is a node id: the file, two colons, the test name. Every test has one, and the failure report prints it, so you can copy it straight back onto the command line.
  • -k takes an expression over test names. "discount and not slow" selects tests whose name contains discount and does not contain slow.
  • -m selects by marker, a label you attach with a decorator such as @pytest.mark.integration. §12.3 shows how to declare them.
  • -s matters more than it looks. pytest captures everything your tests print and shows it only for failures. If you add a print() to debug a passing test and see nothing, that is why.
  • --lf ("last failed") works because pytest remembers which tests failed last time, in a .pytest_cache folder in the project.

--lf and -x together are the tight loop: fix, re-run only what was broken, repeat. On a suite that takes five minutes, that turns each attempt into a second or two.

12.3 Discovery, Layout and Configuration

You never told pytest which functions were tests. It found them by their names.

pytest finds tests by convention: files matching test_*.py or *_test.py, functions starting with test_, and classes named Test* (without an __init__). Nothing is registered; renaming a file out of that pattern silently removes its tests from the suite, which is worth remembering when a suite mysteriously shrinks.

It works like a teacher calling the register. Only names on the list get called. A pupil whose name was misspelt on the list is never called, never marked absent, and nobody notices. Rename tests/test_pricing.py to tests/pricing_tests.py and pytest 9.1.1 prints only this:

no tests ran in 0.05s

There is no error and no warning. The one clue is the exit status: pytest exits with status 5 when it collected nothing, where a passing run exits with 0 and a run with failures exits with 1. A CI job that treats any non-zero status as failure will catch an empty suite; one that only looks for the word failed will not.

A project layout

cart/
├── pyproject.toml
├── src/cart/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   └── pricing.py
└── tests/
    ├── conftest.py            # fixtures and hooks, discovered automatically
    ├── test_pricing.py
    └── integration/
        └── test_checkout.py

Two things to notice:

  • The application lives in src/cart/ and the tests live in a separate tests/ folder beside it. Tests are not part of the package you ship.
