  • conftest.py is a special file name. pytest loads it automatically, and anything defined in it is available to every test in that folder and below. §12.4 is about what goes in it.

Configuration

Configuration belongs in pyproject.toml with everything else:

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
addopts = "-ra --strict-markers --strict-config"
markers = [
    "slow: takes more than a second",
    "integration: needs a real database",
]
filterwarnings = ["error", "ignore::DeprecationWarning:third_party.*"]

Line by line:

  • testpaths tells pytest where to look when you run it with no arguments, so it searches only that folder instead of the whole project.
  • addopts is a list of command-line flags added to every run, so nobody has to remember them.
  • markers declares every marker the project uses, with a one-line description. pytest --markers prints this list.
  • filterwarnings decides what happens to warnings raised during tests. The first entry turns every warning into an error; the second makes an exception for DeprecationWarnings coming from a third-party package you cannot fix.

Four settings that earn their place. -ra prints a summary of everything that was not a plain pass, so skips and xfails (tests marked to be skipped, or expected to fail; §12.8) stop being invisible. --strict-markers turns a typo'd marker into an error rather than a silently-never-selected test — without it, @pytest.mark.integraton is accepted and its test runs in every suite. --strict-config does the same for unknown config keys. And filterwarnings = ["error"] promotes warnings to failures, which is how you find out about a deprecation while there is still time to act rather than on the day it becomes an exception.

The marker typo is worth seeing concretely. Without --strict-markers, pytest 9.1.1 accepts @pytest.mark.integraton, runs the test, and adds a PytestUnknownMarkWarning to the warnings summary at the bottom of the report: Unknown pytest.mark.integraton - is this a typo?. The run still says passed. It is like a parcel with a misspelt label: it does not bounce, it just never reaches the shelf you were going to collect it from. pytest -m integration will never select that test, and the only sign is one line in a summary most people scroll past.

Why the src layout matters for tests

The src layout matters here for the reason given in §11.9: tests import cart the way users do, from the installed package, so a module missing from the wheel fails in CI rather than shipping. Install the project into the venv (pip install -e .) and never add sys.path manipulation to conftest.py.

In §11's terms: you want to test the car that comes off the production line, not the prototype on the designer's desk. If the tests could import straight from the folder, they would pass even when the package you ship is missing a file.

12.4 Fixtures

Most tests need something set up before they run: a temporary folder, a database with one user in it, a logged-in client. Writing that setup at the top of every test is repetitive, and forgetting to clean up afterwards breaks the "independent" rule from §12.1.

A fixture is pytest's answer. Think of a theatre's stage crew. Before each scene they put out the props; after it, they clear them away. The actors never carry furniture. Some things, like the lighting rig, are put up once for the whole run of the play, not once per scene. Fixtures work exactly like that, and the "once per scene or once per run" choice is called the fixture's scope.

A fixture is a function whose return value is injected (handed in automatically) into any test that names it as a parameter. It replaces setUp/tearDown with something composable: fixtures can request other fixtures, and each is created once per whatever scope you give it.

Setup and teardown with yield

Fixtures use yield, the generator keyword from §5.3. Everything before the yield is setup, the yielded value is handed to the test, and everything after is teardown. You can see the mechanism without pytest at all, by driving a generator by hand the way pytest does:

def database():
    print("start database")
    yield {"users": []}             # the value the test receives
    print("stop database")

steps = database()                  # calling a generator function runs nothing yet
db = next(steps)                    # run up to the yield: the setup
print("the test sees:", db)
next(steps, None)                   # run the rest: the teardown

start database
the test sees: {'users': []}
stop database

Line by line:

  • database() creates a generator object but runs none of its body; as §5.3 showed, a generator does nothing until the first next().
  • next(steps) runs the body up to yield and returns the yielded dict. That is the setup.
  • The test would run here. This program just prints what it was given.
  • next(steps, None) resumes the generator after the yield, which runs the teardown. The None stops next from raising StopIteration when the generator finishes.

pytest does those three steps for you, and it does the last one even when the test fails.

Fixtures in pytest

Here is the real thing: two fixtures in conftest.py and two tests that use them.

# tests/conftest.py — fixtures here are available to every test below this directory
import pytest

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def database():
    print("\n  [session] start database")
    yield {"users": []}                    # everything before yield is setup
    print("\n  [session] stop database")   # everything after is teardown

@pytest.fixture
def user(database):                        # fixtures compose: this one requests another
    record = {"name": "ada"}
    database["users"].append(record)
    yield record
    database["users"].remove(record)       # runs even if the test fails

# tests/test_fx.py
def test_one(user, database):
    assert database["users"] == [user]

def test_two(user, database):
    assert len(database["users"]) == 1     # the previous test cleaned up after itself

How the pieces connect:

  • @pytest.fixture marks a function as a fixture. scope="session" means "create it once for the whole test run".
  • The user fixture names database as a parameter, so pytest creates database first and passes it in. That is what "fixtures compose" means.
  • Each test names the fixtures it needs as parameters. pytest reads the parameter names, builds those fixtures, and calls the test with them. You never call a fixture yourself.
  • user has the default scope, function, so it is created fresh for each test and removed again afterwards.

--setup-show prints the lifecycle, which is the fastest way to understand what is being created and when:

$ pytest --setup-show -q
SETUP    S database
        SETUP    F user (fixtures used: database)
        tests/test_fx.py::test_one (fixtures used: database, user) .
        TEARDOWN F user
        SETUP    F user (fixtures used: database)
        tests/test_fx.py::test_two (fixtures used: database, user) .
        TEARDOWN F user
TEARDOWN S database
2 passed in 0.05s

S is session scope, F is function scope. The expensive thing is built once; the per-test state is built and destroyed around each test. That combination — share what is slow, isolate what is mutable — is the entire art of fixtures.

Read it as a stage diary: the lighting rig (database) goes up once, at the start. Before each scene the props (user) go out; after each scene they are cleared. The rig comes down after the last scene.

Choosing a scope

Scope Created once per Use for
function (default) each test anything mutable
class test class rare
module test file a moderately expensive read-only resource
package test package same, one level up
session whole run database container, browser, loaded model (for example a machine-learning model read into memory)

The rule of thumb is one question: can a test change this? If it can, give it function scope, so each test starts clean. If it cannot and it is slow to build, share it with a wider scope.

The teardown must be in the fixture, not the test. The code after yield runs whether the test passed, failed, or raised — that is the guarantee. A try/finally in a test does not cover a failure in setup.

Two more tools

Two more capabilities worth knowing. request.addfinalizer(fn) registers extra cleanup at runtime, and @pytest.fixture(params=[...]) makes a parametrised fixture: every test using it runs once per parameter, which is how you run a whole suite against three database backends (database systems, such as SQLite and PostgreSQL) without touching the tests.

  • request is itself a built-in fixture: an object describing the test that is asking. addfinalizer is useful when you only discover during setup that something needs cleaning up, such as a file you decided to create halfway through.
  • A parametrised fixture is the stage crew building the same scene in three different theatres. The actors do the same play each time; only the venue changes.

Sharing fixtures with conftest.py

conftest.py is the mechanism for sharing. It is discovered automatically by directory — a fixture in tests/conftest.py is visible to every test under tests/, and one in tests/integration/conftest.py only to that subtree. Never import it; never put tests in it.

So in the layout from §12.3, a fixture that only the integration tests need — a real database connection, say — goes in tests/integration/conftest.py, and the quick unit tests never pay for it.

12.5 Parametrisation

Often you want to check one function against a table of inputs and answers. Copying the test five times is tedious, and a loop inside one test has a worse problem: the first failing row stops the loop, and the report says only "the test failed", not which row.

One test body, many cases. The point is not brevity — it is that each case is reported separately, so a failure names the input that broke.

Think of one marking scheme applied to a pile of exam papers. The scheme is written once. Each paper still gets its own mark, and a fail on one paper says which student it was.

import pytest
from cart.pricing import line_total

@pytest.mark.parametrize("price, quantity, discount, expected", [
    (10.0, 1, 0.0, 10.0),
    (10.0, 3, 0.1, 27.0),
    (0.0, 5, 0.5, 0.0),
    pytest.param(19.99, 2, 0.25, 29.98, id="float-rounding"),
])
def test_line_total(price, quantity, discount, expected):
    assert line_total(price, quantity, discount) == expected

How to read the decorator:

  • The first argument is a string naming the parameters, separated by commas. They must match the test function's parameter names.
  • The second argument is a list of rows. Each tuple is one case, with values in the same order as the names.
  • pytest calls test_line_total once per row.
$ pytest -v
tests/test_param.py::test_line_total[10.0-1-0.0-10.0] PASSED             [ 25%]
tests/test_param.py::test_line_total[10.0-3-0.1-27.0] PASSED             [ 50%]
tests/test_param.py::test_line_total[0.0-5-0.5-0.0] PASSED               [ 75%]
tests/test_param.py::test_line_total[float-rounding] PASSED              [100%]

============================== 4 passed in 0.03s ===============================

Four independent test cases, each with an id you can pass straight back to pytest to re-run it alone. pytest.param(..., id=...) replaces the auto-generated id, and takes marks= too — pytest.param(..., marks=pytest.mark.xfail) marks a single case as expected-to-fail without splitting the test up.

The id in square brackets is built from the row's values joined by hyphens, 10.0-1-0.0-10.0. That works for short numbers and becomes unreadable for long strings or objects, which is when an explicit id= pays for itself.

The case that teaches something

That last case is a real result and worth pausing on: 19.99 * 2 * 0.75 displays as 29.985, and round(...) of it is 29.98, not 29.99. The stored float is fractionally below 29.985, so there is nothing to round up. This is not a pytest quirk; it is §1 arithmetic showing up where it will actually cost you money. For currency, keep integer cents or decimal.Decimal — and note that a parametrised table is exactly how you would pin that decision down.

You can see the hidden digits by asking Decimal for the exact value the float holds:

from decimal import Decimal

amount = 19.99 * 2 * (1 - 0.25)
print(amount)
print(round(amount, 2))
print(Decimal(amount))

29.985
29.98
29.9849999999999994315658113919198513031005859375

Line by line:

  • print(amount) shows 29.985, because Python prints the shortest decimal that maps back to the same float.
  • round(amount, 2) gives 29.98. A shopkeeper rounding 29.985 by hand would write 29.99.
  • Decimal(amount) reveals why: the value really stored is a hair below 29.985, so rounding down is correct for the number the computer actually has.

The test row with id="float-rounding" records that behaviour on purpose. If someone later "fixes" line_total to round differently, the row with the name float-rounding is the one that fails, and its name says what the argument was about.

Stacked parametrize decorators

Stacking two parametrize decorators produces the cross-product, which is occasionally what you want and more often an accident:

@pytest.mark.parametrize("currency", ["eur", "usd"])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("quantity", [1, 2, 3])
def test_matrix(currency, quantity):        # 6 cases
    ...

Two currencies times three quantities is six cases. Add a third decorator with four values and it is twenty-four. That grows fast, so stack decorators only when every combination really is worth checking.

Keep the case table data, not logic. If a parametrised test needs an if on which case it is in, it is two tests wearing one coat.

12.6 Test Doubles: monkeypatch, Mock, and Where to Patch

Real code talks to networks, clocks and filesystems. A test double replaces one of those with something predictable. Python offers three tools, in increasing order of power and of the damage they can do.

The name comes from film. A stunt double stands in for the actor in the scenes where the real one would be dangerous, slow or expensive. In a test, the dangerous scene might be charging a real credit card; the slow one, calling a server on another continent; the unpredictable one, asking the clock what time it is.

The simplest double: a fake you write yourself

Before reaching for any library, notice that the simplest double is an ordinary class. Here is a checkout function that saves orders through a "repository" — an object with save and get methods — and an in-memory version of that repository for tests:

class InMemoryOrders:
    def __init__(self):
        self._rows = {}

    def save(self, order_id, total):
        self._rows[order_id] = total

    def get(self, order_id):
        return self._rows[order_id]

def place_order(repo, order_id, prices):
    total = sum(prices)
    repo.save(order_id, total)
    return total

repo = InMemoryOrders()
place_order(repo, "A1", [500, 250])
print("stored total:", repo.get("A1"))

stored total: 750

In production, repo would be a class that talks to PostgreSQL, a widely used database server. In the test it is a dictionary with two methods. place_order cannot tell the difference, because it only ever calls save. This kind of double is called a fake: a working, simplified implementation. It needs no special library, and because it really stores and returns data, the test checks real behaviour.

When writing a fake is too much work, or the thing you need to replace is buried inside code you cannot pass arguments to, the three tools below take over.

monkeypatch

monkeypatch is the pytest fixture for setting an attribute, dict item or environment variable for the duration of one test, and putting it back afterwards. It is the right default because the undo is automatic.

def test_uses_configured_region(monkeypatch, tmp_path):
    monkeypatch.setenv("AWS_REGION", "eu-west-1")
    monkeypatch.setattr("cart.pricing.TAX_RATE", 0.2)
    monkeypatch.delenv("AWS_PROFILE", raising=False)
    monkeypatch.chdir(tmp_path)
    ...

Line by line:

  • setenv sets an environment variable for this test only.
  • setattr("cart.pricing.TAX_RATE", 0.2) replaces a module-level constant. The string form names the module and the attribute in one go.
  • delenv(..., raising=False) removes a variable if it happens to be set on the machine running the tests, and does not complain if it is not.
  • chdir(tmp_path) changes the current directory into a fresh temporary folder (tmp_path is another built-in fixture, §12.8).

When the test ends, pass or fail, every one of those changes is reversed. It is like a hotel room: rearrange the furniture as much as you like, and housekeeping puts it back before the next guest.

unittest.mock

unittest.mock is the standard library's recording stand-in. A MagicMock accepts any call and any attribute, records everything, and can be interrogated afterwards.

Think of a stand-in actor at a rehearsal who will say any line you hand them, and who keeps a notebook of every line they were asked to say. Afterwards you can ask: "were you asked to say this, exactly once?"

from unittest.mock import MagicMock, create_autospec

gateway = MagicMock(name="gateway")
gateway.charge.return_value = {"id": "ch_1", "status": "succeeded"}

result = gateway.charge(amount=1999, currency="eur")
print("returned:", result)
print("called once:", gateway.charge.call_count == 1)
gateway.charge.assert_called_once_with(amount=1999, currency="eur")
print("call args:", gateway.charge.call_args)

# side_effect: a sequence of results, or an exception to raise
gateway.refund.side_effect = [{"status": "ok"}, TimeoutError("gateway down")]
print("first refund:", gateway.refund("ch_1"))
try:
    gateway.refund("ch_2")
except TimeoutError as exc:
    print("second refund raised:", exc)

# The trap: a bare MagicMock invents whatever you ask for, including your typos.
loose = MagicMock()
print("typo silently 'works':", bool(loose.chrage(1999)))

class Gateway:
    def charge(self, amount: int, currency: str) -> dict: ...

strict = create_autospec(Gateway, instance=True)
try:
    strict.chrage(1999)
except AttributeError as exc:
    print("autospec catches it:", exc)
try:
    strict.charge(1999)                      # missing a required argument
except TypeError as exc:
    print("autospec checks the signature:", exc)

returned: {'id': 'ch_1', 'status': 'succeeded'}
called once: True
call args: call(amount=1999, currency='eur')
first refund: {'status': 'ok'}
second refund raised: gateway down
typo silently 'works': True
autospec catches it: Mock object has no attribute 'chrage'
autospec checks the signature: missing a required argument: 'currency'

The program in four parts:

  1. Scripting an answer. gateway.charge.return_value = {...} says "whenever charge is called, return this". Notice that gateway.charge did not exist until it was mentioned; the mock created it on the spot.
  2. Checking the notebook. call_count, assert_called_once_with and call_args ask what happened. assert_called_once_with raises AssertionError if the call was missing, repeated, or had different arguments, so it works as a test assertion.
  3. A sequence of answers. side_effect set to a list returns one item per call. An exception in the list is raised instead of returned, which is how you test "what does my code do when the gateway times out?" without waiting for a real timeout.
  4. The trap. loose.chrage(1999) is a typo for charge, and it "works": the mock invents chrage too, returns another mock, and that mock is truthy. create_autospec(Gateway, instance=True) builds a mock from the real class instead, so it refuses methods Gateway does not have and checks arguments against the real signature.

That contrast is the single most important thing to know about mock. A bare MagicMock cannot fail an assertion about a method that does not exist, so a suite full of them keeps passing after you rename the real method — the worst possible outcome, since it is green and wrong. create_autospec (or patch(..., autospec=True)) builds the double from the real object's signature, so a rename breaks the test the way it should.

In rehearsal terms, the bare MagicMock is the stand-in who will happily say lines that are not in the script. create_autospec is an understudy who has learned the real script: hand them a line that is not in it and they stop the rehearsal.

Where to patch

Often the object to replace is not passed in as an argument; the code under test reaches for it by name. unittest.mock.patch swaps that name for a mock for the length of a with block. The question is which name.

Where to patch. patch replaces a name in a namespace, and the name that matters is the one the code under test looks up, not the one where the function is defined.

import sys, tempfile, pathlib, textwrap
from unittest.mock import patch

root = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(root / "clock.py").write_text("def now():\n    return 'REAL TIME'\n")
(root / "billing.py").write_text(textwrap.dedent("""
    from clock import now              # bound into billing's namespace at import time

    def stamp():
        return f"invoice at {now()}"
"""))
sys.path.insert(0, str(root))
import billing

print("unpatched:", billing.stamp())

with patch("clock.now", return_value="FAKE"):            # patches the wrong name
    print("patching clock.now:  ", billing.stamp())

with patch("billing.now", return_value="FAKE"):          # patches where it is used
    print("patching billing.now:", billing.stamp())

unpatched: invoice at REAL TIME
patching clock.now:   invoice at REAL TIME
patching billing.now: invoice at FAKE

The setup writes two tiny modules into a temporary folder, the same trick as §11's opening example. clock.py has a function now; billing.py imports it with from clock import now and uses it.

from clock import now copied the function object into billing's globals when billing was imported (§11.1). Rebinding clock.now afterwards changes nothing that billing can see. Patch where it is used, not where it is defined — or write import clock and call clock.now(), which makes the lookup happen at call time and both patches work.

An everyday version. A colleague copies your phone number into their own address book. Later you change your number in the company directory. Your colleague still dials the number in their book, and reaches the old phone. To redirect their calls you must change the entry in their address book — the one they actually read. from clock import now is the colleague copying the number; billing.now is their address book entry; patch("billing.now", ...) edits it. This is §1's "names are sticky labels" again: billing.now and clock.now are two labels on one function, and patch moves one label.

Choosing a double

Use the least powerful double that answers the question. In order: a real object; a simple fake you wrote (a dict-backed repository, an in-memory queue); monkeypatch; create_autospec; a bare MagicMock. Every step up buys convenience and pays in tests that pass when the code is broken. And do not mock what you do not own — wrap the third-party client in your own thin interface and fake that, so a change in their API breaks one adapter test (a test of your thin wrapper) instead of forty.

"Wrap it in your own thin interface" in practice: instead of forty tests mocking the payment company's SDK (software development kit: the library a company publishes for using its service), you write one small class of your own, say PaymentGateway, with a charge(amount, currency) method that calls the SDK. Your code uses PaymentGateway. Your tests fake PaymentGateway. When the payment company renames a function, you change one class and its one test; the other forty tests never knew the SDK existed.

12.7 Exceptions, Warnings, and Async Tests

Some behaviour is "this must go wrong in a particular way": a negative quantity must be rejected, an old function must warn that it is deprecated. Tests for those need different tools from assert a == b.

import pytest, warnings

def test_raises_with_message():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match=r"quantity must not be negative") as exc_info:
        line_total(10.0, -1)
    assert exc_info.value.args[0].startswith("quantity")

def test_exception_group():                       # §7.6
    with pytest.raises(ExceptionGroup) as exc_info:
        raise ExceptionGroup("boom", [ValueError("a"), KeyError("b")])
    assert len(exc_info.value.exceptions) == 2

def test_warns():
    with pytest.warns(DeprecationWarning, match="use line_total"):
        old_total(10.0, 3)

def test_no_warning():
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("error")
        line_total(10.0, 3)

What each test does:

  • pytest.raises(ValueError, ...) is a context manager (§2.9's with). The test passes only if the code inside the block raises ValueError. If nothing is raised, or a different exception is, the test fails. as exc_info keeps the caught exception, available as exc_info.value after the block.
  • The exception group test checks a group (§7.6) and then looks inside it: two exceptions were bundled.
  • pytest.warns is the same idea for warnings: the block must emit a DeprecationWarning whose message matches.
  • The last test is the opposite: simplefilter("error") turns any warning into an exception, so if line_total warns about anything, the test fails.

match is a regular expression searched against str(exception), and it is not optional discipline — pytest.raises(ValueError) alone passes when the function raised the wrong ValueError, which is a real way to write a test that never fails.

A smoke alarm and a carbon monoxide alarm both beep. If your test only checks "something beeped", it passes when the wrong alarm goes off. ValueError is one of the most common exceptions in Python — int("abc") raises it, so does unpacking the wrong number of values — so "some ValueError happened" says very little. match checks it was your ValueError, with your message.

Comparing floats with pytest.approx

pytest.approx is the other half of this pair, for the float comparisons §12.5 just demonstrated. The problem it solves fits in three lines:

import math

print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))

0.30000000000000004
False
True

0.1 + 0.2 lands a tiny distance away from 0.3, so == says False. math.isclose asks a better question: "are these two numbers within a small tolerance of each other?" pytest.approx asks the same question inside an assert, and it also works on lists and dicts of numbers:

assert 0.1 + 0.2 == pytest.approx(0.3)
assert [0.1 + 0.2, 1.0] == pytest.approx([0.3, 1.0])
assert 29.985 == pytest.approx(29.99, abs=0.01)

Think of a tailor's tolerance: a sleeve that is within half a centimetre of the pattern counts as correct. By default approx allows a relative difference of one in a million (rel=1e-6); abs=0.01 in the last line sets an absolute tolerance instead, "within one cent". Pick the tolerance from the problem, not from whatever makes the test pass.

Async tests

Async tests need a plugin, because a coroutine function returns a coroutine and pytest cannot await it. Two exist: pytest-asyncio and anyio's plugin (which also runs the test on Trio, an alternative to asyncio).

In §9's kitchen terms: calling an async def function gives you a recipe card, not a cooked meal. Something has to cook it, and that something is an event loop. Plain pytest would call your async test, receive the recipe card, and never cook it. The plugin starts an event loop and runs the coroutine to completion.

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
asyncio_mode = "auto"        # pytest-asyncio: no decorator needed on async tests

import asyncio
import pytest

@pytest.mark.asyncio                       # unnecessary in "auto" mode
async def test_gather_runs_concurrently():
    async def work(n):
        await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
        return n * 2
    assert await asyncio.gather(*(work(i) for i in range(3))) == [0, 2, 4]

@pytest.fixture
async def client():                        # async fixtures work the same way
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    yield {"ready": True}

With asyncio_mode = "auto", every async def test_... is run on an event loop automatically, and async fixtures are awaited for you. In the default "strict" mode you mark each async test with @pytest.mark.asyncio instead; auto mode is the convenient choice when a project uses only asyncio.

Two rules specific to async tests. Never assert on wall-clock durations (real elapsed time) to prove concurrency — that is a flaky test on a loaded CI machine; assert on ordering or on the number of concurrent entries instead. And give every awaited network call a timeout in the test (asyncio.timeout, §9.6), because a hung coroutine otherwise stalls the suite until CI kills the job.

A test that says "three 0.1-second tasks must finish in under 0.15 seconds" passes on your laptop and fails on a CI machine that is busy running twenty other jobs. That is the flickering warning light from §12.1. The result [0, 2, 4] in the order the tasks were given is something the machine's speed cannot change.

12.8 The Built-in Fixtures

pytest ships a set of fixtures that cover most of what tests need from the outside world. Using them instead of hand-rolled equivalents is what keeps tests independent.

You use them exactly like your own fixtures: name one as a parameter and pytest hands it in. Here are the ones you will reach for most, each in a one-job test:

import logging, sys
import pytest

def test_tmp_path(tmp_path):                       # a fresh directory, auto-removed
    target = tmp_path / "notes.txt"
    target.write_text("hello\n", encoding="utf-8")
    assert target.read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip() == "hello"

def test_capsys(capsys):                           # captured stdout/stderr
    print("shipped 3 orders")
    out, err = capsys.readouterr()
    assert "3 orders" in out

def test_caplog(caplog):                           # captured log records (§7.8)
    with caplog.at_level(logging.WARNING, logger="cart"):
        logging.getLogger("cart").warning("stock low: %s", "SKU-9")
    assert caplog.records[0].levelname == "WARNING"
    assert "SKU-9" in caplog.text

def test_monkeypatch(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setenv("CART_ENV", "test")
    monkeypatch.setattr(sys, "maxsize", 99)        # restored automatically afterwards
    assert sys.maxsize == 99

@pytest.mark.skipif(sys.platform == "win32", reason="POSIX only")
def test_skipped_elsewhere():
    assert True

@pytest.mark.xfail(reason="rounding bug, tracked in #412", strict=True)
def test_known_bug():
    assert 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3

One line each:

  • tmp_path is a brand-new, empty folder (a pathlib.Path) for this test alone. Like a hotel room: yours for the stay, cleaned out after you leave, and no other guest's things in it.
  • capsys captures what the test prints. readouterr() hands back everything printed so far, split into standard output and standard error. A tape recorder for print.
  • caplog does the same for the logging module. at_level raises the capture level for one logger inside the with block.
  • monkeypatch you met in §12.6.
  • skipif skips the test when its condition is true, and reports it as skipped (the -ra summary from §12.3 lists every skip).
  • xfail says "this test is expected to fail".
$ pytest -q
.....x                                                                   [100%]
=========================== short test summary info ============================
XFAIL tests/test_builtin.py::test_known_bug - rounding bug, tracked in #412
5 passed, 1 xfailed in 0.06s

Five dots for five passes, and a lower-case x for the expected failure. On Windows the skipped test would show as s instead of a dot.

caplog.records gives you the LogRecord objects themselves, so you can assert on levelname, name and the structured extra fields rather than on formatted text — the right way to test the logging from §7.8.

xfail, skip, and parking broken tests

xfail with strict=True is the useful form: the test is expected to fail, and if it starts passing the suite fails, telling you the bug is fixed and the marker should go. Non-strict xfail silently accepts either outcome, which makes it a way to forget about a bug forever. skip and skipif mean "this cannot run here" — a missing optional dependency, the wrong platform. Neither is a place to park a broken test; a reason linking an issue is the minimum.

Think of a sticky note on a broken printer saying "known fault, engineer booked". A strict xfail is a note that also rings a bell the day the printer starts working again, so someone takes the note down. A non-strict one stays on the printer for years after it was fixed, and everyone keeps walking to the printer on the next floor.

The rest of the set

Also available: tmp_path_factory (session-scoped temp dirs), capfd (captures at file-descriptor level, so it catches output from subprocesses and C libraries that capsys misses), recwarn, and request for introspecting the running test.

pytest --fixtures lists every fixture available in a project, built-in and your own, with its docstring. It is the fastest answer to "is there already a fixture for this?"

12.9 Coverage — and What It Does Not Measure

You have tests. Which parts of the code do they actually exercise? A coverage tool answers that by watching the program while the tests run and recording every line that executed.

Think of driving with a highlighter on a road map, marking every street you drive down. At the end of the month, the unmarked streets are the ones you have never visited. That is useful: a bug on an unmarked street can hide forever. But a highlighted street only proves you drove down it. It does not prove you looked at the houses.

coverage.py records which lines ran. pytest-cov wires it into pytest.

[tool.coverage.run]
branch = true                 # measure branches, not just lines
source = ["src"]

[tool.coverage.report]
show_missing = true
skip_covered = true
fail_under = 90

Line by line:

  • branch = true — explained below; it is the most important line.
  • source = ["src"] measures only your code, not the tests or third-party packages.
  • show_missing adds a column listing the line numbers that never ran.
  • skip_covered hides files that are already at 100%, so the report shows only what needs attention.
  • fail_under = 90 makes coverage report exit with an error status if the total is below 90%, which is how CI enforces a minimum.
$ coverage run -m pytest -q && coverage report
Name                  Stmts   Miss Branch BrPart  Cover   Missing
-----------------------------------------------------------------
src/cart/pricing.py       6      2      4      2    60%   3, 5
-----------------------------------------------------------------
TOTAL                     6      2      4      2    60%

1 file skipped due to complete coverage.
Coverage failure: total of 60 is less than fail-under=90

The columns, left to right:

  • Stmts — statements (roughly, lines of code) in the file: 6.
  • Miss — how many of them never ran: 2.
  • Branch — places where the code can go two ways, counted as possible paths: 4.
  • BrPart — partial branches, decisions that only ever went one way: 2.
  • Cover — the combined score: 60%.
  • Missing — the line numbers that never ran: 3 and 5.

The last line is fail_under at work: the run failed because 60 is below 90.

branch = true is the setting that makes the number mean something. Without it, an if whose body always runs counts as fully covered even though the "skip it" path has never executed once. With it, BrPart counts branches taken only one way, and the Missing column names them.

An example of that. Suppose a function says if total >= 50: discount = 5, and your only test uses a total of 80. Every line runs, so line coverage is 100%. But the case where the if is false — a small order, no discount — has never been tried. Branch coverage reports that missing path; line coverage cannot see it.

coverage html writes a browsable report where every uncovered line is highlighted — far more useful than the percentage for actually finding untested code.

Running is not checking

What coverage does not tell you. It measures execution, not verification. A test that calls every function and asserts nothing scores 100%. It cannot see a missing test for an input you never thought of, and it says nothing about whether the assertions are right. High coverage is weak evidence of a good suite; low coverage is strong evidence of a bad one. That asymmetry is the whole story.

You can prove the first claim with the standard library alone. Python's trace module records which lines run, the same basic job coverage.py does with far more care. Here it watches a "test" that calls a function twice and checks nothing:

import trace

def shipping_cost(total):
    if total >= 50:
        return 0
    return 5

def test_that_checks_nothing():
    shipping_cost(80)
    shipping_cost(10)              # both paths run; no assert anywhere

tracer = trace.Trace(count=True, trace=False)
tracer.runfunc(test_that_checks_nothing)
counts = tracer.results().counts                 # {(filename, line): times run}

code = shipping_cost.__code__
body = range(code.co_firstlineno + 1, code.co_firstlineno + 4)   # the 3 body lines
ran = [line for line in body if (code.co_filename, line) in counts]
print(f"lines of shipping_cost that ran: {len(ran)} of {len(body)}")
print("assertions made: 0")

lines of shipping_cost that ran: 3 of 3
assertions made: 0

Line by line:

  • trace.Trace(count=True, trace=False) creates a tracer that counts executed lines without printing each one.
  • runfunc runs the "test" under the tracer.
  • results().counts is a dictionary keyed by (filename, line number).
  • The next lines work out the three line numbers of shipping_cost's body and check each one against the counts.

Every line ran, both branches included. Perfect coverage, and the test would still pass if shipping_cost returned 500 for every order. Coverage told you the street was driven down. Only an assertion looks at the houses.

Which is why a fail_under gate belongs at a level you can honestly hold — 80–90% for most code — and why chasing 100% produces tests written to satisfy the tool. Use # pragma: no cover sparingly and only for genuinely unreachable code (a if TYPE_CHECKING: block, a defensive raise AssertionError("unreachable")).

Mutation testing: a fire drill for your tests

If you want a check on assertion quality, that is mutation testing: mutmut or cosmic-ray change a > to a >=, re-run the suite, and report every mutation that no test caught. It is slow enough to run nightly rather than per-commit, and it is the only automated answer to "are these assertions doing anything".

It is a fire drill. You do not wait for a real fire to find out whether the alarms work; you light a controlled one and listen. A mutation tool plants a small, deliberate bug — changes >= to >, + to -, True to False — and runs your tests. If some test fails, the bug was "killed": your tests would have caught it. If every test still passes, the mutant "survived", and you have found a line no assertion really checks. Run against test_that_checks_nothing above, every mutant of shipping_cost would survive.

12.10 Property-Based Testing with Hypothesis

Every test so far has used inputs you picked yourself. That is the weakness of hand-written examples: you test the cases you thought of, and bugs live in the cases you did not.

Example-based tests check the cases you thought of. Hypothesis generates hundreds of cases you did not, and when one fails it shrinks it to the smallest input that still fails.

Think of handing a new toy to a toddler. An adult tests the toy the way it was meant to be used. The toddler drops it, sits on it, puts it in the bath, and finds in ten minutes the weakness the factory missed. Hypothesis is the toddler.

The idea, by hand

Before using the library, here is the whole idea in plain Python. my_sort has a bug: it uses set() to sort, which quietly drops repeated numbers. The program generates random lists until one exposes the bug, and then shrinks that list:

import random

def my_sort(numbers):
    return sorted(set(numbers))        # the bug: set() quietly drops repeats

def fails(numbers):
    return my_sort(numbers) != sorted(numbers)     # the property, inverted

rng = random.Random(2)                 # a fixed seed, so every run is the same
for attempt in range(1, 1001):
    numbers = [rng.randint(0, 20) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 8))]
    if fails(numbers):
        break
print(f"attempt {attempt} fails: {numbers}")

shrunk = numbers
while True:
    for i in range(len(shrunk)):
        smaller = shrunk[:i] + shrunk[i + 1:]       # drop one element
        if fails(smaller):
            shrunk = smaller
            break
    else:
        break                                       # nothing smaller fails
print(f"shrunk to: {shrunk}")

attempt 6 fails: [16, 11, 17, 14, 16, 8]
shrunk to: [16, 16]

Line by line:

  • fails states the rule that should hold for every list — "my_sort agrees with the built-in sorted" — and returns True when the rule is broken.
  • The first loop makes random lists of up to eight numbers between 0 and 20. Five lists pass; the sixth breaks the rule.
  • That failing list has six numbers, and only two of them matter. The second loop tries removing one element at a time, keeps any smaller list that still fails, and stops when no single removal fails any more.
  • [16, 16] is the answer: "two equal numbers". That is the bug, stated as plainly as it can be.

Shrinking is how a doctor tracks down a food allergy: drop one ingredient at a time from the meal and see whether the reaction still happens, until only the culprit is left.

The real library does both halves far better. It chooses inputs cleverly (empty lists, huge numbers, odd Unicode: unusual characters from the world's alphabets and symbol sets), and it shrinks values as well as length. Given the same my_sort and the property written as a Hypothesis test, Hypothesis 6.170 reports numbers=[0, 0] — the smallest numbers too, not just the shortest list.

Properties

from hypothesis import given, strategies as st
from cart.text import normalise           # " ".join(s.split()).lower()

@given(st.text())
def test_normalise_is_idempotent(s):
    assert normalise(normalise(s)) == normalise(s)

@given(st.text())
def test_normalise_never_has_double_spaces(s):
    assert "  " not in normalise(s)

How to read it:

  • st.text() is a strategy: a recipe for generating values, here arbitrary strings.
  • @given(st.text()) tells Hypothesis to call the test many times (100 by default), each time with a new generated string as s.
  • The test body states something that must be true for any string. normalise collapses runs of whitespace into single spaces and lowercases, so normalising twice must give the same result as normalising once, and the result can never contain two spaces in a row.

Those are properties: statements true for every input, not for one. The four shapes that cover most real uses:

Property Shape Example
Round-trip decode(encode(x)) == x serialisers, parsers (code that reads text into structured data), compression
Invariant f(x) always satisfies P output is sorted; total is never negative
Idempotence f(f(x)) == f(x) normalisation, deduplication, abs
Oracle fast(x) == obvious(x) an optimisation against the naive version

In everyday terms:

  • Round-trip: translate a sentence into French and back, and you should get the sentence you started with.
  • Invariant: whatever you put in the shopping basket, the total is never negative.
  • Idempotence: pressing the lift button a second time does not call a second lift.
  • Oracle: a new, fast calculator must agree with the slow, obviously correct one. The by-hand example above was an oracle test: my_sort against sorted.

Hypothesis finds the bug you did not look for

Here is the payoff — the same function with a real bug, and what Hypothesis does with it:

# src/cart/report.py
def summarise(prices):
    return f"{len(prices)} items, average {sum(prices) // len(prices)}"

# tests/test_props.py
@given(st.lists(st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=10_000)))
def test_summarise_returns_a_string(prices):
    assert isinstance(summarise(prices), str)

$ pytest -q
    def summarise(prices):
>       return f"{len(prices)} items, average {sum(prices) // len(prices)}"
                                               ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
E       ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
E       Failing test case: test_summarise_returns_a_string(
E           prices=[],
E       )

1 failed in 0.44s

The test only asks "does it return a string?", which sounds too weak to find anything. But to answer it, summarise has to run without crashing, and Hypothesis tried an empty basket. Dividing by len([]) is dividing by zero.

prices=[] is the shrunk result, not the input that first failed — Hypothesis found a failure with some random list, then reduced it repeatedly until nothing smaller failed. The reported counterexample is always the minimal one, which is why the failures are readable.

Keeping found bugs found

Two mechanisms make it usable in CI. Hypothesis keeps a .hypothesis/ database of previously failing examples and replays them first on the next run, so a fixed bug stays fixed deterministically — commit the directory or cache it in CI. And @example(...) pins a specific case permanently alongside the generated ones:

from hypothesis import given, example, settings, strategies as st

@given(st.lists(st.integers()))
@example([])                                   # the regression, forever
@settings(max_examples=500, deadline=None)     # deadline=None for slow code
def test_summarise(prices):
    ...
  • @example([]) makes Hypothesis always try the empty list, on every run, on every machine, whatever the database holds.
  • max_examples=500 raises the number of generated cases from the default 100.
  • deadline=None switches off Hypothesis's per-example time limit (200 milliseconds by default), which otherwise reports a slow example as a failure.

That .hypothesis/ folder is the same idea as the doctor's notes: once an allergy is found, it goes in your file, and every future doctor checks it first.

Strategies for your own objects

Strategies compose, which is what makes it applicable to real domain objects rather than just integers:

orders = st.builds(
    Order,
    id=st.uuids(),
    quantity=st.integers(min_value=1, max_value=100),
    price=st.decimals(min_value=0, max_value=10_000, places=2),
    tags=st.lists(st.text(min_size=1), max_size=5, unique=True),
)

@given(orders)
def test_total_is_never_negative(order):
    assert order.total() >= 0

st.builds(Order, ...) generates Order objects by calling Order(...) with one generated value per argument: a random UUID, a quantity from 1 to 100, a price with two decimal places, and up to five distinct non-empty tags. Each strategy is a small recipe, and builds combines them into a recipe for a whole order.

Use property tests where the properties are real: parsers, serialisers, anything with an inverse, ordering and dedup logic (removing repeats), and arithmetic on money. Do not force them on code whose only property is "it returns what the spec says" (the spec, or specification, being the written description of what it should do), where a parametrised table is clearer and faster.

12.11 ruff: Linting and Formatting

Tests check what code does. A second family of tools checks what code looks like and flags likely mistakes without running anything.

  • A linter reads your source and reports suspicious patterns: an import you never use, a variable that is always overwritten, a mutable default argument. Think of a grammar checker: it does not know what your essay is about, but it knows "their" where "there" belongs.
  • A formatter rewrites your source into one consistent layout: spacing, line breaks, quote style. Think of a newspaper's house style, which decides once how every date and headline is written, so nobody argues about it article by article.

ruff is a linter and formatter that replaces flake8, isort, pyupgrade, pydocstyle, bandit's common rules and black, running fast enough to be imperceptible on save.

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100
target-version = "py311"

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["E", "F", "I", "UP", "B", "SIM", "C4", "RUF"]
ignore = ["E501"]                       # the formatter owns line length

[tool.ruff.lint.per-file-ignores]
"tests/**" = ["S101"]                   # asserts are the point in tests

Line by line:

  • target-version = "py311" tells ruff the oldest Python you support, so it suggests only modern syntax that version understands.
  • select turns on rule families by their letter prefix. Each letter is a group of rules borrowed from an older tool; the list is explained below.
  • ignore = ["E501"] switches off the "line too long" rule, because the formatter already decides line breaks.
  • per-file-ignores relaxes rules for some files. S101 warns about assert in application code (Python skips asserts when run with -O), but in tests assert is the whole point. It only matters once you add the S family, which the list below recommends for code that handles untrusted input.

Here is a short file with a lot wrong in it:

import os
import json
from typing import List


def load(path, keys = []):
    f = open(path)
    data = json.load(f)
    result: List[str] = []
    for k in keys:
        if k in data.keys():
            result.append(str(data[k]))
    return result

$ ruff check --output-format=concise .
messy.py:1:1: I001 [*] Import block is un-sorted or un-formatted
messy.py:1:8: F401 [*] `os` imported but unused
messy.py:3:1: UP035 `typing.List` is deprecated, use `list` instead
messy.py:6:23: B006 Do not use mutable data structures for argument defaults
messy.py:7:9: SIM115 Use a context manager for opening files
messy.py:9:13: UP006 [*] Use `list` instead of `List` for type annotation
messy.py:11:12: SIM118 Use `key in dict` instead of `key in dict.keys()`
Found 7 errors.
[*] 3 fixable with the `--fix` option (2 hidden fixes can be enabled with the `--unsafe-fixes` option).

Each line reads: file, line, column, rule code, message. messy.py:6:23: B006 means line 6, column 23 — the [] in keys = [].

Every one of those is a real defect or a real modernisation, and B006 — the mutable default argument of §1.2 — is a genuine bug the linter caught for free. Note the [*] markers: ruff check --fix applies those automatically, and the two "hidden" fixes are held back because they could change behaviour (deleting an import might remove a side effect).

Two of the seven deserve a translation:

  • SIM115 — f = open(path) is never closed. with open(path) as f: (§2.9) closes it even when json.load raises.
  • SIM118 — k in data.keys() does the same job as k in data, with an extra method call.

Which rules to turn on

The rule families worth enabling on a new project: E/W (pycodestyle), F (pyflakes — real errors), I (import sorting), UP (pyupgrade — modernise for your target-version), B (bugbear — likely bugs), SIM (simplifications), C4 (comprehensions), RUF (ruff's own), and S (bandit security rules) on anything handling untrusted input. Add ANN if you want annotations enforced, and D for docstrings, but adopt them on a new codebase rather than retrofitting them (adding them afterwards) onto a large one in a single commit.

If you are unsure, F and B are the two to start with: F catches outright errors such as an undefined name, and B catches code that runs but probably does not do what you meant.

ruff check .                 # lint
ruff check --fix .           # lint and autofix
ruff format .                # format
ruff format --diff .         # what would change, without changing it
ruff check --statistics .    # a histogram: what to fix first on a legacy codebase

ruff format is a black-compatible formatter: one canonical style, almost nothing to configure, and the argument about brace placement (where brackets and line breaks go) ends permanently. Adopt it in one commit and add that commit's hash to .git-blame-ignore-revs so git blame stays useful.

Why that last step: the formatting commit touches nearly every line, so afterwards git blame (which shows who last changed each line) would name that commit everywhere. Listing it in .git-blame-ignore-revs tells git blame to look past it to the change that really mattered.

Four tools, one job each

The complete quality toolchain for a modern project is four tools with one job each:

Tool Answers Runs in
ruff format Is it laid out consistently? editor on save, pre-commit
ruff check Are there obvious defects and dead code? editor, pre-commit, CI
mypy (§6.13) Do the types actually line up? pre-commit (fast projects), CI
pytest Does it do the right thing? locally, CI

Read the table bottom to top and the questions get cheaper to answer: running the tests takes seconds to minutes, type-checking takes seconds, linting and formatting take milliseconds. That is why the cheap ones run on every save and the expensive ones run in CI.

12.12 pre-commit

Everything above only helps if it runs. pre-commit installs a git hook that runs your checks on the staged files before a commit is created, so nothing unformatted or lint-failing reaches the branch. In git, staged files are the ones you have marked to go into the next commit, and a branch is a line of development that commits are added to.

A git hook is a script git runs automatically at a certain moment; the pre-commit hook runs just before a commit is recorded, and if it fails, the commit does not happen. The pre-commit tool (same name, a separate program, pip install pre-commit) manages that script for you from a config file.

Think of airport security. Your bag is checked before it gets on the plane, not after it lands. Problems found at security are cheap to fix: you take the bottle out and walk through again. Problems found after take-off are not.

# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit
    rev: v0.16.4
    hooks:
      - id: ruff-check
        args: [--fix]
      - id: ruff-format
  - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
    rev: v6.0.0
    hooks:
      - id: trailing-whitespace
      - id: end-of-file-fixer
      - id: check-yaml
      - id: check-added-large-files
  - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/mirrors-mypy
    rev: v2.3.1
    hooks:
      - id: mypy
        additional_dependencies: [types-requests]

How the file is organised:

  • Each entry under repos is a git repository that publishes hooks. rev is the exact tag to use.
  • Under hooks, each id picks one hook from that repository. args passes extra flags; here ruff-check runs with --fix.
  • The middle repository holds small general-purpose checks: strip trailing spaces, make sure files end with a newline, check that YAML files (another configuration format) parse, refuse accidentally committed huge files.
  • additional_dependencies installs extra packages into that hook's environment. mypy needs the type stubs for requests to check code that uses it.
pre-commit install           # write .git/hooks/pre-commit — do this once per clone
pre-commit run --all-files   # run everything now, e.g. when adopting it
pre-commit autoupdate        # bump every `rev:` to the latest tag

pre-commit install is the step people forget. The config file is committed to the repository, but the hook itself lives in .git/hooks/, which git never shares, so every person who clones the project runs install once.

$ pre-commit run --all-files
ruff check...............................................................Failed
- hook id: ruff-check
- files were modified by this hook

Found 1 error (1 fixed, 0 remaining).

ruff format..............................................................Failed
- hook id: ruff-format
- files were modified by this hook

1 file reformatted

trim trailing whitespace.................................................Passed
fix end of files.........................................................Passed
check yaml...............................................................Passed
check for added large files..............................................Passed

Note the behaviour that confuses everyone once: a hook that fixes a file reports Failed. That is correct — the commit is aborted, the fixes are in your working tree, and you stage them and commit again. The hook's job is to guarantee that what gets committed is already clean.

Back at airport security: the officer takes the oversized bottle out of your bag for you, and then sends you back through the scanner. The bag is fixed, but it still has to be checked again. In git terms, git add the fixed files and run git commit once more.

Each hook runs in its own isolated environment pinned by rev:, so every developer and CI runs byte-identical tool versions — which is why pre-commit solves the "works on my machine, fails in CI" formatting argument that a locally-installed linter does not.

Keep the hooks fast. Anything over a couple of seconds gets bypassed with --no-verify and then the hook is decorative. Formatting, linting and small checks belong in pre-commit; the full test suite and slow type checks belong in CI. And run pre-commit run --all-files in CI too, because a local hook is advisory and CI is not.

git commit --no-verify skips the hook entirely. Everyone has the flag, and a hook that makes every commit take thirty seconds teaches people to type it. A security queue that takes an hour gets a side door.

12.13 Running It All in CI

The last step is a place where every check runs on every change, on a machine nobody configured by hand. That is continuous integration (CI): a service that, whenever code is pushed (sent to the shared repository), starts a fresh machine, installs the project from scratch, and runs the whole toolchain. If anything fails, the change is marked red before anyone merges it.

Think of a test kitchen that cooks every new recipe in four different ovens before it goes in the cookbook. Your kitchen at home has its quirks; the test kitchen proves the recipe works without them.

Here is a GitHub Actions workflow for the project in this section:

# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.11", "3.12", "3.13", "3.14"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v10
        with:
          enable-cache: true
      - run: uv sync --frozen --all-extras
      - run: uv run ruff check --output-format=github .
      - run: uv run ruff format --check .
      - run: uv run mypy src
      - run: uv run pytest --cov=src --cov-report=xml -ra

Reading it top to bottom:

  • on: [push, pull_request] — run on every push and every pull request (a proposed change, waiting for review before it is merged).
  • runs-on: ubuntu-latest — a fresh Linux machine each time.
  • matrix — run the whole job once per listed Python version, four jobs in parallel.
  • actions/checkout fetches the code; setup-uv installs uv (§11.12), with a download cache.
  • uv sync --frozen --all-extras installs exactly what the lockfile says, including optional extras.
  • Then the four tools from §12.11's table, each as a run: step. --output-format=github makes ruff's findings appear as comments on the right lines of the pull request. ruff format --check fails if any file would be reformatted, without changing it.
  • --cov=src --cov-report=xml measures coverage while the tests run and writes it in a format coverage services can read.

Four details that matter more than the YAML dialect. --frozen fails if the lockfile is out of date, so CI tests the dependency set you committed rather than resolving fresh and quietly testing something else. The matrix is over the Python versions your requires-python claims — a claim of >=3.11 that is only ever tested on 3.14 is a guess. fail-fast: false so one version's failure does not hide the others. And the lint and format checks come before the tests, because they are the fast ones.

Each of those in kitchen terms:

  • --frozen is cooking from the receipt, not the shopping list (§11): the exact ingredients you tested with, not whatever the shop has today.
  • The matrix is the four ovens. A recipe printed as "works in any oven from 2011 onwards" had better have been tried in the 2011 one.
  • fail-fast: false keeps the other three ovens cooking when one burns the cake, so you learn whether it was one oven or the recipe.
  • Lint first is tasting the sauce before baking the whole dish: a two-second check that can save a five-minute wait.

tox and nox do the same matrix locally, which is worth having when a version-specific failure appears in CI and you need to reproduce it — nox in particular is just Python, so the sessions are readable.

With this file in place, the safety net from the start of the section is complete. The tests catch behaviour changes, coverage shows where the net has holes, Hypothesis throws in the inputs you never imagined, ruff and mypy catch whole classes of mistakes before a test runs, pre-commit stops them at your desk, and CI checks everything again on a machine with no habits of its own.

Exercises

Exercise 12.1 — Four broken tests. Each of these passes today and will not catch the bug it was written for. Say why, and fix it.

def test_charge_calls_gateway():
    gateway = MagicMock()
    checkout(gateway, amount=1999)
    assert gateway.charge.called

def test_rejects_bad_input():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        parse_order("{}")

def test_total():
    assert cart.total() == pytest.approx(0.3)

def test_writes_report():
    generate_report("/tmp/report.csv")
    assert os.path.exists("/tmp/report.csv")
Solution

1. MagicMock plus .called asserts almost nothing. Rename charge to capture in the real gateway and this test still passes, because the mock invents the attribute. It also never checks what was charged, so charging the right amount in the wrong currency passes.

def test_charge_calls_gateway():
    gateway = create_autospec(Gateway, instance=True)
    gateway.charge.return_value = {"status": "succeeded"}
    checkout(gateway, amount=1999)
    gateway.charge.assert_called_once_with(amount=1999, currency="eur")

2. pytest.raises(ValueError) with no match. parse_order("{}") probably raises ValueError for the reason you intended — or from int() on a missing field, or from a typo in the error path. All three pass. Add match=r"missing field 'id'", and prefer a specific exception type of your own over bare ValueError.

3. approx with no expected value in sight. cart.total() on an empty cart is 0.0, and pytest.approx(0.3) has a relative tolerance of 1e-6 — so this test is checking that the total is 0.3, which for an unpopulated cart fixture it is not; if it passes, the fixture is not empty and the test is not testing what its name says. The real fix is to arrange the cart explicitly in the test and assert the exact expected total, using Decimal or integer cents so approx is not needed at all.

4. A shared path outside the test's control. /tmp/report.csv persists between runs, so the assertion passes on the second run even if generate_report has stopped writing anything. It also breaks under pytest -n auto when two workers collide. Use tmp_path, and assert on the content:

def test_writes_report(tmp_path):
    target = tmp_path / "report.csv"
    generate_report(target)
    rows = target.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
    assert rows[0] == "id,total" and len(rows) == 4

The common thread: each of these asserts that something happened, not that the right thing happened. "Did not crash" is the weakest assertion available, and three of the four are really that.

Exercise 12.2 — Design the fixtures. An integration suite needs: a PostgreSQL container (≈8 s to start), a schema loaded into it, a clean set of tables per test, an authenticated API client, and the PAYMENTS_ENABLED environment variable set for one module only. Write the fixture set with scopes, and say why each scope is what it is.

Solution 
# tests/conftest.py
import pytest

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def pg_container():                       # 8 s, so exactly once per run
    with PostgresContainer("postgres:17") as pg:
        yield pg

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def engine(pg_container):                 # schema is expensive and immutable
    engine = create_engine(pg_container.get_connection_url())
    Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
    yield engine
    engine.dispose()

@pytest.fixture                           # function scope: mutable state
def db(engine):
    connection = engine.connect()
    transaction = connection.begin()
    session = Session(bind=connection)
    yield session
    session.close()
    transaction.rollback()                # undo everything the test did
    connection.close()

@pytest.fixture
def client(db):
    app.dependency_overrides[get_session] = lambda: db
    with TestClient(app) as c:
        c.headers["Authorization"] = "Bearer test-token"
        yield c
    app.dependency_overrides.clear()      # never leak overrides into the next test

# tests/test_payments.py — module-scoped env var
@pytest.fixture(scope="module", autouse=True)
def payments_on():
    with pytest.MonkeyPatch.context() as mp:
        mp.setenv("PAYMENTS_ENABLED", "1")
        yield

Session scope for the container and the schema because they are slow and nothing mutates them. Paying 8 seconds per test instead of per run is the difference between a suite people run and one they do not.

Function scope for db, and rollback rather than truncate. Wrapping each test in a transaction that is rolled back is both faster than re-creating tables and stronger: it cannot leave residue behind if the test fails half-way. It does mean the test cannot commit — which is a good constraint, and if code under test needs a real commit, use nested transactions (SAVEPOINT) or truncate instead.

client depends on db so the API and the assertions see the same transaction. Overriding the app's dependency is what makes that possible; clearing the override in teardown is what stops it leaking.

The env var uses MonkeyPatch.context() because the monkeypatch fixture itself is function-scoped and cannot be requested from a module-scoped fixture. autouse=True applies it to every test in the module without each one naming it — appropriate here precisely because it is a module-wide condition rather than something an individual test chooses.

Exercise 12.3 — Write the properties. For a function def slugify(title: str) -> str that lowercases, replaces runs of non-alphanumeric characters with a single hyphen, and strips leading/trailing hyphens: state four properties Hypothesis could check, and write two of them.

Solution

Four properties:

  1. Idempotent — slugify(slugify(s)) == slugify(s). Feeding a slug back in must not change it.
  2. Invariant on the alphabet — the result only ever contains a-z, 0-9 and -.
  3. Invariant on shape — no leading or trailing hyphen, and never two hyphens in a row.
  4. Order-preserving — the alphanumeric characters of the output appear in the same order as the lowercased alphanumerics of the input. This is the one that catches a genuinely wrong implementation rather than a badly formatted one.
import re
from hypothesis import given, example, strategies as st

@given(st.text())
@example("")                # the empty string: the case every implementation forgets
@example("---")             # everything strips away
def test_slugify_is_idempotent(s):
    assert slugify(slugify(s)) == slugify(s)

@given(st.text())
def test_slugify_shape(s):
    out = slugify(s)
    assert re.fullmatch(r"[a-z0-9]*(-[a-z0-9]+)*", out), out

re.fullmatch with that pattern expresses properties 2 and 3 at once — it permits the empty string, forbids leading, trailing and doubled hyphens, and restricts the alphabet.

Two things this exercise is really about. @example("") matters even with generation: Hypothesis will find the empty string quickly, but pinning it makes the regression permanent and the intent visible. And property 4 is the hard one to state and the valuable one to have — the first three are all satisfied by an implementation that returns "" for every input. A property suite that a trivial wrong implementation passes is testing the format, not the function.

Exercise 12.4 — The suite is green and useless. A service reports 94% coverage, 600 tests, a full CI pipeline — and three production incidents in a month that tests should have caught. Name five things you would look for, and what you would do about each.

Solution

1. Tests with no meaningful assertion. grep for tests whose only assertion is assert result is not None, assert x.called, or nothing at all beyond "it did not raise". Coverage counts these at full value. The check: run mutation testing (mutmut run) on the modules that failed in production — every surviving mutant is a line that no assertion constrains.

2. Everything mocked, including the thing under test. If the service layer's tests mock the repository, the repository's tests mock the driver, and no test ever puts them together, then every seam between them is untested. Look at the incidents: if they were integration failures — a wrong column name, a mismatched serialisation format — this is the cause. Add a thin layer of tests that use a real database in a container (Exercise 12.2) and no mocks at all.

3. Line coverage without branch coverage. Turn on branch = true and re-measure; the number will drop. BrPart entries are conditions only ever taken one way — very often the error handling, which is exactly what runs during an incident.

4. Deleted or leaked state between tests. Check for module-level mutable globals, a session-scoped fixture that is mutated, and whether the suite passes with pytest -p no:randomly --lf and under pytest-randomly in a different order. Order-dependence means some tests are passing because of what ran before them, and the ones that would have failed alone are effectively absent.

5. The tests test the code as written, not the requirement. The strongest signal is whether the tests were written after the code by reading it. Take each incident, write the test that would have failed, and note whether it needed new inputs nobody had thought about — if so, the gap is exploratory: add property-based tests (§12.10) for the parsing and calculation code, where "inputs nobody thought about" is exactly what Hypothesis generates.

The framing to carry away: coverage measures which lines ran, not which behaviours are pinned. A suite of 600 tests that all mock their collaborators verifies that the mocks behave the way the test author expected. The three incidents are the measurement that matters, and each one should end with a test that fails against the old code.

SECTION 13

The Standard Library and the Ecosystem

Start with a small program that answers two questions about some orders: who ordered most often, and what the average order was. Before you read the output, look at the imports.

import json, statistics, sys
from collections import Counter

orders = json.loads("""[
  {"customer": "Ada",   "total": 19.99},
  {"customer": "Grace", "total": 7.25},
  {"customer": "Ada",   "total": 45.50}
]""")

print("orders per customer:", Counter(o["customer"] for o in orders))
print("average order:", round(statistics.fmean(o["total"] for o in orders), 2))
print("modules that came with Python:", len(sys.stdlib_module_names) > 200)

orders per customer: Counter({'Ada': 2, 'Grace': 1})
average order: 24.25
modules that came with Python: True

Line by line:

  • json.loads turns text written in the JSON format into ordinary Python lists and dicts. §13.5 covers it.
  • Counter counts things. Give it any iterable and it tallies how often each value appears.
  • statistics.fmean is the average (the "arithmetic mean"), returned as a float.
  • sys.stdlib_module_names is the set of every module name in the standard library. The exact count changes between versions, but it is always well over two hundred.

Nothing in that program was installed. The standard library is the collection of modules that ships with every Python installation, and Python's own motto for it is "batteries included".

Think of moving into a house that came with a well-stocked toolbox in the garage. Before you drive to the hardware shop for a screwdriver, you open the toolbox. Sometimes the shop really does sell something the toolbox lacks, a specialist tool for a specialist job, and then you buy it. But every tool you bring home is one more thing to store, maintain, and replace when it breaks.

Python's reputation rests as much on what you can reach for as on the language itself. This section is a working tour of the parts you will use constantly:

  • the standard library modules that replace most utility code people write by hand,
  • and the four third-party libraries that between them account for an enormous share of professional Python: pydantic, fastapi, numpy and pandas. The tooling from §11 and §12 (uv, pytest, ruff) completes the set.

The aim is not encyclopedic coverage. It is to leave you able to reach for the right thing without searching, and to recognise what a codebase is doing when you open it. The section runs in five parts:

  1. What is already in the toolbox, and the three tools in it that people misuse (§13.1).
  2. Five standard-library tools in depth: paths (§13.2), command-line programs (§13.3), configuration (§13.4), saving and sending objects (§13.5) and a database in a file (§13.6).
  3. Data arriving from outside: checking it with pydantic (§13.7), how web frameworks really work (§13.8), and fastapi (§13.9).
  4. Numbers and tables: numpy (§13.10) and pandas (§13.11).
  5. How to decide whether a new dependency is worth it (§13.12).

13.1 Reach for the Standard Library First

A dependency is a package your project needs that someone else wrote and you install. Installing one takes a second. Living with it takes years.

Every dependency is a permanent cost: a supply-chain risk, a thing to upgrade, a licence to check, and a reason your build can break without you touching it. Read that list slowly, because each item is a real job:

  • A supply-chain risk. The code arrives from strangers, and so does every package it depends on. If any of them is compromised, so are you.
  • A thing to upgrade. Security fixes and new Python versions keep arriving, and each upgrade can change behaviour.
  • A licence to check. Some licences place conditions on how you can ship the software that uses them.
  • A reason your build can break. A new release, a deleted package or a broken wheel can stop your project installing on a day when you changed nothing.

A great deal of what people install is already installed. Here is the toolbox's inventory, arranged by job. Read the right-hand column as "the thing people install, or write by hand, without realising the module exists":

Need Module Instead of
Paths and file operations pathlib os.path string surgery
Command-line arguments argparse hand-parsing sys.argv
Config files tomllib (3.11+), configparser a YAML dependency
Dates and durations datetime, zoneinfo (3.9+) pytz, dateutil for the simple cases
Structured data containers dataclasses, enum, typing.NamedTuple dicts of unknown shape
Counting, grouping, deques collections hand-rolled loops (Exercise 5.2)
Combinatorics, lazy pipelines itertools nested loops (§5.7)
Caching, partials, dispatch functools hand-written memoisation, remembering answers already worked out (§4.8)
Temporary files and dirs tempfile /tmp/ string paths
Subprocesses subprocess os.system
Randomness random, and secrets for anything security-related random for tokens — a real vulnerability, a weakness an attacker can use
Hashing and HMAC (a hash that also proves who made it, using a secret key) hashlib, hmac rolling your own
Embedded database sqlite3 a JSON file you rewrite on every change
HTTP server for a test http.server a framework
Text/CSV csv, textwrap, difflib, re a dependency for one function
Compression and archives zipfile, tarfile, gzip, zlib shelling out to unzip (running the unzip command)
Statistics statistics NumPy for a mean over 40 numbers

You do not need to memorise the table. You need to remember that it exists, and look here before you look at the package index. The next five subsections take the most-used rows one at a time.

Three of those deserve a warning in the other direction: tools that are in the toolbox but are easy to use for the wrong job.

random is for games, not for secrets

random is not a security primitive (a building block you can trust for security) — use secrets.token_urlsafe() for tokens, session ids (the token that keeps a user logged in) and password resets.

The random module is like a shuffled deck of cards that is shuffled the same way every time you give it the same starting point. That starting point is called the seed. Watch what happens when you set it twice:

import random, secrets

random.seed(2026)
first = [random.randint(0, 9) for _ in range(6)]
random.seed(2026)
again = [random.randint(0, 9) for _ in range(6)]
print("same 'random' digits again:", first == again)

token = secrets.token_urlsafe(16)
print("token length:", len(token))
print("only URL-safe characters:", token.replace("-", "").replace("_", "").isalnum())

same 'random' digits again: True
token length: 22
only URL-safe characters: True

Line by line:

  • The two lists are identical, because the same seed replays the same sequence. That is a feature for a simulation or a test you want to repeat.
  • It is a disaster for a password-reset link. random uses an algorithm called the Mersenne Twister, and after someone has seen 624 of its 32-bit outputs they can reconstruct its whole internal state and predict every value that follows. The Python documentation says in so many words that random must not be used for security purposes.
  • secrets.token_urlsafe(16) takes 16 bytes from the operating system's cryptographic random source (randomness collected by the operating system that nobody can predict) and encodes them as 22 characters that are safe to put in a URL (letters, digits, - and _). Nothing in your program can replay it.

Dates need a timezone

datetime.now() without a timezone produces a naive datetime that will eventually be compared against an aware one and raise; use datetime.now(tz=timezone.utc), store UTC, and convert at the edges.

A naive datetime has no timezone attached. It is like a note that says "meet at 9:30" without saying which city. An aware datetime carries its timezone, so it names one exact moment. Python refuses to compare the two, because it cannot know whether they are the same moment:

from datetime import datetime, timezone
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

naive = datetime(2026, 8, 23, 9, 30)                        # "9:30, somewhere"
aware = datetime(2026, 8, 23, 9, 30, tzinfo=timezone.utc)   # 9:30 in UTC, one exact moment
print("naive tzinfo:", naive.tzinfo, "| aware tzinfo:", aware.tzinfo)

try:
    naive < aware
except TypeError as exc:
    print("TypeError:", exc)

print("the same moment in London:", aware.astimezone(ZoneInfo("Europe/London")).isoformat())

naive tzinfo: None | aware tzinfo: UTC
TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes
the same moment in London: 2026-08-23T10:30:00+01:00

Line by line:
