        2      Ada     EU  45.50 2026-08-03
        3    Grace     US   7.25 2026-08-03

rows, cols: (5, 5)
EU orders over 20: 2

        count     sum   mean
region
EU          3  164.49  54.83
US          2   19.25   9.62

region      EU     US
month
2026-08  65.49   7.25
2026-09  99.00  12.00

Line by line:

  • io.StringIO makes a string behave like an open file, so the CSV can live in the example. read_csv would read a real file the same way.
  • parse_dates=["placed_on"] turns that column's text into real dates.
  • df.dtypes shows each column's type. head(3) is the first three rows.
  • df[(df.region == "EU") & (df.total > 20)] keeps rows matching both conditions. df.region is a shorter spelling of df["region"].
  • groupby("region")["total"].agg(["count", "sum", "mean"]) splits the rows by region, then counts, totals and averages each group's total: three EU orders summing to 164.49.
  • .dt.to_period("M") turns each date into its month. pivot_table then makes one row per month and one column per region, holding the sum, with fill_value=0 for empty cells.

The operations that cover most work: read_csv/read_parquet/read_sql to load; df[mask] with boolean conditions to filter (& and |, with parentheses — and and or do not work on Series); df.loc[rows, cols] for label-based selection and df.iloc for positional; groupby(...).agg(...); merge for joins; pivot_table for cross-tabs (summary tables of one category against another); assign to add columns without mutating; dropna/fillna for missing data; and .dt/.str accessors for datetime and string operations on a whole column.

Two of those trip up everyone once, so here they are, running:

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"region": ["EU", "US"], "total": [19.99, 7.25]})
try:
    df[(df.region == "EU") and (df.total > 5)]
except ValueError as exc:
    print("ValueError:", exc)

print("loc[0, 'total']:", df.loc[0, "total"])   # by label: row labelled 0, column "total"
print("iloc[1, 1]:     ", df.iloc[1, 1])         # by position: second row, second column

ValueError: The truth value of a Series is ambiguous. Use a.empty, a.bool(), a.item(), a.any() or a.all().
loc[0, 'total']: 19.99
iloc[1, 1]:      7.25

Line by line:

  • and asks Python's ordinary question "is this whole thing true?". A column of several True/False values has no single answer, so pandas refuses. & combines the two columns element by element, which is what you meant. The parentheses are needed because & binds more tightly than ==.
  • loc selects by label and iloc by position. Here the labels happen to be 0 and 1, so they look alike; after filtering or sorting they no longer match, and that is when mixing them up bites.

Two things in that output are worth noting because they are recent. The customer column has dtype str, not object — pandas 3.0 made a proper string dtype the default, which is faster and no longer silently accepts mixed types. And datetime64[us] shows that pandas now preserves the resolution the data implies rather than forcing nanoseconds. Code written against pandas 1.x may assume object and datetime64[ns].

Two habits prevent most pandas pain. Chain, do not mutate — df.assign(...).query(...).groupby(...) is easier to reason about than a sequence of in-place edits, and pandas 3.0's copy-on-write makes the old SettingWithCopyWarning dance obsolete. And never iterate rows with iterrows(); it is slow and it loses dtypes. If you cannot express something as a vectorised operation or a groupby, apply is the escape hatch, and it is still a Python-level loop.

Chaining reads like a recipe: take the orders, add a month column, keep the EU ones, group by month. Each step makes a new table and leaves the one before it alone, so you can stop after any step and look. Copy-on-write means a new table shares its data with the old one until either is changed, so chaining is cheap.

polars is worth knowing about as the modern alternative: a different API built on Arrow (a standard in-memory format for columns of data), with lazy evaluation and multi-threaded execution, typically several times faster on large frames. For work at a scale where pandas struggles it is the first thing to try, and its expression API is closer to SQL than to pandas.

13.12 Choosing a Dependency

Adopting a dog costs very little on the day. Feeding it, walking it and paying the vet for the next twelve years is the real price. A dependency is the same: pip install takes a second, and the package then lives in your project for as long as the project does.

You will make this decision constantly, and the cost of a bad one is measured in years.

Is it in the standard library? Check first. It is already installed, already audited, and it will still work in ten years.
Is it maintained? Recent releases, issues answered, more than one maintainer, and a stated support policy for Python versions.
What does it drag in? pip download or uv tree shows the transitive set. Forty packages for one function is forty things that can break.
Does it ship types and wheels? A py.typed marker and a wheel for your platform mean it will work with your checker and install without a compiler.
Could you replace it? A dependency behind your own thin interface can be swapped. One whose types are threaded through your domain model cannot.

Read the five questions in order, because each one is cheaper to answer than the next:

  • Standard library first. The toolbox in the garage, from §13.1.
  • Maintained? A package whose last release was four years ago will not get the fix for the next security hole, or support the next Python version.
  • What it drags in. A package's own dependencies become yours. uv tree (uv is §11.12's tool) prints the whole family tree.
  • Types and wheels. A wheel (§11.10) is a pre-built package; without one for your platform, installing means compiling, which needs a compiler.
  • Replaceable? If only one small module of yours talks to the package, swapping it later means rewriting that module. If its types appear everywhere, swapping it means rewriting everything.

Two security habits belong here rather than in a separate chapter. Typosquatting is real: python -m pip install requets installs whatever someone registered under that name, and it runs at install time. Read the name you typed. And pin with hashes for anything deployed (§11.11) so the artefact you tested is the artefact that runs. pip-audit checks an environment against the advisory database (a public list of known security problems in packages) and belongs in CI, next to the tests.

Typosquatting is registering a name one typo away from a popular package, like a fake website one letter away from your bank's. The standard library's difflib shows how close those names are:

import difflib

popular = ["requests", "numpy", "pandas", "pydantic", "fastapi", "pytest"]
for typed in ["requets", "pandsa", "numpy"]:
    match = difflib.get_close_matches(typed, popular, n=1)[0]
    print(f"{typed:8} ->", "exact" if typed == match else f"one slip from {match!r}")

requets  -> one slip from 'requests'
pandsa   -> one slip from 'pandas'
numpy    -> exact

get_close_matches finds the most similar names in a list. A single dropped or swapped letter keeps a name very close to the original, which is exactly what makes it hard to spot when you type it and easy for an attacker to register.

That is the section's toolbox complete. Look in the garage first, and when you do go to the shop, buy the tool that will still be worth owning in five years. §14 puts the whole course's tools to work on one project.

Exercises

Exercise 13.1 — Replace the dependencies. This script's imports include three things the standard library already does. Rewrite it, and say what each replacement gains.

import os
import requests
import yaml
from dateutil.parser import parse as parse_date

config = yaml.load(open("config.yaml"))
outdir = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "reports", config["name"])
os.makedirs(outdir, exist_ok=True)
cutoff = parse_date(config["cutoff"])
Solution 
import tomllib
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

with open(Path(__file__).parent / "config.toml", "rb") as fh:   # tomllib needs binary
    config = tomllib.load(fh)

outdir = Path(__file__).parent / "reports" / config["name"]
outdir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
cutoff = datetime.fromisoformat(config["cutoff"])

yaml → tomllib. TOML is in the standard library from 3.11 and gives real types, so cutoff could be a native datetime in the file itself. If the file must stay YAML, the minimum change is yaml.safe_load — the original yaml.load without a Loader constructs arbitrary Python objects and is a code-execution hole. Note also the original leaks a file handle; tomllib.load here is inside a with.

os.path → pathlib. One expression instead of three functions, and mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) replaces makedirs.

dateutil → datetime.fromisoformat. Since 3.11 it parses the full ISO 8601 range, which is what a config file should contain. dateutil is still the right answer for parsing unpredictable human-written dates — that is a different problem.

requests is not replaced — and that is the point of the exercise. urllib.request exists, but it is unpleasant enough that requests or httpx earns its place. Knowing which dependencies are worth it matters more than minimising the count; httpx is the modern choice because it also does async and HTTP/2 with the same API.

Exercise 13.2 — Find four bugs. This endpoint has four defects: one security, one correctness, one durability, one design.

@app.post("/orders")
async def create_order(request: Request):
    data = json.loads(await request.body())
    con = sqlite3.connect("orders.db")
    con.execute(
        f"INSERT INTO orders (customer, total) VALUES ('{data['customer']}', {data['total']})"
    )
    con.close()
    return {"status": "created", "customer": data["customer"]}
Solution

Security — SQL injection. data['customer'] is formatted straight into the statement, so a customer name of x'); DROP TABLE orders; -- executes. Use ? placeholders. This is not mitigated by validating elsewhere; parameterisation is the fix.

Correctness — no validation at all. A missing total raises KeyError and returns a 500; a total of "abc" or -100 is accepted. Take a pydantic model as the parameter and let FastAPI reject bad input with a 422 (§13.9). That also removes the manual json.loads.

Durability — nothing is committed. sqlite3 opens a transaction implicitly and con.close() discards it, so every order is silently lost while the endpoint returns 201. Use with con:. A connection per request is the second half of this problem: opening the database on every request is slow and, under an async server, blocks the event loop.

Design — a blocking driver in an async def handler. sqlite3 is synchronous, so every request stalls the loop and the server's concurrency collapses under load (§9.11). Either make the handler def — FastAPI runs it in a thread pool — or use an async driver such as aiosqlite.

class OrderIn(BaseModel):
    customer: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=100)
    total: int = Field(ge=0)                       # integer cents

@app.post("/orders", status_code=201)
def create_order(order: OrderIn, db: Annotated[sqlite3.Connection, Depends(get_db)]):
    with db:
        cur = db.execute("INSERT INTO orders (customer, total) VALUES (?, ?)",
                         (order.customer, order.total))
    return {"id": cur.lastrowid, "customer": order.customer}

Note the handler is now def, the connection arrives from a dependency (so tests can override it), and the response includes the id — the original told the client nothing it could use.

Exercise 13.3 — Which tool? For each task, choose between the standard library, NumPy, pandas, and a database, and justify it.

  1. Average of 40 numbers in a CLI tool.
  2. Count occurrences of each error code in a 3 GB log file.
  3. Element-wise arithmetic on a 10-million-row numeric column.
  4. Joining two CSV files on a key and grouping the result.
  5. Storing a desktop application's user data, queried in several ways.
Solution

1. statistics.fmean. Adding NumPy to a CLI for this costs ~20 MB and a second of import time to save one line. fmean is faster than mean and returns a float.

2. collections.Counter over a generator. The file does not fit comfortably in memory, and the operation is one streaming pass:

counts = Counter(m.group(1) for line in path.open(encoding="utf-8")
                 if (m := ERROR_RE.search(line)))

Reading a 3 GB file into a DataFrame to count a column is the wrong shape of solution — and if you need pandas anyway, read_csv(..., chunksize=...) streams.

3. NumPy. This is exactly what it is for: one dtype, one contiguous block, whole-array arithmetic in compiled code. pandas would also work — it is NumPy underneath — but the labels and index cost memory you have no use for.

4. pandas. A join plus a group-by on labelled columns is its core competence, and merge handles the join semantics you would otherwise write by hand. If the files are large enough to be slow, polars or loading both into SQLite and writing a JOIN are both reasonable.

5. SQLite. Multiple query shapes over persistent structured data is the definition of a database. A JSON file rewritten on every change loses data on a crash, cannot be queried without loading all of it, and has no transactions. sqlite3 costs no dependency and no server.

The pattern: match the tool to the data's shape and size, not to its familiarity. The most common real error is the last one — reaching for pandas because it is known, when the data is a stream (2) or a store (5) rather than a table.

Exercise 13.4 — Draw the boundary. A service reads a JSON message from a queue, writes a row to PostgreSQL, and calls a third-party API. Say where validation happens, which types cross which boundary, and what pickle should be allowed to touch.

Solution

Validate once, at each edge, immediately on arrival.

queue message (bytes) — untrusted
json.loads → dict → Message.model_validate(...)
the only place raw input is trusted
↓
domain object (dataclass) — validated
the core works only with these, and imports no validation library
repository.save(order)
parameterised SQL, no dicts; schema constraints as the last line of defence
gateway.charge(order)
its own request model — and the response is validated too

Three boundaries, three validations. The queue message is untrusted and gets a pydantic model. The third-party API's response is also untrusted — it is someone else's code, it changes without notice, and validating it turns "a field went missing" into a clear error at the boundary instead of an AttributeError three layers deep. The database is trusted for shape (the schema enforces it) but its constraints (NOT NULL, CHECK, foreign keys) are the last line of defence, and should exist even though the application validates first.

Types across the boundaries. Bytes in, pydantic model at the edge, then convert to plain dataclasses for the core (§13.7). The core should not import pydantic: it makes the domain logic testable without constructing validated models, and it means a change of validation library does not reach into your business rules. Going out, convert domain objects to the request model the gateway needs.

pickle touches none of it. Nothing here is inside a single trust boundary: a queue is written by other services, a database can be written by other applications, and a third-party API is by definition foreign. Use JSON on the wire, real columns in the database, and reserve pickle for multiprocessing and a local cache you alone write and read.

The reason this shape is worth the ceremony: every one of these boundaries will eventually deliver something you did not expect, and the difference between a clear rejection at the edge and a corrupt row written at 3 a.m. is exactly where the validation sits.

SECTION 14

Capstone Project: Sentinel, an Async Service Monitor

Start with the smallest possible version of this project: one function that asks "is anything answering on this port?"

import asyncio


async def is_answering(host, port):
    try:
        reader, writer = await asyncio.open_connection(host, port)
    except OSError as exc:
        return f"no answer ({type(exc).__name__})"
    writer.close()
    await writer.wait_closed()
    return "answering"


async def main():
    async def hang_up(reader, writer):
        writer.close()

    server = await asyncio.start_server(hang_up, "127.0.0.1", 0)
    port = server.sockets[0].getsockname()[1]
    print("a server we just started:", await is_answering("127.0.0.1", port))
    print("port 1, where nothing listens:", await is_answering("127.0.0.1", 1))
    server.close()
    await server.wait_closed()

asyncio.run(main())

a server we just started: answering
port 1, where nothing listens: no answer (ConnectionRefusedError)

Line by line:

  • asyncio.start_server(hang_up, "127.0.0.1", 0) starts a real server on this machine. Port 0 means "any free port, you choose", and getsockname()[1] reads back the port the operating system picked.
  • hang_up is what the server does with each visitor: it closes the connection straight away. That is enough, because the question here is only whether something answered.
  • asyncio.open_connection dials a host and port. If something answers, you get a reader and a writer, and the function closes them politely.
  • Nothing listens on port 1, so the operating system refuses the connection at once. That arrives as ConnectionRefusedError, which is a kind of OSError, so the except turns it into a sentence instead of a crash.

That function is the seed of a real tool. Sentinel is a service health monitor. A service here is a program on a server that others rely on, such as a website, a database or a cache, and a health monitor checks that each one is answering. Sentinel reads a TOML file describing services, checks them all concurrently, records the results in SQLite, prints a report, and exits with a status code CI can act on. It uses no third-party libraries at all — the standard library is enough, and building it that way is the point.

Everything in this course exists in this project. Classes, decorators, generators, typing, errors, asyncio, packaging and testing all turn up, each one doing a job you can point at.

Picture a nurse doing a ward round:

  • There is a list of patients at the nurses' station. That is the configuration.
  • The nurse visits each bed and checks on the patient. That is a check.
  • Several nurses work the round at once, but only as many as are on shift. That is the concurrency limit.
  • Nobody stands at one bed all night. That is the deadline.
  • If a patient is asleep, the nurse tries again a little later. That is the retry.
  • Everything goes on the chart at the foot of the bed. That is the store.
  • At handover, the patients who need attention are at the top of the sheet. That is the report.

The analogy comes back throughout the section, because each part of the program answers a question a careful nurse would ask.

This section is a project brief with a worked solution. Build it yourself first, from the requirements and the build order. Read the solution when you are finished, or when you are properly stuck — comparing your design to another one is where most of the value is.

The section runs in four parts:

  1. The brief: what you are building (§14.1), the order to build it in (§14.2), and the five decisions that are harder than they look (§14.3).
  2. The worked solution, layer by layer: types and errors (§14.4), the checks (§14.5), retry and the runner (§14.6), and the store and report (§14.7).
  3. Proof: a demo against real servers (§14.8), the tests (§14.9), and the package and its command line (§14.10).
  4. Looking back and looking forward: what the project used from each section (§14.11), and where to take it next (§14.12).

14.1 What You Are Building

Here is a run of the finished tool. Read it the way an operator would, from the top:

$ sentinel check --config services.toml
DOWN billing         3.2 ms  billing: HTTP 503
DOWN legacy        201.7 ms  timed out
OK   api            12.4 ms  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
OK   cache           0.8 ms  connected
SLOW reports        54.1 ms  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
2 of 5 down
$ echo $?
1

Line by line:

  • Each line is one service: its status, its name, how long the check took, and what it said.
  • The two DOWN lines come first. On a handover sheet, the patients who need you go at the top.
  • billing answered, but with HTTP 503, which means "I am up, but I cannot serve you". legacy did not answer at all before its deadline.
  • cache says connected rather than an HTTP status line. It is checked by opening a connection, not by asking a web question.
  • reports is SLOW: it answered correctly, but it took longer than its threshold allows.
  • The last line is a summary for a human. echo $? prints the program's exit status, and 1 is the summary for a machine: "something is wrong".

The requirements, in full:

  1. Configuration is a TOML file with a [target.<name>] table per service: host, port, an optional path (present means "speak HTTP", absent means "just open a TCP connection"; TCP is the basic protocol for a reliable connection between two machines, and opening one is enough to show something is listening), an optional timeout and an optional slow_after_ms. A malformed config fails at startup with a message naming the offending target.
  2. Checks run concurrently, with a configurable ceiling on how many run at once.
  3. Every check has a deadline. A target that never answers must not stall the run.
  4. A transient failure is retried with exponential backoff before being called down.
  5. Results are stored in SQLite with a timestamp, so sentinel history and an uptime percentage per target (the share of checks in which it was up) are available later.
  6. The report is sorted with failures first, and the process exits 0 when everything is up and 1 otherwise.
  7. Errors are the program's own types, not raw OSErrors escaping to the top level.
  8. It is a package: pip install -e . gives you a sentinel command.
  9. It is tested without a network, without sleep, and without mocking the thing under test.

A few words in that list are worth unpacking before you start:

  • Concurrently means the checks overlap in time. Five services that each take 200 ms should take about 200 ms together, not a second. §9 is the toolkit for this.
  • A transient failure is one that might not happen if you try again a moment later: a dropped connection, a network hiccup. A sleeping patient, not an absent one.
  • Exponential backoff means each retry waits twice as long as the one before. It gives a struggling service room to recover instead of hammering it.
  • An exit status (or exit code) is the number a program hands back to whatever started it. 0 means success; anything else means something went wrong. Shell scripts and CI systems read it to decide what to do next.

14.2 Build Order

Build it bottom-up; each stage is runnable and testable before the next one exists.

Think of the nurse again. Before the first ward round, someone checks that the thermometer works on one patient. Nobody starts by organising a round of forty beds with a thermometer that has never been switched on. Building bottom-up is the same idea: you test each piece on its own, so when you put pieces together, any new problem must be in the new part.

1. Types first. Status, Target, CheckResult, and the exception hierarchy. Everything else is written against these.
2. Config parsing. TOML text → list[Target], raising ConfigError with a useful message. Testable with a string; no files needed.
3. One check. tcp_check against a server you start in the test. Then http_check.
4. The runner. Timeout, then retry, then concurrency, then the task group — in that order, so each behaviour is added to something that already works.
5. The store. Schema, insert, two queries. SQLite in memory in tests, a file in production.
6. The CLI and the packaging. Last, because everything under it is already proven.

Why this order, step by step:

  • Types first, because they are the words the rest of the program is written in. Once Target and CheckResult exist, every other function has a clear input and a clear output.
  • Config parsing next, because it only needs strings. You can test it with a TOML string in a test, without a single file on disk.
  • One check, because a check that cannot talk to one server will not talk to five. The opening example of this section is already most of tcp_check.
  • The runner, built in layers. Add the timeout and see it work. Then add retry, and see both work. Each layer is added to something that already works, so when something breaks you know which layer did it.
  • The store, which does not care how the results were made, only what they contain.
  • The CLI last. By now it is a thin layer that reads arguments and calls functions you have already tested.

Here is where each piece ends up. This is the src layout from §11.9:

sentinel-monitor/
├── pyproject.toml
├── README.md
├── src/
│   └── sentinel/
│       ├── __init__.py      # §14.4 to §14.7: types, checks, runner, store
│       └── cli.py           # §14.10: the command line
└── tests/
    ├── __init__.py          # empty; lets the tests import from .conftest
    ├── conftest.py          # fake_service, from §14.8
    └── test_sentinel.py     # §14.9

14.3 The Hard Parts

Five decisions will take longer than the rest of the project put together. They are worth thinking about before you start. Each one gets a small, runnable experiment, so you can see the problem before you meet it in the real code.

Where the deadline goes

Where does the timeout go? Inside the check, or around it? Around it — asyncio.timeout (§9.6) wrapping the whole check means a target with a slow DNS lookup (turning a name such as example.com into a network address), a slow connect and a slow response is still bounded by one number, and the check itself stays free of timing code. Note that the timeout must be inside the semaphore's async with or a target that waits for a slot will have its own deadline eaten by the queue.

Two words in that paragraph need a quick reminder:

  • A semaphore (§9.9) is a counter of free slots. async with sem: waits until a slot is free, takes it, and gives it back at the end. It is the number of nurses on shift.
  • A deadline is how long one check may take. The question is when the clock starts: when the check is queued, or when it actually begins?

Imagine a patient's check is allowed fifteen minutes, but the clock starts when the patient is added to the list, not when a nurse reaches the bed. If the nurses are busy elsewhere, the fifteen minutes run out while the patient is still waiting, and the chart says "no response" for a patient nobody visited. Here is that bug in miniature. There is one slot, two checks, and each check needs 100 ms of a 150 ms deadline:

import asyncio


async def deadline_includes_the_queue(sem):
    async with asyncio.timeout(0.15):          # the clock starts here...
        async with sem:                         # ...while we may still be waiting
            await asyncio.sleep(0.1)            # the check itself: 100 ms


async def deadline_starts_with_the_check(sem):
    async with sem:                             # wait for a free slot first
        async with asyncio.timeout(0.15):       # then start the clock
            await asyncio.sleep(0.1)


async def two_checks_one_slot(check):
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(1)
    results = await asyncio.gather(check(sem), check(sem), return_exceptions=True)
    return ["ok" if r is None else type(r).__name__ for r in results]

print("timeout around the semaphore:", asyncio.run(two_checks_one_slot(deadline_includes_the_queue)))
print("timeout inside the semaphore:", asyncio.run(two_checks_one_slot(deadline_starts_with_the_check)))

timeout around the semaphore: ['ok', 'TimeoutError']
timeout inside the semaphore: ['ok', 'ok']

Line by line:

  • asyncio.Semaphore(1) means one check at a time, so the second check must wait 100 ms for the first to finish.
  • gather(..., return_exceptions=True) runs both and hands back an exception as a value instead of raising it, so both outcomes can be printed.
  • In the first version, the second check spends 100 ms queuing and then needs another 100 ms. That is 200 ms against a 150 ms deadline, so it fails with TimeoutError without a single byte being sent.
  • In the second version, its clock only starts once it holds the slot, so it gets its full 150 ms and both succeed.

The same reasoning applies to measuring a check, not just limiting it. If the stopwatch starts before the wait for a slot, a healthy service that queued behind others looks slow. Sentinel's runner starts both the deadline and the stopwatch inside the semaphore, for this reason.

One failure must not stop the round

How do concurrency and cancellation interact? TaskGroup (§9.5) cancels its siblings when a task raises. That is exactly what you do not want here: one unreachable host must not abort the run. So run_one catches its own failures and returns a CheckResult describing them — the task group only sees success. Letting an exception escape the task and then trying to reassemble the results from an ExceptionGroup is possible, and much worse.

In ward-round terms: one nurse finds an empty bed, and every other nurse is called off the round. That is what a TaskGroup does when one of its tasks raises. Watch it happen:

import asyncio

log = []


async def legacy():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    raise ConnectionRefusedError("legacy refused the connection")


async def api():
    try:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
        log.append("api: checked")
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        log.append("api: cancelled before it could finish")
        raise


async def main():
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            tg.create_task(legacy())
            tg.create_task(api())
    except* ConnectionRefusedError as group:
        log.append(f"the group re-raised: {group.exceptions[0]!r}")

asyncio.run(main())
print(*log, sep="\n")

api: cancelled before it could finish
the group re-raised: ConnectionRefusedError('legacy refused the connection')

Line by line:

  • legacy fails after 10 ms. api is healthy, but needs 100 ms.
  • The moment legacy raises, the task group cancels api. api never gets to write "checked": its only line in the log is the one its except CancelledError wrote on the way out.
  • The group then raises the failure wrapped in an ExceptionGroup (§9.5), which except* unwraps. The monitor has lost the healthy result and has an exception to deal with.

Now make each task catch its own failure and turn it into a result. A refused connection becomes a line on the chart, not an alarm that ends the round:

import asyncio

log = []


async def legacy():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    raise ConnectionRefusedError("legacy refused the connection")


async def api():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    log.append("api: checked")
    return "HTTP/1.1 200 OK"


async def run_one(name, check):
    try:
        return f"{name}: up, {await check()}"
    except OSError as exc:                      # a failure becomes a result
        return f"{name}: down, {exc}"


async def main():
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tasks = [tg.create_task(run_one("legacy", legacy)),
                 tg.create_task(run_one("api", api))]
    print(*[t.result() for t in tasks], sep="\n")
    print(log)

asyncio.run(main())

legacy: down, legacy refused the connection
api: up, HTTP/1.1 200 OK
['api: checked']

Both checks report, and the task group never saw an exception, so it had no reason to cancel anything. That is the whole design of Sentinel's run_one in fifteen lines.

Data or error?

What is a failure, and what is a result? A refused connection is a normal outcome of a monitoring tool — it is data, not an error. ConfigError is an error: the program cannot proceed. Draw that line deliberately (§7.2), because it decides which layer each try belongs in.

Here is the test that decides which is which. Ask: "Could the program still do its job?"

  • A service is down. The program's job is to find out whether services are down, so it just did its job. That is data: it goes into a CheckResult.
  • The ward list is unreadable. Nobody knows which beds to visit, so the round cannot begin. That is an error: it becomes a ConfigError, the program stops, and it says why.

Once you have drawn that line, the place for each try follows. Data is caught deep down, right next to the check that produced it (run_one). Errors travel up to the top of the program (main in §14.10), where there is someone to tell.

Testing time without waiting

How do you test time-dependent behaviour without waiting? By making the durations parameters and choosing tiny ones. The retry backoff starts at 10 ms, so a three-attempt failure costs 30 ms; the "slow" threshold is per-target, so a test sets it to 10 ms and a 50 ms server is reliably slow. Never assert on an absolute duration (§12.7).

You can check the 30 ms in that paragraph without running a network at all. Three attempts means two waits between them, and each wait doubles:

attempts, base_delay = 3, 0.01

waits = [base_delay * 2 ** (attempt - 1) for attempt in range(1, attempts)]
print("waits between attempts:", waits)
print("total time spent waiting:", round(sum(waits), 3), "seconds")

waits between attempts: [0.01, 0.02]
total time spent waiting: 0.03 seconds

Line by line:

  • range(1, attempts) is 1, 2: there is a wait after the first and second attempts, but none after the last, because there is nothing left to wait for.
  • 2 ** (attempt - 1) is 1, then 2, so the waits are 10 ms and then 20 ms. That is the doubling of exponential backoff.
  • In production you would pass base_delay=1.0 and wait one second, then two. The code is the same; only the number changes.

The general rule: anything that waits should take the waiting time as a parameter. Then the test can pass a tiny number, and the same code runs in milliseconds.

A real server on a free port

How do you test network code without a network? asyncio.start_server on port 0 gives you a real server on a real socket on a port the OS picks — no mocks, no fixed ports, no collisions under pytest -n auto, and the code under test is exercised for real. This is the single most useful technique in the project.

The opening example already used it. Here is the property that makes it safe for tests, in four lines of plain socket code:

import socket

first = socket.create_server(("127.0.0.1", 0))
second = socket.create_server(("127.0.0.1", 0))
port_a, port_b = first.getsockname()[1], second.getsockname()[1]

print("asked for port 0, got a real port:", port_a > 0 and port_b > 0)
print("two servers, two different ports:", port_a != port_b)
first.close()
second.close()

asked for port 0, got a real port: True
two servers, two different ports: True

Line by line:

  • Both servers asked for port 0, and the operating system gave each one a free port of its own.
  • So two tests running at the same time, as pytest -n auto does with the pytest-xdist plugin, can each start their own server without fighting over port 8080.
  • Nothing is pretend. A real socket is opened, real bytes travel through it, and the code under test cannot tell the difference from production.

It is like practising on a training ward: real beds, real equipment, real volunteers, but nobody is actually ill. A mock (§12.6) is a photograph of a bed. You can learn from a photograph, but it will never show you that the bed's wheels stick.

14.4 Types and Errors

Two small ideas first, then the code. The first is what frozen=True and StrEnum actually do:

from dataclasses import FrozenInstanceError, dataclass
from enum import StrEnum


class Status(StrEnum):
    UP = "up"
    DOWN = "down"
    SLOW = "slow"


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Target:
    name: str
    port: int


print("str(Status.SLOW):", str(Status.SLOW))
print("equal to the plain string:", Status.SLOW == "slow")

api = Target("api", 8080)
try:
    api.port = 9090
except FrozenInstanceError as exc:
    print("refused:", exc)
print("has a per-instance __dict__:", hasattr(api, "__dict__"))

str(Status.SLOW): slow
equal to the plain string: True
refused: cannot assign to field 'port'
has a per-instance __dict__: False

Line by line:

  • A StrEnum member is a string. str() gives "slow", and it compares equal to "slow", so it can go straight into a database or a JSON document.
  • frozen=True makes the dataclass refuse changes after it is built. Trying to change port raises FrozenInstanceError.
  • slots=True stores the fields in fixed slots instead of a dictionary per object (§1.7), so there is no __dict__.

The second idea is when a default value is worked out:

import time
from dataclasses import dataclass, field


@dataclass
class Once:
    at: float = time.monotonic()                        # runs once, when the class is made


@dataclass
class EachTime:
    at: float = field(default_factory=time.monotonic)   # runs for every new object


first = Once()
time.sleep(0.01)
second = Once()
print("plain default, same timestamp on both:", first.at == second.at)

first = EachTime()
time.sleep(0.01)
second = EachTime()
print("default_factory, same timestamp on both:", first.at == second.at)

plain default, same timestamp on both: True
default_factory, same timestamp on both: False

Line by line:

  • time.monotonic() in Once is called exactly once, when Python runs the class statement. Every Once object gets that same number, however much later it is created.
  • field(default_factory=time.monotonic) stores the function, not its result. The dataclass calls it each time a new object is made, so each object gets its own time.

Think of a rubber stamp with a date on it. A plain default is a stamp carved once, on the day it was made; it prints that day forever. default_factory is a date stamp with turning wheels, set fresh every time you use it.

Now the real thing. This is the first part of src/sentinel/__init__.py, and it holds the imports for the whole module:

import asyncio
import functools
import logging
import sqlite3
import time
import tomllib
from collections.abc import Awaitable, Callable, Iterable, Iterator
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import UTC, datetime
from enum import StrEnum
from typing import Protocol, Self

log = logging.getLogger("sentinel")


class SentinelError(Exception):
    """Base class for every error this package raises deliberately."""


class ConfigError(SentinelError):
    """The configuration is unusable; the program cannot start."""


class CheckFailed(SentinelError):
    """A target answered, but not acceptably."""

    def __init__(self, target: str, reason: str) -> None:
        super().__init__(f"{target}: {reason}")
        self.target = target
        self.reason = reason


class Status(StrEnum):
    UP = "up"
    DOWN = "down"
    SLOW = "slow"


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Target:
    name: str
    host: str
    port: int
    path: str | None = None
    timeout: float = 2.0
    slow_after_ms: float = 500.0

    @classmethod
    def from_toml(cls, name: str, raw: dict[str, object]) -> Self:
        def need(key: str) -> object:
            if key not in raw:
                raise ConfigError(f"target {name!r} is missing {key!r}")
            return raw[key]

        try:
            return cls(
                name=name,
                host=str(need("host")),
                port=int(str(need("port"))),          # str() first: raw is dict[str, object]
                path=str(raw["path"]) if "path" in raw else None,
                timeout=float(str(raw.get("timeout", 2.0))),
                slow_after_ms=float(str(raw.get("slow_after_ms", 500.0))),
            )
        except (TypeError, ValueError) as exc:
            raise ConfigError(f"target {name!r}: {exc}") from exc


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class CheckResult:
    target: str
    status: Status
    elapsed_ms: float
    detail: str = ""
    at: datetime = field(default_factory=lambda: datetime.now(UTC))

    @property
    def ok(self) -> bool:
        return self.status is not Status.DOWN

Read it from the top, one piece at a time:

  • log is the module's logger, named "sentinel" (§7.8). Nothing is printed through it unless the program turns logging up.
  • SentinelError is the family name for every error this package raises on purpose. ConfigError and CheckFailed are its two children. A caller who wants "anything Sentinel complained about" catches the parent.
  • CheckFailed stores the target and the reason separately, as well as building a readable message. Code can read .reason; a person reads str(exc).
  • Status has three members, UP, DOWN and SLOW.
  • Target is one service from the configuration. from_toml builds one from the dictionary tomllib produced, and need is a small helper that complains clearly about a missing key.
  • CheckResult is one line on the chart: who, what status, how long, what they said, and when. ok is True for anything that is not DOWN, so a slow service still counts as up.
  • UTC is the same object as timezone.utc (§13.1), under the shorter name Python 3.11 added. Every timestamp is stored in UTC.

Four choices in there are the ones a reviewer would ask about.

Values that cannot change

frozen=True, slots=True (§3.9): a Target is a value read from configuration and a CheckResult is a record of something that happened — neither should ever be mutated, and slots removes the per-instance __dict__ for objects you may have thousands of.

A chart entry that someone can quietly edit after the fact is worthless. If a CheckResult could change after it was made, a bug anywhere in the program could rewrite history, and the store would faithfully save the rewritten version. Freezing it makes that bug impossible instead of merely unlikely.

Three states, not two

A three-member StrEnum, not a boolean (§3.10). "Slow" is a real state that a boolean cannot express, and StrEnum means str(status) is "up", so it goes into SQLite and out of a JSON encoder unchanged.

A boolean is a light switch: on or off. A service's health is more like a traffic light. Green is fine, red is down, and amber means "working, but something is wrong, look soon". is_up: bool would have to call amber either green or red, and either answer loses information an operator needs.

One error type for every bad config

from_toml translates every failure into ConfigError (§7.4), so a caller has one exception type to handle. The str() around each value is not decoration: tomllib returns dict[str, object], and int(some_object) does not type-check — going through str makes the conversion honest, and int("no") still raises the ValueError that becomes the message target 'a': invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'no'.

Here is where that message comes from, one step at a time:

import tomllib

raw = tomllib.loads('[target.a]\nhost = "h"\nport = "no"')["target"]["a"]
print(raw)
try:
    int(str(raw["port"]))
except ValueError as exc:
    print("ValueError:", exc)

{'host': 'h', 'port': 'no'}
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'no'

Line by line:

  • TOML is perfectly happy with port = "no". It is a valid string. The problem is only that a port must be a number, and TOML does not know that.
  • int(str(...)) raises ValueError with Python's own explanation.
  • from_toml catches it and raises ConfigError(f"target {name!r}: {exc}") from exc. The message gains the target's name, which is the piece the operator needs, and from exc keeps the original error attached for anyone debugging (§7.4).

Without the translation, a caller would need to catch ValueError, TypeError and ConfigError, and would have to know which line of from_toml raises which. With it, there is one door out, and it has a label on it.

A fresh timestamp for every result

default_factory for at (§3.9): a mutable or "computed now" default must not be evaluated once at class-definition time, which is what a plain default would do — the same bug as §1.2's mutable default argument.

You saw the stamp with turning wheels above. Here it matters directly: with a plain default, every result in a run of a week would carry the time the program started, and the history query in §14.7, which sorts by time, would return them in no meaningful order.

14.5 Checks

A check is anything you can call with a target and await to get a description back. That is all the runner needs to know. Here is that idea on its own, with a check that inherits from nothing:

import asyncio
from typing import Protocol


class Check(Protocol):
    async def __call__(self, target: str) -> str: ...


async def always_fine(target: str) -> str:              # inherits from nothing
    return f"{target}: pretend all is well"


async def run_check(check: Check, target: str) -> str:
    return await check(target)

print(asyncio.run(run_check(always_fine, "api")))

status_line = "HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable"
print(status_line.split(" "))
print("code:", int(status_line.split(" ")[1]))

api: pretend all is well
['HTTP/1.1', '503', 'Service', 'Unavailable']
code: 503

Line by line:

  • Check describes a shape: "an async callable that takes a target and returns a string". It is a Protocol, so nothing has to inherit from it.
  • always_fine is a plain async def. It has the right shape, so a type checker accepts it wherever a Check is expected.
  • The last three lines are how the HTTP check reads an answer. The first line of every HTTP response is a status line: the protocol version, a three-digit code, and a short phrase. Splitting on spaces puts the code at index 1.

The real checks, then. One opens a connection and hangs up. The other asks a web question and reads the first line of the answer:

class Check(Protocol):
    async def __call__(self, target: Target) -> str: ...


async def tcp_check(target: Target) -> str:
    _reader, writer = await asyncio.open_connection(target.host, target.port)
    writer.close()
    await writer.wait_closed()
    return "connected"


async def http_check(target: Target) -> str:
    reader, writer = await asyncio.open_connection(target.host, target.port)
    try:
        request = (
            f"GET {target.path} HTTP/1.1\r\n"
            f"Host: {target.host}\r\n"
            "Connection: close\r\n\r\n"
        )
        writer.write(request.encode("ascii"))
        await writer.drain()
        status_line = (await reader.readline()).decode("ascii", "replace").strip()
        if not status_line.startswith("HTTP/"):
            raise CheckFailed(target.name, f"not an HTTP response: {status_line!r}")
        code = int(status_line.split(" ")[1])
        if code >= 400:
            raise CheckFailed(target.name, f"HTTP {code}")
        return status_line
    finally:
        writer.close()
        await writer.wait_closed()


def pick_check(target: Target) -> Check:
    return http_check if target.path is not None else tcp_check

Line by line:

  • tcp_check is the opening example with the try removed. It does not catch OSError itself, because deciding what a failure means is the runner's job, one layer up. The leading underscore in _reader says "I know this is unused", which is what the linter asks for.
  • http_check writes a minimal HTTP/1.1 request by hand. \r\n ends each line, as the protocol requires, and the blank line at the end says "that is the whole request". Connection: close asks the server to hang up afterwards.
  • writer.drain() waits until the bytes have really been handed to the operating system, so a slow network cannot make the program pile up unsent data.
  • reader.readline() reads only the status line. That is all a health check needs.
  • Anything that is not an HTTP response, and any code of 400 or above, becomes a CheckFailed. A code below 400 is a healthy answer, and the status line itself becomes the detail in the report.
  • pick_check chooses by the presence of path, exactly as requirement 1 says.

Check is a Protocol (§6.6), so a check is any async callable with that signature. Nothing inherits from it, and a test can pass a plain async def that returns a canned string, one fixed in advance. That is structural typing doing real work: the runner depends on a shape, not on a class hierarchy.

Think of a hospital that says "anyone with a nursing licence can do the round", rather than "only nurses trained at this hospital". The runner asks for the licence, the shape, not for the family tree.

Why the finally matters

The try/finally around the HTTP exchange is not decoration. Without it, a CheckFailed raised on a 503 leaks the socket, and after a few hundred checks the process runs out of file descriptors — the kind of bug that only appears in production, on the third day.

A file descriptor is the small number the operating system hands out for each open file or socket, and every process has a limit on how many it may hold at once. A leaked socket is a borrowed library book never returned. One is harmless. Keep doing it and the library stops lending. You can watch the library stop lending by lowering the limit (this uses the resource module, so it runs on macOS and Linux):

import errno
import resource
import socket

soft, hard = resource.getrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_NOFILE)
resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_NOFILE, (40, hard))   # a small limit, to see it quickly

leaked = []
try:
    while True:
        leaked.append(socket.socket())                     # opened, never closed
except OSError as exc:
    print("OSError:", exc.strerror)
    print("it is EMFILE:", exc.errno == errno.EMFILE)
    print("gave up before 40 sockets:", len(leaked) < 40)

for s in leaked:
    s.close()
resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_NOFILE, (soft, hard))

OSError: Too many open files
it is EMFILE: True
gave up before 40 sockets: True

Line by line:

  • setrlimit lowers this process's limit to 40 open descriptors, so the failure arrives in a fraction of a second instead of after thousands of checks.
  • The loop opens sockets and never closes them, which is exactly what http_check would do on every 503 without its finally.
  • The failure is EMFILE, "Too many open files". It arrives before 40 sockets, because the process already had some descriptors open (standard input, output and error, at least).
  • Once a process is in this state, everything that needs a descriptor fails: new checks, opening the database, even writing a log file. The real limit is usually 256 or more, which is why the bug waits until the third day.

finally runs whether the try body returned, raised CheckFailed, or was cancelled by the timeout. That is the only way to be sure every socket is returned.

14.6 Retry and the Runner

Two warm-ups first. The first is about applying a decorator by hand:

import functools


def shout(fn):
    @functools.wraps(fn)
    def wrapper(*args):
        return fn(*args).upper()
    return wrapper


def hello(name):
    return f"hello, {name}"


loud = shout(hello)               # exactly what @shout above `def hello` would do
print(loud("ada"))
print("still called:", loud.__name__)

HELLO, ADA
still called: hello

@shout above a def is only a shorthand for hello = shout(hello) (§4.4). Writing the call yourself is useful when you only find out which function to decorate while the program is running. functools.wraps copies the original's name and docstring onto the wrapper, so logs and tracebacks still say hello.

The second warm-up is a retry loop, without a decorator around it, against a service that drops the connection twice and then answers:

import asyncio

attempts_made = 0


async def flaky():
    global attempts_made
    attempts_made += 1
    if attempts_made < 3:
        raise ConnectionResetError("the connection dropped")
    return "answered"


async def with_retries(fn, attempts=3, base_delay=0.01):
    for attempt in range(1, attempts + 1):
        try:
            return await fn()
        except OSError as exc:
            print(f"attempt {attempt} failed: {exc}")
            if attempt == attempts:
                raise
            await asyncio.sleep(base_delay * 2 ** (attempt - 1))

print(asyncio.run(with_retries(flaky)), "on attempt", attempts_made)
print("TimeoutError is an OSError:", issubclass(TimeoutError, OSError))

attempt 1 failed: the connection dropped
attempt 2 failed: the connection dropped
answered on attempt 3
TimeoutError is an OSError: True

Line by line:

  • The first two calls raise ConnectionResetError, another kind of OSError. Each failure is printed, followed by a wait of 10 ms and then 20 ms.
  • The third call succeeds, and return await fn() hands its answer straight back. The loop ends there.
  • If the last attempt had failed too, the bare raise would re-raise that error unchanged, so the caller sees the real reason.
  • The last line is a fact worth knowing: TimeoutError is itself a subclass of OSError. Sentinel still names both in its except, because the reader of the code should not need to know that.

This is the sleeping patient. The nurse does not write "unresponsive" after one knock. They come back a little later, then a little later again, and only then write it down.

Now the real retry, as a decorator factory, and the runner that uses it:

def retry[**P, R](
    attempts: int = 3, base_delay: float = 0.01
) -> Callable[[Callable[P, Awaitable[R]]], Callable[P, Awaitable[R]]]:
    """Retry a coroutine function on transient network errors, with backoff."""
    def decorate(fn: Callable[P, Awaitable[R]]) -> Callable[P, Awaitable[R]]:
        @functools.wraps(fn)
        async def wrapper(*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R:
            last: Exception | None = None
            for attempt in range(1, attempts + 1):
                try:
                    return await fn(*args, **kwargs)
                except (OSError, TimeoutError) as exc:
                    last = exc
                    log.debug("attempt %d/%d failed: %s", attempt, attempts, exc)
                    if attempt < attempts:
                        await asyncio.sleep(base_delay * 2 ** (attempt - 1))
            assert last is not None
            raise last
        return wrapper
    return decorate


async def run_one(target: Target, sem: asyncio.Semaphore) -> CheckResult:
    check = retry()(pick_check(target))
    async with sem:                                  # bound concurrency
        started = time.perf_counter()                # time the check, not the queue
        try:
            async with asyncio.timeout(target.timeout):    # bound total time
                detail = await check(target)
        except TimeoutError:
            return CheckResult(target.name, Status.DOWN,
                               (time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000, "timed out")
        except (OSError, CheckFailed) as exc:
            return CheckResult(target.name, Status.DOWN,
                               (time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000, str(exc))
    elapsed = (time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000
    status = Status.SLOW if elapsed > target.slow_after_ms else Status.UP
    return CheckResult(target.name, status, elapsed, detail)


async def run_all(targets: Iterable[Target], concurrency: int = 10) -> list[CheckResult]:
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency)
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tasks = [tg.create_task(run_one(t, sem), name=t.name) for t in targets]
    return [t.result() for t in tasks]

Read the three functions in the order a check travels through them:

  • run_all makes one semaphore for the whole round, starts one task per target inside a task group, and collects every result when the group is done. Naming each task after its target makes debugging output readable.
  • run_one handles one target. It wraps the right check in retry(), waits for a slot, starts the stopwatch, and runs the check under a deadline. Every way the check can end becomes a CheckResult.
  • retry sits closest to the network. It tries up to three times and only gives up when the last attempt fails.
  • The timeout surrounds the whole retry, so three attempts and their waits must all fit in one deadline. That is "bounded by one number" from §14.3.
  • After the async with sem: block, the slot is handed back and the status is decided: SLOW if the check took longer than the target allows, UP otherwise.

This is the heart of the program, and every line is a decision from §8 and §9.

A decorator chosen at runtime

retry()(pick_check(target)) applies a decorator at runtime rather than with @ syntax, because which function is being decorated depends on the target. A decorator is just a function that takes a function (§4.4); @ is syntactic sugar (a shorter way to write the same thing) for exactly this call.

There are two pairs of brackets because retry is a decorator factory: retry() builds a decorator with the default settings, and the second call applies it to the chosen check. retry(attempts=5)(...) would build a different one.

Types that survive the wrapper

The decorator is generic in both directions — [**P, R] (§6.10) says it preserves whatever parameters and return type the wrapped coroutine had. Without that, retry returns Callable[..., Any] and every caller silently loses its types; mypy --strict rejects the untyped version outright, which is how this one came to be written that way.

Read [**P, R] as two blanks to fill in. P stands for "whatever parameters the wrapped function takes", and R for "whatever it returns". The signature then says: give me a function taking P and returning an awaitable R, and I will give you back one with exactly the same shape. Wrapping http_check produces something a type checker still knows takes a Target and returns a str.

What is worth retrying

CheckFailed is deliberately not retried. A 503 is an answer, and retrying it three times turns a monitoring tool into a small denial-of-service, the name for flooding a service with more requests than it can handle. Only OSError and TimeoutError — genuinely transient conditions — are.

A patient who is asleep might answer next time. A patient who says "I feel terrible" has answered, and asking them three more times does not help them, it just tires them out. A 503 is the second kind. A server already struggling under load is the last thing that needs every monitor in the building asking it three times as often.

Waiting without blocking

asyncio.sleep for backoff, never time.sleep (§9.11). time.sleep would block the event loop and stall every other check in flight.

There is only one thread (§9.3). time.sleep puts the whole thread to sleep, so every other check stops too. await asyncio.sleep says "wake me later, and look after the others meanwhile", which is the only kind of waiting allowed inside async code.

Where the stopwatch and the deadline start

The semaphore is outside the timeout. Reversed, a target queuing behind nine others would spend its deadline waiting for a slot and time out without a single packet (a unit of data sent over the network) being sent.

You measured that in §14.3. The same holds for the stopwatch: started is read after the slot is acquired, so elapsed_ms measures how long the service took to answer, not how long the check waited for a nurse. Read before the async with sem:, a healthy 50 ms service checked with concurrency=1 behind another one is reported as taking about 100 ms, and comes back SLOW against an 80 ms threshold. The chart would blame the patient for the nurse's queue.

A runner that never raises

run_one never raises. That is what keeps TaskGroup from cancelling the other checks when one host is unreachable, and it is why the return type is a CheckResult describing a failure rather than an exception.

This is the second experiment from §14.3, at full size. Every outcome a check can have, success, slowness, refusal, a bad answer, a deadline, ends up in the same type, and the task group only ever sees tasks that finished normally.

Results after the group

t.result() after the async with is safe because the task group has already awaited every task. Reading .result() on a task that has not finished raises InvalidStateError.

Here is that rule on its own:

import asyncio


async def main():
    task = asyncio.create_task(asyncio.sleep(0.01, result="done"))
    try:
        task.result()
    except asyncio.InvalidStateError as exc:
        print("asked too early:", exc)
    await task
    print("asked after awaiting:", task.result())

asyncio.run(main())

asked too early: Result is not set.
asked after awaiting: done

asyncio.sleep accepts a result= argument and returns it when the sleep ends, which makes it a handy stand-in for any slow job that produces a value. Asking before it has finished raises; asking after await returns "done". run_all reads the results after the async with block, so by then every task has finished.

14.7 Store and Report

One thing first, because the code relies on it. A with block on a SQLite connection is not what most people expect:

import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE result (target TEXT)")

with con:                                        # a transaction: commit at the end
    con.execute("INSERT INTO result VALUES ('api')")
print("rows, still connected after the with:", con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM result").fetchone()[0])

con.close()                                      # this is what actually closes it
try:
    con.execute("SELECT 1")
except sqlite3.ProgrammingError as exc:
    print("after close():", exc)

rows, still connected after the with: 1
after close(): Cannot operate on a closed database.

Line by line:

  • with con: starts a transaction and commits it when the block ends, or rolls it back if the block raised (§13.6).
  • After the block, the connection is still open and the row is there. A with on a file closes the file; a with on a connection does not close the connection.
  • Only close() closes it, and after that any use raises ProgrammingError.

So Store below needs both: its own with to close the connection, and with self.con: inside save for the transaction.

SCHEMA = """
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS result (
    id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    target  TEXT    NOT NULL,
    status  TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('up', 'down', 'slow')),
    ms      REAL    NOT NULL CHECK (ms >= 0),
    detail  TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    at      TEXT    NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS result_target_at ON result (target, at);
"""


class Store:
    def __init__(self, path: str) -> None:
        self.con = sqlite3.connect(path)
        self.con.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
        self.con.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
        self.con.executescript(SCHEMA)

    def __enter__(self) -> Self:
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *exc_info: object) -> None:
        self.con.close()

    def save(self, results: Iterable[CheckResult]) -> int:
        rows = [(r.target, str(r.status), r.elapsed_ms, r.detail, r.at.isoformat())
                for r in results]
        with self.con:                                    # transaction, not close
            cur = self.con.executemany(
                "INSERT INTO result (target, status, ms, detail, at) VALUES (?,?,?,?,?)",
                rows,
            )
        return cur.rowcount

    def history(self, target: str, limit: int = 10) -> list[sqlite3.Row]:
        return self.con.execute(
            "SELECT status, ms, at FROM result WHERE target = ? ORDER BY at DESC LIMIT ?",
            (target, limit),
        ).fetchall()

    def uptime(self) -> dict[str, float]:
        rows = self.con.execute(
            "SELECT target, "
            "       SUM(CASE WHEN status != 'down' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS up "
            "FROM result GROUP BY target"
        ).fetchall()
        return {r["target"]: round(r["up"] * 100, 1) for r in rows}


def format_results(results: Iterable[CheckResult]) -> Iterator[str]:
    symbols = {Status.UP: "OK  ", Status.SLOW: "SLOW", Status.DOWN: "DOWN"}
    for r in sorted(results, key=lambda r: (r.status is not Status.DOWN, r.target)):
        yield f"{symbols[r.status]} {r.target:<12} {r.elapsed_ms:6.1f} ms  {r.detail}"


def exit_code(results: Iterable[CheckResult]) -> int:
    return 0 if all(r.ok for r in results) else 1


def load_targets(text: str) -> list[Target]:
    try:
        raw = tomllib.loads(text)
    except tomllib.TOMLDecodeError as exc:
        raise ConfigError(f"invalid TOML: {exc}") from exc
    targets = raw.get("target")
    if not isinstance(targets, dict) or not targets:
        raise ConfigError("no [target.*] tables found")
    return [Target.from_toml(name, body) for name, body in targets.items()]

Read it as the chart, the handover sheet, and the ward list:

  • SCHEMA is the chart's layout. The CHECK constraints make the database itself refuse a status it does not know or a negative time, so a bug elsewhere cannot write nonsense into history. The index on (target, at) makes "the latest results for one target" fast however long the history grows.
  • Store opens the database, sets row_factory = sqlite3.Row so rows can be read by column name (row["status"]), and creates the table if it is not there yet. PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON (§13.6) does nothing for this one table, but it is the habit that protects you the day a second table is added.
  • save turns each result into a tuple of plain values. ? placeholders keep the values out of the SQL text (§13.6), and executemany inserts all of them in one transaction.
  • history returns the newest rows for one target. The timestamps are ISO 8601 strings in UTC (the international date format, year first, such as 2026-08-23T09:30:00+00:00), which sort as text in time order, so ORDER BY at works on them directly.
  • uptime counts, per target, the share of results that were not down. The * 1.0 makes SQLite divide as decimals rather than whole numbers.
  • format_results builds the handover sheet, exit_code turns all of it into one number, and load_targets reads the ward list, rejecting bad TOML or a file with no targets before anything else runs.

Store is a context manager (§2.9) because a connection is a resource, and __exit__ accepting *exc_info closes it whether the body succeeded or raised. Note that with self.con: inside save is a transaction, not a close (§13.6) — the two with statements do entirely different things and both are needed.

Let the database count

The aggregation is SQL, not Python. Aggregation means combining many rows into one number, such as a count or an average. uptime() could have pulled every row and counted in a comprehension; letting SQLite do it means the work happens where the index is and the memory cost does not grow with history.

Picture asking the records office "what share of last year's checks on bed 12 were fine?" You could have them post you every chart, and count yourself at the kitchen table. Or the clerk, who already has the files in order, can count and phone you one number. A year of five-minute checks on twenty targets is over two million rows. Fetching them all into Python to produce twenty numbers is the kitchen-table version.

Failures first

format_results is a generator (§5.3), so the CLI can stream it to stdout (standard output, where print writes), a test can take next() of it, and nothing builds a list that is immediately thrown away. The sort key (r.status is not Status.DOWN, r.target) puts failures first because False sorts before True — a small idiom worth recognising.

Here is the idiom on its own, with plain tuples:

rows = [("api", "up"), ("billing", "down"), ("cache", "up"), ("legacy", "down")]

print("False < True:", False < True)
for name, status in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (r[1] != "down", r[0])):
    print(status, name)

False < True: True
down billing
down legacy
up api
up cache

Line by line:

  • The key for each row is a pair. For billing it is (False, "billing"); for api it is (True, "api").
  • Python compares pairs item by item. The first items decide: every False comes before every True, so every down row comes first.
  • Within each group, the second item, the name, puts them in alphabetical order.

The line format is worth reading too. {r.target:<12} pads the name on the right to twelve characters, and {r.elapsed_ms:6.1f} prints the time with one decimal place, padded on the left to six characters:

for name, ms in [("api", 12.4), ("legacy", 201.7)]:
    print(f"[{name:<12}] [{ms:6.1f}]")

[api         ] [  12.4]
[legacy      ] [ 201.7]

That is what makes the columns of §14.1's report line up, with the times right-aligned so the decimal points sit under one another.

And a generator does no work until someone asks for a line:

def numbered(lines):
    for n, line in enumerate(lines, start=1):
        print(f"  (making line {n})")
        yield f"{n}. {line}"


report = numbered(["billing is down", "api is up", "cache is up"])
print("nothing made yet")
print(next(report))

nothing made yet
  (making line 1)
1. billing is down

Calling numbered(...) made nothing at all; the first line was made only when next() asked for it, and the other two were never made. That is why a test can take next(format_results(...)) and check only the top line, which is the one that matters: the worst news.

14.8 Proving It Works

The demo starts three real servers on OS-assigned ports, points the monitor at them plus one address that is guaranteed to refuse, and checks all five concurrently. No mocks anywhere.

This is the training ward from §14.3: three volunteers with scripted answers, one empty bed, and one volunteer who answers slowly. fake_service is the script. Each server reads the first line of the request, optionally waits, and replies with a fixed status line and a two-byte body.

async def fake_service(status_line: bytes, delay: float = 0.0):
    """A minimal HTTP server, used here and in the tests."""
    async def handle(reader, writer):
        await reader.readline()
        if delay:
            await asyncio.sleep(delay)
        writer.write(status_line + b"\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\nhi")
        await writer.drain()
        writer.close()
    server = await asyncio.start_server(handle, "127.0.0.1", 0)   # port 0: OS picks
    return server, server.sockets[0].getsockname()[1]


async def main() -> None:
    good, p_good = await fake_service(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK")
    bad,  p_bad  = await fake_service(b"HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable")
    slow, p_slow = await fake_service(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK", delay=0.05)

    targets = load_targets(f"""
        [target.api]
        host = "127.0.0.1"
        port = {p_good}
        path = "/health"

        [target.billing]
        host = "127.0.0.1"
        port = {p_bad}
        path = "/health"

        [target.reports]
        host = "127.0.0.1"
        port = {p_slow}
        path = "/health"
        slow_after_ms = 10

        [target.cache]
        host = "127.0.0.1"
        port = {p_good}

        [target.legacy]
        host = "127.0.0.1"
        port = 1
        timeout = 0.2
    """)

    results = await run_all(targets, concurrency=4)
    for r in sorted(results, key=lambda r: r.target):
        detail = "connection refused" if "Errno" in r.detail else r.detail
        print(f"{r.target:<8} {r.status.value:<4} {detail}")
    print("exit code:", exit_code(results))

    with Store(":memory:") as store:
        store.save(results)
        store.save(results)                       # a second round, same outcomes
        print("uptime %:", store.uptime())
        print("history rows for billing:", len(store.history("billing")))

    for s in (good, bad, slow):
        s.close()
        await s.wait_closed()

asyncio.run(main())

api      up   HTTP/1.1 200 OK
billing  down billing: HTTP 503
cache    up   connected
legacy   down connection refused
reports  slow HTTP/1.1 200 OK
exit code: 1
uptime %: {'api': 100.0, 'billing': 0.0, 'cache': 100.0, 'legacy': 0.0, 'reports': 100.0}
history rows for billing: 2

Five targets, four distinct outcomes, one run. cache has no path, so it took the TCP branch and reported connected; reports answered in 50 ms against a 10 ms threshold and came back slow; billing answered correctly with a 503 and is down without being retried; legacy was refused three times, with backoff, in well under its 200 ms deadline.

A few details of the demo itself, line by line:

  • The TOML text is an f-string, so the ports the operating system picked are written straight into the configuration. load_targets cannot tell it apart from a file.
  • concurrency=4 with five targets means one check had to wait for a slot. Because the stopwatch starts inside the semaphore, the wait does not show up in anyone's time.
  • The demo sorts by name and prints only a status word and a detail, not the times. Times change from run to run, so printing them would make the output different every time; names and statuses do not change.
  • The refusal message contains an error number that differs between operating systems ([Errno 61] on macOS, [Errno 111] on Linux), so the demo prints connection refused in its place.
  • Saving the same round twice gives two rows per target, so history("billing") returns 2. Uptime is a share, so it does not change: billing was down both times, 0.0.

14.9 The Tests

These live in tests/test_sentinel.py. The fake_service helper from §14.8 goes in tests/conftest.py, and an empty tests/__init__.py makes tests a package, which is what lets the relative import from .conftest import ... work.

import re

import pytest
from sentinel import (CheckResult, ConfigError, Status, Store, Target,
                      exit_code, load_targets, run_all)

from .conftest import fake_service          # the server helper from §14.8

@pytest.fixture
async def service():
    """Start a real server; yield its port; shut it down afterwards."""
    servers = []

    async def start(status_line=b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK", delay=0.0):
        server, port = await fake_service(status_line, delay)
        servers.append(server)
        return port

    yield start
    for server in servers:
        server.close()
        await server.wait_closed()


@pytest.mark.parametrize("toml_text, message", [
    ('[target.a]\nport = 80',              "missing 'host'"),
    ('[target.a]\nhost = "h"',             "missing 'port'"),
    ('[target.a]\nhost = "h"\nport = "no"', "invalid literal"),
    ('',                                   "no [target.*] tables"),
])
def test_config_errors_name_the_problem(toml_text, message):
    with pytest.raises(ConfigError, match=re.escape(message)):
        load_targets(toml_text)


async def test_http_503_is_down_and_not_retried(service):
    port = await service(b"HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable")
    target = Target("billing", "127.0.0.1", port, path="/health")
    [result] = await run_all([target])
    assert result.status is Status.DOWN
    assert "HTTP 503" in result.detail


async def test_slow_target_is_slow_not_down(service):
    port = await service(delay=0.05)
    target = Target("reports", "127.0.0.1", port, path="/", slow_after_ms=10)
    [result] = await run_all([target])
    assert result.status is Status.SLOW and result.ok


async def test_one_dead_target_does_not_cancel_the_others(service):
    port = await service()
    targets = [Target("good", "127.0.0.1", port, path="/"),
               Target("dead", "127.0.0.1", 1, timeout=0.2)]
    results = {r.target: r.status for r in await run_all(targets)}
    assert results == {"good": Status.UP, "dead": Status.DOWN}


def test_uptime_counts_slow_as_up():
    with Store(":memory:") as store:
        store.save([CheckResult("a", Status.UP, 1.0),
                    CheckResult("a", Status.SLOW, 900.0),
                    CheckResult("a", Status.DOWN, 5.0)])
        assert store.uptime() == {"a": 66.7}


def test_exit_code_is_one_when_anything_is_down():
    assert exit_code([CheckResult("a", Status.UP, 1.0)]) == 0
    assert exit_code([CheckResult("a", Status.UP, 1.0),
                      CheckResult("b", Status.DOWN, 1.0)]) == 1

Read the tests one at a time:

  • service is a fixture that hands the test a function. Each call starts another real server and returns its port, and the fixture remembers every server so it can shut them all down after the test, even a failing one (§12.4). This is the "factory as fixture" shape.
  • test_config_errors_name_the_problem feeds four broken configurations to load_targets and checks that each raises ConfigError with the right words. re.escape is needed because match reads its argument as a regular expression, and [target.*] is full of characters with special meaning there.
  • test_http_503_is_down_and_not_retried checks that a 503 is DOWN and that the detail names the code. [result] = ... unpacks a list that must contain exactly one item, so the test also fails if run_all ever returns two.
  • test_slow_target_is_slow_not_down uses a 50 ms server and a 10 ms threshold. It checks both halves of "slow": the status is SLOW and ok is still True.
  • test_one_dead_target_does_not_cancel_the_others puts a healthy server and an empty port in the same round, which is §14.3's second experiment as a test.
  • test_uptime_counts_slow_as_up saves one up, one slow and one down result. Two out of three is 66.7 per cent once rounded, so slow must have counted as up.
  • test_exit_code_is_one_when_anything_is_down needs no async and no server at all, because exit_code is a plain function of its input.

The async def tests and the async fixture need no decorator, because asyncio_mode = "auto" in pyproject.toml (§14.10) tells the pytest-asyncio plugin to treat every coroutine test as async (§12.7). Run pytest and it reports nine passes: the parametrised test counts once per case, so four plus five.

Notice what is not here. Nothing is mocked — the HTTP tests speak to a real socket, and the store tests use a real database. There is no sleep and no assertion on a duration; "slow" is tested by setting the threshold to 10 ms rather than by making the test slow. And test_one_dead_target_does_not_cancel_the_others pins the single most subtle behaviour in the program, which is exactly the kind of thing that a refactor (a change to how code is written that should not change what it does) breaks silently.

That last test is the safety net under the trickiest part of the tightrope (§12). Someone tidying run_one next year might reasonably think "this function catches too much, let the errors propagate". That change looks harmless and every other test still passes. This one fails, and its name says exactly why the catch is there.

The parametrised config test is the shape §12.5 argued for: four cases, four names in the output, and a failure tells you which malformed file stopped producing a good message.

14.10 Shipping It

The project file comes first. It names the package, declares that it needs nothing installed to run, lists the tools you need to develop it, and creates the sentinel command:

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
name = "sentinel-monitor"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Concurrent service health checks with history."
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
license = "MIT"
dependencies = []                       # the point: there are none

[dependency-groups]
dev = ["pytest>=8", "pytest-asyncio>=1.0", "ruff>=0.6", "mypy>=1.11"]

[project.scripts]
