sentinel = "sentinel.cli:main"

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]
packages = ["src/sentinel"]             # the project name and the package name differ

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
asyncio_mode = "auto"
addopts = "-ra --strict-markers"

[tool.mypy]
strict = true

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["E", "F", "I", "UP", "B", "SIM", "RUF"]

Table by table:

  • [build-system] says which tool turns the source into an installable package: here, hatchling (§11.9).
  • [project] is the package's identity card. dependencies = [] is the whole point of the project. requires-python = ">=3.12" is there because the retry[**P, R] syntax arrived in 3.12.
  • [dependency-groups] lists the tools a developer needs, which a user installing the package never gets (§11.9).
  • [project.scripts] creates the command: installing the package puts a sentinel program on your PATH that calls main in sentinel/cli.py and exits with whatever main returns (§11.13).
  • [tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel] tells hatchling where the code is. Hatchling looks for a folder named after the project, and the project is called sentinel-monitor while the folder is src/sentinel. Without this table, pip install -e . stops with "Unable to determine which files to ship inside the wheel".
  • The [tool.*] tables configure the tools: pytest in async mode with strict markers (§12.7), mypy in strict mode (§6), and ruff with a set of rule families (§12.11). line-length = 100 raises ruff's default of 88, which the longer SQL lines in Store exceed. With these settings, mypy --strict src reports no issues and ruff check src reports none either.

The command line goes in src/sentinel/cli.py, which begins by importing what it uses:

import argparse
import asyncio
import logging
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from sentinel import (
    ConfigError,
    Store,
    exit_code,
    format_results,
    load_targets,
    run_all,
)

The CLI is the last piece, and it is small because everything below it is finished:

def build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="sentinel")
    parser.add_argument("--db", default="sentinel.db", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="count", default=0)
    sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    check = sub.add_parser("check", help="check every target once")
    check.add_argument("--config", type=Path, required=True)
    check.add_argument("--concurrency", type=int, default=10)

    hist = sub.add_parser("history", help="recent results for one target")
    hist.add_argument("target")
    hist.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=10)
    return parser


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    args = build_parser().parse_args(argv)
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=[logging.WARNING, logging.INFO, logging.DEBUG][min(args.verbose, 2)],
        format="%(levelname)-8s %(name)s %(message)s",
    )
    try:
        with Store(str(args.db)) as store:
            if args.command == "check":
                targets = load_targets(args.config.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
                results = asyncio.run(run_all(targets, args.concurrency))
                store.save(results)
                for line in format_results(results):
                    print(line)
                down = sum(1 for r in results if not r.ok)
                print(f"{down} of {len(results)} down")
                return exit_code(results)
            for row in store.history(args.target, args.limit):
                print(f"{row['at']}  {row['status']:<4} {row['ms']:6.1f} ms")
            return 0
    except ConfigError as exc:
        print(f"sentinel: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    except FileNotFoundError as exc:
        print(f"sentinel: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2

Line by line:

  • build_parser describes the command line, using the subcommand pattern from §13.3: sentinel check --config FILE and sentinel history TARGET. --db and -v belong to the main parser, so they come before the subcommand.
  • main takes argv as a parameter instead of reading sys.argv itself. A test can call main(["check", "--config", "x.toml"]) and check the number it returns, without starting a new process.
  • logging.basicConfig turns the number of -v flags into a log level, so -vv shows the log.debug lines from retry.
  • asyncio.run appears exactly once in the whole program, here at the top (§9.3). Everything below it is async; everything above it is ordinary code.
  • The check branch saves before it prints, so the history is complete even if printing fails halfway.
  • Both except clauses print one line to standard error and return 2. A missing config file is FileNotFoundError, raised by read_text.

The -v mapping works like this:

import logging

for verbose in range(4):
    level = [logging.WARNING, logging.INFO, logging.DEBUG][min(verbose, 2)]
    print(f"{'-' + 'v' * verbose if verbose else '(no flag)':<10} {logging.getLevelName(level)}")

(no flag)  WARNING
-v         INFO
-vv        DEBUG
-vvv       DEBUG

action="count" counts how many times the flag appears, and min(verbose, 2) stops -vvv from running off the end of the three-item list.

Three exit codes

Three exit codes with three meanings: 0 everything up, 1 something is down, 2 the tool could not run at all. That distinction is what makes it usable from a shell script or a CI job, and it is why main catches ConfigError here rather than letting a traceback reach the user — an operator does not need your stack, they need the name of the target with the bad port.

This is the handover in one word. "All fine." "Someone needs you." "I could not do the round, the ward list was unreadable." The doctor on call reacts differently to each, and so does a CI job. Here is what the shell sees when a Python program ends with each of them:

import subprocess
import sys

for code in (0, 1, 2):
    finished = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", f"raise SystemExit({code})"])
    print("the shell sees exit status", finished.returncode)

the shell sees exit status 0
the shell sees exit status 1
the shell sees exit status 2

raise SystemExit(n) is what sys.exit(n) does, and it is also what the generated sentinel command does with the number main returns. subprocess.run (§8.10) starts a separate Python and reports its exit status as returncode.

The choice of 2 is not arbitrary. It is the number argparse itself uses when the command line is wrong:

import argparse
import contextlib
import io

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="sentinel")
sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)
sub.add_parser("check")

print(parser.parse_args(["check"]))

errors = io.StringIO()
try:
    with contextlib.redirect_stderr(errors):
        parser.parse_args([])                    # forgot the subcommand
except SystemExit as exc:
    print("argparse exit status:", exc.code)
print(errors.getvalue().splitlines()[-1])

Namespace(command='check')
argparse exit status: 2
sentinel: error: the following arguments are required: command

Line by line:

  • With a subcommand, parse_args returns a Namespace whose command says which one was chosen.
  • Without one, argparse prints a usage message and an error to standard error, then exits with status 2. redirect_stderr catches that text so the example can show its last line.

So Sentinel's three codes line up with the convention a shell user already knows: 2 always means "I was not able to do what you asked", whether argparse noticed the problem or main did.

Run against the three servers from §14.8 and a real unreachable address, the installed command prints the report in §14.1's shape, failures first, and exits 1. A config whose port is "no" prints sentinel: target 'a': invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'no' and exits 2, and so does a config file that does not exist.

14.11 What It Demonstrates

Here is the whole course, seen from inside one program. Each row is a section, and where its ideas turned up:

Section Where it appears
1–2 Object model, dunders frozen/slots dataclasses, StrEnum, __enter__/__exit__
3 Classes dataclasses, classmethod constructor, properties
4 Functions and decorators the retry decorator factory, functools.wraps
5 Iteration format_results as a generator; Store as a context manager (§2.9)
6 Typing Protocol for Check, Self, str \| None, strict mypy
7 Errors and logging the exception hierarchy, raise ... from, log.debug with %s
8–9 Concurrency TaskGroup, Semaphore, asyncio.timeout, cancellation discipline
11 Packaging pyproject.toml, src layout, a console-script entry point
12 Testing real servers instead of mocks, parametrisation, async fixtures
13 Ecosystem tomllib, sqlite3, pathlib, argparse — and no dependencies

Section 10, performance, is missing from the table on purpose. Sentinel spends almost all of its time waiting for the network, and §10's first rule is to measure before optimising. There is nothing here worth optimising until a measurement says otherwise.

14.12 Where to Take It

Each of these is a real extension, not busywork, and each one forces a design decision the current code does not have to make.

  • A watch subcommand that runs forever on an interval and handles SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly. You will need asyncio.get_running_loop().add_signal_handler and a cancellation path that still flushes the store.
  • Notifications on a state change rather than on every failure — which means reading the previous status out of the store and deciding what "flapping" means.
  • A plugin system for check types, using entry points (§11.13), so a separate package can add a redis_check without you editing Sentinel.
  • Percentile latency in the report: p50 and p95 per target from the history table. statistics.quantiles does it in Python; a window function (a SQL feature that calculates across a group of related rows) does it in SQL. Try both and compare.
  • Property-based tests (§12.10) for load_targets: generate valid TOML from a strategy and assert it round-trips, then generate invalid TOML and assert it always raises ConfigError rather than anything else.
  • Structured logging with extra={"target": ..., "ms": ...} and a JSON formatter, so the output is queryable (§7.8).

A few hints, so each one starts in the right place:

  • SIGINT is what Ctrl-C sends, and SIGTERM is what a service manager or container platform sends when it wants a program to stop. "Cleanly" means the round in progress is saved before the program exits.
  • Flapping is a service that goes down, up, down, up, every few minutes. Without a rule for it, the nurse wakes the doctor every five minutes for the same patient.
  • A percentile answers "how slow is it for most people?" p95 is the time 95 per cent of checks were faster than, which tells you more than an average, because one very slow answer barely moves an average.

Every one of these makes the program bigger, and each is a good test of whether its parts were drawn in the right places. If adding notifications means changing run_one, something in the design is wrong. If it only means reading from the store, the layers are doing their job.

That is the course's last project, and it was built from nothing but the toolbox that came with Python. A nurse's round works because each step is simple and each step is checked. A program like this works for the same reason: small pieces, each one tested, put together in an order where you always know which piece is new.

You started this course able to write Python. You now understand why Python behaves the way it does — which is the difference between code that works and code you can be trusted with.

Remember the four lines from the start: b = a, then b.append(3), and a changed too. At the time that may have looked like a quirk. Now you can say exactly what happened: there was one list with two labels on it (§1.2). That is the mechanic hearing the noise and naming the part. The rest of this page is a short tour of what you can now do, a list for the moments when Python still surprises you, and a few habits worth keeping.

What you can now do

Each item is one section's worth of skill, in the order you learned it.

  1. Explain the language's behaviour from the object model. Names bind to objects, everything is an object, attribute lookup follows the MRO through descriptors, and almost every surprise in Python — mutable defaults, identity versus equality, why += changes a list in place but builds a new tuple — falls out of those rules rather than needing to be memorised.
  2. Design classes that fit the language. Dunder methods so your objects work with len, in, with, [] and the operators; dataclasses for records; __slots__ when there are a million of them; ABCs and protocols to state what you require.
  3. Use functions as the first-class values they are. Closures, decorators that preserve signatures, functools for caching and dispatch, and the knowledge of exactly when a default argument is evaluated.
  4. Write lazy pipelines. Generators, the iterator protocol, itertools, and context managers — processing a file larger than memory without thinking twice about it.
  5. Run a type checker in CI and mean it. Protocols, generics, variance, TypedDict, overloads, narrowing, and the judgement to know where annotations earn their keep and where they are noise.
  6. Handle failure deliberately. An exception hierarchy of your own, chaining that preserves the cause, exception groups, structured logging that is queryable, and a debugger you can attach to a running process.
  7. Choose the right concurrency for the workload. Threads, processes, free-threaded builds, subinterpreters and asyncio — and the ability to say which one a given bottleneck needs, and why the other three would not help.
  8. Write asyncio that does not fall over. Task groups, cancellation, timeouts, backpressure, and the discipline never to block the event loop.
  9. Make things faster on evidence. Profile before optimising, know that the answer is usually a data structure, and measure again afterwards.
  10. Ship it. An installable project with a lockfile, a test suite that fails when the code is wrong, a linter and a formatter that run automatically, and a package on PyPI with an entry point.
  11. Build a whole program from the parts. The Sentinel capstone (§14) used something from nearly every section: dataclasses and enums for its records, a Protocol for its checks, a task group and a semaphore for its concurrency, SQLite for its history, tests for its behaviour, and a pyproject.toml that turns it into a command anyone can install.

That is a working professional's toolkit. There is no part of a normal Python codebase you should now find opaque.

When Python surprises you

You will still be surprised sometimes. Everyone is. The difference now is that most surprises come from a handful of mechanisms, and you have seen all of them.

Use the table like a doctor uses a symptom list. Find the question that matches what you are seeing, then go to the subsection that explains the mechanism behind it.

Symptom Where the answer is
"Why did my default argument keep its value from last time?" §1.2 — defaults are evaluated once, at definition
"Why is a is b False when a == b?" §1.4 — identity, equality, and interning
"Why does mutating one object change another?" §1.2 — names are bindings, not boxes
"Why is my class attribute shared between instances?" §1.6 — class attributes are shared until shadowed
"Why did += change my list but not my tuple?" §2.6 — __iadd__ mutates in place; without it, += builds a new object
"Why did my __radd__ not fire?" §2.6 — reflected methods belong to the other operand
"Why did the subclass ignore my method?" §3.5 — MRO and C3 linearisation
"Why does my generator only work once?" §5.1 — an iterator is exhausted, not rewound
"Why does mypy reject a list[Dog] where list[Animal] is wanted?" §6.5 — invariance
"Why is my exception's cause missing?" §7.4 — raise ... from
"Why do my threads not go faster?" §8.2 — the GIL
"Why did my whole server stop while one request ran?" §9.11 — a blocking call on the event loop
"Why is this slow when it looks simple?" §10.5 — the complexity, not the constant factor
"Why does my import work here and not there?" §11.2 — sys.path and what is on it
"Why does my patched function not get called?" §12.6 — patch where it is used
"Why is my setting True when the environment says false?" §13.4 — bool() of any non-empty string is True
"Why did my SQLite insert vanish?" §13.6 — nothing was committed before the connection closed
"Why did a healthy task time out?" §14.3 — the deadline was started before it got a slot from the semaphore
"Why does my program run out of files after a few hours?" §14.5 — a socket or file that is never closed

Habits worth keeping

Knowing the mechanisms is half of it. The other half is a few habits that stop the surprises from happening in the first place.

Run the code. Almost every claim about Python can be settled in a REPL in under ten seconds. That habit keeps catching things that feel obviously true and are not. Two examples from this course: four threads incrementing a shared counter on 3.14 will very likely not lose updates, which does not make the code correct (§8.4); and a frozen=True dataclass is hashable only if every one of its fields is (§3.9).

Read the source. The standard library is Python you can open. inspect.getsource, or just following the traceback, answers more questions than searching does.

Prefer the boring construction. A dict, a list comprehension and a function beat a metaclass almost every time. The advanced machinery in this course exists so that you recognise it in other people's code and reach for it in the rare case that earns it.

Make the invalid state unrepresentable. A frozen dataclass, a StrEnum instead of a string, integer cents instead of a float, Literal instead of "one of these four strings" — each one moves a class of bug from runtime to the type checker, or eliminates it entirely.

Validate at the boundary, trust inside it. Everything that crosses into your program is untyped until you check it, and everything after that check should be a real object with a real type. Think of passport control: everyone is checked once, at the border, and inside the country nobody asks again.

Leave the diagnostics behind. Structured logs, exception chaining, a test that reproduces the incident. The version of you that gets paged at 3 a.m. is a different person with much less context.

Where to go next

You have the engine knowledge. Here are four ways to keep building on it.

  • Read a real codebase. CPython's Lib/ is the obvious one; httpx, attrs, rich and pydantic are all readable, well tested and modern. Pick one, find an open issue labelled "good first issue", and write the patch.
  • Follow the language. Each release's What's New is short and worth the twenty minutes. PEPs are the reasoning behind the changes, and reading a few — 484, 492, 557, 634, 649, 703 — explains the shape of modern Python better than any summary.
  • Pick a depth. Async services and the web; data engineering with Arrow, Polars and Parquet; scientific computing with NumPy and JAX; or the interpreter itself — the free-threaded build and subinterpreters are the most interesting thing to happen to CPython in a decade, and both are young enough to contribute to. If the web is your direction, the Django course in this collection is the natural next step.
  • Teach it. Explaining the descriptor protocol to someone else is how you find out whether you understand it.

Python rewards curiosity unusually well, because so little of it is hidden. When something surprises you, the mechanism is there to be found — and you now know where to look.
